abstract: Many optimization models of neural networks need constraints to restrict the space of outputs to a subspace which satisfies external criteria. Optimizations using energy methods yield "forces" which act upon the state of the neural network. The penalty method, in which quadratic energy constraints are added to an existing optimization energy, has become popular recently, but is not guaranteed to satisfy the constraint conditions when there are other forces on the neural model or when there are multiple constraints. In this paper, we present the basic differential multiplier method (BDMM), which satisfies constraints exactly; we create forces which gradually apply the constraints over time, using "neurons" that estimate Lagrange multipliers. The basic differential multiplier method is a differential version of the method of multipliers from Numerical Analysis. We prove that the differential equations locally converge to a constrained minimum. Examples of applications of the differential method of multipliers include enforcing permutation codewords in the analog decoding problem and enforcing valid tours in the traveling salesman problem.

paragraphs: Neural optimization systems often need to improve an objective while keeping their outputs within a set of valid solutions. Adding a quadratic penalty for invalid outputs is one common approach. The paper explains that this does not guarantee constraint satisfaction when other forces influence the network or several constraints interact.

The proposed basic differential multiplier method introduces neurons that estimate Lagrange multipliers. These estimates generate forces that progressively enforce the constraints as the network evolves. The method turns the numerical method of multipliers into a continuous dynamical process, making constraint enforcement an active part of the network’s behavior.

The authors prove local convergence of the differential equations to a constrained minimum and state that the method satisfies constraints exactly. Local convergence concerns behavior near the relevant solution; it does not establish convergence from every starting point. Applications include producing valid permutation codewords in analog decoding and valid traveling-salesman tours. In both settings, the method addresses the need for an optimized answer to obey the rules that make it usable.
summary.tldr: The differential multiplier method uses evolving multiplier neurons to enforce constraints exactly, with a proof of local convergence to a constrained minimum.

title: Constrained Differential Optimization

abstract: The Boltzmann Machine has been introduced as a means to perform global optimization for multimodal objective functions using the principles of simulated annealing. In this paper we consider its utility as a spurious-free content-addressable memory, and provide bounds on its performance in this context. We show how to exploit the machine's ability to escape local minima, in order to use it, at a constant temperature, for unambiguous associative pattern-retrieval in noisy environments. An association rule, which creates a sphere of influence around each stored pattern, is used along with the Machine's dynamics to match the machine's noisy input with one of the pre-stored patterns. Spurious fIxed points, whose regions of attraction are not recognized by the rule, are skipped, due to the Machine's fInite probability to escape from any state. The results apply to the Boltzmann machine and to the asynchronous net of binary threshold elements (Hopfield model'). They provide the network designer with worst-case and best-case bounds for the network's performance, and allow polynomial-time tradeoff studies of design parameters.

paragraphs: This paper studies the Boltzmann machine as a memory that retrieves stored patterns from noisy inputs. The challenge is to obtain an unambiguous stored answer while avoiding spurious states that do not represent valid memories. The authors use the machine's ability to escape local minima as part of the retrieval process.

An association rule assigns a sphere of influence to each stored pattern. Together with the network dynamics, this rule determines when a noisy input has been associated with a valid memory. Spurious fixed points outside recognized regions are skipped because the machine has a nonzero probability of escaping any state. The proposed retrieval operates at a constant temperature.

The paper provides best-case and worst-case performance bounds, with results applying to the Boltzmann machine and the asynchronous binary-threshold Hopfield model. It also enables polynomial-time studies of tradeoffs among design parameters. The significance is that retrieval behavior becomes something a designer can bound and analyze, while random state changes help prevent invalid attractors from becoming final answers.
summary.tldr: An association rule and stochastic network dynamics enable noisy pattern retrieval that bypasses spurious states, with explicit performance bounds.

title: Convergence and Pattern-Stabilization in the Boltzmann Machine

abstract: In this paperl we show that neural networks for speech recognition can be constructed in a modular fashion by exploiting the hidden structure of previously trained phonetic subcategory networks. The performance of resulting larger phonetic nets was found to be as good as the performance of the subcomponent nets by themselves. This approach avoids the excessive learning times that would be necessary to train larger networks and allows for incremental learning. Large time-delay neural networks constructed incrementally by applying these modular training techniques achieved a recognition performance of 96.0% for all consonants.
originalAbstract: In this paperl we show that neural networks for speech recognition can be constructed in a modular fashion by exploiting the hidden structure of previously trained phonetic subcategory networks. The performance of resulting larger phonetic nets was found to be as good as the performance of the subcomponent nets by themselves. This approach avoids the excessive learning times that would be necessary to train larger networks and allows for incremental learning. Large time-delay neural networks constructed incrementally by applying these modular training techniques achieved a recognition performance of 96.0% for all consonants.

paragraphs: This paper investigates how to build larger speech-recognition networks from smaller networks that already recognize phonetic subcategories. Its central idea is to reuse the hidden structure learned by those component networks. That structure becomes part of a larger system, allowing knowledge acquired during earlier training to contribute directly to an expanded recognition task.

The authors apply this modular construction to time-delay neural networks and build the larger networks incrementally. This matters because training a large network can demand excessive learning time. Reusing trained components offers a way to extend the system through successive additions while preserving useful internal representations already obtained.

The resulting larger phonetic networks performed as well as their component networks did individually. An incrementally constructed network achieved 96.0% recognition performance across all consonants. Together, these findings support modular training as a practical route to expanding phonetic coverage: the larger recognizer retained component-level performance while the construction method addressed the training burden associated with larger networks.
summary.tldr: Reusing trained phonetic subnetworks enables incremental construction of larger speech recognizers, reaching 96.0% consonant recognition.

title: Consonant Recognition by Modular Construction of Large Phonemic Time-Delay Neural Networks

abstract: We present two connectionist architectures for chunking of symbolic rewrite rules. One uses backpropagation learning, the other competitive learning. Although they were developed for chunking the same sorts of rules, the two differ in their representational abilities and learning behaviors.
originalAbstract: We present two connectionist architectures for chunking of symbolic rewrite rules. One uses backpropagation learning, the other competitive learning. Although they were developed for chunking the same sorts of rules, the two differ in their representational abilities and learning behaviors.

paragraphs: This paper presents two neural architectures for chunking symbolic rewrite rules. Rewrite rules describe transformations between symbolic expressions, and chunking concerns how such rule-based material is organized into learned units. The task connects an explicitly symbolic form of knowledge with representations learned by a neural system.

One architecture uses backpropagation, while the other uses competitive learning. Both are developed for the same kinds of rules, which gives the comparison a common target. The distinction is therefore not simply that the systems address different symbolic tasks; they bring different learning approaches and representations to a shared category of task.

The authors report differences in both representational ability and learning behavior. Those are separate considerations: what a system can represent need not be the same question as how it acquires that representation. The paper's stated contribution is this comparison between two connectionist approaches to rule chunking. It highlights that choosing a neural architecture for symbolic material involves considering the representation it supports as well as its learning procedure.
summary.tldr: Two neural approaches to chunking symbolic rewrite rules differ in both what they can represent and how they learn.

title: Rule Representations in a Connectionist Chunker

abstract: The focused gamma network is proposed as one of the possible implementations of the gamma neural model. The focused gamma network is compared with the focused backpropagation network and TDNN for a time series prediction problem, and with ADALINE in a system identification problem.
originalAbstract: The focused gamma network is proposed as one of the possible implementations of the gamma neural model. The focused gamma network is compared with the focused backpropagation network and TDNN for a time series prediction problem, and with ADALINE in a system identification problem.

paragraphs: This paper proposes the focused gamma network as an implementation of the gamma neural model. It examines the network through two modeling applications involving data that change over time. The contribution described is an implemented network approach placed in comparison with other methods on those applications.

The first application is time-series prediction, where the modeling task is to predict values in a sequence. Here the focused gamma network is compared with a focused backpropagation network and a time-delay neural network, or TDNN. This comparison places the proposed implementation alongside two alternative network approaches within the same type of prediction problem.

The second application is system identification, which concerns constructing a model of a system's behavior. For this task, the comparison is with ADALINE. Together, the applications examine the focused gamma implementation from two related perspectives: predicting a changing sequence and modeling a system. The abstract establishes these comparison settings without stating a performance ordering among the methods.
summary.tldr: The focused gamma network is introduced and compared with other models on time-series prediction and system identification.

title: Modeling Applications with the Focused Gamma Net

abstract: Platt's resource-allocation network (RAN) (Platt, 1991a, 1991b) is modified for a reinforcement-learning paradigm and to "restart" existing hidden units rather than adding new units. After restart(cid:173) ing, units continue to learn via back-propagation. The resulting restart algorithm is tested in a Q-Iearning network that learns to solve an inverted pendulum problem. Solutions are found faster on average with the restart algorithm than without it.
originalAbstract: Platt's resource-allocation network (RAN) (Platt, 1991a, 1991b) is modified for a reinforcement-learning paradigm and to "restart" existing hidden units rather than adding new units. After restart(cid:173) ing, units continue to learn via back-propagation. The resulting restart algorithm is tested in a Q-Iearning network that learns to solve an inverted pendulum problem. paragraphs: The paper explores a way to change a neural network's hidden representation while it learns through reinforcement. It adapts a resource-allocation network for use with Q-learning. The distinctive change is to restart existing hidden units instead of adding new ones, making reuse of the current network part of the learning process.

A restart is followed by continued training through backpropagation. The procedure therefore combines a discrete intervention in a hidden unit with ongoing adjustment of its parameters. The idea matters because adapting a representation need not always mean expanding the network; the method investigates whether revisiting existing units can help learning progress.

The authors test the resulting algorithm on an inverted-pendulum problem. The Q-learning network finds solutions faster on average when restarting is used than when it is omitted. This provides task-specific evidence that hidden-unit restarting can improve the learning process. The reported outcome concerns average speed of finding a solution, tying the representation change directly to progress on the control task.
summary.tldr: Restarting existing hidden units helps a Q-learning network solve an inverted-pendulum problem faster on average.

title: Q-Learning with Hidden-Unit Restarting

abstract: Solvable models of nonlinear learning machines are proposed, and learning in artificial neural networks is studied based on the theory of ordinary differential equations. A learning algorithm is con(cid:173) structed, by which the optimal parameter can be found without any recursive procedure. The solvable models enable us to analyze the reason why experimental results by the error backpropagation often contradict the statistical learning theory.
originalAbstract: Solvable models of nonlinear learning machines are proposed, and learning in artificial neural networks is studied based on the theory of ordinary differential equations. A learning algorithm is con(cid:173) structed, by which the optimal parameter can be found without any recursive procedure. The solvable models enable us to analyze the reason why experimental results by the error backpropagation often contradict the statistical learning theory.

paragraphs: The paper proposes nonlinear learning models that can be solved mathematically. Its purpose is to make aspects of neural network learning accessible to direct analysis, rather than relying only on observed training behavior. The authors study learning using the theory of ordinary differential equations.

Within these solvable models, they construct a learning algorithm that finds an optimal parameter without a recursive procedure. This provides a setting in which the relationship between the model, its parameters, and the learning solution can be examined explicitly. The claim concerns the proposed solvable models; it is not presented as a universal solution for arbitrary neural networks.

The models are also used to investigate why experimental results from error backpropagation can appear to contradict statistical learning theory. Their value is therefore explanatory as well as algorithmic. A mathematically tractable learning system offers a way to study the source of that disagreement and connect training behavior with theoretical expectations. The abstract states this analytical purpose without specifying the resulting explanation.
summary.tldr: Solvable nonlinear learning models enable nonrecursive parameter optimization and analysis of apparent disagreements between backpropagation experiments and learning theory.

title: Solvable Models of Artificial Neural Networks

abstract: A rich body of data exists showing that recollection of specific infor(cid:173) mation makes an important contribution to recognition memory, which is distinct from the contribution of familiarity, and is not adequately cap(cid:173) tured by existing unitary memory models. Furthennore, neuropsycholog(cid:173) ical evidence indicates that recollection is sub served by the hippocampus. We present a model, based largely on known features of hippocampal anatomy and physiology, that accounts for the following key character(cid:173) istics of recollection: 1) false recollection is rare (i.e., participants rarely claim to recollect having studied nonstudied items), and 2) increasing in(cid:173) terference leads to less recollection but apparently does not compromise the quality of recollection (i.e., the extent to which recollected infonna(cid:173) tion veridically reflects events that occurred at study).

paragraphs: Recognizing something can involve a feeling of familiarity or the recovery of specific details about a previous encounter. This paper focuses on the second process, recollection. It develops a model based largely on hippocampal anatomy and physiology, motivated by evidence connecting that brain structure to recollection and by the difficulty of explaining recollection through a single, undifferentiated memory process.

The model addresses two particular features of recognition memory. First, people rarely report recollecting a studied event for an item they never studied. Second, interference reduces how often recollection occurs, while apparently leaving the accuracy of successfully recollected information intact. These are separate requirements: a model must explain both whether details are recovered and how trustworthy those details are.

The contribution is an account that captures both patterns within a biologically motivated framework. Its significance is the distinction between recollection becoming less available and recollection becoming less accurate. The reported behavior supports treating those outcomes separately when explaining recognition memory.
summary.tldr: A hippocampal model explains why interference can reduce recollection without reducing the accuracy of what is recollected.

title: A Hippocampal Model of Recognition Memory

abstract: Based on computational principles, the concept of an internal model for adaptive control has been divided into a forward and an inverse model. However, there is as yet little evidence that learning control by the eNS is through adaptation of one or the other. Here we examine two adaptive control architectures, one based only on the inverse model and other based on a combination of forward and inverse models. We then show that for reaching movements of the hand in novel force fields, only the learning of the forward model results in key characteristics of performance that match the kine(cid:173) matics of human subjects. In contrast, the adaptive control system that relies only on the inverse model fails to produce the kinematic patterns observed in the subjects, despite the fact that it is more stable. Our results provide evidence that learning control of novel dynamics is via formation of a forward model.

paragraphs: The paper investigates what kind of internal model supports human adaptation to unfamiliar movement dynamics. It compares two adaptive-control architectures: one using only an inverse model, and another combining forward and inverse models. The aim is to distinguish their explanations of learning by comparing their movement patterns with those of human subjects.

The comparison concerns hand-reaching movements in novel force fields. Among the architectures examined, learning a forward model produces key performance characteristics that match human movement kinematics. The inverse-only architecture fails to reproduce those observed patterns, even though it is more stable. This makes the detailed form of the movement an important source of evidence beyond whether a controller remains stable.

The findings support the idea that adapting to novel dynamics involves forming a forward model. The strength of the conclusion comes from the contrast between the tested architectures and the human movement data. It is evidence for a particular account of adaptation in this setting, with the forward-model architecture capturing characteristics that the tested inverse-only alternative does not.
summary.tldr: Comparisons with human reaching movements support forward-model learning as an account of adaptation to novel force fields.

title: Evidence for a Forward Dynamics Model in Human Adaptive Motor Control

abstract: In this paper, we address two issues of long-standing interest in the re(cid:173) inforcement learning literature. First, what kinds of performance guar(cid:173) antees can be made for Q-learning after only a finite number of actions? Second, what quantitative comparisons can be made between Q-learning and model-based (indirect) approaches, which use experience to estimate next-state distributions for off-line value iteration? We first show that both Q-learning and the indirect approach enjoy rather rapid convergence to the optimal policy as a function of the num(cid:173) ber of state transitions observed. In particular, on the order of only (Nlog(1/c)/c2 )(log(N) + loglog(l/c)) transitions are sufficient for both algorithms to come within c of the optimal policy, in an idealized model that assumes the observed transitions are "well-mixed" throughout an N-state MDP. Thus, the two approaches have roughly the same sample complexity. Perhaps surprisingly, this sample complexity is far less than what is required for the model-based approach to actually construct a good approximation to the next-state distribution. The result also shows that the amount of memory required by the model-based approach is closer to N than to N 2 • For either approach, to remove the assumption that the observed tran(cid:173) sitions are well-mixed, we consider a model in which the transitions are determined by a fixed, arbitrary exploration policy. Bounds on the number of transitions required in order to achieve a desired level of performance are then related to the stationary distribution and mixing time of this policy.

paragraphs: The paper asks how much experience Q-learning and a model-based reinforcement-learning approach need to produce a near-optimal policy. The model-based method estimates next-state distributions and then performs offline value iteration. The authors compare the two approaches through finite-sample guarantees, measuring experience by the number of observed state transitions.

In an idealized model where transitions are well mixed across an N-state Markov decision process, both approaches have roughly the same sample complexity. The stated sufficient bound grows approximately linearly with N and inversely with the square of the desired error tolerance, with additional logarithmic factors. Achieving a good policy requires substantially less data than accurately reconstructing the next-state distribution, and the model-based memory requirement is closer to linear than quadratic in N.

The authors also consider transitions generated by a fixed, arbitrary exploration policy. This removes the idealized well-mixed assumption, but makes the bounds depend on that policy's stationary distribution and mixing time. The results therefore distinguish learning from broadly distributed experience from learning under a particular exploration process.
summary.tldr: Finite-sample bounds give Q-learning and model-based learning similar sample complexity under well-mixed sampling, with exploration-dependent bounds beyond that setting.

title: Finite-Sample Convergence Rates for Q-Learning and Indirect Algorithms

abstract: In this paper we present a novel approach to multichannel blind separation/generalized deconvolution, assuming that both mixing and demixing models are described by stable linear state-space sys(cid:173) tems. We decompose the blind separation problem into two pro(cid:173) cess: separation and state estimation. Based on the minimization of Kullback-Leibler Divergence, we develop a novel learning algo(cid:173) rithm to train the matrices in the output equation. To estimate the state of the demixing model, we introduce a new concept, called hidden innovation, to numerically implement the Kalman filter. Computer simulations are given to show the validity and high ef(cid:173) fectiveness of the state-space approach. 1

paragraphs: This paper proposes a method for recovering sources from multiple observed channels when the sources have been mixed and filtered. Its central modeling assumption is that both the mixing process and the system used to undo it can be described by stable linear state-space systems. This provides a common representation for the original transformation and its reversal.

The method divides the task into source separation and state estimation. For separation, the authors derive a learning algorithm that adjusts the matrices in the output equation by minimizing Kullback-Leibler divergence. For state estimation, they introduce a quantity called hidden innovation to support a numerical implementation of the Kalman filter.

This division lets the method address the output mapping and the internal state of the demixing model as distinct parts of one procedure. The authors report computer simulations demonstrating the validity and high effectiveness of the state-space approach. The evidence supports the proposed combination within the studied setup, whose formulation depends on the stable linear models specified at the outset.
summary.tldr: A stable linear state-space formulation separates filtered sources by combining divergence-based learning with Kalman state estimation.

title: Blind Separation of Filtered Sources Using State-Space Approach

abstract: An on-line recursive algorithm for training support vector machines, one vector at a time, is presented. Adiabatic increments retain the Kuhn(cid:173) Tucker conditions on all previously seen training data, in a number of steps each computed analytically. The incremental procedure is re(cid:173) versible, and decremental "unlearning" offers an efficient method to ex(cid:173) actly evaluate leave-one-out generalization performance. Interpretation of decremental unlearning in feature space sheds light on the relationship between generalization and geometry of the data.

Adiabatic increments retain the Kuhn(cid:173) Tucker conditions on all previously seen training data, in a number of steps each computed analytically. The incremental procedure is re(cid:173) versible, and decremental "unlearning" offers an efficient method to ex(cid:173) actly evaluate leave-one-out generalization performance. Interpretation of decremental unlearning in feature space sheds light on the relationship between generalization and geometry of the data.

paragraphs: The paper presents a support vector machine training procedure that processes one training vector at a time. Its central concern is how to incorporate a new example while preserving the optimization conditions associated with previously seen examples. This gives online learning a precise relationship to the constraints defining the support vector solution.

The update proceeds through gradual increments that retain the Kuhn–Tucker conditions on earlier training data. Each step is computed analytically. These conditions describe the relationship between the solution and its optimization constraints, so maintaining them is more specific than simply making a small change to the classifier's parameters after receiving a new observation.

The incremental process is reversible, allowing examples to be removed through decremental unlearning. The authors use this capability to evaluate leave-one-out generalization performance exactly and efficiently: each example can be assessed with its contribution removed from training. They also interpret removal geometrically in feature space, connecting the effect of individual observations with the relationship between data geometry and generalization.
summary.tldr: A reversible SVM update preserves optimization conditions while adding examples and enables efficient exact leave-one-out evaluation by removing them.

title: Incremental and Decremental Support Vector Machine Learning

abstract: We present efficient algorithms for all-point-pairs problems , or 'N(cid:173) body '-like problems, which are ubiquitous in statistical learning. We focus on six examples, including nearest-neighbor classification, kernel density estimation, outlier detection , and the two-point correlation. These include any problem which abstractly requires a comparison of each of the N points in a dataset with each other point and would naively be solved using N 2 distance computations. In practice N is often large enough to make this infeasible. We present a suite of new geometric t echniques which are applicable in principle to any 'N-body' computation including large-scale mixtures of Gaussians, RBF neural networks, and HMM 's. Our algorithms exhibit favorable asymptotic scaling and are empirically several orders of magnitude faster than the naive computation, even for small datasets. We are aware of no exact algorithms for these problems which are more effi(cid:173) cient either empirically or theoretically. In addition, our framework yields simple and elegant algorithms. It also permits two important generalizations beyond the standard all-point-pairs problems, which are more difficult. These are represented by our final examples, the multiple two-point correlation and the notorious n-point correlation.

paragraphs: Many statistical learning computations appear to require comparing every data point with every other point. The straightforward approach uses a number of distance calculations proportional to the square of the dataset size, which can become infeasible. The paper develops geometric algorithms for this shared computational structure across six examples.

The examples include nearest-neighbor classification, kernel density estimation, outlier detection, and two-point correlation. The authors present techniques applicable in principle to other N-body-style computations, including those arising in Gaussian mixtures, radial basis function networks, and hidden Markov models. This groups several learning problems around a common computational challenge.

The algorithms have favorable asymptotic scaling and are empirically several orders of magnitude faster than naive computation, even on small datasets. The authors report knowing no more efficient exact algorithms for these problems, either theoretically or empirically. Their framework also extends to more difficult correlation computations, illustrated by multiple two-point correlation and n-point correlation. The contribution combines speed improvements with a broader geometric framework for related computations.
summary.tldr: Geometric algorithms accelerate all-pairs statistical learning computations by several orders of magnitude in experiments and extend to harder correlation problems.

title: `N-Body' Problems in Statistical Learning

abstract: A mixed-signal paradigm is presented for high-resolution parallel inner- product computation in very high dimensions, suitable for efﬁcient im- plementation of kernels in image processing. At the core of the externally digital architecture is a high-density, low-power analog array performing binary-binary partial matrix-vector multiplication. Full digital resolution is maintained even with low-resolution analog-to-digital conversion, ow- ing to random statistics in the analog summation of binary products. A random modulation scheme produces near-Bernoulli statistics even for highly correlated inputs. The approach is validated with real image data, and with experimental results from a CID/DRAM analog array prototype in 0.5

paragraphs: The paper presents a hardware approach for computing high-dimensional inner products in parallel, aimed at efficient image-processing kernels. Its external interface is digital, while a dense, low-power analog array performs partial matrix-vector calculations on binary inputs. The architecture combines digital representation with analog computation at the core of the operation.

A central result is that full digital resolution can be maintained even when the analog-to-digital converter has low resolution. The approach relies on the random statistics of summed binary products. To support those statistics when inputs are strongly correlated, the authors introduce random modulation that makes the resulting behavior approximately Bernoulli. The statistical design is therefore part of how the hardware achieves its stated precision.

Validation uses real image data and experimental results from a CID/DRAM analog array prototype. These demonstrations support the feasibility of combining dense analog computation with a digital interface for this task. The contribution links numerical resolution, input randomization, and circuit architecture in a method intended for very high-dimensional kernel calculations.
summary.tldr: A mixed-signal architecture uses randomized binary computations to preserve digital resolution with low-resolution analog conversion.

title: Stochastic Mixed-Signal VLSI Architecture for High-Dimensional Kernel Machines

abstract: We consider the problem of learning to attain multiple goals in a dynamic envi- ronment, which is initially unknown. In addition, the environment may contain arbitrarily varying elements related to actions of other agents or to non-stationary moves of Nature. This problem is modelled as a stochastic (Markov) game between the learning agent and an arbitrary player, with a vector-valued reward function. The objective of the learning agent is to have its long-term average reward vector belong to a given target set. We devise an algorithm for achieving this task, which is based on the theory of approachability for stochastic games. This algorithm com- bines, in an appropriate way, a ﬂnite set of standard, scalar-reward learning algo- rithms. Su–cient conditions are given for the convergence of the learning algorithm to a general target set. The specialization of these results to the single-controller Markov decision problem are discussed as well.

Su–cient conditions are given for the convergence of the learning algorithm to a general target set. The specialization of these results to the single-controller Markov decision problem are discussed as well.

paragraphs: The paper studies reinforcement learning with several goals in an initially unknown dynamic environment. Some environmental changes may vary arbitrarily because of other agents or nonstationary external influences. The authors model this as a stochastic game between the learner and an arbitrary player, with each outcome producing a vector of rewards.

The learner’s objective is for its long-run average reward vector to belong to a specified target set. This expresses success through several reward components together. The proposed algorithm draws on approachability theory for stochastic games and appropriately combines a finite collection of standard learning algorithms that each use scalar rewards.

The authors provide sufficient conditions for convergence to a general target set. These conditions establish when the steering construction succeeds, without claiming success for every environment or target. They also discuss the specialization to a single-controller Markov decision problem. The contribution is a way to build a multiple-goal learning procedure from scalar learners while retaining a conditional theoretical account of its long-run behavior.
summary.tldr: A steering algorithm combines scalar-reward learners to approach a target set of average reward vectors under sufficient convergence conditions.

title: The Steering Approach for Multi-Criteria Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Integration in the head-direction system is a computation by which hor- izontal angular head velocity signals from the vestibular nuclei are in- tegrated to yield a neural representation of head direction. In the thala- mus, the postsubiculum and the mammillary nuclei, the head-direction representation has the form of a place code: neurons have a preferred head direction in which their ﬁring is maximal [Blair and Sharp, 1995, Blair et al., 1998, ?]. Integration is a difﬁcult computation, given that head-velocities can vary over a large range. Previous models of the head-direction system relied on the assumption that the integration is achieved in a ﬁring-rate-based attractor network with a ring structure. In order to correctly integrate head-velocity signals during high-speed head rotations, very fast synaptic dynamics had to be assumed. Here we address the question whether integration in the head-direction system is possible with slow synapses, for example excitatory NMDA and inhibitory GABA(B) type synapses. For neural networks with such slow synapses, rate-based dynamics are a good approximation of spik- ing neurons [Ermentrout, 1994]. We ﬁnd that correct integration during high-speed head rotations imposes strong constraints on possible net- work architectures.

paragraphs: The head-direction system must convert signals about how quickly the head is turning into a representation of its direction. This requires integration: accumulating changes in angle over time. In several brain regions, direction is represented by neurons that fire most strongly when the head points toward their preferred direction.

The difficulty is that head movements span a wide range of speeds. Earlier models used a ring-shaped attractor network described through firing rates, but accurate integration during fast rotations required very fast synaptic dynamics. The paper asks whether integration can instead work with slow synapses, including excitatory NMDA and inhibitory GABA(B) types.

For networks with such slow synapses, firing-rate dynamics provide a good approximation to spiking neurons. Within this setting, the authors find that accurate integration at high rotation speeds places strong constraints on network architecture. The contribution is therefore an architectural constraint on proposed mechanisms: a plausible account must accommodate both slow synaptic responses and rapid changes in head direction.
summary.tldr: Accurately integrating rapid head turns with slow synapses places strong constraints on the architecture of head-direction networks.

title: A theory of neural integration in the head-direction system

abstract: We propose a new algorithm to estimate the intrinsic dimension of data sets. The method is based on geometric properties of the data and re- quires neither parametric assumptions on the data generating model nor input parameters to set. The method is compared to a similar, widely- used algorithm from the same family of geometric techniques. Experi- ments show that our method is more robust in terms of the data generating distribution and more reliable in the presence of noise.
originalAbstract: We propose a new algorithm to estimate the intrinsic dimension of data sets. The method is based on geometric properties of the data and re- quires neither parametric assumptions on the data generating model nor input parameters to set. The method is compared to a similar, widely- used algorithm from the same family of geometric techniques. Experi- ments show that our method is more robust in terms of the data generating distribution and more reliable in the presence of noise.

paragraphs: A dataset's intrinsic dimension describes the dimensionality of its underlying structure. This paper proposes an algorithm for estimating that dimension from the geometry of the observed data. As indicated by its title, the approach uses packing numbers, making geometric organization the basis for the estimate rather than a specified model of how the data were generated.

Two design features make the method straightforward to apply: it requires neither parametric assumptions about the generating process nor input parameters for the user to choose. These properties reduce the need to commit to a particular distributional model or configure the estimator before using it. They are part of the method's stated formulation.

The authors compare their estimator with a similar, widely used geometric algorithm. In the reported experiments, the proposed method is more robust to the data-generating distribution and more reliable in the presence of noise. These findings support its practical appeal within that comparison, particularly when estimating dimension from data whose geometry is affected by noisy observations.
summary.tldr: A parameter-free geometric dimension estimator shows greater robustness to distribution changes and noise than a related method in experiments.

title: Intrinsic Dimension Estimation Using Packing Numbers

abstract: We consider a statistical framework for learning in a class of net- works of spiking neurons. Our aim is to show how optimal local learning rules can be readily derived once the neural dynamics and desired functionality of the neural assembly have been speciﬂed, in contrast to other models which assume (sub-optimal) learning rules. Within this framework we derive local rules for learning tem- poral sequences in a model of spiking neurons and demonstrate its superior performance to correlation (Hebbian) based approaches. We further show how to include mechanisms such as synaptic de- pression and outline how the framework is readily extensible to learning in networks of highly complex spiking neurons. A stochas- tic quantal vesicle release mechanism is considered and implications on the complexity of learning discussed.
originalAbstract: We consider a statistical framework for learning in a class of net- works of spiking neurons. Our aim is to show how optimal local learning rules can be readily derived once the neural dynamics and desired functionality of the neural assembly have been speciﬂed, in contrast to other models which assume (sub-optimal) learning rules. Within this framework we derive local rules for learning tem- poral sequences in a model of spiking neurons and demonstrate its superior performance to correlation (Hebbian) based approaches. We further show how to include mechanisms such as synaptic de- pression and outline how the framework is readily extensible to learning in networks of highly complex spiking neurons. A stochas- tic quantal vesicle release mechanism is considered and implications on the complexity of learning discussed.

paragraphs: The paper proposes a statistical framework for deriving learning rules in networks of spiking neurons. The starting point is to specify both the neurons' dynamics and the function the network should perform. From those choices, the framework derives optimal local learning rules, tying their optimality to the particular model and task.

The authors apply this approach to learning temporal sequences. They derive local rules for a spiking-neuron model and demonstrate better performance than correlation-based Hebbian approaches. The significance is methodological as well as empirical: the learning rule follows from the stated dynamics and desired function, providing a principled alternative to assuming a rule in advance.

The framework can incorporate synaptic depression, and the authors outline how it could extend to networks with more complex spiking neurons. They also consider stochastic release of discrete vesicles and discuss what this implies for learning complexity. These additions connect the statistical derivation to richer neural mechanisms while keeping the relationship between neuronal dynamics and learning central.
summary.tldr: A statistical framework derives local learning rules from spiking-neuron dynamics and demonstrates improved temporal-sequence learning over Hebbian approaches.

title: Learning in Spiking Neural Assemblies

abstract: We apply the replica method of Statistical Physics combined with a vari- ational method to the approximate analytical computation of bootstrap averages for estimating the generalization error. We demonstrate our ap- proach on regression with Gaussian processes and compare our results with averages obtained by Monte-Carlo sampling.
originalAbstract: We apply the replica method of Statistical Physics combined with a vari- ational method to the approximate analytical computation of bootstrap averages for estimating the generalization error. We demonstrate our ap- proach on regression with Gaussian processes and compare our results with averages obtained by Monte-Carlo sampling.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to calculate bootstrap averages used to estimate generalization error: how well a learned predictor performs beyond its training observations. The quantity of interest is an average over bootstrap resampling. The authors investigate an analytical approximation to that average, bringing methods from statistical physics into the assessment of predictive models.

Their approach combines the replica method with a variational method. Together, these tools provide a way to approximate the desired average through mathematical analysis. The contribution is therefore a method for evaluating bootstrap quantities, with generalization-error estimation as its purpose, rather than a new predictor trained directly for the regression task.

The authors demonstrate the approach using Gaussian process regression and compare its results with averages obtained through Monte Carlo sampling. This comparison connects the analytical calculation to a sampling-based calculation of the target quantities. The stated contribution is an approximate analytical route and its demonstration in that setting; the abstract reports the comparison without claiming a particular accuracy advantage, speedup, or exact agreement.
summary.tldr: The paper combines replica and variational methods to approximate bootstrap averages for generalization-error estimation in Gaussian process regression.

title: A Statistical Mechanics Approach to Approximate Analytical Bootstrap Averages

abstract: Online algorithms for classification often require vast amounts of memory and computation time when employed in conjunction with kernel functions. In this paper we describe and analyze a simple approach for an on-the-fly reduction of the number of past examples used for prediction. Experiments performed with real datasets show that using the proposed algorithmic approach with a single epoch is competitive with the support vector machine (SVM) although the latter, being a batch algorithm, accesses each training example multiple times.
originalAbstract: Online algorithms for classification often require vast amounts of memory and computation time when employed in conjunction with kernel functions. In this paper we describe and analyze a simple approach for an on-the-fly reduction of the number of past examples used for prediction. Experiments performed with real datasets show that using the proposed algorithmic approach with a single epoch is competitive with the support vector machine (SVM) although the latter, being a batch algorithm, accesses each training example multiple times.

paragraphs: The paper addresses the memory and computation costs of online classification with kernels. In this setting, predictions can depend on many previously seen examples. Keeping and using a large history can make an otherwise incremental learning procedure expensive, motivating a way to reduce the examples retained for prediction.

The authors describe and analyze a simple method that performs this reduction while learning proceeds. Its focus is the number of past examples used by the classifier, connecting resource control directly to the representation used for future predictions. The approach is designed to make that reduction on the fly as training examples are processed.

Experiments on real datasets show that the proposed approach is competitive with a support vector machine after just one pass through the training data. The compared SVM is a batch method that accesses each example multiple times. The result supports the practical value of reducing the retained history during online learning while achieving competitive classification performance in the reported experiments.
summary.tldr: An online method reduces the past examples needed for kernel prediction and remains competitive with an SVM after one training pass.

title: Online Classification on a Budget

abstract: We have designed and tested a single-chip analog VLSI sensor that detects imminent collisions by measuring radially expansive optic flow. The design of the chip is based on a model proposed to explain leg-extension behavior in flies during landing approaches. A new elementary motion detector (EMD) circuit was developed to measure optic flow. This EMD circuit models the bandpass nature of large monopolar cells (LMCs) immediately postsynaptic to photoreceptors in the fly visual system. A 16 × 16 array of 2-D motion detectors was fabricated on a 2.24 mm × 2.24 mm die in a standard 0.5-µm CMOS process. The chip consumes 140 µW of power from a 5 V supply. With the addition of wide-angle optics, the sensor is able to detect collisions around 500 ms before impact in complex, real-world scenes.
originalAbstract: We have designed and tested a single-chip analog VLSI sensor that detects imminent collisions by measuring radially expansive optic flow. This EMD circuit models the bandpass nature of large monopolar cells (LMCs) immediately postsynaptic to photoreceptors in the fly visual system. paragraphs: The paper presents a single-chip visual sensor that detects approaching collisions from outward-expanding patterns of image motion. This radial expansion provides a visual signal of an impending impact. The design draws on a model developed to explain how flies time leg extension while approaching a landing surface, translating that biological idea into analog circuitry.

The authors developed an elementary motion detector that models the bandpass behavior of cells immediately downstream of fly photoreceptors. A fabricated chip contains a 16-by-16 array of two-dimensional motion detectors on a 2.24-by-2.24-millimeter die. It uses a standard 0.5-micrometer CMOS process and consumes 140 microwatts from a 5-volt supply.

With wide-angle optics added, the tested sensor can detect collisions approximately 500 milliseconds before impact in complex real-world scenes. The result connects a biologically motivated computation with a working, low-power device. The optics are part of the stated collision-detection setup, and the reported warning time is approximate rather than a fixed guarantee for every encounter.
summary.tldr: A fly-inspired analog vision chip detects approaching collisions about 500 milliseconds before impact with wide-angle optics while consuming 140 microwatts.

title: A Low-Power Analog VLSI Visual Collision Detector

abstract: We develop an approach for estimation with Gaussian Markov processes that imposes a smoothness prior while allowing for discontinuities. In- stead of propagating information laterally between neighboring nodes in a graph, we study the posterior distribution of the hidden nodes as a whole—how it is perturbed by invoking discontinuities, or weakening the edges, in the graph. We show that the resulting computation amounts to feed-forward fan-in operations reminiscent of V1 neurons. Moreover, using suitable matrix preconditioners, the incurred matrix inverse and determinant can be approximated, without iteration, in the same compu- tational style. Simulation results illustrate the merits of this approach.
originalAbstract: We develop an approach for estimation with Gaussian Markov processes that imposes a smoothness prior while allowing for discontinuities. In- stead of propagating information laterally between neighboring nodes in a graph, we study the posterior distribution of the hidden nodes as a whole—how it is perturbed by invoking discontinuities, or weakening the edges, in the graph. We show that the resulting computation amounts to feed-forward fan-in operations reminiscent of V1 neurons. Moreover, using suitable matrix preconditioners, the incurred matrix inverse and determinant can be approximated, without iteration, in the same compu- tational style. Simulation results illustrate the merits of this approach.

paragraphs: This paper develops estimation methods for Gaussian Markov processes that favor smoothness while still permitting discontinuities. These requirements must coexist: neighboring hidden quantities should generally vary smoothly, but some graph connections must allow abrupt changes. The authors investigate how weakening edges changes the posterior distribution over hidden nodes.

Their analysis considers that distribution as a whole rather than propagating information laterally between neighboring nodes. The resulting computation takes the form of feed-forward operations that collect multiple inputs, resembling the computational organization of V1 neurons. This provides an alternative way to organize inference when the model's smoothness relationships are perturbed.

The method also encounters matrix inverses and determinants. With suitable matrix preconditioners, the authors show that these quantities can be approximated without iteration using the same computational style. Simulations illustrate the approach's merits. The contribution is a route to non-iterative approximation and estimation that accommodates broken smoothness connections, with the matrix-approximation result specifically depending on appropriate preconditioning.
summary.tldr: Analyzing graph-edge perturbations enables feed-forward estimation with smoothness and discontinuities, including non-iterative matrix approximations under suitable preconditioning.

title: Non-iterative Estimation with Perturbed Gaussian Markov Processes

abstract: Predictive state representations (PSRs) are a method of modeling dynamical systems using only observable data, such as actions and observations, to describe their model. PSRs use predictions about the outcome of future tests to summarize the system state. The best existing techniques for discovery and learning of PSRs use a Monte Carlo approach to explicitly estimate these outcome probabilities. In this paper, we present a new algorithm for discovery and learning of PSRs that uses a gradient descent approach to compute the predictions for the current state. The algorithm takes advantage of the large amount of structure inherent in a valid prediction matrix to constrain its predictions. Furthermore, the algorithm can be used online by an agent to constantly improve its prediction quality; something that current state of the art discovery and learning algorithms are unable to do. We give empirical results to show that our constrained gradient algorithm is able to discover core tests using very small amounts of data, and with larger amounts of data can compute accurate predictions of the system dynamics.
originalAbstract: Predictive state representations (PSRs) are a method of modeling dynamical systems using only observable data, such as actions and observations, to describe their model. PSRs use predictions about the outcome of future tests to summarize the system state. The best existing techniques for discovery and learning of PSRs use a Monte Carlo approach to explicitly estimate these outcome probabilities. In this paper, we present a new algorithm for discovery and learning of PSRs that uses a gradient descent approach to compute the predictions for the current state. The algorithm takes advantage of the large amount of structure inherent in a valid prediction matrix to constrain its predictions. Furthermore, the algorithm can be used online by an agent to constantly improve its prediction quality; something that current state of the art discovery and learning algorithms are unable to do. We give empirical results to show that our constrained gradient algorithm is able to discover core tests using very small amounts of data, and with larger amounts of data can compute accurate predictions of the system dynamics.

paragraphs: Predictive state representations describe a dynamical system through observable actions and observations. They summarize its current state using predictions about outcomes of future tests. Learning such a representation involves discovering useful tests as well as estimating the predictions that describe the system's behavior.

The paper introduces a gradient descent algorithm for both discovery and learning. It uses the structure of a valid prediction matrix to constrain its predictions, incorporating relationships that valid predictions must respect. This differs from the Monte Carlo approach used by the existing techniques discussed in the abstract, which explicitly estimate test-outcome probabilities.

The algorithm can operate online, allowing an agent to keep improving predictions as it interacts with the system. Empirical results show discovery of core tests with very small amounts of data and accurate predictions of system dynamics when more data are available. These findings support both parts of the learning task. The main contribution combines structural constraints with an update procedure suitable for continuing discovery and prediction during operation.
summary.tldr: A constrained gradient algorithm discovers and learns predictive state representations online, with empirical support for data-efficient discovery and accurate prediction.

title: Online Discovery and Learning of Predictive State Representations

abstract: Computation of a satisfactory control policy for a Markov decision process when the parameters of the model are not exactly known is a problem encountered in many practical applications. The traditional robust approach is based on a worstcase analysis and may lead to an overly conservative policy. In this paper we consider the tradeoff between nominal performance and the worst case performance over all possible models. Based on parametric linear programming, we propose a method that computes the whole set of Pareto efficient policies in the performancerobustness plane when only the reward parameters are subject to uncertainty. In the more general case when the transition probabilities are also subject to error, we show that the strategy with the "optimal" tradeoff might be non-Markovian and hence is in general not tractable.
originalAbstract: Computation of a satisfactory control policy for a Markov decision process when the parameters of the model are not exactly known is a problem encountered in many practical applications. The traditional robust approach is based on a worstcase analysis and may lead to an overly conservative policy. In this paper we consider the tradeoff between nominal performance and the worst case performance over all possible models. Based on parametric linear programming, we propose a method that computes the whole set of Pareto efficient policies in the performancerobustness plane when only the reward parameters are subject to uncertainty. In the more general case when the transition probabilities are also subject to error, we show that the strategy with the "optimal" tradeoff might be non-Markovian and hence is in general not tractable.

paragraphs: A controller often has to choose actions using a Markov decision process whose parameters are uncertain. Optimizing only for the worst possible model can produce overly conservative behavior. This paper instead examines the relationship between performance under the nominal model and performance under the worst case among the possible models.

When uncertainty affects only rewards, the authors use parametric linear programming to compute the complete set of Pareto-efficient policies in this two-objective space. These are policies for which improving one objective requires sacrificing the other. The resulting set describes the available compromises, giving a fuller picture than a single worst-case-optimal policy.

The situation changes when transition probabilities are also uncertain. The authors show that a strategy achieving the optimal tradeoff might need to be non-Markovian, so its decisions may depend on more than the current state. The general problem is consequently not tractable. The paper therefore identifies both a computable reward-uncertainty case and a significant difficulty introduced by uncertain dynamics.
summary.tldr: The paper computes performance–robustness tradeoffs for uncertain rewards and shows why uncertain transitions make the general problem harder.

title: The Robustness-Performance Tradeoff in Markov Decision Processes

abstract: Multinomial logistic regression provides the standard penalised maximum- likelihood solution to multi-class pattern recognition problems. More recently, the development of sparse multinomial logistic regression models has found ap- plication in text processing and microarray classiﬁcation, where explicit identiﬁ- cation of the most informative features is of value. In this paper, we propose a sparse multinomial logistic regression method, in which the sparsity arises from the use of a Laplace prior, but where the usual regularisation parameter is inte- grated out analytically. Evaluation over a range of benchmark datasets reveals this approach results in similar generalisation performance to that obtained using cross-validation, but at greatly reduced computational expense.
originalAbstract: Multinomial logistic regression provides the standard penalised maximum- likelihood solution to multi-class pattern recognition problems. More recently, the development of sparse multinomial logistic regression models has found ap- plication in text processing and microarray classiﬁcation, where explicit identiﬁ- cation of the most informative features is of value. In this paper, we propose a sparse multinomial logistic regression method, in which the sparsity arises from the use of a Laplace prior, but where the usual regularisation parameter is inte- grated out analytically. Evaluation over a range of benchmark datasets reveals this approach results in similar generalisation performance to that obtained using cross-validation, but at greatly reduced computational expense.

paragraphs: Multinomial logistic regression predicts membership across several classes. Sparse versions are useful when identifying informative features matters alongside prediction, as in text processing and microarray classification. This paper proposes a Bayesian approach that encourages sparsity while changing how the strength of that encouragement is handled.

The model uses a Laplace prior to produce sparse coefficients. A usual regularization parameter controls the amount of regularization, but here the authors integrate that parameter out analytically. This incorporates it into the mathematical treatment instead of selecting its value through the cross-validation procedure used for comparison. The method thus targets a computational burden associated with fitting a sparse multiclass model.

Across benchmark datasets, the authors report generalization performance similar to that obtained using cross-validation, at greatly reduced computational expense. The finding concerns maintaining comparable prediction on unseen data while making model fitting less costly. It supports analytical treatment of the regularization parameter as a practical alternative in the evaluated problems, while retaining the sparse formulation that makes informative features explicit.
summary.tldr: Analytically integrating out regularization strength yields sparse multiclass logistic regression with comparable generalization at lower reported computational cost.

title: Sparse Multinomial Logistic Regression via Bayesian L1 Regularisation

abstract: In this paper, we consider collaborative ﬁltering as a ranking problem. We present a method which uses Maximum Margin Matrix Factorization and optimizes rank- ing instead of rating. We employ structured output prediction to optimize directly for ranking scores. Experimental results show that our method gives very good ranking scores and scales well on collaborative ﬁltering tasks.
originalAbstract: In this paper, we consider collaborative ﬁltering as a ranking problem. We present a method which uses Maximum Margin Matrix Factorization and optimizes rank- ing instead of rating. We employ structured output prediction to optimize directly for ranking scores. Experimental results show that our method gives very good ranking scores and scales well on collaborative ﬁltering tasks.

paragraphs: Collaborative filtering can be framed around the order in which items should be presented to a user. In that setting, the central output is a ranking: which items should appear ahead of others. The paper adopts this perspective and makes ranking quality the explicit target of learning.

The proposed method uses maximum-margin matrix factorization together with structured output prediction. Matrix factorization supplies the collaborative model, while structured prediction allows the learning objective to operate on rankings. This matters because a ranking describes relationships among multiple items, and the authors optimize ranking scores directly instead of using rating prediction as the training target.

The experiments report very good ranking scores and favorable scaling on collaborative-filtering tasks. These findings support the practicality of aligning the optimization objective with the ordered recommendations the method is meant to produce. The paper's stated contribution is therefore both methodological and empirical: it connects a factorization approach to direct ranking optimization and demonstrates useful performance and scalability in the tested tasks.
summary.tldr: COFI RANK combines maximum-margin matrix factorization with structured prediction to optimize recommendation rankings directly.

title: COFI RANK - Maximum Margin Matrix Factorization for Collaborative Ranking

abstract: Many types of regularization schemes have been employed in statistical learning, each one motivated by some assumption about the problem domain. In this paper, we present a unified asymptotic analysis of smooth regularizers, which allows us to see how the validity of these assumptions impacts the success of a particular regularizer. In addition, our analysis motivates an algorithm for optimizing regularization parameters, which in turn can be analyzed within our framework. We apply our analysis to several examples, including hybrid generative-discriminative learning and multi-task learning.
originalAbstract: Many types of regularization schemes have been employed in statistical learning, each one motivated by some assumption about the problem domain. In this paper, we present a unified asymptotic analysis of smooth regularizers, which allows us to see how the validity of these assumptions impacts the success of a particular regularizer. In addition, our analysis motivates an algorithm for optimizing regularization parameters, which in turn can be analyzed within our framework. We apply our analysis to several examples, including hybrid generative-discriminative learning and multi-task learning.

paragraphs: Regularization introduces preferences into statistical learning, and different preferences reflect different assumptions about a problem. This paper asks how the validity of those assumptions affects whether a regularizer succeeds. Its focus is smooth regularization in parametric models, examined through an asymptotic analysis that describes behavior as the amount of data grows.

The authors provide a unified framework for studying smooth regularizers. This matters because it connects the motivation for a regularization scheme with its statistical consequences. Instead of treating each scheme as a separate technique, the analysis offers a common way to understand how assumptions about the problem influence the value of the resulting regularization.

The analysis also motivates an algorithm for choosing regularization parameters, and that algorithm can itself be studied within the same framework. Applications include hybrid generative-discriminative learning and multi-task learning. The contribution therefore connects theoretical assessment with parameter selection across several learning settings, with conclusions framed by the paper's smoothness and asymptotic scope.
summary.tldr: A unified asymptotic analysis connects the success of smooth regularizers to their underlying assumptions and motivates regularization parameter selection.

title: Asymptotically Optimal Regularization in Smooth Parametric Models

abstract: We propose a new probabilistic model for analyzing dynamic evolutions of relational data, such as additions, deletions and split & merge, of relation clusters like communities in social networks. Our proposed model abstracts observed time-varying object-object relationships into relationships between object clusters. We extend the infinite Hidden Markov model to follow dynamic and time-sensitive changes in the structure of the relational data and to estimate a number of clusters simultaneously. We show the usefulness of the model through experiments with synthetic and real-world data sets.
originalAbstract: We propose a new probabilistic model for analyzing dynamic evolutions of relational data, such as additions, deletions and split & merge, of relation clusters like communities in social networks. Our proposed model abstracts observed time-varying object-object relationships into relationships between object clusters. We extend the infinite Hidden Markov model to follow dynamic and time-sensitive changes in the structure of the relational data and to estimate a number of clusters simultaneously. We show the usefulness of the model through experiments with synthetic and real-world data sets.

paragraphs: Relational data describe connections between objects, such as relationships among people in a social network. Those connections can change as groups appear, disappear, split, or merge. This paper proposes a probabilistic model for analyzing such evolving group structure, with communities in social networks serving as an example of the kind of pattern it seeks to capture.

The model represents observed relationships between individual objects through relationships between clusters of objects. It extends the infinite Hidden Markov model to track changes in relational structure over time. The number of clusters is estimated alongside their temporal evolution, bringing the questions of how many groups exist and how their structure changes into the same analysis.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the model's usefulness. The contribution is a framework that treats changing cluster structure as part of the phenomenon to be modeled. This gives the analysis a way to describe additions, deletions, and reorganizations of groups through a shared probabilistic representation.
summary.tldr: A dynamic relational model jointly estimates evolving object clusters and their number, including changes such as splits and merges.

title: Dynamic Infinite Relational Model for Time-varying Relational Data Analysis

abstract: Heavy-tailed distributions are often used to enhance the robustness of regression and classification methods to outliers in output space. Often, however, we are confronted with ``outliers'' in input space, which are isolated observations in sparsely populated regions. We show that heavy-tailed process priors (which we construct from Gaussian processes via a copula), can be used to improve robustness of regression and classification estimators to such outliers by selectively shrinking them more strongly in sparse regions than in dense regions. We carry out a theoretical analysis to show that selective shrinkage occurs provided the marginals of the heavy-tailed process have sufficiently heavy tails. The analysis is complemented by experiments on biological data which indicate significant improvements of estimates in sparse regions while producing competitive results in dense regions.

We show that heavy-tailed process priors (which we construct from Gaussian processes via a copula), can be used to improve robustness of regression and classification estimators to such outliers by selectively shrinking them more strongly in sparse regions than in dense regions. We carry out a theoretical analysis to show that selective shrinkage occurs provided the marginals of the heavy-tailed process have sufficiently heavy tails. The analysis is complemented by experiments on biological data which indicate significant improvements of estimates in sparse regions while producing competitive results in dense regions.

paragraphs: Outliers can be unusual because of their output values, but they can also be isolated in the input space. This paper focuses on observations in sparsely populated input regions. It asks how regression and classification methods can respond more cautiously to those observations while retaining useful estimates in regions with denser evidence.

The authors construct heavy-tailed process priors from Gaussian processes using a copula. These priors can produce selective shrinkage: estimates in sparse regions are pulled back more strongly than estimates in dense regions. The theoretical analysis establishes this behavior when the marginal distributions of the process have sufficiently heavy tails, making tail behavior a substantive condition of the result.

Experiments on biological data complement the analysis. They indicate significant improvements in sparse regions while maintaining competitive results in dense regions. The contribution extends the role of heavy-tailed modeling beyond handling unusual outputs, showing how a prior over functions can address uneven input coverage. The reported gains support adapting shrinkage to where observations are scarce.
summary.tldr: Sufficiently heavy-tailed process priors can shrink estimates more strongly in sparse input regions, improving robustness to isolated observations.

title: Heavy-Tailed Process Priors for Selective Shrinkage

abstract: Off-policy learning, the ability for an agent to learn about a policy other than the one it is following, is a key element of Reinforcement Learning, and in recent years there has been much work on developing Temporal Different (TD) algorithms that are guaranteed to converge under off-policy sampling. It has remained an open question, however, whether anything can be said a priori about the quality of the TD solution when off-policy sampling is employed with function approximation. In general the answer is no: for arbitrary off-policy sampling the error of the TD solution can be unboundedly large, even when the approximator can represent the true value function well. In this paper we propose a novel approach to address this problem: we show that by considering a certain convex subset of off-policy distributions we can indeed provide guarantees as to the solution quality similar to the on-policy case. Furthermore, we show that we can efficiently project on to this convex set using only samples generated from the system. The end result is a novel TD algorithm that has approximation guarantees even in the case of off-policy sampling and which empirically outperforms existing TD methods.

paragraphs: Off-policy learning evaluates a policy using experience generated while following another policy. For temporal difference learning with function approximation, convergence alone does not establish that the resulting value estimate is good. The paper shows that arbitrary off-policy sampling can produce unboundedly large error even when the approximation system can represent the true value function well.

The authors address this problem by identifying a particular convex subset of off-policy sampling distributions. Within this set, they can guarantee solution quality in a way similar to the on-policy case. The restriction on sampling distributions is therefore central: the guarantee does not extend to arbitrary off-policy sampling.

They also show how to project efficiently onto this convex set using only samples generated by the system. This makes the theoretical restriction part of a usable procedure, leading to a new temporal difference algorithm with approximation guarantees under off-policy sampling. Experiments show it outperforming existing temporal difference methods. The contribution links a condition ensuring solution quality to a practical way of enforcing that condition.
summary.tldr: Restricting off-policy sampling to a suitable convex set yields temporal difference approximation guarantees and a practical sample-based algorithm.

title: The Fixed Points of Off-Policy TD

abstract: The CUR matrix decomposition is an important extension of Nyström approximation to a general matrix. It approximates any data matrix in terms of a small number of its columns and rows. In this paper we propose a novel randomized CUR algorithm with an expected relative-error bound. The proposed algorithm has the advantages over the existing relative-error CUR algorithms that it possesses tighter theoretical bound and lower time complexity, and that it can avoid maintaining the whole data matrix in main memory. Finally, experiments on several real-world datasets demonstrate significant improvement over the existing relative-error algorithms.
