paragraphs: CUR decomposition approximates a data matrix using a small selection of its own columns and rows. This makes the selected parts of the original data central to the representation. The paper develops a randomized algorithm for constructing this approximation, addressing both the quality of the result and the resources needed to compute it.

The algorithm comes with an expected relative-error guarantee. The word expected matters: the stated theoretical bound concerns the randomized procedure in expectation. Compared with existing relative-error CUR algorithms, the proposed method offers a tighter theoretical bound and lower time complexity. It can also operate without keeping the entire data matrix in main memory, addressing a separate practical obstacle for large matrices.

Experiments on several real-world datasets report significant improvements over existing relative-error algorithms. The contribution therefore combines mathematical guarantees with computational advantages and empirical support. Its significance is that approximation quality, runtime, and memory requirements are addressed together, making CUR decomposition more practical when storing and processing the complete matrix is expensive.
summary.tldr: A randomized CUR algorithm offers a tighter expected relative-error bound, lower time complexity, and reduced main-memory requirements.

title: A Scalable CUR Matrix Decomposition Algorithm: Lower Time Complexity and Tighter Bound

abstract: We analyze a reweighted version of the Kikuchi approximation for estimating the log partition function of a product distribution defined over a region graph. We establish sufficient conditions for the concavity of our reweighted objective function in terms of weight assignments in the Kikuchi expansion, and show that a reweighted version of the sum product algorithm applied to the Kikuchi region graph will produce global optima of the Kikuchi approximation whenever the algorithm converges. When the region graph has two layers, corresponding to a Bethe approximation, we show that our sufficient conditions for concavity are also necessary. Finally, we provide an explicit characterization of the polytope of concavity in terms of the cycle structure of the region graph. We conclude with simulations that demonstrate the advantages of the reweighted Kikuchi approach.

We establish sufficient conditions for the concavity of our reweighted objective function in terms of weight assignments in the Kikuchi expansion, and show that a reweighted version of the sum product algorithm applied to the Kikuchi region graph will produce global optima of the Kikuchi approximation whenever the algorithm converges. When the region graph has two layers, corresponding to a Bethe approximation, we show that our sufficient conditions for concavity are also necessary. Finally, we provide an explicit characterization of the polytope of concavity in terms of the cycle structure of the region graph. We conclude with simulations that demonstrate the advantages of the reweighted Kikuchi approach.

paragraphs: The Kikuchi approximation provides a way to estimate a log partition function using a region graph. This paper studies a reweighted version, asking which assignments of weights make its objective concave. Concavity matters because it gives the approximate optimization problem a structure that supports guarantees about the quality of an optimizer.

The authors establish sufficient conditions on the weights. They also show that a reweighted sum-product algorithm produces a global optimum of the Kikuchi approximation whenever it converges. Both qualifications matter: the result concerns the approximate objective, and the conclusion is conditional on convergence. It does not assert that every run must converge.

For region graphs with two layers, corresponding to the Bethe approximation, the weight conditions are necessary as well as sufficient. The paper further characterizes the polytope of concavity through the graph's cycle structure. Simulations demonstrate advantages of the reweighted approach, connecting these structural results to observed inference performance.
summary.tldr: The paper identifies weights that make reweighted Kikuchi objectives concave and establishes global optimality of the approximation when its message-passing algorithm converges.

title: Concavity of reweighted Kikuchi approximation

abstract: Learning in recurrent neural networks has been a topic fraught with difficulties and problems. We here report substantial progress in the unsupervised learning of recurrent networks that can keep track of an input signal. Specifically, we show how these networks can learn to efficiently represent their present and past inputs, based on local learning rules only. Our results are based on several key insights. First, we develop a local learning rule for the recurrent weights whose main aim is to drive the network into a regime where, on average, feedforward signal inputs are canceled by recurrent inputs. We show that this learning rule minimizes a cost function. Second, we develop a local learning rule for the feedforward weights that, based on networks in which recurrent inputs already predict feedforward inputs, further minimizes the cost. Third, we show how the learning rules can be modified such that the network can directly encode non-whitened inputs. Fourth, we show that these learning rules can also be applied to a network that feeds a time-delayed version of the network output back into itself. As a consequence, the network starts to efficiently represent both its signal inputs and their history. We develop our main theory for linear networks, but then sketch how the learning rules could be transferred to balanced, spiking networks.

paragraphs: The paper develops unsupervised local learning rules for recurrent networks that represent both current inputs and their recent history. Its main theory concerns linear networks. The aim is to learn useful short-term memory through updates based on local information, with an explicit cost function connecting the rules to efficient representation.

The recurrent-weight rule drives the network toward a regime where recurrent inputs cancel feedforward signal inputs on average. The authors show that this rule minimizes a cost. Once recurrent activity predicts feedforward input, a separate rule for feedforward weights reduces the cost further. They also modify the rules to accommodate non-whitened inputs directly.

Applying the learning rules to a network that receives a delayed version of its own output leads it to represent both incoming signals and their history. This links the predictive cancellation mechanism to memory formation. The authors additionally sketch how the rules could transfer to balanced spiking networks; that extension is presented as a possible transfer beyond the developed linear-network theory.
summary.tldr: Local unsupervised learning rules train linear recurrent networks to efficiently represent present inputs and their history.

title: Unsupervised learning of an efficient short-term memory network

abstract: A new Bayesian formulation is developed for nonlinear support vector machines (SVMs), based on a Gaussian process and with the SVM hinge loss expressed as a scaled mixture of normals. We then integrate the Bayesian SVM into a factor model, in which feature learning and nonlinear classifier design are performed jointly; almost all previous work on such discriminative feature learning has assumed a linear classifier. Inference is performed with expectation conditional maximization (ECM) and Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC). An extensive set of experiments demonstrate the utility of using a nonlinear Bayesian SVM within discriminative feature learning and factor modeling, from the standpoints of accuracy and interpretability

We then integrate the Bayesian SVM into a factor model, in which feature learning and nonlinear classifier design are performed jointly; almost all previous work on such discriminative feature learning has assumed a linear classifier. Inference is performed with expectation conditional maximization (ECM) and Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC). An extensive set of experiments demonstrate the utility of using a nonlinear Bayesian SVM within discriminative feature learning and factor modeling, from the standpoints of accuracy and interpretability

paragraphs: The paper develops a Bayesian version of a nonlinear support vector machine. It combines a Gaussian process with a representation of the SVM hinge loss as a scaled mixture of normal distributions. These ingredients provide a formulation in which nonlinear SVM classification can be handled using Bayesian inference methods.

The authors then place this classifier inside a factor model so that feature learning and classifier design happen jointly. This connects the representation learned from the data with the nonlinear decision rule that uses it. The distinction matters because, according to the abstract, almost all earlier work on this kind of discriminative feature learning assumed a linear classifier. The new formulation expands the classifier available within that joint learning process.

Inference uses expectation conditional maximization and Markov Chain Monte Carlo. An extensive experimental evaluation supports the usefulness of the nonlinear Bayesian SVM for both discriminative feature learning and factor modeling. The stated benefits concern accuracy and interpretability, connecting predictive performance with the ability to understand the learned model. The abstract reports these benefits without specifying numerical gains.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian nonlinear SVM enables joint feature and classifier learning within factor models, with experiments supporting accuracy and interpretability benefits.

title: Bayesian Nonlinear Support Vector Machines and Discriminative Factor Modeling

abstract: Perception is often described as a predictive process based on an optimal inference with respect to a generative model. We study here the principled construction of a generative model specifically crafted to probe motion perception. In that context, we first provide an axiomatic, biologically-driven derivation of the model. This model synthesizes random dynamic textures which are defined by stationary Gaussian distributions obtained by the random aggregation of warped patterns. Importantly, we show that this model can equivalently be described as a stochastic partial differential equation. Using this characterization of motion in images, it allows us to recast motion-energy models into a principled Bayesian inference framework. Finally, we apply these textures in order to psychophysically probe speed perception in humans. In this framework, while the likelihood is derived from the generative model, the prior is estimated from the observed results and accounts for the perceptual bias in a principled fashion.

paragraphs: This paper develops a generative model of moving textures to investigate human motion perception. The motivation is to connect controlled visual stimuli with the idea that perception involves inference under a model of how sensory observations arise. The authors derive their texture model from explicit principles informed by biology.

The model creates random dynamic textures by aggregating warped patterns, producing stationary Gaussian distributions. The authors also show that the same model can be expressed as a stochastic partial differential equation. This equivalent description links the generation of moving images to a mathematical account of their evolution, allowing motion-energy models to be formulated within Bayesian inference.

The textures are then used in human experiments on perceived speed. Within the proposed framework, the generative model supplies the likelihood, while the prior is estimated from the observed responses. That prior accounts for perceptual bias in the model. The contribution therefore connects stimulus construction, motion modeling, and interpretation of behavioral results through a shared probabilistic framework.
summary.tldr: A biologically motivated texture model connects moving-image generation with Bayesian explanations of human speed perception.

title: Biologically Inspired Dynamic Textures for Probing Motion Perception

abstract: Multilabel classification is rapidly developing as an important aspect of modern predictive modeling, motivating study of its theoretical aspects. To this end, we propose a framework for constructing and analyzing multilabel classification metrics which reveals novel results on a parametric form for population optimal classifiers, and additional insight into the role of label correlations. In particular, we show that for multilabel metrics constructed as instance-, micro- and macro-averages, the population optimal classifier can be decomposed into binary classifiers based on the marginal instance-conditional distribution of each label, with a weak association between labels via the threshold. Thus, our analysis extends the state of the art from a few known multilabel classification metrics such as Hamming loss, to a general framework applicable to many of the classification metrics in common use. Based on the population-optimal classifier, we propose a computationally efficient and general-purpose plug-in classification algorithm, and prove its consistency with respect to the metric of interest. Empirical results on synthetic and benchmark datasets are supportive of our theoretical findings.

paragraphs: Multilabel prediction assigns several possible labels to an instance, and different evaluation metrics can favor different prediction rules. This paper builds a framework for analyzing those metrics and characterizing classifiers that are optimal for the underlying population. It also clarifies how relationships between labels enter the optimal decision.

For the instance-, micro-, and macro-averaged metrics covered by the analysis, the population-optimal classifier decomposes into binary decisions based on each label's conditional marginal distribution. The labels retain a weak association through the decision threshold. Thus, the framework explains how per-label probability information can support a joint evaluation objective without requiring all label relationships to enter each binary decision directly.

Using this characterization, the authors propose a computationally efficient, general-purpose plug-in classifier and prove consistency for the metric being optimized. This extends analysis beyond a few previously understood metrics, including Hamming loss, to many commonly used measures. Experiments on synthetic and benchmark datasets support the theory, connecting the population-level characterization to a practical classification procedure.
summary.tldr: A framework for multilabel metrics yields population-optimal threshold rules and an efficient plug-in classifier with consistency guarantees.

title: Consistent Multilabel Classification

abstract: There are two major types of uncertainty one can model. Aleatoric uncertainty captures noise inherent in the observations. On the other hand, epistemic uncertainty accounts for uncertainty in the model - uncertainty which can be explained away given enough data. Traditionally it has been difficult to model epistemic uncertainty in computer vision, but with new Bayesian deep learning tools this is now possible. We study the benefits of modeling epistemic vs. aleatoric uncertainty in Bayesian deep learning models for vision tasks. For this we present a Bayesian deep learning framework combining input-dependent aleatoric uncertainty together with epistemic uncertainty. We study models under the framework with per-pixel semantic segmentation and depth regression tasks. Further, our explicit uncertainty formulation leads to new loss functions for these tasks, which can be interpreted as learned attenuation. This makes the loss more robust to noisy data, also giving new state-of-the-art results on segmentation and depth regression benchmarks.

paragraphs: A vision model can be uncertain because its observations are noisy or because the model itself lacks enough knowledge. The paper distinguishes these as aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty. The latter can be reduced with sufficient data, while the former concerns noise inherent in what is observed. The authors study the benefits of representing both.

Their Bayesian deep-learning framework combines epistemic uncertainty with input-dependent aleatoric uncertainty. Allowing observation noise to depend on the input means the model can represent different noise levels across observations. The framework is studied on per-pixel semantic segmentation and depth regression, connecting uncertainty modeling to predictions about image content and scene depth.

The explicit treatment of uncertainty also yields new training losses interpreted as learned attenuation. These losses make training more robust to noisy data, so uncertainty affects the learning process as well as how predictions are described. The authors report new state-of-the-art results on segmentation and depth-regression benchmarks. The findings support combining the two uncertainty types within the evaluated vision models.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian vision framework models observation noise and model uncertainty together, producing noise-robust losses and strong segmentation and depth results.

title: What Uncertainties Do We Need in Bayesian Deep Learning for Computer Vision?

abstract: We consider online linear regression: at each round, an adversary reveals a covariate vector, the learner predicts a real value, the adversary reveals a label, and the learner suffers the squared prediction error. The aim is to minimize the difference between the cumulative loss and that of the linear predictor that is best in hindsight. Previous work demonstrated that the minimax optimal strategy is easy to compute recursively from the end of the game; this requires the entire sequence of covariate vectors in advance. We show that, once provided with a measure of the scale of the problem, we can invert the recursion and play the minimax strategy without knowing the future covariates. Further, we show that this forward recursion remains optimal even against adaptively chosen labels and covariates, provided that the adversary adheres to a set of constraints that prevent misrepresentation of the scale of the problem. This strategy is horizon-independent in that the regret and minimax strategies depend on the size of the constraint set and not on the time-horizon, and hence it incurs no more regret than the optimal strategy that knows in advance the number of rounds of the game. We also provide an interpretation of the minimax algorithm as a follow-the-regularized-leader strategy with a data-dependent regularizer and obtain an explicit expression for the minimax regret.

paragraphs: In online linear regression, a learner predicts a number after seeing each input vector, then receives the label and incurs squared error. Performance is measured against the best fixed linear predictor chosen afterward. Earlier work could compute the minimax strategy backward from the game's end, but needed the entire input sequence in advance.

The authors show how to reverse that computation into a forward recursion when a measure of the problem's scale is supplied. The learner can then follow the minimax strategy without knowing future inputs. Optimality also holds against adaptively chosen inputs and labels, provided the adversary obeys constraints that prevent it from misrepresenting the supplied scale.

The resulting strategy and regret depend on the constraint set's size rather than the number of rounds. Consequently, the strategy incurs no more regret than the optimum that knows the horizon beforehand. The paper also interprets the algorithm as follow-the-regularized-leader with a data-dependent regularizer and gives an explicit minimax regret expression. The scale information and adversarial constraints are essential qualifications to the stated guarantee.
summary.tldr: Given scale information and suitable adversarial constraints, online linear regression can achieve minimax performance without knowing future inputs or the horizon.

title: Horizon-Independent Minimax Linear Regression

abstract: The change-point detection problem seeks to identify distributional changes at an unknown change-point k* in a stream of data. This problem appears in many important practical settings involving personal data, including biosurveillance, fault detection, finance, signal detection, and security systems. The field of differential privacy offers data analysis tools that provide powerful worst-case privacy guarantees. We study the statistical problem of change-point problem through the lens of differential privacy. We give private algorithms for both online and offline change-point detection, analyze these algorithms theoretically, and then provide empirical validation of these results.

We study the statistical problem of change-point problem through the lens of differential privacy. We give private algorithms for both online and offline change-point detection, analyze these algorithms theoretically, and then provide empirical validation of these results.

paragraphs: Change-point detection asks where a stream of observations switches from one underlying distribution to another. The point of change is unknown and must be inferred from the data. This problem arises in settings such as biosurveillance, fault detection, finance, and security, where the observations can also contain personal information.

The paper studies this statistical task under differential privacy, a framework for providing worst-case privacy guarantees. Its contribution includes private algorithms for both online and offline detection. These cover two ways of handling the problem: looking for a change as observations arrive and analyzing a collection of observations after they have been gathered.

The authors analyze the algorithms theoretically and provide empirical validation of their results. The significance is the joint treatment of change detection and privacy: locating a distributional shift is studied with privacy protection built into the analysis. Covering both online and offline settings makes the contribution relevant to monitoring ongoing streams as well as examining historical data for a previously unknown change.
summary.tldr: The paper develops and evaluates differentially private algorithms for detecting distributional changes in online and offline data.

title: Differentially Private Change-Point Detection

abstract: A normalizing flow models a complex probability density as an invertible transformation of a simple base density. Flows based on either coupling or autoregressive transforms both offer exact density evaluation and sampling, but rely on the parameterization of an easily invertible elementwise transformation, whose choice determines the flexibility of these models. Building upon recent work, we propose a fully-differentiable module based on monotonic rational-quadratic splines, which enhances the flexibility of both coupling and autoregressive transforms while retaining analytic invertibility. We demonstrate that neural spline flows improve density estimation, variational inference, and generative modeling of images.

Flows based on either coupling or autoregressive transforms both offer exact density evaluation and sampling, but rely on the parameterization of an easily invertible elementwise transformation, whose choice determines the flexibility of these models. Building upon recent work, we propose a fully-differentiable module based on monotonic rational-quadratic splines, which enhances the flexibility of both coupling and autoregressive transforms while retaining analytic invertibility. We demonstrate that neural spline flows improve density estimation, variational inference, and generative modeling of images.

paragraphs: Normalizing flows represent complicated probability distributions by transforming a simple base distribution through an invertible mapping. Coupling and autoregressive flows support exact density evaluation and sampling, but their flexibility depends on the individual transformations they use. Those transformations must be expressive while still allowing the mapping to be reversed efficiently.

The paper introduces a fully differentiable module built from monotonic rational-quadratic splines. These provide a more flexible choice of elementwise transformation while retaining an analytic inverse. The module can be used with both coupling and autoregressive constructions, so the contribution applies to two established ways of building flow models.

The authors demonstrate improvements in density estimation, variational inference, and image generation. These findings connect the choice of transformation inside a flow to its usefulness across several modeling tasks. The approach matters because increased expressiveness comes while preserving analytic invertibility, a property central to the flow construction. It changes a building block of the model while keeping the exact density and sampling capabilities that motivate these architectures.
summary.tldr: Monotonic rational-quadratic splines make normalizing flows more flexible while preserving analytic invertibility.

title: Neural Spline Flows

abstract: Consider a player that in each of T rounds chooses one of K arms. An adversary chooses the cost of each arm in a bounded interval, and a sequence of feedback delays \left{ d_{t}\right} that are unknown to the player. After picking arm a_{t} at round t, the player receives the cost of playing this arm d_{t} rounds later. In cases where t+d_{t}>T, this feedback is simply missing. We prove that the EXP3 algorithm (that uses the delayed feedback upon its arrival) achieves a regret of O\left(\sqrt{\ln K\left(KT+\sum_{t=1}^{T}d_{t}\right)}\right). For the case where \sum_{t=1}^{T}d_{t} and T are unknown, we propose a novel doubling trick for online learning with delays and prove that this adaptive EXP3 achieves a regret of O\left(\sqrt{\ln K\left(K^{2}T+\sum_{t=1}^{T}d_{t}\right)}\right). We then consider a two player zero-sum game where players experience asynchronous delays. We show that even when the delays are large enough such that players no longer enjoy the “no-regret property”, (e.g., where d_{t}=O\left(t\log t\right)) the ergodic average of the strategy profile still converges to the set of Nash equilibria of the game. The result is made possible by choosing an adaptive step size \eta_{t} that is not summable but is square summable, and proving a “weighted regret bound” for this general case.
originalAbstract: Consider a player that in each of T rounds chooses one of K arms. An adversary chooses the cost of each arm in a bounded interval, and a sequence of feedback delays \left{ d_{t}\right} that are unknown to the player. After picking arm a_{t} at round t, the player receives the cost of playing this arm d_{t} rounds later. In cases where t+d_{t}>T, this feedback is simply missing. We prove that the EXP3 algorithm (that uses the delayed feedback upon its arrival) achieves a regret of O\left(\sqrt{\ln K\left(KT+\sum_{t=1}^{T}d_{t}\right)}\right). For the case where \sum_{t=1}^{T}d_{t} and T are unknown, we propose a novel doubling trick for online learning with delays and prove that this adaptive EXP3 achieves a regret of O\left(\sqrt{\ln K\left(K^{2}T+\sum_{t=1}^{T}d_{t}\right)}\right). We then consider a two player zero-sum game where players experience asynchronous delays. We show that even when the delays are large enough such that players no longer enjoy the “no-regret property”, (e.g., where d_{t}=O\left(t\log t\right)) the ergodic average of the strategy profile still converges to the set of Nash equilibria of the game. The result is made possible by choosing an adaptive step size \eta_{t} that is not summable but is square summable, and proving a “weighted regret bound” for this general case.

paragraphs: The paper studies adversarial bandits where feedback arrives after unknown delays. In each round, the learner chooses one of K actions and eventually observes only that action's cost. Costs and delays are adversarially chosen, and feedback scheduled beyond the T-round horizon is missing.

Using delayed observations when they arrive, EXP3 achieves regret O(sqrt(ln K times (KT plus the sum of delays))). When both the horizon and total delay are unknown, a new doubling procedure makes the method adaptive, with a bound that replaces KT by K squared times T. The results explicitly quantify how accumulated delay enters learning performance.

The authors also analyze two-player zero-sum games with asynchronous feedback. Even in some delay regimes where ordinary no-regret behavior is lost, the ergodic average of strategies still converges to the Nash equilibrium set. This result uses a weighted regret bound and adaptive step sizes whose sum diverges while the sum of their squares converges.
summary.tldr: Delayed-feedback EXP3 admits explicit regret bounds, while weighted analysis also establishes equilibrium convergence in some severe-delay game settings.

title: Online EXP3 Learning in Adversarial Bandits with Delayed Feedback

abstract: In this work we address the challenging problem of multiview 3D surface reconstruction. We introduce a neural network architecture that simultaneously learns the unknown geometry, camera parameters, and a neural renderer that approximates the light reflected from the surface towards the camera. The geometry is represented as a zero level-set of a neural network, while the neural renderer, derived from the rendering equation, is capable of (implicitly) modeling a wide set of lighting conditions and materials. We trained our network on real world 2D images of objects with different material properties, lighting conditions, and noisy camera initializations from the DTU MVS dataset. We found our model to produce state of the art 3D surface reconstructions with high fidelity, resolution and detail.

paragraphs: Reconstructing a 3D surface from multiple images requires accounting for both object shape and how the object appears under lighting. This paper introduces an architecture that jointly learns the unknown geometry, camera parameters, and a neural renderer. The renderer approximates light reflected from the surface toward the camera.

The surface is represented as the zero level-set of a neural network: the locations where its output equals zero define the geometry. A separate rendering component is derived from the rendering equation and can implicitly represent a broad range of materials and lighting conditions. This gives geometry and appearance distinct roles within the jointly trained architecture.

The authors train on real object images from the DTU MVS dataset, covering different materials, lighting conditions, and noisy initial camera estimates. They report state-of-the-art surface reconstructions with high fidelity, resolution, and detail. These findings support the joint treatment of geometry, camera estimation, and appearance modeling for the varied image conditions included in the evaluation.
summary.tldr: A neural architecture jointly learns surface geometry, camera parameters, and appearance to reconstruct detailed 3D objects from multiple images.

title: Multiview Neural Surface Reconstruction by Disentangling Geometry and Appearance

abstract: Signed networks are graphs where edges are annotated with a positive or negative sign, indicating whether an edge interaction is friendly or antagonistic. Signed networks can be used to study a variety of social phenomena, such as mining polarized discussions in social media, or modeling relations of trust and distrust in online review platforms. In this paper we study the problem of detecting $k$ conflicting groups in a signed network. Our premise is that each group is positively connected internally and negatively connected with the other $k-1$ groups. An important aspect of our formulation is that we are not searching for a complete partition of the signed network, instead, we allow other nodes to be neutral with respect to the conflict structure we are searching. As a result, the problem we tackle differs from previously studied problems, such as correlation clustering and $k$-way partitioning. To solve the conflicting-group discovery problem, we derive a novel formulation in which each conflicting group is naturally characterized by the solution to the maximum discrete Rayleigh's quotient (\maxdrq) problem. We present two spectral methods for finding approximate solutions to the \maxdrq problem, which we analyze theoretically. Our experimental evaluation shows that, compared to state-of-the-art baselines, our methods find solutions of higher quality, are faster, and recover ground truth conflicting groups with higher accuracy.

paragraphs: A signed network records whether relationships are friendly or antagonistic. The paper searches for several groups whose members connect positively within each group and negatively across groups. This captures a particular form of conflict, such as opposing communities in a discussion or patterns of trust and distrust.

A central modeling choice is to let some nodes remain neutral. The algorithm does not have to assign everyone to a conflicting camp, which distinguishes the problem from methods that partition an entire network. To express the desired structure mathematically, the authors formulate each group's discovery through a maximum discrete Rayleigh quotient problem and develop two spectral methods that approximately solve it.

The paper provides theoretical analysis of these approximation methods and evaluates them experimentally. In the reported comparisons, they find higher-quality solutions, run faster, and recover known conflicting groups more accurately than the tested state-of-the-art baselines. The formulation matters because it searches for conflict within a network without assuming that conflict explains every node's relationships.
summary.tldr: Two spectral methods identify mutually antagonistic groups in signed networks while allowing unrelated nodes to remain neutral.

title: Discovering conflicting groups in signed networks

abstract: It is a truth universally acknowledged that an observed association without known mechanism must be in want of a causal estimate. Causal estimates from observational data will be biased in the presence of ‘unobserved confounding’. However, we might hope that the influence of unobserved confounders is weak relative to a ‘large’ estimated effect. The purpose of this paper is to develop Austen plots, a sensitivity analysis tool to aid such judgments by making it easier to reason about potential bias induced by unobserved confounding. We formalize confounding strength in terms of how strongly the unobserved confounding influences treatment assignment and outcome. For a target level of bias, an Austen plot shows the minimum values of treatment and outcome influence required to induce that level of bias. Austen plots generalize the classic sensitivity analysis approach of Imbens [Imb03]. Critically, Austen plots allow any approach for modeling the observed data. We illustrate the tool by assessing biases for several real causal inference problems, using a variety of machine learning approaches for the initial data analysis. Code, demo data, and a tutorial are available at github.com/anishazaveri/austen_plots.

paragraphs: An estimated effect from observational data can be biased by unmeasured factors that influence both treatment assignment and outcomes. A large estimated effect alone does not reveal how vulnerable it is to such confounding. This paper introduces Austen plots to make that vulnerability easier to reason about after an initial analysis.

The method describes confounding strength along two dimensions: influence on treatment assignment and influence on the outcome. For a chosen amount of bias, the plot shows the minimum treatment and outcome influences needed to produce it. This turns an abstract concern about missing variables into a concrete sensitivity question about the strength of their possible effects.

Austen plots generalize an established sensitivity-analysis approach while allowing any method for modeling the observed data. The authors demonstrate them on several real causal-inference problems using different machine learning methods for the initial analysis. Their role is to help assess how much unobserved confounding would be required to alter a conclusion, rather than to establish that such confounding is absent.
summary.tldr: Austen plots show how strongly unobserved confounding would need to affect treatment and outcomes to induce a chosen level of bias.

title: Sense and Sensitivity Analysis: Simple Post-Hoc Analysis of Bias Due to Unobserved Confounding

abstract: In this paper, we study k-means++ and k-means||, the two most popular algorithms for the classic k-means clustering problem. We provide novel analyses and show improved approximation and bi-criteria approximation guarantees for k-means++ and k-means||. Our results give a better theoretical justification for why these algorithms perform extremely well in practice.
originalAbstract: In this paper, we study k-means++ and k-means||, the two most popular algorithms for the classic k-means clustering problem. We provide novel analyses and show improved approximation and bi-criteria approximation guarantees for k-means++ and k-means||. Our results give a better theoretical justification for why these algorithms perform extremely well in practice.

paragraphs: This paper revisits the theoretical understanding of k-means++ and its parallel counterpart, k-means||. Both are popular algorithms for the classic k-means clustering problem. The contribution consists of new analyses of these existing algorithms, with the aim of explaining more convincingly why they work so well in practice.

The authors improve approximation guarantees, which characterize how an algorithm's solution quality compares with the ideal clustering objective. They also improve bicriteria approximation guarantees, which assess quality while permitting a relaxation of another part of the clustering requirement. Considering both forms provides more than one way to describe the algorithms' theoretical behavior.

These results strengthen the mathematical justification for widely used methods. Their significance lies in obtaining better guarantees for algorithms already valued for practical performance, bringing the analysis closer to that practical experience. The stated finding is an improvement in what can be proved about k-means++ and k-means||, rather than a claim that the analysis itself changes how those algorithms execute.
summary.tldr: New analyses strengthen approximation and bicriteria guarantees for k-means++ and k-means||.

title: Improved Guarantees for k-means++ and k-means++ Parallel

abstract: Self-supervised learning methods have witnessed a recent surge of interest after proving successful in multiple application fields. In this work, we leverage these techniques, and we propose 3D versions for five different self-supervised methods, in the form of proxy tasks. Our methods facilitate neural network feature learning from unlabeled 3D images, aiming to reduce the required cost for expert annotation. The developed algorithms are 3D Contrastive Predictive Coding, 3D Rotation prediction, 3D Jigsaw puzzles, Relative 3D patch location, and 3D Exemplar networks. Our experiments show that pretraining models with our 3D tasks yields more powerful semantic representations, and enables solving downstream tasks more accurately and efficiently, compared to training the models from scratch and to pretraining them on 2D slices. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our methods on three downstream tasks from the medical imaging domain: i) Brain Tumor Segmentation from 3D MRI, ii) Pancreas Tumor Segmentation from 3D CT, and iii) Diabetic Retinopathy Detection from 2D Fundus images. In each task, we assess the gains in data-efficiency, performance, and speed of convergence. Interestingly, we also find gains when transferring the learned representations, by our methods, from a large unlabeled 3D corpus to a small downstream-specific dataset. We achieve results competitive to state-of-the-art solutions at a fraction of the computational expense. We publish our implementations for the developed algorithms (both 3D and 2D versions) as an open-source library, in an effort to allow other researchers to apply and extend our methods on their datasets.

paragraphs: This paper studies how medical imaging models can learn useful features from unlabeled three-dimensional images before training on a specific task. The motivation is to reduce dependence on costly expert annotations. The authors develop 3D versions of five self-supervised tasks: contrastive predictive coding, rotation prediction, jigsaw puzzles, relative patch location, and exemplar learning.

These proxy tasks provide training signals from the images themselves. The resulting pretrained representations are evaluated on brain tumor segmentation from MRI, pancreas tumor segmentation from CT, and diabetic retinopathy detection from fundus images. This includes testing whether features learned from 3D data can help a task involving 2D images.

In the reported experiments, 3D pretraining improves accuracy and efficiency compared with training from scratch or pretraining on 2D slices. The authors also observe benefits when transferring from a large unlabeled 3D collection to a small task-specific dataset. Their results are competitive with leading solutions at substantially lower computational expense, and they release implementations to support further use.
summary.tldr: Five 3D self-supervised pretraining methods improve medical imaging performance and efficiency in the reported experiments.

title: 3D Self-Supervised Methods for Medical Imaging

abstract: Unlike normal-form games, where correlated equilibria have been studied for more than 45 years, extensive-form correlation is still generally not well understood. Part of the reason for this gap is that the sequential nature of extensive-form games allows for a richness of behaviors and incentives that are not possible in normal-form settings. This richness translates to a significantly different complexity landscape surrounding extensive-form correlated equilibria. As of today, it is known that finding an optimal extensive-form correlated equilibrium (EFCE), extensive-form coarse correlated equilibrium (EFCCE), or normal-form coarse correlated equilibrium (NFCCE) in a two-player extensive-form game is computationally tractable when the game does not include chance moves, and intractable when the game involves chance moves. In this paper we significantly refine this complexity threshold by showing that, in two-player games, an optimal correlated equilibrium can be computed in polynomial time, provided that a certain condition is satisfied. We show that the condition holds, for example, when all chance moves are public, that is, both players observe all chance moves. This implies that an optimal EFCE, EFCCE and NFCCE can be computed in polynomial time in the game size in two-player games with public chance moves.

paragraphs: Sequential games allow patterns of information and incentives that do not arise in a single simultaneous choice. This makes computing correlated equilibria more complicated. The prior complexity boundary described in the paper distinguishes two-player games without chance moves, where optimal solutions are tractable, from games with chance moves, where the general problem is intractable.

The authors refine that boundary by identifying a condition under which an optimal correlated equilibrium can still be computed in polynomial time. They show that the condition holds when every chance move is public, meaning both players observe its outcome. Public chance therefore supplies a concrete class of games for which random events need not destroy computational tractability.

The result covers extensive-form correlated equilibrium, extensive-form coarse correlated equilibrium, and normal-form coarse correlated equilibrium. For two-player games with public chance moves, an optimal solution of each type can be computed in time polynomial in game size. The contribution replaces a broad distinction based on the presence of chance with a more precise sufficient condition that accounts for what players observe.
summary.tldr: Optimal correlated equilibria of three types are polynomial-time computable in two-player sequential games with public chance moves.

title: Polynomial-Time Computation of Optimal Correlated Equilibria in Two-Player Extensive-Form Games with Public Chance Moves and Beyond

abstract: Effectively modeling phenomena present in highly nonlinear dynamical systems whilst also accurately quantifying uncertainty is a challenging task, which often requires problem-specific techniques. We present a novel, domain-agnostic approach to tackling this problem, using compositions of physics-informed random features, derived from ordinary differential equations. The architecture of our model leverages recent advances in approximate inference for deep Gaussian processes, such as layer-wise weight-space approximations which allow us to incorporate random Fourier features, and stochastic variational inference for approximate Bayesian inference. We provide evidence that our model is capable of capturing highly nonlinear behaviour in real-world multivariate time series data. In addition, we find that our approach achieves comparable performance to a number of other probabilistic models on benchmark regression tasks.

paragraphs: Highly nonlinear dynamical systems are difficult to model because their behavior can be complex and predictions also need meaningful uncertainty estimates. Methods often depend on techniques tailored to a particular problem. This paper proposes a domain-agnostic approach that combines building blocks derived from ordinary differential equations.

Those building blocks are physics-informed random features, composed to form the model. The architecture uses approximate inference methods developed for deep Gaussian processes. In particular, layer-wise approximations expressed through weights allow random Fourier features to be incorporated, while stochastic variational inference supplies approximate Bayesian inference. Together, these components support a compositional probabilistic model for nonlinear behavior.

Experiments provide evidence that the approach can capture strong nonlinear patterns in real-world time series containing multiple variables. On benchmark regression tasks, it performs comparably to several other probabilistic models. The findings support the usefulness of combining differential-equation-derived features with probabilistic inference, including beyond the dynamical-system examples, without claiming uniformly superior predictive performance.
summary.tldr: Composed features derived from differential equations enable probabilistic modeling of nonlinear dynamics, with supporting time-series and regression results.

title: Compositional Modeling of Nonlinear Dynamical Systems with ODE-based Random Features

abstract: This work presents several expected generalization error bounds based on the Wasserstein distance. More specifically, it introduces full-dataset, single-letter, and random-subset bounds, and their analogous in the randomized subsample setting from Steinke and Zakynthinou [1]. Moreover, when the loss function is bounded and the geometry of the space is ignored by the choice of the metric in the Wasserstein distance, these bounds recover from below (and thus, are tighter than) current bounds based on the relative entropy. In particular, they generate new, non-vacuous bounds based on the relative entropy. Therefore, these results can be seen as a bridge between works that account for the geometry of the hypothesis space and those based on the relative entropy, which is agnostic to such geometry. Furthermore, it is shown how to produce various new bounds based on different information measures (e.g., the lautum information or several $f$-divergences) based on these bounds and how to derive similar bounds with respect to the backward channel using the presented proof techniques.

paragraphs: Generalization bounds describe the expected gap between a model’s performance on its training data and on new data. This paper develops bounds using Wasserstein distance, which can incorporate the geometry of the hypothesis space. It provides full-dataset, single-letter, and random-subset versions, together with counterparts for a randomized subsample setting.

The authors connect these bounds to existing approaches based on relative entropy. When the loss is bounded and the chosen Wasserstein metric ignores geometry, the new bounds recover those earlier bounds from below, making them tighter in that setting. The results also yield new relative-entropy bounds that are non-vacuous, meaning they provide informative control.

This establishes a bridge between geometric analyses and information-theoretic analyses that do not use geometry. The paper further derives bounds involving other information measures, including lautum information and several f-divergences. Its proof techniques also produce analogous bounds for the backward channel. The contribution is therefore a family of related guarantees, with the tighter comparison to relative entropy tied to the stated bounded-loss and metric conditions.
summary.tldr: Wasserstein-based generalization bounds connect geometric and information-theoretic analyses and tighten relative-entropy bounds under stated conditions.

title: Tighter Expected Generalization Error Bounds via Wasserstein Distance

abstract: Models for audio generation are typically trained on hours of recordings. Here, we illustrate that capturing the essence of an audio source is typically possible from as little as a few tens of seconds from a single training signal. Specifically, we present a GAN-based generative model that can be trained on one short audio signal from any domain (e.g. speech, music, etc.) and does not require pre-training or any other form of external supervision. Once trained, our model can generate random samples of arbitrary duration that maintain semantic similarity to the training waveform, yet exhibit new compositions of its audio primitives. This enables a long line of interesting applications, including generating new jazz improvisations or new a-cappella rap variants based on a single short example, producing coherent modifications to famous songs (e.g. adding a new verse to a Beatles song based solely on the original recording), filling-in of missing parts (inpainting), extending the bandwidth of a speech signal (super-resolution), and enhancing old recordings without access to any clean training example. We show that in all cases, no more than 20 seconds of training audio commonly suffice for our model to achieve state-of-the-art results. This is despite its complete lack of prior knowledge about the nature of audio signals in general.

paragraphs: This paper investigates how much audio is needed to learn a generative model of a particular sound source. Its GAN-based approach trains on a single short recording, without pretraining or external supervision. The intended scope includes different audio domains, such as speech and music, rather than a model trained beforehand for one specific kind of recording.

After training, the model can produce random audio of arbitrary duration. The generated signal remains semantically similar to the example while arranging its audio primitives into new compositions. The distinction matters: learning from one recording is used to support new variations and extensions, rather than merely reproducing the original waveform.

The authors demonstrate applications including musical variation, filling missing audio, extending speech bandwidth, and improving old recordings without clean training examples. Across these applications, they report that no more than 20 seconds of training audio commonly suffice for state-of-the-art results. The qualification is important: the claim is that short examples commonly work in the reported settings, not that every recording provides enough information for every audio task.
summary.tldr: A GAN trained on one short recording generates related audio variations and supports restoration tasks without pretraining or external supervision.

title: Catch-A-Waveform: Learning to Generate Audio from a Single Short Example

abstract: Our main contribution in this work is an empirical finding that random General Value Functions (GVFs), i.e., deep action-conditional predictions---random both in what feature of observations they predict as well as in the sequence of actions the predictions are conditioned upon---form good auxiliary tasks for reinforcement learning (RL) problems. In particular, we show that random deep action-conditional predictions when used as auxiliary tasks yield state representations that produce control performance competitive with state-of-the-art hand-crafted auxiliary tasks like value prediction, pixel control, and CURL in both Atari and DeepMind Lab tasks. In another set of experiments we stop the gradients from the RL part of the network to the state representation learning part of the network and show, perhaps surprisingly, that the auxiliary tasks alone are sufficient to learn state representations good enough to outperform an end-to-end trained actor-critic baseline. We opensourced our code at https://github.com/Hwhitetooth/random_gvfs.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning systems can learn state representations through auxiliary prediction tasks alongside the main control task. This paper investigates whether those auxiliary tasks need careful hand design. It studies random General Value Functions: predictions randomized both in the observation features they target and in the action sequences on which the predictions depend.

The central empirical finding is that these random, deep, action-conditional predictions provide useful training signals. On Atari and DeepMind Lab tasks, representations learned with these auxiliary objectives support control performance competitive with established hand-crafted alternatives, including value prediction, pixel control, and CURL. Random selection of prediction targets and action conditions therefore works well in the evaluated settings.

A second experiment prevents gradients from the reinforcement learning component from updating the state representation. The auxiliary tasks then provide the representation's learning signal on their own. Even under this separation, the resulting system outperforms an end-to-end trained actor-critic baseline. This shows that, in those experiments, random predictive tasks alone can learn representations sufficiently useful for strong control performance.
summary.tldr: Random action-conditional prediction tasks learn useful reinforcement learning representations, competing with designed auxiliaries and sometimes succeeding without control gradients.

title: Learning State Representations from Random Deep Action-conditional Predictions

abstract: Adversarial robustness has received increasing attention along with the study of adversarial examples. So far, existing works show that robust models not only obtain robustness against various adversarial attacks but also boost the performance in some downstream tasks. However, the underlying mechanism of adversarial robustness is still not clear. In this paper, we interpret adversarial robustness from the perspective of linear components, and find that there exist some statistical properties for comprehensively robust models. Specifically, robust models show obvious hierarchical clustering effect on their linearized sub-networks, when removing or replacing all non-linear components (e.g., batch normalization, maximum pooling, or activation layers). Based on these observations, we propose a novel understanding of adversarial robustness and apply it on more tasks including domain adaption and robustness boosting. Experimental evaluations demonstrate the rationality and superiority of our proposed clustering strategy. Our code is available at https://github.com/bymavis/Adv_Weight_NeurIPS2021.
originalAbstract: Adversarial robustness has received increasing attention along with the study of adversarial examples. So far, existing works show that robust models not only obtain robustness against various adversarial attacks but also boost the performance in some downstream tasks. However, the underlying mechanism of adversarial robustness is still not clear. In this paper, we interpret adversarial robustness from the perspective of linear components, and find that there exist some statistical properties for comprehensively robust models. Specifically, robust models show obvious hierarchical clustering effect on their linearized sub-networks, when removing or replacing all non-linear components (e.g., batch normalization, maximum pooling, or activation layers). Based on these observations, we propose a novel understanding of adversarial robustness and apply it on more tasks including domain adaption and robustness boosting. Experimental evaluations demonstrate the rationality and superiority of our proposed clustering strategy. Our code is available at https://github.com/bymavis/Adv_Weight_NeurIPS2021.

paragraphs: Models trained for adversarial robustness can also improve performance on some downstream tasks, but the mechanism behind these benefits remains unclear. This paper investigates robustness by examining the linear components of neural networks. The aim is to identify statistical structure associated with robust models that may be obscured by the full network's nonlinear operations.

The authors remove or replace nonlinear components, including batch normalization, maximum pooling, and activation layers, to examine linearized subnetworks. They observe a pronounced hierarchical clustering effect in comprehensively robust models. This suggests that studying the remaining linear structure provides a useful perspective on robustness, alongside evaluating how the intact model responds to adversarial attacks.

Building on these observations, the authors develop a clustering strategy and apply it to domain adaptation and robustness improvement. Their experiments support the strategy's effectiveness and the interpretation motivating it. The stated contribution combines an observed structural property with practical applications; the abstract presents clustering as a way to understand and exploit robustness, without establishing it as a complete causal explanation.
summary.tldr: Robust models exhibit hierarchical clustering in their linearized subnetworks, motivating a strategy for domain adaptation and robustness improvement.

title: Clustering Effect of Adversarial Robust Models

abstract: Self-supervised learning algorithms, including BERT and SimCLR, have enabled significant strides in fields like natural language processing, computer vision, and speech processing. However, these algorithms are domain-specific, meaning that new self-supervised learning algorithms must be developed for each new setting, including myriad healthcare, scientific, and multimodal domains. To catalyze progress toward domain-agnostic methods, we introduce DABS: a Domain-Agnostic Benchmark for Self-supervised learning. To perform well on DABS, an algorithm is evaluated on seven diverse domains: natural images, multichannel sensor data, English text, speech recordings, multilingual text, chest x-rays, and images with text descriptions. Each domain contains an unlabeled dataset for pretraining; the model is then is scored based on its downstream performance on a set of labeled tasks in the domain. We also present e-Mix and ShED: two baseline domain-agnostic algorithms; their relatively modest performance demonstrates that significant progress is needed before self-supervised learning is an out-of-the-box solution for arbitrary domains. Code for benchmark datasets and baseline algorithms is available at https://github.com/alextamkin/dabs.

paragraphs: Self-supervised learning uses unlabeled data to prepare models for later tasks. Successful approaches have emerged in language, vision, and speech, but the paper describes them as largely tailored to their domains. DABS asks whether methods can work across substantially different kinds of data, reducing the need to design a new algorithm for each setting.

The benchmark spans seven domains: natural images, multichannel sensor readings, English text, speech, multilingual text, chest x-rays, and images paired with descriptions. Each domain supplies unlabeled data for pretraining. Evaluation then measures how well the resulting model performs on labeled tasks within that domain, connecting pretraining to the usefulness of what the model learned.

The authors introduce two domain-agnostic baseline algorithms, e-Mix and ShED. Their comparatively modest results indicate that substantial progress remains before self-supervised learning becomes an out-of-the-box solution for arbitrary domains. By releasing the benchmark and baseline code, the work turns that broad ambition into a collection of concrete, shared evaluation problems.
summary.tldr: DABS evaluates self-supervised learning across seven domains, and its two general-purpose baselines show substantial room for improvement.

title: DABS: a Domain-Agnostic Benchmark for Self-Supervised Learning

abstract: We introduce EventNarrative, a knowledge graph-to-text dataset from publicly available open-world knowledge graphs. Given the recent advances in event-driven Information Extraction (IE), and that prior research on graph-to-text only focused on entity-driven KGs, this paper focuses on event-centric data. However, our data generation system can still be adapted to other types of KG data. Existing large-scale datasets in the graph-to-text area are non-parallel, meaning there is a large disconnect between the KGs and text. The datasets that have a paired KG and text, are small scale and manually generated or generated without a rich ontology, making the corresponding graphs sparse. Furthermore, these datasets contain many unlinked entities between their KG and text pairs. EventNarrative consists of approximately 230,000 graphs and their corresponding natural language text, six times larger than the current largest parallel dataset. It makes use of a rich ontology, all the KGs entities are linked to the text, and our manual annotations confirm a high data quality. Our aim is two-fold: to help break new ground in event-centric research where data is lacking and to give researchers a well-defined, large-scale dataset in order to better evaluate existing and future knowledge graph-to-text models. We also evaluate two types of baselines on EventNarrative: a graph-to-text specific model and two state-of-the-art language models, which previous work has shown to be adaptable to the knowledge graph-to-text domain.

It uses a rich ontology, and every graph entity is linked to the paired text. Manual annotation confirms high data quality, supporting the usefulness of these pairs for evaluation.

The authors evaluate a model designed specifically for graph-to-text generation and two state-of-the-art language models previously shown adaptable to this task. They also explain that the data generation system can be adapted to other graph types. The main contribution is a large, aligned evaluation resource that opens event-centric generation to more systematic study.
summary.tldr: EventNarrative supplies approximately 230,000 aligned event graphs and texts, with linked entities and baseline evaluations for graph-to-text generation.

title: EventNarrative: A Large-scale Event-centric Dataset for Knowledge Graph-to-Text Generation

abstract: We identify label errors in the test sets of 10 of the most commonly-used computer vision, natural language, and audio datasets, and subsequently study the potential for these label errors to affect benchmark results. Errors in test sets are numerous and widespread: we estimate an average of at least 3.3% errors across the 10 datasets, where for example label errors comprise at least 6% of the ImageNet validation set. Putative label errors are identified using confident learning algorithms and then human-validated via crowdsourcing (51% of the algorithmically-flagged candidates are indeed erroneously labeled, on average across the datasets). Traditionally, machine learning practitioners choose which model to deploy based on test accuracy -- our findings advise caution here, proposing that judging models over correctly labeled test sets may be more useful, especially for noisy real-world datasets. Surprisingly, we find that lower capacity models may be practically more useful than higher capacity models in real-world datasets with high proportions of erroneously labeled data. For example, on ImageNet with corrected labels: ResNet-18 outperforms ResNet-50 if the prevalence of originally mislabeled test examples increases by just 6%. On CIFAR-10 with corrected labels: VGG-11 outperforms VGG-19 if the prevalence of originally mislabeled test examples increases by just 5%. Test set errors across the 10 datasets can be viewed at https://labelerrors.com and all label errors can be reproduced by https://github.com/cleanlab/label-errors.

paragraphs: A model's test accuracy depends on the correctness of the labels used to judge it. This paper investigates labeling errors in ten widely used vision, language, and audio test sets. It estimates an average error rate of at least 3.3% across those datasets, including at least 6% in the ImageNet validation set.

The authors use confident learning algorithms to flag suspected errors, then ask crowdsourced human reviewers to validate them. On average, 51% of flagged candidates are confirmed as mislabeled. This distinction matters: an algorithm's suspicion is a starting point for review, rather than automatic evidence that a label is wrong.

The study shows that label corrections and the prevalence of originally mislabeled examples can affect model rankings. On corrected ImageNet labels, ResNet-18 surpasses ResNet-50 when that prevalence increases by 6%; a corresponding 5% increase reverses the VGG-11 versus VGG-19 comparison on CIFAR-10. These conditional findings suggest that smaller models may be more useful in some noisy-data settings and motivate greater care when choosing models from benchmark accuracy.
summary.tldr: Widespread test-label errors can change benchmark conclusions, including which model appears preferable under particular noisy-data conditions.

title: Pervasive Label Errors in Test Sets Destabilize Machine Learning Benchmarks

abstract: Motivated by recent applications requiring differential privacy in the setting of adaptive streams, we investigate the question of optimal instantiations of the matrix mechanism in this setting. We prove fundamental theoretical results on the applicability of matrix factorizations to the adaptive streaming setting, and provide a new parameter-free fixed-point algorithm for computing optimal factorizations. We instantiate this framework with respect to concrete matrices which arise naturally in the machine learning setting, and train user-level differentially private models with the resulting optimal mechanisms, yielding significant improvements on a notable problem in federated learning with user-level differential privacy.

paragraphs: This paper studies differential privacy for adaptive streams, where later computations can depend on earlier results. Its focus is the matrix mechanism and how to instantiate it optimally in that setting. The motivation comes from machine learning applications in which privacy-preserving computations occur throughout an evolving training process.

The authors establish theoretical results showing how matrix factorizations apply to adaptive streaming. They also introduce a parameter-free fixed-point algorithm for finding optimal factorizations. This supplies both a foundation for using the mechanism in an adaptive setting and a computational procedure for choosing its factorization, connecting the privacy framework to an implementable optimization method.

The framework is instantiated for concrete matrices that arise in machine learning. The resulting mechanisms are then used to train models with user-level differential privacy, and the authors report significant improvements on a federated learning problem. The stated empirical finding concerns that application. The broader contribution is a principled method for computing optimal private linear mechanisms and applying them within adaptive learning.
summary.tldr: The paper develops optimal matrix mechanisms for adaptive streams and applies them to improve user-level private federated learning.

title: Improved Differential Privacy for SGD via Optimal Private Linear Operators on Adaptive Streams

abstract: Recent advances in TCP congestion control (CC) have achieved tremendous success with deep reinforcement learning (RL) approaches, which use feedforward neural networks (NN) to learn complex environment conditions and make better decisions. However, such ``black-box'' policies lack interpretability and reliability, and often, they need to operate outside the traditional TCP datapath due to the use of complex NNs. This paper proposes a novel two-stage solution to achieve the best of both worlds: first to train a deep RL agent, then distill its (over-)parameterized NN policy into white-box, light-weight rules in the form of symbolic expressions that are much easier to understand and to implement in constrained environments. At the core of our proposal is a novel symbolic branching algorithm that enables the rule to be aware of the context in terms of various network conditions, eventually converting the NN policy into a symbolic tree. The distilled symbolic rules preserve and often improve performance over state-of-the-art NN policies while being faster and simpler than a standard neural network. We validate the performance of our distilled symbolic rules on both simulation and emulation environments. Our code is available at https://github.com/VITA-Group/SymbolicPCC.

paragraphs: Deep reinforcement learning can learn effective TCP congestion-control policies, but neural policies are difficult to interpret and can be cumbersome to run in constrained networking environments. This paper proposes a two-stage process: first learn a neural policy, then distill its behavior into lightweight symbolic expressions that are easier to understand and implement.

The central technique is symbolic branching. It produces a symbolic tree whose rules account for different network conditions, allowing the distilled controller to respond to context. This gives the symbolic policy a way to express conditional decisions while retaining a simpler representation than the original neural network. The aim is to preserve learned decision quality in a more accessible form.

Evaluations in simulation and emulation show that the symbolic rules preserve, and often improve, performance relative to the compared leading neural policies. They are also faster and simpler than a standard neural network. These findings support symbolic distillation as a practical route from a learned controller to deployable rules, while the stated evidence concerns the tested environments rather than a universal reliability guarantee.
summary.tldr: Symbolic branching distills learned TCP controllers into interpretable rules that preserve or improve tested performance while running faster.

title: Symbolic Distillation for Learned TCP Congestion Control

abstract: Feature attribution for kernel methods is often heuristic and not individualised for each prediction. To address this, we turn to the concept of Shapley values (SV), a coalition game theoretical framework that has previously been applied to different machine learning model interpretation tasks, such as linear models, tree ensembles and deep networks. By analysing SVs from a functional perspective, we propose RKHS-SHAP, an attribution method for kernel machines that can efficiently compute both Interventional and Observational Shapley values using kernel mean embeddings of distributions. We show theoretically that our method is robust with respect to local perturbations - a key yet often overlooked desideratum for consistent model interpretation. Further, we propose Shapley regulariser, applicable to a general empirical risk minimisation framework, allowing learning while controlling the level of specific feature's contributions to the model. We demonstrate that the Shapley regulariser enables learning which is robust to covariate shift of a given feature and fair learning which controls the SVs of sensitive features.

paragraphs: Explaining a kernel model requires identifying how individual features contribute to a particular prediction. Existing attribution methods are often heuristic or insufficiently specific to the prediction being explained. This paper develops RKHS-SHAP using Shapley values, a game-theoretic framework for assigning contributions among participants, here interpreted as input features.

The method analyzes Shapley values as functions and uses kernel mean embeddings to represent distributions. This enables efficient computation of both interventional and observational Shapley values for kernel machines. The authors also establish theoretical robustness to local perturbations, addressing whether small changes produce stable explanations. That property matters because an attribution that changes sharply near a prediction can be difficult to interpret consistently.

The paper further introduces a Shapley regularizer for empirical risk minimization, allowing feature contributions to be controlled during training. The authors demonstrate robustness to covariate shift in a specified feature and fairness-oriented learning that controls sensitive features' Shapley values. Thus, attribution becomes both an explanation tool and a means of shaping model behavior.
summary.tldr: RKHS-SHAP efficiently explains kernel predictions with Shapley values and enables training that controls specified feature contributions.

title: RKHS-SHAP: Shapley Values for Kernel Methods

abstract: Pre-trained vision-language models (e.g., CLIP) have shown promising zero-shot generalization in many downstream tasks with properly designed text prompts. Instead of relying on hand-engineered prompts, recent works learn prompts using the training data from downstream tasks. While effective, training on domain-specific data reduces a model's generalization capability to unseen new domains. In this work, we propose test-time prompt tuning (TPT), a method that can learn adaptive prompts on the fly with a single test sample. TPT optimizes the prompt by minimizing the entropy with confidence selection so that the model has consistent predictions across different augmented views of each test sample. In evaluating generalization to natural distribution shifts, TPT improves the zero-shot top-1 accuracy of CLIP by 3.6\% on average, surpassing previous prompt tuning approaches that require additional task-specific training data. In evaluating cross-dataset generalization with unseen categories, TPTperforms on par with the state-of-the-art approaches that use additional training data.

paragraphs: Pretrained vision-language models can recognize new categories through text prompts, but prompt design affects their performance. Learning prompts from downstream training data can help while also reducing generalization to unfamiliar domains. Test-time prompt tuning addresses this tension by adapting a prompt using a single test example as it arrives.

TPT generates augmented views of that example and optimizes the prompt through entropy minimization with confidence selection. The procedure aims to produce consistent predictions across the different views. Its adaptation signal therefore comes from the current test sample, avoiding a requirement for additional task-specific training data to learn the prompt.

For natural distribution shifts, the authors report an average 3.6% improvement in CLIP's zero-shot top-1 accuracy, exceeding earlier prompt-tuning approaches that use extra task-specific data. On cross-dataset generalization involving unseen categories, TPT performs on par with state-of-the-art approaches that use additional training data. These results show that per-sample prompt adaptation can improve generalization in the evaluated settings without a separate downstream prompt-training dataset.
summary.tldr: TPT adapts prompts from a single test sample, improving CLIP's reported zero-shot performance under natural distribution shifts without task-specific training data.

title: Test-Time Prompt Tuning for Zero-Shot Generalization in Vision-Language Models

abstract: In multi-agent coverage control problems, agents navigate their environment to reach locations that maximize the coverage of some density. In practice, the density is rarely known $\textit{a priori}$, further complicating the original NP-hard problem. Moreover, in many applications, agents cannot visit arbitrary locations due to $\textit{a priori}$ unknown safety constraints. In this paper, we aim to efficiently learn the density to approximately solve the coverage problem while preserving the agents' safety. We first propose a conditionally linear submodular coverage function that facilitates theoretical analysis. Utilizing this structure, we develop MacOpt, a novel algorithm that efficiently trades off the exploration-exploitation dilemma due to partial observability, and show that it achieves sublinear regret. Next, we extend results on single-agent safe exploration to our multi-agent setting and propose SafeMac for safe coverage and exploration. We analyze SafeMac and give first of its kind results: near optimal coverage in finite time while provably guaranteeing safety. We extensively evaluate our algorithms on synthetic and real problems, including a bio-diversity monitoring task under safety constraints, where SafeMac outperforms competing methods.
