paragraphs: Coverage control asks multiple agents to position themselves so that they collectively cover an important spatial density. The problem becomes harder when that density is initially unknown and some locations may be unsafe under constraints that are also unknown. The agents must learn where to go while accounting for both coverage and safety.

The authors introduce a conditionally linear, submodular coverage function that makes theoretical analysis possible. Building on that structure, MacOpt balances exploring the environment with using current knowledge to improve coverage. The paper proves sublinear regret for this algorithm, establishing a long-run guarantee for its handling of partial information.

SafeMac extends the approach by adapting single-agent safe-exploration results to multiple agents. The authors prove finite-time near-optimal coverage together with safety guarantees in their analyzed setting. Evaluations include synthetic and real problems, with a biodiversity-monitoring task involving safety constraints where SafeMac outperforms competing methods. The contribution links learning an unknown coverage objective with safe exploration, rather than assuming either the important locations or the safe regions are already fully known.
summary.tldr: MacOpt and SafeMac learn unknown coverage objectives, with SafeMac providing finite-time near-optimal coverage and safety guarantees in the analyzed setting.

title: Near-Optimal Multi-Agent Learning for Safe Coverage Control

abstract: Transformer architecture has become the fundamental element of the widespread natural language processing~(NLP) models. With the trends of large NLP models, the increasing memory and computation costs hinder their efficient deployment on resource-limited devices. Therefore, transformer quantization attracts wide research interest. Recent work recognizes that structured outliers are the critical bottleneck for quantization performance. However, their proposed methods increase the computation overhead and still leave the outliers there. To fundamentally address this problem, this paper delves into the inherent inducement and importance of the outliers. We discover that $\boldsymbol \gamma$ in LayerNorm (LN) acts as a sinful amplifier for the outliers, and the importance of outliers varies greatly where some outliers provided by a few tokens cover a large area but can be clipped sharply without negative impacts. Motivated by these findings, we propose an outlier suppression framework including two components: Gamma Migration and Token-Wise Clipping. The Gamma Migration migrates the outlier amplifier to subsequent modules in an equivalent transformation, contributing to a more quantization-friendly model without any extra burden. The Token-Wise Clipping takes advantage of the large variance of token range and designs a token-wise coarse-to-fine pipeline, obtaining a clipping range with minimal final quantization loss in an efficient way. This framework effectively suppresses the outliers and can be used in a plug-and-play mode. Extensive experiments prove that our framework surpasses the existing works and, for the first time, pushes the 6-bit post-training BERT quantization to the full-precision (FP) level. Our code is available at https://github.com/wimh966/outlier_suppression.

paragraphs: Low-bit quantization can reduce Transformer memory and computation costs, but unusually large values make accurate quantization difficult. This paper investigates both the origin and importance of these outliers. The authors identify LayerNorm’s gamma parameter as an amplifier and find that some large values associated with a few tokens can be sharply clipped without harming performance.

Their framework combines Gamma Migration with Token-Wise Clipping. Gamma Migration moves the amplifying factor into subsequent modules through an equivalent transformation, producing a more quantization-friendly model without additional overhead. Token-Wise Clipping exploits differences in value ranges across tokens, using a coarse-to-fine procedure to select a clipping range that minimizes final quantization loss efficiently.

The method is designed for plug-and-play use. Extensive experiments show improvements over existing approaches, and the authors report that six-bit post-training quantization of BERT reaches full-precision performance in their evaluation. The significance lies in treating outliers according to their cause and contribution: preserving every extreme value is not always necessary for maintaining model quality, and restructuring the computation can make low-bit representations more effective.
summary.tldr: Gamma Migration and Token-Wise Clipping suppress quantization outliers, bringing six-bit post-training BERT to full-precision performance in the reported evaluation.

title: Outlier Suppression: Pushing the Limit of Low-bit Transformer Language Models

abstract: A major task of sports analytics is player evaluation. Previous methods commonly measured the impact of players' actions on desirable outcomes (e.g., goals or winning) without considering the risk induced by stochastic game dynamics. In this paper, we design an uncertainty-aware Reinforcement Learning (RL) framework to learn a risk-sensitive player evaluation metric from stochastic game dynamics. To embed the risk of a player’s movements into the distribution of action-values, we model their 1) aleatoric uncertainty, which represents the intrinsic stochasticity in a sports game, and 2) epistemic uncertainty, which is due to a model's insufficient knowledge regarding Out-of-Distribution (OoD) samples. We demonstrate how a distributional Bellman operator and a feature-space density model can capture these uncertainties. Based on such uncertainty estimation, we propose a Risk-sensitive Game Impact Metric (RiGIM) that measures players' performance over a season by conditioning on a specific confidence level. Empirical evaluation, based on over 9M play-by-play ice hockey and soccer events, shows that RiGIM correlates highly with standard success measures and has a consistent risk sensitivity.
originalAbstract: A major task of sports analytics is player evaluation. Previous methods commonly measured the impact of players' actions on desirable outcomes (e.g., goals or winning) without considering the risk induced by stochastic game dynamics. In this paper, we design an uncertainty-aware Reinforcement Learning (RL) framework to learn a risk-sensitive player evaluation metric from stochastic game dynamics. To embed the risk of a player’s movements into the distribution of action-values, we model their 1) aleatoric uncertainty, which represents the intrinsic stochasticity in a sports game, and 2) epistemic uncertainty, which is due to a model's insufficient knowledge regarding Out-of-Distribution (OoD) samples. We demonstrate how a distributional Bellman operator and a feature-space density model can capture these uncertainties. Based on such uncertainty estimation, we propose a Risk-sensitive Game Impact Metric (RiGIM) that measures players' performance over a season by conditioning on a specific confidence level. Empirical evaluation, based on over 9M play-by-play ice hockey and soccer events, shows that RiGIM correlates highly with standard success measures and has a consistent risk sensitivity.

paragraphs: Player evaluation often measures how actions contribute to desirable outcomes such as goals or wins. This paper adds explicit consideration of risk from uncertain game dynamics. It develops a reinforcement-learning framework that represents uncertainty in action values and uses that representation to evaluate players over a season.

The framework distinguishes two sources of uncertainty. Aleatoric uncertainty reflects randomness intrinsic to the game, while epistemic uncertainty reflects the model's limited knowledge about out-of-distribution examples. A distributional Bellman operator and a feature-space density model capture these sources. The resulting Risk-sensitive Game Impact Metric, or RiGIM, conditions player evaluation on a specified confidence level.

The authors evaluate RiGIM using more than nine million play-by-play events from ice hockey and soccer. They report strong correlation with standard success measures together with consistent risk sensitivity. These findings suggest that the metric retains a connection to familiar measures of sporting success while incorporating how uncertain an action's assessed impact is, rather than reporting only its estimated contribution.
summary.tldr: RiGIM evaluates sports players using action-value uncertainty and a chosen confidence level, showing strong success correlations and consistent risk sensitivity.

title: Uncertainty-Aware Reinforcement Learning for Risk-Sensitive Player Evaluation in Sports Game

abstract: Most existing benchmarks for grounding language in interactive environments either lack realistic linguistic elements, or prove difficult to scale up due to substantial human involvement in the collection of data or feedback signals. We develop WebShop – a simulated e-commerce website environment with 1.18 million real-world products and 12,087 crowd-sourced text instructions. In this environment, an agent needs to navigate multiple types of webpages and issue diverse actions to find, customize, and purchase a product given an instruction. WebShop provides several challenges including understanding compositional instructions, query (re-)formulation, dealing with noisy text in webpages, and performing strategic exploration. We collect over 1,600 human trajectories to first validate the benchmark, then train and evaluate a diverse range of agents using reinforcement learning, imitation learning, and pre-trained image and language models. Our best model achieves a task success rate of 29%, which significantly outperforms rule heuristics but is far lower than expert human performance (59%). We also analyze agent and human trajectories and ablate various model components to provide insights for developing future agents with stronger language understanding and decision making abilities. Finally, we show our agent trained on WebShop exhibits non-trivial sim-to-real transfer when evaluated on amazon.com and ebay.com, indicating the potential value of our benchmark for developing practical web agents that can operate in the wild.

title: WebShop: Towards Scalable Real-World Web Interaction with Grounded Language Agents

abstract: Augmenting algorithms with learned predictions is a promising approach for going beyond worst-case bounds. Dinitz, Im, Lavastida, Moseley, and Vassilvitskii~(2021) have demonstrated that warm-starts with learned dual solutions can improve the time complexity of the Hungarian method for weighted perfect bipartite matching. We extend and improve their framework in a principled manner via \textit{discrete convex analysis} (DCA), a discrete analog of convex analysis. We show the usefulness of our DCA-based framework by applying it to weighted perfect bipartite matching, weighted matroid intersection, and discrete energy minimization for computer vision. Our DCA-based framework yields time complexity bounds that depend on the $\ell_\infty$-distance from a predicted solution to an optimal solution, which has two advantages relative to the previous $\ell_1$-distance-dependent bounds: time complexity bounds are smaller, and learning of predictions is more sample efficient. We also discuss whether to learn primal or dual solutions from the DCA perspective.

paragraphs: A learned prediction can give an optimization algorithm a useful starting point, potentially reducing the work needed to reach an optimal solution. Earlier work demonstrated this idea for weighted perfect bipartite matching using predicted dual solutions. This paper develops a broader framework for such warm starts through discrete convex analysis.

Discrete convex analysis supplies a counterpart to convex analysis for discrete optimization problems. The authors apply their framework to weighted perfect bipartite matching, weighted matroid intersection, and discrete energy minimization in computer vision. These applications show how the same mathematical perspective can guide prediction-assisted algorithms across several problem types.

The resulting runtime bounds depend on the largest coordinate error between the predicted and optimal solutions, expressed through the infinity norm. Earlier bounds depended on the sum of coordinate errors through the one norm. The paper establishes smaller time-complexity bounds and more sample-efficient prediction learning with its approach. It also uses this perspective to discuss whether learning primal or dual solutions is preferable.
summary.tldr: Discrete convex analysis yields prediction-based warm starts with improved runtime bounds and more sample-efficient learning.

title: Discrete-Convex-Analysis-Based Framework for Warm-Starting Algorithms with Predictions

abstract: While existing automatic differentiation (AD) frameworks allow flexibly composing model architectures, they do not provide the same flexibility for composing learning algorithms---everything has to be implemented in terms of back propagation. To address this gap, we invent Automatic Propagation (AP) software, which generalizes AD, and allows custom and composable construction of complex learning algorithms. The framework allows packaging custom learning algorithms into propagators that automatically implement the necessary computations, and can be reused across different computation graphs. We implement Proppo, a prototype AP software package built on top of the Pytorch AD framework. To demonstrate the utility of Proppo, we use it to implement Monte Carlo gradient estimation techniques, such as reparameterization and likelihood ratio gradients, as well as the total propagation algorithm and Gaussian shaping gradients, which were previously used in model-based reinforcement learning, but do not have any publicly available implementation. Finally, in minimalistic experiments, we show that these methods allow increasing the gradient accuracy by orders of magnitude, particularly when the machine learning system is at the edge of chaos.

paragraphs: Automatic differentiation makes it easy to combine model components, but the paper argues that learning algorithms remain constrained by having to express everything through backpropagation. The authors introduce Automatic Propagation to extend that flexibility to the learning procedure itself. Custom algorithms are packaged as propagators that perform their required computations and can be reused across computation graphs.

The authors demonstrate it with Monte Carlo gradient estimators, including reparameterization and likelihood-ratio gradients. They also implement total propagation and Gaussian shaping gradients, techniques previously used in model-based reinforcement learning that lacked publicly available implementations.

Minimal experiments show that these methods can improve gradient accuracy by orders of magnitude, particularly near the edge of chaos. The result is tied to those experimental settings. More broadly, the software contribution is a way to make specialized learning computations reusable and composable, giving algorithm designers a framework that extends beyond conventional automatic differentiation.
summary.tldr: Proppo generalizes automatic differentiation into reusable propagators for composing learning algorithms, demonstrated with specialized gradient estimators.

title: Proppo: a Message Passing Framework for Customizable and Composable Learning Algorithms

abstract: In this paper, we propose a new method for knowledge base completion (KBC): instance-based learning (IBL). For example, to answer (Jill Biden, lived city,? ), instead of going directly to Washington D.C., our goal is to find Joe Biden, who has the same lived city as Jill Biden. Through prototype entities, IBL provides interpretability. We develop theories for modeling prototypes and combining IBL with translational models. Experiments on various tasks confirmed the IBL model's effectiveness and interpretability.In addition, IBL shed light on the mechanism of rule-based KBC models. Previous research has generally agreed that rule-based models provide rules with semantically compatible premise and hypothesis. We challenge this view. We begin by demonstrating that some logical rules represent {\it instance-based equivalence} (i.e. prototypes) rather than semantic compatibility. These are denoted as {\it IBL rules}. Surprisingly, despite occupying only a small portion of the rule space, IBL rules outperform non-IBL rules in all four benchmarks. %KBC can be achieved using only IBL rules in two benchmarks without sacrificing effectiveness. We use a variety of experiments to demonstrate that rule-based models work because they have the ability to represent instance-based equivalence via IBL rules. The findings provide new insights of how rule-based models work and how to interpret their rules.

paragraphs: Knowledge base completion fills missing relationships between entities. This paper proposes doing so through prototype entities: to infer an entity's missing relationship, find another entity that shares the relevant relationship. The prototype supplies an interpretable intermediate connection, making the prediction explainable through a concrete instance.

The authors develop theory for modeling these prototypes and for combining instance-based learning with translational models. Experiments across several tasks support the resulting model's effectiveness and interpretability. The contribution therefore includes both a prediction method and a way to express why a particular entity is useful evidence for a missing fact.

The paper also reexamines how rule-based completion methods work. Some rules, it argues, express instance-based equivalence rather than a semantically compatible link between premise and conclusion. Although these instance-based rules occupy only a small part of the rule space, they outperform the remaining rules on all four studied benchmarks. Additional experiments support their role in rule-based models' effectiveness, suggesting that interpreting rules requires attention to the prototype relationships they encode.
summary.tldr: Prototype-based reasoning improves interpretable knowledge base completion and offers evidence that instance equivalence helps explain the success of rule-based models.

title: Instance-based Learning for Knowledge Base Completion

abstract: The binding problem is one of the fundamental challenges that prevent the artificial neural network (ANNs) from a compositional understanding of the world like human perception, because disentangled and distributed representations of generative factors can interfere and lead to ambiguity when complex data with multiple objects are presented. In this paper, we propose a brain-inspired unsupervised hybrid neural network (HNN) that introduces temporal binding theory originated from neuroscience into ANNs by integrating spike timing dynamics (via spiking neural networks, SNNs) with reconstructive attention (by ANNs). Spike timing provides an additional dimension for grouping, while reconstructive feedback coordinates the spikes into temporal coherent states. Through iterative interaction of ANN and SNN, the model continuously binds multiple objects at alternative synchronous firing times in the SNN coding space. The effectiveness of the model is evaluated on five artificially generated datasets of binary images. By visualization and analysis, we demonstrate that the binding is explainable, soft, flexible, and hierarchical. Notably, the model is trained on single object datasets without explicit supervision on grouping, but can successfully bind multiple objects on test datasets, showing its compositional generalization capability. Further results show its binding ability in dynamic situations.

paragraphs: When several objects appear together, distributed representations can mix their attributes and make it unclear which features belong to which object. This is the binding problem. The paper proposes an unsupervised hybrid network that combines an artificial neural network with a spiking neural network to organize object information through time.

Spike timing supplies an extra dimension for grouping features. Reconstructive attention from the artificial neural network feeds back into the spiking system, coordinating activity into temporally coherent groups. Through repeated interaction, different objects become associated with different synchronous firing times. The approach uses this timing structure to separate objects within the shared coding space.

The model is evaluated on five artificially generated binary-image datasets. Although trained on single-object data without explicit grouping supervision, it successfully binds multiple objects at test time, demonstrating compositional generalization in these settings. Visualizations and analyses characterize the binding as explainable, soft, flexible, and hierarchical, and further results show binding in dynamic situations. The findings support temporal coordination as a useful mechanism for learned object grouping.
summary.tldr: A hybrid spiking and artificial neural network learns temporal object grouping from single-object training data and generalizes to multiple objects in synthetic images.

title: Dance of SNN and ANN: Solving binding problem by combining spike timing and reconstructive attention

abstract: Self-supervised learning allows AI systems to learn effective representations from large amounts of data using tasks that do not require costly labeling. Mode collapse, i.e., the model producing identical representations for all inputs, is a central problem to many self-supervised learning approaches, making self-supervised tasks, such as matching distorted variants of the inputs, ineffective. In this article, we argue that a straightforward application of information maximization among alternative latent representations of the same input naturally solves the collapse problem and achieves competitive empirical results. We propose a self-supervised learning method, CorInfoMax, that uses a second-order statistics-based mutual information measure that reflects the level of correlation among its arguments. Maximizing this correlative information measure between alternative representations of the same input serves two purposes: (1) it avoids the collapse problem by generating feature vectors with non-degenerate covariances; (2) it establishes relevance among alternative representations by increasing the linear dependence among them. An approximation of the proposed information maximization objective simplifies to a Euclidean distance-based objective function regularized by the log-determinant of the feature covariance matrix. The regularization term acts as a natural barrier against feature space degeneracy. Consequently, beyond avoiding complete output collapse to a single point, the proposed approach also prevents dimensional collapse by encouraging the spread of information across the whole feature space. Numerical experiments demonstrate that CorInfoMax achieves better or competitive performance results relative to the state-of-the-art SSL approaches.

CorInfoMax addresses this collapse problem through information maximization between alternative representations of an input, aiming to preserve both their agreement and their informational diversity.

Numerical experiments report performance that is better than or competitive with state-of-the-art self-supervised approaches, supporting the proposed information-maximization criterion as a practical training method.
summary.tldr: CorInfoMax matches alternative representations while using covariance-based information maximization to prevent complete and dimensional collapse.

title: Self-Supervised Learning with an Information Maximization Criterion

abstract: The input to the {line-sets $k$-median} problem is an integer $k \geq 1$, and a set $\mathcal{L} = \{L_1,\dots,L_n\}$that contains $n$ sets of lines in $\mathbb{R}^d$. The goal is to compute a set $C$ of $k$ centers (points in $\mathbb{R}^d$) that minimizes the sum $\sum_{L \in \mathcal{L}}\min_{\ell\in L, c\in C}\mathrm{dist}(\ell,c)$ of Euclidean distances from each set to its closest center, where $\mathrm{dist}(\ell,c):=\min_{x\in \ell}\norm{x-c}_2$.An \emph{$\varepsilon$-coreset} for this problem is a weighted subset of sets in $\mathcal{L}$ that approximates this sum up to $1 \pm \varepsilon$ multiplicative factor, for every set $C$ of $k$ centers. We prove that \emph{every} such input set $\set{L}$ has a small $\varepsilon$-coreset, and provide the first coreset construction for this problem and its variants. The coreset consists of $O(\log^2n)$ weighted line-sets from $\set{L}$, and is constructed in $O(n\log n)$ time for every fixed $d, k\geq 1$ and $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$. The main technique is based on a novel reduction to a ``fair clustering'' of colored points to colored centers. We then provide a coreset for this coloring problem, which may be of independent interest. Open source code and experiments are also provided.

paragraphs: The paper studies a clustering problem whose inputs are sets of lines rather than individual points. The task is to choose k point centers. Each input set contributes the smallest distance between any of its lines and any center, and the objective is to minimize the sum of those contributions.

The authors construct a coreset: a small weighted selection of the original line sets that approximately preserves this objective. The guarantee applies to every possible choice of k centers, with multiplicative error controlled by epsilon. This means the summary represents the clustering objective across candidate solutions, rather than only approximating one selected solution.

For fixed dimension, number of centers, and accuracy parameter, every input has a coreset containing O(log² n) weighted line sets, constructible in O(n log n) time. The main technique reduces the problem to fair clustering involving colored points and colored centers. The paper also provides a coreset for that intermediate problem, alongside experiments and open-source code. Its central result is a provably compact representation of the original geometric optimization task.
summary.tldr: The paper constructs small weighted summaries that preserve line-set clustering costs for every choice of centers.

title: Coreset for Line-Sets Clustering

abstract: Graph few-shot learning is of great importance among various graph learning tasks. Under the few-shot scenario, models are often required to conduct classification given limited labeled samples. Existing graph few-shot learning methods typically leverage Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) and perform classification across a series of meta-tasks. Nevertheless, these methods generally rely on the original graph (i.e., the graph that the meta-task is sampled from) to learn node representations. Consequently, the learned representations for the same nodes are identical in all meta-tasks. Since the class sets are different across meta-tasks, node representations should be task-specific to promote classification performance. Therefore, to adaptively learn node representations across meta-tasks, we propose a novel framework that learns a task-specific structure for each meta-task. To handle the variety of nodes across meta-tasks, we extract relevant nodes and learn task-specific structures based on node influence and mutual information. In this way, we can learn node representations with the task-specific structure tailored for each meta-task. We further conduct extensive experiments on five node classification datasets under both single- and multiple-graph settings to validate the superiority of our framework over the state-of-the-art baselines.

Existing approaches often train across many classification tasks but compute node representations from the same original graph. As a result, a node can receive the same representation even when the set of classes being distinguished changes from task to task.

This paper proposes learning a separate graph structure for each task so that node representations can adapt to the current classification problem. The method extracts relevant nodes and uses node influence and mutual information to learn the task-specific structure. This changes the relationships used to represent a node, allowing the representation to reflect the task’s particular distinctions.

The authors evaluate the framework on five node-classification datasets, covering settings with one graph and with multiple graphs. They report improvements over state-of-the-art baselines. The findings support the idea that few-shot adaptation on graphs can benefit from changing the structure used for representation learning, rather than relying on a fixed graph representation across all tasks.
summary.tldr: Learning a graph structure for each few-shot task produces adaptive node representations and improves classification in the reported evaluations.

title: Graph Few-shot Learning with Task-specific Structures

abstract: PopSign is a smartphone-based bubble-shooter game that helps hearing parentsof deaf infants learn sign language. To help parents practice their ability to sign,PopSign is integrating sign language recognition as part of its gameplay. Fortraining the recognizer, we introduce the PopSign ASL v1.0 dataset that collectsexamples of 250 isolated American Sign Language (ASL) signs using Pixel 4Asmartphone selfie cameras in a variety of environments. It is the largest publiclyavailable, isolated sign dataset by number of examples and is the first dataset tofocus on one-handed, smartphone signs. We collected over 210,000 examplesat 1944x2592 resolution made by 47 consenting Deaf adult signers for whomAmerican Sign Language is their primary language. We manually reviewed 217,866of these examples, of which 175,023 (approximately 700 per sign) were the signintended for the educational game. 39,304 examples were recognizable as a signbut were not the desired variant or were a different sign. We provide a training setof 31 signers, a validation set of eight signers, and a test set of eight signers. Abaseline LSTM model for the 250-sign vocabulary achieves 82.1% accuracy (81.9%class-weighted F1 score) on the validation set and 84.2% (83.9% class-weightedF1 score) on the test set. Gameplay suggests that accuracy will be sufficient forcreating educational games involving sign language recognition.

paragraphs: PopSign is a smartphone game intended to help hearing parents of deaf infants learn sign language. To support recognition-based signing practice, this paper introduces a dataset of 250 isolated American Sign Language signs recorded with Pixel 4A selfie cameras in varied environments. The collection focuses on one-handed signing while using a smartphone.

The dataset contains over 210,000 examples from 47 consenting Deaf adults whose primary language is ASL. Manual review covered 217,866 recordings: 175,023 matched the sign intended for the game, while 39,304 were recognizable signs but used another variant or represented another sign. Those distinctions make the annotations relevant to the game's specific educational vocabulary.

The authors divide signers into separate training, validation, and test groups of 31, eight, and eight people. A baseline LSTM reaches 82.1% validation accuracy and 84.2% test accuracy, with corresponding class-weighted F1 scores of 81.9% and 83.9%. Gameplay suggests this accuracy may suffice for educational recognition games. The demonstrated scope is isolated signs in the specified vocabulary, matching the dataset's intended use.
summary.tldr: PopSign ASL supplies a large smartphone-recorded dataset of 250 isolated signs to support sign-recognition learning games.

title: PopSign ASL v1.0: An Isolated American Sign Language Dataset Collected via Smartphones

abstract: Modern language models excel at integrating across long temporal scales needed to encode linguistic meaning and show non-trivial similarities to biological neural systems. Prior work suggests that human brain responses to language exhibit hierarchically organized "integration windows" that substantially constrain the overall influence of an input token (e.g., a word) on the neural response. However, little prior work has attempted to use integration windows to characterize computations in large language models (LLMs). We developed a simple word-swap procedure for estimating integration windows from black-box language models that does not depend on access to gradients or knowledge of the model architecture (e.g., attention weights). Using this method, we show that trained LLMs exhibit stereotyped integration windows that are well-fit by a convex combination of an exponential and a power-law function, with a partial transition from exponential to power-law dynamics across network layers. We then introduce a metric for quantifying the extent to which these integration windows vary with structural boundaries (e.g., sentence boundaries), and using this metric, we show that integration windows become increasingly yoked to structure at later network layers. None of these findings were observed in an untrained model, which as expected integrated uniformly across its input. These results suggest that LLMs learn to integrate information in natural language using a stereotyped pattern: integrating across position-yoked, exponential windows at early layers, followed by structure-yoked, power-law windows at later layers. The methods we describe in this paper provide a general-purpose toolkit for understanding temporal integration in language models, facilitating cross-disciplinary research at the intersection of biological and artificial intelligence.

This paper studies those influence patterns as integration windows. In trained models, the measured windows fit a mixture of exponential and power-law functions. Across layers, the pattern partially shifts from exponential toward power-law behavior. The authors also introduce a measure of how windows relate to structural boundaries, such as sentence endings, and find stronger alignment with linguistic structure in later layers.

An untrained model does not show these patterns and instead integrates uniformly across its input. The findings suggest that training produces a characteristic progression: earlier layers integrate more according to position, while later layers respond more to structure. The toolkit offers a way to investigate temporal integration and compare questions studied in artificial language models and biological language processing.
summary.tldr: Word-swap measurements suggest trained language models shift from position-based integration toward more structure-sensitive integration in later layers.

title: Large language models transition from integrating across position-yoked, exponential windows to structure-yoked, power-law windows

abstract: Performative prediction is a recently proposed framework where predictions guide decision-making and hence influence future data distributions. Such performative phenomena are ubiquitous in various areas, such as transportation, finance, public policy, and recommendation systems. To date, work on performative prediction has only focused on unconstrained problems, neglecting the fact that many real-world learning problems are subject to constraints. This paper bridges this gap by studying performative prediction under inequality constraints. Unlike most existing work that provides only performative stable points, we aim to find the optimal solutions. Anticipating performative gradient is a challenging task, due to the agnostic performative effect on data distributions. To address this issue, we first develop a robust primal-dual framework that requires only approximate gradients up to a certain accuracy, yet delivers the same order of performance as the stationary stochastic primal-dual algorithm without performativity. Based on this framework, we then propose an adaptive primal-dual algorithm for location families. Our analysis demonstrates that the proposed adaptive primal-dual algorithm attains $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{T})$ regret and constraint violations, using only $\sqrt{T} + 2T$ samples, where $T$ is the time horizon. To our best knowledge, this is the first study and analysis on the optimality of the performative prediction problem under inequality constraints. Finally, we validate the effectiveness of our algorithm and theoretical results through numerical simulations.

paragraphs: Performative prediction studies settings where predictions influence decisions and thereby change future data. This paper adds inequality constraints to that feedback problem and seeks optimal solutions, going beyond finding points that are merely stable under deployment. The challenge is that the way predictions alter the data distribution is unknown, making the relevant optimization gradient difficult to anticipate.

The authors first develop a robust primal-dual framework that works with approximate gradients accurate enough for its requirements. It matches the order of performance of a stationary stochastic primal-dual algorithm without performative effects. They then construct an adaptive algorithm for location families, a specified class of distributions, to make the framework operational in that setting.

The analysis gives O(√T) cumulative regret and constraint violations using √T + 2T samples over horizon T. Because these quantities grow sublinearly, their per-round averages shrink as the horizon grows; the result does not mean literal zero cumulative regret at every finite horizon. Numerical simulations support the algorithm and theory, demonstrating an approach to optimizing predictions while accounting for both feedback and constraints.
summary.tldr: An adaptive primal-dual method achieves sublinear regret and constraint violations for constrained performative prediction within location families.

title: Zero-Regret Performative Prediction Under Inequality Constraints

abstract: Computer end users have spent billions of hours completing daily tasks like tabular data processing and project timeline scheduling. Most of these tasks are repetitive and error-prone, yet most end users lack the skill to automate these burdensome works. With the advent of large language models (LLMs), directing software with natural language user requests become a reachable goal. In this work, we propose a SheetCopilot agent that takes natural language task and control spreadsheet to fulfill the requirements. We propose a set of atomic actions as an abstraction of spreadsheet software functionalities. We further design a state machine-based task planning framework for LLMs to robustly interact with spreadsheets. We curate a representative dataset containing 221 spreadsheet control tasks and establish a fully automated evaluation pipeline for rigorously benchmarking the ability of LLMs in software control tasks. Our SheetCopilot correctly completes 44.3\% of tasks for a single generation, outperforming the strong code generation baseline by a wide margin. Our project page: https://sheetcopilot.github.io/.

paragraphs: SheetCopilot is an agent that translates natural-language requests into spreadsheet operations. It targets repetitive tasks that users may find burdensome or error-prone but lack the programming skills to automate. The central problem is turning a request into a sequence of software actions that actually fulfills the user's requirements.

The authors define atomic actions that abstract spreadsheet functionality and build a state-machine-based planning framework around them. This gives the language model a structured way to plan and interact with the spreadsheet. The contribution includes both this action interface and the planning arrangement used to control the software.

To evaluate the system, the paper introduces a dataset of 221 spreadsheet-control tasks and a fully automated evaluation pipeline. SheetCopilot correctly completes 44.3 percent of tasks with a single generation, substantially outperforming a strong code-generation baseline. This demonstrates an empirical advantage for the proposed control framework while also showing that many benchmark tasks remain unsolved in that setting. The benchmark makes successful task completion the basis for assessing language-model-driven spreadsheet automation.
summary.tldr: SheetCopilot combines atomic spreadsheet actions with structured planning, completing 44.3 percent of 221 benchmark tasks in a single generation.

title: SheetCopilot: Bringing Software Productivity to the Next Level through Large Language Models

abstract: Aimed at adapting a generative model to a novel generation task with only a few given data samples, the capability of few-shot generation is crucial for many real-world applications with limited data, \emph{e.g.}, artistic domains.Instead of training from scratch, recent works tend to leverage the prior knowledge stored in previous datasets, which is quite similar to the memory mechanism of human intelligence, but few of these works directly imitate the memory-recall mechanism that humans make good use of in accomplishing creative tasks, \emph{e.g.}, painting and writing.Inspired by the memory mechanism of human brain, in this work, we carefully design a variational structured memory module (VSM), which can simultaneously store both episodic and semantic memories to assist existing generative models efficiently recall these memories during sample generation.Meanwhile, we introduce a bionic memory updating strategy for the conversion between episodic and semantic memories, which can also model the uncertainty during conversion.Then, we combine the developed VSM with various generative models under the Bayesian framework, and evaluate these memory-augmented generative models with few-shot generation tasks, demonstrating the effectiveness of our methods.

paragraphs: Few-shot generation asks a model to adapt to a new generation task using only a small number of examples. Prior knowledge from earlier datasets can help, but this paper focuses specifically on how that knowledge is stored and recalled. It draws inspiration from human memory mechanisms used during creative activities.

The authors introduce a variational structured memory module that stores both episodic and semantic memories. The module is designed to help existing generative models recall these memories while producing samples. A separate memory-updating strategy handles conversion between the two memory forms and models uncertainty in that conversion, making the changing memory representation an explicit part of the approach.

The memory module is combined with several generative models within a Bayesian framework. Evaluations on few-shot generation tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of these memory-augmented models. The contribution is therefore a reusable memory mechanism for generative modeling: it organizes prior experience, supports recall during generation, and accounts for uncertainty as stored memories change, all in service of adapting from limited new data.
summary.tldr: A variational memory module helps generative models adapt from few examples by storing, updating, and recalling episodic and semantic memories.

title: Few-shot Generation via Recalling Brain-Inspired Episodic-Semantic Memory

abstract: Brain-machine interfaces (BMIs) can restore motor function to people with paralysis but are currently limited by the accuracy of real-time decoding algorithms. Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) using modern training techniques have shown promise in accurately predicting movements from neural signals but have yet to be rigorously evaluated against other decoding algorithms in a closed-loop setting. Here we compared RNNs to other neural network architectures in real-time, continuous decoding of finger movements using intracortical signals from nonhuman primates. Across one and two finger online tasks, LSTMs (a type of RNN) outperformed convolutional and transformer-based neural networks, averaging 18% higher throughput than the convolution network. On simplified tasks with a reduced movement set, RNN decoders were allowed to memorize movement patterns and matched able-bodied control. Performance gradually dropped as the number of distinct movements increased but did not go below fully continuous decoder performance. Finally, in a two-finger task where one degree-of-freedom had poor input signals, we recovered functional control using RNNs trained to act both like a movement classifier and continuous decoder. Our results suggest that RNNs can enable functional real-time BMI control by learning and generating accurate movement patterns.

paragraphs: Brain-machine interfaces need to translate neural activity into useful movements in real time. This paper evaluates recurrent neural networks in closed-loop finger-control tasks, where decoding operates as part of ongoing control. The experiments use intracortical recordings from nonhuman primates and compare recurrent models with convolutional and transformer-based neural networks.

Across online tasks involving one or two fingers, LSTMs outperform the other tested architectures, averaging 18% higher throughput than the convolutional network. The authors also investigate how much a decoder can benefit from memorizing movement patterns. When tasks contain a reduced set of movements, recurrent decoders match able-bodied control. Performance declines as the movement set expands, but remains at least as high as fully continuous decoding.

A further experiment addresses a two-finger task in which one movement dimension has poor neural inputs. Training an RNN to combine movement classification with continuous decoding recovers functional control. Together, these findings suggest that learning reusable movement patterns can help real-time BMI performance, with the usefulness of memorization depending on the range of movements required.
summary.tldr: Recurrent decoders improve real-time finger control in primate BMI experiments by combining continuous decoding with learned movement patterns.

title: Balancing memorization and generalization in RNNs for high performance brain-machine Interfaces

abstract: Simulation is an essential tool to develop and benchmark autonomous vehicle planning software in a safe and cost-effective manner. However, realistic simulation requires accurate modeling of multi-agent interactive behaviors to be trustworthy, behaviors which can be highly nuanced and complex. To address these challenges, we introduce Waymax, a new data-driven simulator for autonomous driving in multi-agent scenes, designed for large-scale simulation and testing. Waymax uses publicly-released, real-world driving data (e.g., the Waymo Open Motion Dataset) to initialize or play back a diverse set of multi-agent simulated scenarios. It runs entirely on hardware accelerators such as TPUs/GPUs and supports in-graph simulation for training, making it suitable for modern large-scale, distributed machine learning workflows. To support online training and evaluation, Waymax includes several learned and hard-coded behavior models that allow for realistic interaction within simulation. To supplement Waymax, we benchmark a suite of popular imitation and reinforcement learning algorithms with ablation studies on different design decisions, where we highlight the effectiveness of routes as guidance for planning agents and the ability of RL to overfit against simulated agents.

paragraphs: Autonomous-driving planners need simulation environments that support large-scale testing and meaningful interactions among road users. Waymax is a data-driven simulator built for multi-agent driving scenes. It uses publicly released real-world driving data to initialize scenarios or replay recorded behavior, providing a varied foundation for training and evaluation.

The simulator runs entirely on accelerators such as GPUs and TPUs and supports simulation within the training computation graph. This design makes it suitable for distributed machine-learning workflows. Learned and hard-coded behavior models allow simulated agents to interact during online training and evaluation, complementing the use of recorded scenarios with responsive behavior.

The authors also benchmark imitation-learning and reinforcement-learning algorithms and examine different design decisions through ablation studies. They highlight the usefulness of routes as guidance for planning agents and show that reinforcement learning can overfit to simulated agents. That finding matters when interpreting simulation performance: success can reflect adaptation to the particular agents used in training. Waymax contributes both scalable infrastructure and evidence about choices that shape planning results within it.
summary.tldr: Waymax enables accelerator-based multi-agent driving simulation and benchmarks planning choices, including route guidance and overfitting to simulated agents.

title: Waymax: An Accelerated, Data-Driven Simulator for Large-Scale Autonomous Driving Research

abstract: Machine learning based decision-support tools in criminal justice systems are subjects of intense discussions and academic research. There are important open questions about the utility and fairness of such tools. Academic researchers often rely on a few small datasets that are not sufficient to empirically study various real-world aspects of these questions. In this paper, we contribute WCLD, a curated large dataset of 1.5 million criminal cases from circuit courts in the U.S. state of Wisconsin. We used reliable public data from 1970 to 2020 to curate attributes like prior criminal counts and recidivism outcomes. The dataset contains large number of samples from five racial groups, in addition to information like sex and age (at judgment and first offense). Other attributes in this dataset include neighborhood characteristics obtained from census data, detailed types of offense, charge severity, case decisions, sentence lengths, year of filing etc. We also provide pseudo-identifiers for judge, county and zipcode. The dataset will not only enable researchers to more rigorously study algorithmic fairness in the context of criminal justice, but also relate algorithmic challenges with various systemic issues. We also discuss in detail the process of constructing the dataset and provide a datasheet. The WCLD dataset is available at https://clezdata.github.io/wcld/.

summary.tldr: WCLD provides 1.5 million Wisconsin criminal-case records with demographic, case, and contextual attributes for studying algorithmic fairness and systemic issues.

title: WCLD: Curated Large Dataset of Criminal Cases from Wisconsin Circuit Courts

abstract: Vision-language pretrained models have seen remarkable success, but their application to safety-critical settings is limited by their lack of interpretability. To improve the interpretability of vision-language models such as CLIP, we propose a multi-modal information bottleneck (M2IB) approach that learns latent representations that compress irrelevant information while preserving relevant visual and textual features. We demonstrate how M2IB can be applied to attribution analysis of vision-language pretrained models, increasing attribution accuracy and improving the interpretability of such models when applied to safety-critical domains such as healthcare. Crucially, unlike commonly used unimodal attribution methods, M2IB does not require ground truth labels, making it possible to audit representations of vision-language pretrained models when multiple modalities but no ground-truth data is available. Using CLIP as an example, we demonstrate the effectiveness of M2IB attribution and show that it outperforms gradient-based, perturbation-based, and attention-based attribution methods both qualitatively and quantitatively.

paragraphs: Vision-language models can perform well while remaining difficult to interpret. This paper proposes a way to examine which visual and textual information matters in their representations. Its motivation includes safety-critical applications, where understanding the information a model uses is an important concern.

The method, multi-modal information bottleneck attribution, or M2IB, learns latent representations that suppress irrelevant information while retaining relevant features from both modalities. This provides a basis for attribution analysis that considers images and text together. A central feature is that the method does not require ground-truth labels, enabling representation audits when paired modalities are available but labeled answers are not.

Using CLIP as the example model, the authors report qualitative and quantitative improvements over gradient-based, perturbation-based, and attention-based attribution methods. The results support more accurate attribution and improved interpretability in the evaluated setting. The contribution is particularly useful for auditing representations without labels: it offers evidence about what information is retained and used, while the stated findings concern explanatory quality rather than a guarantee of safe deployment.
summary.tldr: M2IB explains image-text representations by preserving relevant multimodal information and improves CLIP attribution without requiring ground-truth labels.

title: Visual Explanations of Image-Text Representations via Multi-Modal Information Bottleneck Attribution

abstract: We investigate robust model-free reinforcement learning algorithms designed for environments that may be dynamic or even adversarial. Traditional state-based policies often struggle to accommodate the challenges imposed by the presence of unmodeled disturbances in such settings. Moreover, optimizing linear state-based policies pose an obstacle for efficient optimization, leading to nonconvex objectives, even in benign environments like linear dynamical systems.Drawing inspiration from recent advancements in model-based control, we intro- duce a novel class of policies centered on disturbance signals. We define several categories of these signals, which we term pseudo-disturbances, and develop corresponding policy classes based on them. We provide efficient and practical algorithms for optimizing these policies.Next, we examine the task of online adaptation of reinforcement learning agents in the face of adversarial disturbances. Our methods seamlessly integrate with any black-box model-free approach, yielding provable regret guarantees when dealing with linear dynamics. These regret guarantees unconditionally improve the best-known results for bandit linear control in having no dependence on the state-space dimension. We evaluate our method over various standard RL benchmarks and demonstrate improved robustness.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning agents can struggle when environments contain changing or adversarial disturbances that their policies do not model. This paper also identifies an optimization difficulty: even linear policies based on state can lead to nonconvex objectives in linear dynamical systems. It develops an alternative family of policies organized around disturbance-related signals.

The authors define several kinds of signals called pseudo-disturbances and construct corresponding policy classes. Inspired by model-based control, these classes support efficient, practical optimization algorithms in a model-free setting. The resulting methods can integrate with any black-box model-free approach, providing a way to adapt an existing agent online when disturbances are adversarial.

For linear dynamics, the paper proves regret guarantees that improve the best-known bandit linear control results by removing dependence on state-space dimension. That theoretical claim is specifically tied to linear dynamics. Evaluations across standard reinforcement learning benchmarks also show improved robustness. Together, the analysis and experiments support disturbance-centered adaptation as a useful design principle for agents operating under changing conditions.
summary.tldr: Policies based on pseudo-disturbances improve online robustness and obtain state-dimension-independent regret guarantees for linear dynamics.

title: Online Nonstochastic Model-Free Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We explore the fundamental problem of sorting through the lens of learning-augmented algorithms, where algorithms can leverage possibly erroneous predictions to improve their efficiency. We consider two different settings: In the first setting, each item is provided a prediction of its position in the sorted list. In the second setting, we assume there is a ``quick-and-dirty'' way of comparing items, in addition to slow-and-exact comparisons. For both settings, we design new and simple algorithms using only $O(\sum_i \log \eta_i)$ exact comparisons, where $\eta_i$ is a suitably defined prediction error for the $i$th element. In particular, as the quality of predictions deteriorates, the number of comparisons degrades smoothly from $O(n)$ to $O(n\log n)$. We prove that this comparison complexity is theoretically optimal with respect to the examined error measures. An experimental evaluation against existing adaptive and non-adaptive sorting algorithms demonstrates the potential of applying learning-augmented algorithms in sorting tasks.

For both settings, we design new and simple algorithms using only $O(\sum_i \log \eta_i)$ exact comparisons, where $\eta_i$ is a suitably defined prediction error for the $i$th element. paragraphs: Sorting can be expensive when exact comparisons between items are slow. This paper investigates whether imperfect predictions can reduce the number of those comparisons. It studies two sources of help: a predicted sorted position for each item, and a fast but potentially inaccurate comparison procedure available alongside a slower exact one.

For both settings, the authors design simple algorithms whose exact-comparison cost depends on suitably defined errors for individual elements. The bound sums logarithms of those errors. As predictions worsen, the required number of exact comparisons transitions smoothly from linear in the number of items to the familiar n log n scale.

The authors prove that these comparison bounds are optimal for the error measures they examine. This gives a precise account of how prediction quality can translate into savings without requiring predictions to be perfect. Experiments against existing adaptive and nonadaptive sorting algorithms demonstrate practical potential. The result concerns exact-comparison efficiency, tying the value of predictive information to a measurable part of the sorting workload.
summary.tldr: Prediction-assisted sorting algorithms use fewer exact comparisons when predictions are good and degrade smoothly as prediction errors grow.

title: Sorting with Predictions

abstract: No-regret learners seek to minimize the difference between the loss they cumulated through the actions they played, and the loss they would have cumulated in hindsight had they consistently modified their behavior according to some strategy transformation function. The size of the set of transformations considered by the learner determines a natural notion of rationality. As the set of transformations each learner considers grows, the strategies played by the learners recover more complex game-theoretic equilibria, including correlated equilibria in normal-form games and extensive-form correlated equilibria in extensive-form games. At the extreme, a no-swap-regret agent is one that minimizes regret against the set of all functions from the set of strategies to itself. While it is known that the no-swap-regret condition can be attained efficiently in nonsequential (normal-form) games, understanding what is the strongest notion of rationality that can be attained efficiently in the worst case in sequential (extensive-form) games is a longstanding open problem. In this paper we provide a positive result, by showing that it is possible, in any sequential game, to retain polynomial-time (in the game tree size) iterations while achieving sublinear regret with respect to all linear transformations of the mixed strategy space, a notion called no-linear-swap regret. This notion of hindsight rationality is as strong as no-swap-regret in nonsequential games, and stronger than no-trigger-regret in sequential games—thereby proving the existence of a subset of extensive-form correlated equilibria robust to linear deviations, which we call linear-deviation correlated equilibria, that can be approached efficiently.

paragraphs: Regret measures how much better a learner could have done by consistently changing its past behavior according to an allowed transformation. In sequential games, the challenge is to strengthen that standard while keeping learning computationally efficient.

summary.tldr: The paper proves efficient learning with sublinear regret against all linear strategy transformations in any sequential game.

title: Polynomial-Time Linear-Swap Regret Minimization in Imperfect-Information Sequential Games

abstract: Categorical random variables can faithfully represent the discrete and uncertain aspects of data as part of a discrete latent variable model. Learning in such models necessitates taking gradients with respect to the parameters of the categorical probability distributions, which is often intractable due to their combinatorial nature. A popular technique to estimate these otherwise intractable gradients is the Log-Derivative trick. This trick forms the basis of the well-known REINFORCE gradient estimator and its many extensions. While the Log-Derivative trick allows us to differentiate through samples drawn from categorical distributions, it does not take into account the discrete nature of the distribution itself. Our first contribution addresses this shortcoming by introducing the CatLog-Derivative trick -- a variation of the Log-Derivative trick tailored towards categorical distributions. Secondly, we use the CatLog-Derivative trick to introduce IndeCateR, a novel and unbiased gradient estimator for the important case of products of independent categorical distributions with provably lower variance than REINFORCE. Thirdly, we empirically show that IndeCateR can be efficiently implemented and that its gradient estimates have significantly lower bias and variance for the same number of samples compared to the state of the art.

paragraphs: Models with discrete latent variables represent uncertainty through choices among categories. Training them requires gradients with respect to the probabilities of those choices, but accounting for all possible combinations can be intractable. The common log-derivative trick estimates these gradients from samples and underlies REINFORCE. The paper asks how explicitly using categorical structure can improve that estimation.

The authors introduce the CatLog-Derivative trick, a categorical version of the existing identity. They then derive IndeCateR, an estimator for products of independent categorical distributions. In this setting, the estimator is unbiased, meaning its average estimate matches the target gradient, and has provably lower variance than REINFORCE. The independence condition identifies the setting of this particular theoretical result.

Empirical comparisons show that IndeCateR can be implemented efficiently and produces estimates with significantly lower bias and variance than the compared state-of-the-art methods at the same sample count. The findings distinguish a theoretical guarantee against REINFORCE from broader experimental comparisons. Together, they support exploiting the distribution's discrete structure to obtain more reliable training signals.
summary.tldr: CatLog yields an unbiased gradient estimator for independent categorical variables with provably lower variance than REINFORCE.

title: Differentiable Sampling of Categorical Distributions Using the CatLog-Derivative Trick

abstract: Text-to-image generation has recently witnessed remarkable achievements. We introduce a text-conditional image diffusion model, termed RAPHAEL, to generate highly artistic images, which accurately portray the text prompts, encompassing multiple nouns, adjectives, and verbs. This is achieved by stacking tens of mixture-of-experts (MoEs) layers, i.e., space-MoE and time-MoE layers, enabling billions of diffusion paths (routes) from the network input to the output. Each path intuitively functions as a "painter" for depicting a particular textual concept onto a specified image region at a diffusion timestep. Comprehensive experiments reveal that RAPHAEL outperforms recent cutting-edge models, such as Stable Diffusion, ERNIE-ViLG 2.0, DeepFloyd, and DALL-E 2, in terms of both image quality and aesthetic appeal. Firstly, RAPHAEL exhibits superior performance in switching images across diverse styles, such as Japanese comics, realism, cyberpunk, and ink illustration. Secondly, a single model with three billion parameters, trained on 1,000 A100 GPUs for two months, achieves a state-of-the-art zero-shot FID score of 6.61 on the COCO dataset. Furthermore, RAPHAEL significantly surpasses its counterparts in human evaluation on the ViLG-300 benchmark. We believe that RAPHAEL holds the potential to propel the frontiers of image generation research in both academia and industry, paving the way for future breakthroughs in this rapidly evolving field. More details can be found on a webpage: https://raphael-painter.github.io/.

paragraphs: RAPHAEL is a text-conditioned diffusion model designed to generate artistic images that reflect prompts containing multiple objects, attributes, and actions. Its central architectural idea is to stack many mixture-of-experts layers across space and diffusion time. Their combinations create billions of possible routes through the network.

The authors describe each route intuitively as a painter responsible for a textual concept in a particular image region at a particular diffusion timestep. This connects the architecture to the challenge of depicting several parts of a prompt together. The reported experiments also examine the model’s ability to produce different styles, including comics, realism, cyberpunk, and ink illustration.

The evaluated model has three billion parameters and was trained using 1,000 A100 GPUs for two months. It achieves a zero-shot COCO FID of 6.61, reported as state of the art, and outperforms the compared systems in ViLG-300 human evaluation. The authors also report stronger image quality and aesthetic appeal than the named competing models. These findings support the proposed mixture architecture within the substantial training setup described.
summary.tldr: RAPHAEL combines spatial and temporal expert layers into many diffusion routes, reporting strong text-to-image quality and aesthetic results.

title: RAPHAEL: Text-to-Image Generation via Large Mixture of Diffusion Paths

abstract: The lack of standardized benchmarks for reinforcement learning (RL) in sustainability applications has made it difficult to both track progress on specific domains and identify bottlenecks for researchers to focus their efforts. In this paper, we present SustainGym, a suite of five environments designed to test the performance of RL algorithms on realistic sustainable energy system tasks, ranging from electric vehicle charging to carbon-aware data center job scheduling. The environments test RL algorithms under realistic distribution shifts as well as in multi-agent settings. We show that standard off-the-shelf RL algorithms leave significant room for improving performance and highlight the challenges ahead for introducing RL to real-world sustainability tasks.

paragraphs: SustainGym addresses a benchmarking gap in reinforcement learning for sustainable energy systems. Without standardized environments, researchers have difficulty tracking progress within an application and identifying the problems that most need attention. The paper contributes a shared evaluation suite intended to make those comparisons and research priorities easier to establish.

The suite contains five environments covering realistic energy-system tasks, including electric-vehicle charging and carbon-aware scheduling of data-center jobs. It evaluates algorithms under realistic distribution shifts and in settings involving multiple agents. These features extend the evaluation beyond performance under a single fixed set of conditions, reflecting challenges relevant to the intended applications.

The authors find that standard, readily available reinforcement-learning algorithms leave substantial room for improvement. This result makes the suite useful as a way to expose weaknesses as well as measure progress. The contribution is a set of demanding sustainability-oriented tests and evidence that existing methods do not yet resolve their challenges, helping frame further work toward applying reinforcement learning in real energy systems.
summary.tldr: SustainGym provides five realistic sustainable-energy benchmarks that reveal substantial room to improve standard reinforcement-learning algorithms.

title: SustainGym: Reinforcement Learning Environments for Sustainable Energy Systems

abstract: The choice of a graph learning (GL) model (i.e., a GL algorithm and its hyperparameter settings) has a significant impact on the performance of downstream tasks. However, selecting the right GL model becomes increasingly difficult and time consuming as more and more GL models are developed. Accordingly, it is of great significance and practical value to equip users of GL with the ability to perform a near-instantaneous selection of an effective GL model without manual intervention. Despite the recent attempts to tackle this important problem, there has been no comprehensive benchmark environment to evaluate the performance of GL model selection methods. To bridge this gap, we present GLEMOS in this work, a comprehensive benchmark for instantaneous GL model selection that makes the following contributions. (i) GLEMOS provides extensive benchmark data for fundamental GL tasks, i.e., link prediction and node classification, including the performances of 366 models on 457 graphs on these tasks. (ii) GLEMOS designs multiple evaluation settings, and assesses how effectively representative model selection techniques perform in these different settings. (iii) GLEMOS is designed to be easily extended with new models, new graphs, and new performance records. (iv) Based on the experimental results, we discuss the limitations of existing approaches and highlight future research directions. To promote research on this significant problem, we make the benchmark data and code publicly available at https://namyongpark.github.io/glemos.

paragraphs: Choosing a graph learning model means choosing both an algorithm and its hyperparameters. As the range of candidates grows, this decision becomes increasingly costly. GLEMOS addresses the evaluation problem behind automated, near-instantaneous selection: researchers need a shared way to test whether a selection technique recommends effective models across different graphs.

The benchmark contains performance records for 366 models on 457 graphs, covering node classification and link prediction. These records provide evidence against which selection methods can be assessed. GLEMOS also defines multiple evaluation settings and evaluates representative techniques, making it possible to examine model selection under more than one experimental arrangement.

The framework is designed to accept additional models, graphs, and performance records, allowing its coverage to expand. The authors use their experimental results to discuss shortcomings of existing selection approaches and identify research directions. GLEMOS thus contributes infrastructure for comparing and improving selectors, rather than claiming that the model-selection problem itself has been solved. Its public data and code support further work on that goal.
summary.tldr: GLEMOS benchmarks automated graph-model selection using performance records for 366 models on 457 graphs across two fundamental tasks.

title: GLEMOS: Benchmark for Instantaneous Graph Learning Model Selection

abstract: Effectively modeling long spatiotemporal sequences is challenging due to the need to model complex spatial correlations and long-range temporal dependencies simultaneously. ConvLSTMs attempt to address this by updating tensor-valued states with recurrent neural networks, but their sequential computation makes them slow to train. In contrast, Transformers can process an entire spatiotemporal sequence, compressed into tokens, in parallel. However, the cost of attention scales quadratically in length, limiting their scalability to longer sequences. Here, we address the challenges of prior methods and introduce convolutional state space models (ConvSSM) that combine the tensor modeling ideas of ConvLSTM with the long sequence modeling approaches of state space methods such as S4 and S5. First, we demonstrate how parallel scans can be applied to convolutional recurrences to achieve subquadratic parallelization and fast autoregressive generation. We then establish an equivalence between the dynamics of ConvSSMs and SSMs, which motivates parameterization and initialization strategies for modeling long-range dependencies. The result is ConvS5, an efficient ConvSSM variant for long-range spatiotemporal modeling. ConvS5 significantly outperforms Transformers and ConvLSTM on a long horizon Moving-MNIST experiment while training $3\times$ faster than ConvLSTM and generating samples $400\times$ faster than Transformers. In addition, ConvS5 matches or exceeds the performance of state-of-the-art methods on challenging DMLab, Minecraft and Habitat prediction benchmarks and enables new directions for modeling long spatiotemporal sequences.

ConvLSTMs retain spatial structure in their internal states, but their sequential calculations slow training. Transformers allow parallel processing, yet their attention cost grows quadratically with sequence length. This paper develops convolutional state space models to address these competing computational demands.

The approach combines tensor-valued states with techniques from long-sequence state space models. These results demonstrate the approach’s combination of predictive performance and efficiency on the evaluated sequences.
summary.tldr: ConvS5 combines spatially structured states with efficient sequence computation to improve long-range prediction and generation.

title: Convolutional State Space Models for Long-Range Spatiotemporal Modeling

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have exhibited an impressive ability to perform In-Context Learning (ICL) from only a few examples. Recent works have indicated that the functions learned by ICL can be represented through compressed vectors derived from the transformer. However, the working mechanisms and optimization of these vectors are yet to be thoroughly explored. In this paper, we address this gap by presenting a comprehensive analysis of these compressed vectors, drawing parallels to the parameters trained with gradient descent, and introducing the concept of state vector. Inspired by the works on model soup and momentum-based gradient descent, we propose inner and momentum optimization methods that are applied to refine the state vector progressively as test-time adaptation. Moreover, we simulate state vector aggregation in the multiple example setting, where demonstrations comprising numerous examples are usually too lengthy for regular ICL, and further propose a divide-and-conquer aggregation method to address this challenge. We conduct extensive experiments using Llama-2 and GPT-J in both zero-shot setting and few-shot setting. The experimental results show that our optimization method effectively enhances the state vector and achieves the state-of-the-art performance on diverse tasks.

paragraphs: In-context learning lets a language model use examples supplied with a task. Earlier work suggests that the functions learned this way can be represented by compressed vectors extracted from the Transformer. This paper investigates how those representations work and how they can be improved, introducing the term state vector for the object being studied.

The authors draw parallels between state vectors and parameters learned through gradient descent. Inspired by model soup and momentum-based optimization, they develop inner and momentum optimization methods that progressively refine the vector during test-time adaptation. This makes the compressed representation itself a target for improvement rather than treating its initial extraction as the end of the process.

The paper also examines aggregation when many demonstrations would make ordinary in-context learning too lengthy. A divide-and-conquer method combines state-vector information to address that setting. Experiments using Llama-2 and GPT-J cover zero-shot and few-shot tasks. The authors report improved state vectors and state-of-the-art performance across the evaluated tasks, supporting optimization and aggregation as useful extensions of compressed in-context representations.
summary.tldr: The paper improves compressed representations of in-context learning through test-time optimization and aggregation of information from multiple demonstrations.

title: In-Context Learning State Vector with Inner and Momentum Optimization

abstract: We propose to explore an interesting and promising problem, Cloud Object Detector Adaptation (CODA), where the target domain leverages detections provided by a large cloud model to build a target detector. Despite with powerful generalization capability, the cloud model still cannot achieve error-free detection in a specific target domain. In this work, we present a novel Cloud Object detector adaptation method by Integrating different source kNowledge (COIN). The key idea is to incorporate a public vision-language model (CLIP) to distill positive knowledge while refining negative knowledge for adaptation by self-promotion gradient direction alignment. To that end, knowledge dissemination, separation, and distillation are carried out successively. Knowledge dissemination combines knowledge from cloud detector and CLIP model to initialize a target detector and a CLIP detector in target domain. By matching CLIP detector with the cloud detector, knowledge separation categorizes detections into three parts: consistent, inconsistent and private detections such that divide-and-conquer strategy can be used for knowledge distillation. Consistent and private detections are directly used to train target detector; while inconsistent detections are fused based on a consistent knowledge generation network, which is trained by aligning the gradient direction of inconsistent detections to that of consistent detections, because it provides a direction toward an optimal target detector. Experiment results demonstrate that the proposed COIN method achieves the state-of-the-art performance.
