paragraphs: COIN studies how to build a detector for a target domain using detections supplied by a large cloud model. The motivation is that strong generalization does not make the cloud model error-free in every domain. COIN therefore brings in CLIP as another knowledge source and organizes adaptation around agreement and disagreement between sources.

The method first combines cloud and CLIP knowledge to initialize a target detector and a CLIP detector. It then compares detections from the CLIP detector and cloud detector, separating them into consistent, inconsistent, and private groups. Consistent and private detections directly support target-detector training, while disagreements receive a separate fusion procedure.

For inconsistent detections, a knowledge-generation network learns to align their gradient directions with those produced by consistent detections. This uses agreement as a guide for refining conflicting information before distillation. The authors report state-of-the-art performance in their experiments. The approach's central contribution is a concrete mechanism for treating source agreement and conflict differently during detector adaptation.
summary.tldr: COIN adapts a target detector by combining cloud and CLIP knowledge and refining disagreements through gradient alignment.

title: Cloud Object Detector Adaptation by Integrating Different Source Knowledge

abstract: We address the challenges of Byzantine-robust training in asynchronous distributed machine learning systems, aiming to enhance efficiency amid massive parallelization and heterogeneous compute resources. Asynchronous systems, marked by independently operating workers and intermittent updates, uniquely struggle with maintaining integrity against Byzantine failures, which encompass malicious or erroneous actions that disrupt learning. The inherent delays in such settings not only introduce additional bias to the system but also obscure the disruptions caused by Byzantine faults. To tackle these issues, we adapt the Byzantine framework to asynchronous dynamics by introducing a novel weighted robust aggregation framework. This allows for the extension of robust aggregators and a recent meta-aggregator to their weighted versions, mitigating the effects of delayed updates. By further incorporating a recent variance-reduction technique, we achieve an optimal convergence rate for the first time in an asynchronous Byzantine environment. Our methodology is rigorously validated through empirical and theoretical analysis, demonstrating its effectiveness in enhancing fault tolerance and optimizing performance in asynchronous ML systems.

paragraphs: Asynchronous distributed learning allows workers to operate independently and send updates intermittently. This supports heterogeneous computing resources, but delayed updates introduce bias and complicate the detection of harmful contributions. Byzantine failures, which include malicious or erroneous worker behavior, therefore interact with the timing differences already present in the system.

The paper introduces weighted robust aggregation tailored to these asynchronous dynamics. It extends robust aggregators and a recent meta-aggregator into weighted forms to mitigate the effects of delayed updates. This makes update timing part of the aggregation framework used to preserve learning integrity, rather than treating robustness and asynchronous execution as separate concerns.

The authors combine this framework with a recent variance-reduction technique and establish an optimal convergence rate in the asynchronous Byzantine setting they study. They support the method with both theoretical and empirical analysis. The contribution connects fault tolerance with efficient learning: weighting handles the complications introduced by delayed updates, while variance reduction helps obtain the stated convergence result in the presence of disruptive workers.
summary.tldr: Weighted robust aggregation and variance reduction enable an optimal convergence rate in the paper’s asynchronous Byzantine learning setting.

title: Weight for Robustness: A Comprehensive Approach towards Optimal Fault-Tolerant Asynchronous ML

abstract: We measure the out-of-domain uncertainty in the prediction of Neural Networks using a statistical notion called "Lens Depth'' (LD) combined with Fermat Distance, which is able to capture precisely the "depth'' of a point with respect to a distribution in feature space, without any distributional assumption. Our method also has no trainable parameter. The method is applied directly in the feature space at test time and does not intervene in training process. As such, it does not impact the performance of the original model. The proposed method gives excellent qualitative results on toy datasets and can give competitive or better uncertainty estimation on standard deep learning datasets compared to strong baseline methods.

paragraphs: This paper estimates uncertainty associated with inputs outside a neural network's familiar data domain. It approaches the problem through the network's feature space, where inputs are represented as points. The central question is how deeply a new point sits within the distribution of those representations, providing a geometric basis for assessing unfamiliarity.

The method combines Lens Depth, a statistical measure of depth within a distribution, with Fermat Distance. Together, they measure the position of a point relative to the feature distribution without assuming a particular distributional form. The procedure has no trainable parameters and operates directly at test time, so it can be applied without changing the network's training process.

Because the uncertainty calculation leaves the original model untouched, the authors state that it does not affect that model's predictive performance. They report strong qualitative behavior on toy datasets and uncertainty estimates that can match or exceed strong baselines on standard deep learning datasets. The contribution is therefore a separate, training-independent uncertainty assessment whose reported competitiveness depends on the evaluated setting.
summary.tldr: Combining Lens Depth with Fermat Distance provides a parameter-free, test-time measure of out-of-domain uncertainty in neural network features.

title: Combining Statistical Depth and Fermat Distance for Uncertainty Quantification

abstract: Vision Language Models (VLMs) excel in zero-shot image classification by pairing images with textual category names. The expanding variety of Pre-Trained VLMs enhances the likelihood of identifying a suitable VLM for specific tasks. To better reuse the VLM resource and fully leverage its potential on different zero-shot image classification tasks, a promising strategy is selecting appropriate Pre-Trained VLMs from the VLM Zoo, relying solely on the text data of the target dataset without access to the dataset’s images. In this paper, we analyze two inherent challenges in assessing the ability of a VLM in this Language-Only VLM selection: the “Modality Gap”—the disparity in VLM’s embeddings across two different modalities, making text a less reliable substitute for images; and the “Capability Gap”— the discrepancy between the VLM’s overall ranking and its ranking for target dataset, hindering direct prediction of a model’s dataset-specific performance from its general performance. We propose VLM Selection With gAp Bridging (SWAB) to mitigate the negative impact of two gaps. SWAB first adopts optimal transport to capture the relevance between open-source and target datasets with a transportation matrix. It then uses this matrix to transfer useful statistics of VLMs from open-source datasets to the target dataset for bridging two gaps. By bridging two gaps to obtain better substitutes for test images, SWAB can accurately predict the performance ranking of different VLMs on the target task without the need for the dataset’s images. Experiments across various VLMs and image classification datasets validate SWAB’s effectiveness. Code is available at: https://github.com/YCaigogogo/SWAB.

paragraphs: Choosing a vision-language model for image classification is difficult when only the target dataset's text is available. A model that performs well overall may not be the strongest choice for a particular collection of categories. SWAB addresses the task of predicting which pre-trained model will perform best without inspecting the target images.

The paper identifies two obstacles. The modality gap means that text and image representations differ, making text an imperfect stand-in for visual examples. The capability gap means that a model's general ranking may differ from its ranking on the target task. Together, these gaps undermine selection based only on textual representations or broad measures of model quality.

SWAB uses optimal transport to describe relationships between open-source datasets and the target dataset. It then transfers useful model statistics through those relationships to reduce both gaps and construct better substitutes for the unavailable images. Experiments across multiple models and classification datasets support the approach's effectiveness. Its contribution is making language-only selection more sensitive to the specific task by drawing on relevant evidence from other datasets.
summary.tldr: SWAB transfers statistics from related datasets to rank vision-language models for a target classification task without using its images.

title: Bridge the Modality and Capability Gaps in Vision-Language Model Selection

abstract: Medical time series (MedTS) data, such as Electroencephalography (EEG) and Electrocardiography (ECG), play a crucial role in healthcare, such as diagnosing brain and heart diseases. Existing methods for MedTS classification primarily rely on handcrafted biomarkers extraction and CNN-based models, with limited exploration of transformer-based models. In this paper, we introduce Medformer, a multi-granularity patching transformer tailored specifically for MedTS classification. Our method incorporates three novel mechanisms to leverage the unique characteristics of MedTS: cross-channel patching to leverage inter-channel correlations, multi-granularity embedding for capturing features at different scales, and two-stage (intra- and inter-granularity) multi-granularity self-attention for learning features and correlations within and among granularities. We conduct extensive experiments on five public datasets under both subject-dependent and challenging subject-independent setups. Results demonstrate Medformer's superiority over 10 baselines, achieving top averaged ranking across five datasets on all six evaluation metrics. These findings underscore the significant impact of our method on healthcare applications, such as diagnosing Myocardial Infarction, Alzheimer's, and Parkinson's disease. We release the source code at https://github.com/DL4mHealth/Medformer.

paragraphs: Medical recordings such as EEG and ECG contain signals across multiple channels and time scales. Medformer is a transformer designed to use those characteristics for classification. The paper positions it alongside approaches based on handcrafted biomarkers and convolutional networks, addressing the comparatively limited exploration of transformers for these data.

Its design has three connected parts. Cross-channel patching captures relationships between channels. Multi-granularity embeddings represent patterns at different scales. A two-stage attention mechanism then learns relationships within each granularity and across granularities. Together, these components let the model combine information about where signals occur across channels with how they develop over different temporal spans.

The authors evaluate Medformer on five public datasets under both subject-dependent and more challenging subject-independent setups. Against ten baselines, it obtains the highest average ranking across the datasets on all six evaluation metrics. These classification results support the usefulness of the architecture for the studied medical time-series tasks, including applications involving myocardial infarction, Alzheimer's disease, and Parkinson's disease.
summary.tldr: Medformer combines cross-channel information and multiple temporal scales to improve classification of medical time series.

title: Medformer: A Multi-Granularity Patching Transformer for Medical Time-Series Classification

abstract: Designing a fast and effective entropy model is challenging but essential for practical application of neural codecs. Beyond spatial autoregressive entropy models, more efficient backward adaptation-based entropy models have been recently developed. They not only reduce decoding time by using smaller number of modeling steps but also maintain or even improve rate--distortion performance by leveraging more diverse contexts for backward adaptation. Despite their significant progress, we argue that their performance has been limited by the simple adoption of the design convention for forward adaptation: using only a single type of hyper latent representation, which does not provide sufficient contextual information, especially in the first modeling step. In this paper, we propose a simple yet effective entropy modeling framework that leverages sufficient contexts for forward adaptation without compromising on bit-rate. Specifically, we introduce a strategy of diversifying hyper latent representations for forward adaptation, i.e., using two additional types of contexts along with the existing single type of context. In addition, we present a method to effectively use the diverse contexts for contextualizing the current elements to be encoded/decoded. By addressing the limitation of the previous approach, our proposed framework leads to significant performance improvements. Experimental results on popular datasets show that our proposed framework consistently improves rate-distortion performance across various bit-rate regions, e.g., 3.73\% BD-rate gain over the state-of-the-art baseline on the Kodak dataset.

paragraphs: Neural image compression depends on an entropy model that helps encode an image's representation efficiently. The model must balance decoding speed with the tradeoff between file size and reconstruction quality. Recent approaches reduce the number of modeling steps and use varied contexts from backward adaptation, but this paper identifies an information bottleneck in their forward adaptation.

Specifically, those approaches retain a single type of hyper latent representation for forward adaptation. The authors argue that this supplies insufficient context, especially at the first modeling step. Their framework introduces two additional context types and a method for using the combined information to contextualize the elements currently being encoded or decoded.

The approach aims to supply richer context without compromising bit rate. Experiments on popular datasets show consistent improvements in rate-distortion performance across several bit-rate regions, including a reported 3.73% BD-rate gain over the state-of-the-art baseline on Kodak. The finding indicates that the diversity and use of contextual information remain valuable design choices for efficient neural codecs.
summary.tldr: Adding and effectively combining more types of context improves neural image compression's rate-distortion performance.

title: Diversify, Contextualize, and Adapt: Efficient Entropy Modeling for Neural Image Codec

abstract: Recent advancements in 3D generation have leveraged synthetic datasets with ground truth 3D assets and predefined camera trajectories. However, the potential of adopting real-world datasets, which can produce significantly more realistic 3D scenes, remains largely unexplored. In this work, we delve into the key challenge of the complex and scene-specific camera trajectories found in real-world captures. We introduce Director3D, a robust open-world text-to-3D generation framework, designed to generate both real-world 3D scenes and adaptive camera trajectories. To achieve this, (1) we first utilize a Trajectory Diffusion Transformer, acting as the \emph{Cinematographer}, to model the distribution of camera trajectories based on textual descriptions. Next, a Gaussian-driven Multi-view Latent Diffusion Model serves as the \emph{Decorator}, modeling the image sequence distribution given the camera trajectories and texts. This model, fine-tuned from a 2D diffusion model, directly generates pixel-aligned 3D Gaussians as an immediate 3D scene representation for consistent denoising. Lastly, the 3D Gaussians are further refined by a novel SDS++ loss as the \emph{Detailer}, which incorporates the prior of the 2D diffusion model. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Director3D outperforms existing methods, offering superior performance in real-world 3D generation.

paragraphs: Director3D addresses text-driven 3D generation using real-world captures, where camera motion is more complex and scene-dependent than the predefined trajectories common in synthetic datasets. Its framework generates both a scene and a camera trajectory suited to the text. This makes camera movement part of the generation problem rather than a fixed input chosen independently.

The system divides the work into three stages. A trajectory diffusion transformer first generates camera motion from the description. A multi-view latent diffusion model then produces an image sequence conditioned on that motion and the text. This second model directly generates pixel-aligned 3D Gaussians, providing an immediate scene representation that supports consistency during denoising.

A final stage refines those Gaussians with the proposed SDS++ loss, drawing on knowledge from a 2D diffusion model. The authors report that Director3D outperforms existing methods in their real-world 3D generation experiments. The approach matters because it connects scene-specific camera trajectories, coordinated image generation, and explicit 3D refinement within one framework designed to exploit real-world data.
summary.tldr: Director3D jointly generates text-conditioned camera trajectories and 3D scenes, then refines the scenes using a 2D diffusion model.

title: Director3D: Real-world Camera Trajectory and 3D Scene Generation from Text

abstract: We present BricksRL, a platform designed to democratize access to robotics for reinforcement learning research and education. BricksRL facilitates the creation, design, and training of custom LEGO robots in the real world by interfacing them with the TorchRL library for reinforcement learning agents. The integration of TorchRL with the LEGO hubs, via Bluetooth bidirectional communication, enables state-of-the-art reinforcement learning training on GPUs for a wide variety of LEGO builds. This offers a flexible and cost-efficient approach for scaling and also provides a robust infrastructure for robot-environment-algorithm communication. We present various experiments across tasks and robot configurations, providing built plans and training results. Furthermore, we demonstrate that inexpensive LEGO robots can be trained end-to-end in the real world to achieve simple tasks, with training times typically under 120 minutes on a normal laptop. Moreover, we show how users can extend the capabilities, exemplified by the successful integration of non-LEGO sensors. By enhancing accessibility to both robotics and reinforcement learning, BricksRL establishes a strong foundation for democratized robotic learning in research and educational settings.

paragraphs: BricksRL makes physical robot learning more accessible by connecting custom LEGO robots to reinforcement learning software. Its purpose is to support research and teaching with inexpensive, configurable hardware that users can build and train in the real world. The platform includes robot construction plans and training results across several tasks and configurations.

The technical connection runs through TorchRL and two-way Bluetooth communication with LEGO hubs. This supplies the communication infrastructure linking the robot, its environment, and the learning algorithm, while allowing reinforcement learning training on GPUs. Because the interface supports different LEGO builds, users can explore multiple robot designs within the same software framework.

The experiments show that inexpensive LEGO robots can learn simple tasks through end-to-end training on physical hardware, typically in under 120 minutes using a normal laptop. The authors also demonstrate integration with sensors from outside the LEGO ecosystem. Together, these findings show a practical route to adaptable robotics experiments and classroom activities, with the stated training-time result applying to the simple tasks demonstrated.
summary.tldr: BricksRL connects LEGO robots to TorchRL, enabling inexpensive real-world learning experiments with simple tasks typically trained in under two hours.

title: BricksRL: A Platform for Democratizing Robotics and Reinforcement Learning Research and Education with LEGO

abstract: As a marriage between offline RL and meta-RL, the advent of offline meta-reinforcement learning (OMRL) has shown great promise in enabling RL agents to multi-task and quickly adapt while acquiring knowledge safely. Among which, context-based OMRL (COMRL) as a popular paradigm, aims to learn a universal policy conditioned on effective task representations. In this work, by examining several key milestones in the field of COMRL, we propose to integrate these seemingly independent methodologies into a unified framework. Most importantly, we show that the pre-existing COMRL algorithms are essentially optimizing the same mutual information objective between the task variable $M$ and its latent representation $Z$ by implementing various approximate bounds. Such theoretical insight offers ample design freedom for novel algorithms. As demonstrations, we propose a supervised and a self-supervised implementation of $I(Z; M)$, and empirically show that the corresponding optimization algorithms exhibit remarkable generalization across a broad spectrum of RL benchmarks, context shift scenarios, data qualities and deep learning architectures. This work lays the information theoretic foundation for COMRL methods, leading to a better understanding of task representation learning in the context of reinforcement learning. Given itsgenerality, we envision our framework as a promising offline pre-training paradigm of foundation models for decision making.

paragraphs: Context-based offline meta-reinforcement learning aims to train a shared policy that can handle multiple tasks using representations learned from existing data. The task representation tells the policy which situation it should adapt to. This paper asks whether several established approaches to learning these representations can be understood through one underlying objective.

The authors show that the examined methods optimize approximate bounds on the same mutual information between a task variable and its latent representation. In plain terms, they encourage the representation to retain information that identifies the task. This connection explains apparently different algorithms through a shared information-theoretic framework and provides room to design alternative approximations.

The paper demonstrates that flexibility through supervised and self-supervised implementations of the objective. Experiments report strong generalization across reinforcement learning benchmarks, context shifts, data quality levels, and neural architectures. These results support the framework as both an explanatory account and an algorithm-design tool. The authors also propose its potential as an offline pretraining approach for decision-making foundation models, presenting that broader application as a future possibility.
summary.tldr: The paper unifies context-based offline meta-RL methods through task–representation mutual information and develops supervised and self-supervised implementations.

title: Towards an Information Theoretic Framework of Context-Based Offline Meta-Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Diffusion Transformer (DiT) is emerging as a cutting-edge trend in the landscape of generative diffusion models for image generation. Recently, masked-reconstruction strategies have been considered to improve the efficiency and semantic consistency in training DiT but suffer from deficiency in contextual information extraction. In this paper, we provide a new insight to reveal that noisy-to-noisy masked-reconstruction harms sufficient utilization of contextual information. We further demonstrate the insight with theoretical analysis and empirical study on the mutual information between unmasked and masked patches. Guided by such insight, we propose a novel training paradigm named MC-DiT for fully learning contextual information via diffusion denoising at different noise variances with clean-to-clean mask-reconstruction. Moreover, to avoid model collapse, we design two complementary branches of DiT decoders for enhancing the use of noisy patches and mitigating excessive reliance on clean patches in reconstruction. Extensive experimental results on 256$\times$256 and 512$\times$512 image generation on the ImageNet dataset demonstrate that the proposed MC-DiT achieves state-of-the-art performance in unconditional and conditional image generation with enhanced convergence speed.

paragraphs: Masked reconstruction trains an image model to infer hidden patches from visible ones. For diffusion transformers, this can improve training efficiency and semantic consistency, but the paper identifies a weakness when both the visible information and reconstruction targets are noisy. Noise limits how effectively the model can use relationships between image regions.

The authors support this explanation through theoretical analysis and empirical measurements of mutual information between masked and unmasked patches. They then propose MC-DiT, which combines diffusion denoising at different noise levels with clean-to-clean masked reconstruction. The clean reconstruction task is intended to make contextual relationships more accessible during learning.

A further design choice prevents the model from becoming overly dependent on clean patches: two complementary decoder branches strengthen its use of noisy patches and counter that dependence. On ImageNet generation at 256 × 256 and 512 × 512 resolution, the authors report state-of-the-art conditional and unconditional generation results with faster convergence. The findings connect a diagnosis of lost contextual information to a revised training procedure.
summary.tldr: MC-DiT combines clean-patch reconstruction with diffusion denoising and complementary decoders to improve contextual learning and image generation.

title: MC-DiT: Contextual Enhancement via Clean-to-Clean Reconstruction for Masked Diffusion Models

abstract: The persistent challenge of bias in machine learning models necessitates robust solutions to ensure parity and equal treatment across diverse groups, particularly in classification tasks. Current methods for mitigating bias often result in information loss and an inadequate balance between accuracy and fairness. To address this, we propose a novel methodology grounded in bilevel optimization principles. Our deep learning-based approach concurrently optimizes for both accuracy and fairness objectives, and under certain assumptions, achieving proven Pareto optimal solutions while mitigating bias in the trained model. Theoretical analysis indicates that the upper bound on the loss incurred by this method is less than or equal to the loss of the Lagrangian approach, which involves adding a regularization term to the loss function. We demonstrate the efficacy of our model primarily on tabular datasets such as UCI Adult and Heritage Health. When benchmarked against state-of-the-art fairness methods, our model exhibits superior performance, advancing fairness-aware machine learning solutions and bridging the accuracy-fairness gap. The implementation of FairBiNN is available on https://github.com/yazdanimehdi/FairBiNN.

paragraphs: FairBiNN addresses the challenge of improving fairness across groups while maintaining classification accuracy. The authors argue that existing bias-mitigation methods can lose useful information and strike an inadequate balance between these objectives. Their approach uses bilevel optimization to coordinate accuracy and fairness within a deep-learning framework.

Under certain assumptions, the method has a proof of Pareto optimality. This means the resulting solution balances the objectives so that improving one cannot occur without worsening another within the relevant optimization setting. The authors also derive an upper bound on the method's loss that is no greater than the loss of a Lagrangian approach, which incorporates fairness through an added regularization term.

Experiments primarily use tabular datasets, including UCI Adult and Heritage Health. The authors report superior performance against state-of-the-art fairness methods, supporting the practical value of the proposed optimization structure. The theoretical result remains conditional on its assumptions, while the experiments provide evidence of an improved accuracy–fairness balance on the evaluated classification problems.
summary.tldr: FairBiNN uses bilevel optimization to balance accuracy and fairness, with conditional Pareto-optimality guarantees and strong tabular-data results.

title: Fair Bilevel Neural Network (FairBiNN): On Balancing fairness and accuracy via Stackelberg Equilibrium

abstract: Given a source and a target probability measure, the Monge problem studies efficient ways to map the former onto the latter.This efficiency is quantified by defining a *cost* function between source and target data. Such a cost is often set by default in the machine learning literature to the squared-Euclidean distance, $\ell^2\_2(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}):=\tfrac12\|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{y}\|\_2^2$.The benefits of using *elastic* costs, defined using a regularizer $\tau$ as $c(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}):=\ell^2_2(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})+\tau(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{y})$, was recently highlighted in (Cuturi et al. 2023). Such costs shape the *displacements* of Monge maps $T$, namely the difference between a source point and its image $T(\mathbf{x})-\mathbf{x}$, by giving them a structure that matches that of the proximal operator of $\tau$.In this work, we make two important contributions to the study of elastic costs:*(i)* For any elastic cost, we propose a numerical method to compute Monge maps that are provably optimal. This provides a much-needed routine to create synthetic problems where the ground-truth OT map is known, by analogy to the Brenier theorem, which states that the gradient of any convex potential is always a valid Monge map for the $\ell_2^2$ cost; *(ii)* We propose a loss to *learn* the parameter $\theta$ of a parameterized regularizer $\tau_\theta$, and apply it in the case where $\tau_{A}({\bf z}):=\|A^\perp {\bf z}\|^2_2$. This regularizer promotes displacements that lie on a low-dimensional subspace of $\mathbb{R}^d$, spanned by the $p$ rows of $A\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times d}$. We illustrate the soundness of our procedure on synthetic data, generated using our first contribution, in which we show near-perfect recovery of $A$'s subspace using only samples. We demonstrate the applicability of this method by showing predictive improvements on single-cell data tasks.

paragraphs: The Monge problem seeks an efficient map from one probability distribution to another, with efficiency determined by a chosen transport cost. This paper studies elastic costs, which add a regularizer to squared Euclidean distance. The extra term shapes how points move, allowing displacement structure to influence which transport map is preferred.

The first contribution is a numerical method for computing provably optimal Monge maps for any elastic cost. This provides a way to construct synthetic problems with known ground-truth transport maps. The second contribution is a loss for learning the parameters of the regularizer, so the structure encouraged by the transport cost can itself be inferred.

The authors apply this learning procedure to a regularizer that encourages displacements within a low-dimensional subspace. On synthetic data generated using their first contribution, they recover that subspace almost perfectly from samples alone. They also report predictive improvements on single-cell data tasks. Together, the two contributions connect controlled tests with a practical method for learning how transport displacements should be structured.
summary.tldr: The paper constructs optimal transport maps for elastic costs and learns regularizers that encourage useful low-dimensional displacement structure.

title: Learning Elastic Costs to Shape Monge Displacements

abstract: We study learning problems on correlated stochastic block models with two balanced communities. Our main result gives the first efficient algorithm for graph matching in this setting. In the most interesting regime where the average degree is logarithmic in the number of vertices, this algorithm correctly matches all but a vanishing fraction of vertices with high probability, whenever the edge correlation parameter $s$ satisfies $s^2 > \alpha \approx 0.338$, where $\alpha$ is Otter's tree-counting constant. Moreover, we extend this to an efficient algorithm for exact graph matching whenever this is information-theoretically possible, positively resolving an open problem of Rácz and Sridhar (NeurIPS 2021). Our algorithm generalizes the recent breakthrough work of Mao, Wu, Xu, and Yu (STOC 2023), which is based on centered subgraph counts of a large family of trees termed chandeliers. A major technical challenge that we overcome is dealing with the additional estimation errors that are necessarily present due to the fact that, in relevant parameter regimes, the latent community partition cannot be exactly recovered from a single graph. As an application of our results, we give an efficient algorithm for exact community recovery using multiple correlated graphs in parameter regimes where it is information-theoretically impossible to do so using just a single graph.

summary.tldr: The paper gives efficient graph-matching algorithms for correlated two-community models, with conditional guarantees for near-complete and exact recovery.

title: Efficient Graph Matching for Correlated Stochastic Block Models

abstract: Machine learning (ML) algorithms can often differ in performance across domains. Understanding why their performance differs is crucial for determining what types of interventions (e.g., algorithmic or operational) are most effective at closing the performance gaps. Aggregate decompositions express the total performance gap as the gap due to a shift in the feature distribution $p(X)$ plus the gap due to a shift in the outcome's conditional distribution $p(Y|X)$. While this coarse explanation is helpful for guiding root cause analyses, it provides limited details and can only suggest coarse fixes involving all variables in an ML system. Detailed decompositions quantify the importance of each variable to each term in the aggregate decomposition, which can provide a deeper understanding and suggest more targeted interventions. Although parametric methods exist for conducting a full hierarchical decomposition of an algorithm's performance gap at the aggregate and detailed levels, current nonparametric methods only cover parts of the hierarchy; many also require knowledge of the entire causal graph. We introduce a nonparametric hierarchical framework for explaining why the performance of an ML algorithm differs across domains, without requiring causal knowledge. Furthermore, we derive debiased, computationally-efficient estimators and statistical inference procedures to construct confidence intervals for the explanations.

paragraphs: A machine learning system can perform differently across domains because its inputs change, because the relationship between inputs and outcomes changes, or both. Separating these sources helps explain a performance gap. However, an explanation at that broad level does not reveal which variables deserve closer attention when choosing a response.

This paper introduces a hierarchical framework that connects broad explanations to detailed ones. At the aggregate level, it separates shifts in the feature distribution from shifts in outcomes conditional on those features. At the detailed level, it quantifies individual variables' contributions to those components. The framework is nonparametric and does not require prior knowledge of the causal relationships among all variables.

The authors also derive computationally efficient, debiased estimators and procedures for attaching confidence intervals to the explanations. This makes uncertainty part of the analysis rather than leaving users with contributions alone. The result supports more targeted investigation of performance discrepancies, while its explanations do not themselves establish that a particular intervention will causally eliminate a gap.
summary.tldr: A nonparametric framework explains performance gaps at both distribution and variable levels, with confidence intervals and no required causal graph.

title: A hierarchical decomposition for explaining ML performance discrepancies

abstract: G-code (Geometric code) or RS-274 is the most widely used computer numerical control (CNC) and 3D printing programming language. G-code provides machine instructions for the movement of the 3D printer, especially for the nozzle, stage, and extrusion of material for extrusion-based additive manufacturing. Currently, there does not exist a large repository of curated CAD models along with their corresponding G-code files for additive manufacturing. To address this issue, we present Slice-100K, a first-of-its-kind dataset of over 100,000 G-code files, along with their tessellated CAD model, LVIS (Large Vocabulary Instance Segmentation) categories, geometric properties, and renderings. We build our dataset from triangulated meshes derived from Objaverse-XL and Thingi10K datasets. We demonstrate the utility of this dataset by finetuning GPT-2 on a subset of the dataset for G-code translation from a legacy G-code format (Sailfish) to a more modern, widely used format (Marlin). Our dataset can be found here. Slice-100K will be the first step in developing a multimodal foundation model for digital manufacturing.

paragraphs: A digital shape and the instructions needed to print it are different kinds of information. In extrusion-based 3D printing, G-code controls movements of the nozzle and stage as well as material extrusion. The paper addresses the absence of a large curated repository pairing CAD geometry with the corresponding machine instructions.

Slice-100K contains more than 100,000 G-code files together with tessellated CAD models, object categories, geometric properties, and renderings. It is built from triangulated meshes drawn from Objaverse-XL and Thingi10K. Pairing these forms of information gives researchers a dataset connecting object geometry and visual representations to the instructions used for manufacturing.

To demonstrate a use of the dataset, the authors finetune GPT-2 on a subset for translation between G-code formats, moving from the legacy Sailfish format to Marlin. This establishes a concrete language-modeling application for the paired manufacturing data. The paper presents the dataset as a first step toward multimodal foundation models for digital manufacturing, rather than claiming to have already produced such a model.
summary.tldr: Slice-100K pairs over 100,000 G-code files with geometry and visual metadata, demonstrating its use for translating printer instruction formats.

title: Slice-100K: A Multimodal Dataset for Extrusion-based 3D Printing

abstract: In this paper, we propose a novel benchmark, named VastTrack, aiming to facilitate the development of general visual tracking via encompassing abundant classes and videos. VastTrack consists of a few attractive properties: (1) Vast Object Category. In particular, it covers targets from 2,115 categories, significantly surpassing object classes of existing popular benchmarks (e.g., GOT-10k with 563 classes and LaSOT with 70 categories). Through providing such vast object classes, we expect to learn more general object tracking. (2) Larger scale. Compared with current benchmarks, VastTrack provides 50,610 videos with 4.2 million frames, which makes it to date the largest dataset in term of the number of videos, and hence could benefit training even more powerful visual trackers in the deep learning era. (3) Rich Annotation. Besides conventional bounding box annotations, VastTrack also provides linguistic descriptions with more than 50K sentences for the videos. Such rich annotations of VastTrack enable the development of both vision-only and vision-language tracking. In order to ensure precise annotation, each frame in the videos is manually labeled with multi-stage of careful inspections and refinements. To understand performance of existing trackers and to provide baselines for future comparison, we extensively evaluate 25 representative trackers. The results, not surprisingly, display significant drops compared to those on current datasets due to lack of abundant categories and videos from diverse scenarios for training, and more efforts are urgently required to improve general visual tracking. Our VastTrack, the toolkit, and evaluation results are publicly available at https://github.com/HengLan/VastTrack.

paragraphs: VastTrack is a benchmark designed to push visual tracking toward a wider range of objects and situations. It contains 50,610 videos, 4.2 million frames, and targets from 2,115 categories. That category coverage substantially exceeds the cited tracking benchmarks GOT-10k and LaSOT, giving researchers a broader resource for developing and testing general tracking ability.

The dataset combines bounding boxes with more than 50,000 sentences describing its videos. This supports trackers that rely only on visual information as well as systems that also use language. Each frame is manually annotated, with multiple rounds of inspection and refinement intended to improve annotation precision.

The authors evaluate 25 representative trackers and find substantial performance drops compared with results on existing datasets. They attribute these drops to insufficient training diversity in object categories and scenarios. The benchmark thus exposes a gap between strong performance on established collections and broader tracking capability. Its scale and annotations are intended to support further progress, while the published evaluations establish comparison points for future trackers.
summary.tldr: VastTrack broadens visual tracking to 2,115 object categories and reveals substantial generalization gaps in existing trackers.

title: VastTrack: Vast Category Visual Object Tracking

abstract: In question-answering scenarios, humans can assess whether the available information is sufficient and seek additional information if necessary, rather than providing a forced answer. In contrast, Vision Language Models (VLMs) typically generate direct, one-shot responses without evaluating the sufficiency of the information. To investigate this gap, we identify a critical and challenging task in the Visual Question Answering (VQA) scenario: can VLMs indicate how to adjust an image when the visual information is insufficient to answer a question? This capability is especially valuable for assisting visually impaired individuals who often need guidance to capture images correctly. To evaluate this capability of current VLMs, we introduce a human-labeled dataset as a benchmark for this task. Additionally, we present an automated framework that generates synthetic training data by simulating ``where to know'' scenarios. Our empirical results show significant performance improvements in mainstream VLMs when fine-tuned with this synthetic data. This study demonstrates the potential to narrow the gap between information assessment and acquisition in VLMs, bringing their performance closer to humans.

paragraphs: A visual question may be impossible to answer from the image currently available. Humans can recognize this and seek another view, whereas vision-language models commonly produce a direct response. This paper studies whether a model can instead explain how to adjust an image so that the missing visual information becomes available.

The task connects assessing information sufficiency with guiding information acquisition. The authors introduce a human-labeled dataset to evaluate this capability and an automated framework that creates synthetic training examples by simulating situations where more visual information is needed. They identify assistance for visually impaired people capturing images as a particularly valuable application of this guidance.

Fine-tuning mainstream vision-language models with the synthetic examples produces significant performance improvements in the reported experiments. This suggests that training on information-seeking situations can strengthen a capability that direct question answering does not adequately exercise. The findings show potential to bring models closer to human behavior in assessing and acquiring information, without establishing that the broader human-model gap has been closed.
summary.tldr: A new benchmark and synthetic training framework improve VLMs' ability to guide image adjustments when a question needs more visual information.

title: Right this way: Can VLMs Guide Us to See More to Answer Questions?

abstract: Diffusion Transformers have recently demonstrated unprecedented generative capabilities for various tasks. The encouraging results, however, come with the cost of slow inference, since each denoising step requires inference on a transformer model with a large scale of parameters. In this study, we make an interesting and somehow surprising observation: the computation of a large proportion of layers in the diffusion transformer, through introducing a caching mechanism, can be readily removed even without updating the model parameters. In the case of U-ViT-H/2, for example, we may remove up to 93.68% of the computation in the cache steps (46.84% for all steps), with less than 0.01 drop in FID. To achieve this, we introduce a novel scheme, named Learning-to-Cache (L2C), that learns to conduct caching in a dynamic manner for diffusion transformers. Specifically, by leveraging the identical structure of layers in transformers and the sequential nature of diffusion, we explore redundant computations between timesteps by treating each layer as the fundamental unit for caching. To address the challenge of the exponential search space in deep models for identifying layers to cache and remove, we propose a novel differentiable optimization objective. An input-invariant yet timestep-variant router is then optimized, which can finally produce a static computation graph. Experimental results show that L2C largely outperforms samplers such as DDIM and DPM-Solver, alongside prior cache-based methods at the same inference speed.

paragraphs: Diffusion transformers repeatedly run a large network during denoising, making generation slow. This paper observes that many layer computations can be replaced through caching without changing the underlying model parameters. Learning-to-Cache turns that redundancy into an optimization problem: determine which layers can reuse computations across diffusion timesteps.

Searching every possible caching configuration would grow exponentially with network depth. The authors instead introduce a differentiable objective and optimize a router whose decisions vary by timestep but remain independent of the input. This learned schedule can produce a static computation graph, combining timestep-specific caching choices with a fixed execution structure.

For U-ViT-H/2, the paper reports removing up to 93.68% of computation in cache steps, corresponding to 46.84% across all steps, with an FID change below 0.01. Experiments also report better performance than DDIM, DPM-Solver, and earlier caching methods at matched inference speed. The distinction between cache-step and overall savings is essential to interpreting the reported acceleration.
summary.tldr: Learning-to-Cache learns timestep-specific layer reuse to accelerate diffusion transformers while preserving generation quality in reported experiments.

title: Learning-to-Cache: Accelerating Diffusion Transformer via Layer Caching

abstract: Transformers have demonstrated great power in the recent development of large foundational models. In particular, the Vision Transformer (ViT) has brought revolutionary changes to the field of vision, achieving significant accomplishments on the experimental side. However, their theoretical capabilities, particularly in terms of generalization when trained to overfit training data, are still not fully understood. To address this gap, this work delves deeply into the \textit{benign overfitting} perspective of transformers in vision. To this end, we study the optimization of a Transformer composed of a self-attention layer with softmax followed by a fully connected layer under gradient descent on a certain data distribution model. By developing techniques that address the challenges posed by softmax and the interdependent nature of multiple weights in transformer optimization, we successfully characterized the training dynamics and achieved generalization in post-training. Our results establish a sharp condition that can distinguish between the small test error phase and the large test error regime, based on the signal-to-noise ratio in the data model. The theoretical results are further verified by experimental simulation. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to characterize benign overfitting for Transformers.

paragraphs: Benign overfitting describes a situation in which a model overfits its training data yet still performs well on unseen examples. This paper investigates that phenomenon for a vision-oriented Transformer. Its aim is to explain theoretically when fitting the training set is compatible with good generalization in the model under study.

The analysis considers a Transformer with one softmax self-attention layer followed by a fully connected layer, trained by gradient descent under a particular data-distribution model. The authors develop techniques for handling softmax and the dependence between multiple trainable weights. These allow them to characterize training dynamics and analyze generalization after training.

The central result is a sharp condition based on the data model's signal-to-noise ratio that separates small-test-error and large-test-error regimes. Experimental simulations support the theoretical findings. This provides a specific account of when benign overfitting occurs for the analyzed architecture and distribution, with the scope of the conclusion tied to that mathematical setting.
summary.tldr: A theoretical analysis identifies a signal-to-noise condition separating good and poor generalization for an overfitted Transformer under a specified data model.

title: Unveil Benign Overfitting for Transformer in Vision: Training Dynamics, Convergence, and Generalization

abstract: The inner workings of neural networks can be better understood if we can fully decipher the information encoded in neural activations. In this paper, we argue that this information is embodied by the subset of inputs that give rise to similar activations. We propose InversionView, which allows us to practically inspect this subset by sampling from a trained decoder model conditioned on activations. This helps uncover the information content of activation vectors, and facilitates understanding of the algorithms implemented by transformer models. We present four case studies where we investigate models ranging from small transformers to GPT-2. In these studies, we show that InversionView can reveal clear information contained in activations, including basic information about tokens appearing in the context, as well as more complex information, such as the count of certain tokens, their relative positions, and abstract knowledge about the subject. We also provide causally verified circuits to confirm the decoded information.

paragraphs: InversionView investigates what a neural activation contains by examining inputs that produce similar activations. The paper’s central argument is that this collection of inputs embodies the information represented by the activation. Inspecting the shared content of those inputs offers a way to interpret internal representations and understand the computations they support.

To make that inspection practical, the method trains a decoder that samples inputs while conditioned on an activation. These samples expose information associated with the activation vector. The approach is applied in four case studies spanning small transformers through GPT-2, connecting the decoded information to questions about the algorithms implemented by those models.

The studies reveal basic contextual token information as well as token counts, relative positions, and abstract information about a subject. The researchers also provide causally verified circuits to confirm the decoded content. These findings show how input reconstruction can help make internal information legible, with circuit-level evidence supporting the interpretations presented in the case studies.
summary.tldr: InversionView samples inputs associated with neural activations to reveal their information content, supported by causally verified circuits.

title: InversionView: A General-Purpose Method for Reading Information from Neural Activations

abstract: Diffusion models show remarkable image generation performance following text prompts, but risk generating sexual contents. Existing approaches, such as prompt filtering, concept removal, and even sexual contents mitigation methods, struggle to defend against adversarial attacks while maintaining benign image quality. In this paper, we propose a novel approach called Distorting Embedding Space (DES), a text encoder-based defense mechanism that effectively tackles these issues through innovative embedding space control. DES transforms unsafe embeddings, extracted from a text encoder using unsafe prompts, toward carefully calculated safe embedding regions to prevent unsafe contents generation, while reproducing the original safe embeddings. DES also neutralizes the ``nudity'' embedding, by aligning it with neutral embedding to enhance robustness against adversarial attacks. As a result, extensive experiments on explicit content mitigation and adaptive attack defense show that DES achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) defense, with attack success rate (ASR) of 9.47\% on FLUX.1, a recent popular model, and 0.52\% on the widely adopted Stable Diffusion v1.5. These correspond to ASR reductions of 76.5\% and 63.9\% compared to previous SOTA methods, EraseAnything and AdvUnlearn, respectively. Furthermore, DES maintains benign image quality, achieving Frechet Inception Distance and CLIP score comparable to those of the original FLUX.1 and Stable Diffusion v1.5.

paragraphs: The paper tackles the difficulty of suppressing sexual image generation while preserving the quality of benign outputs. Prompt filtering and concept-removal methods can struggle against adversarial prompts. Distorting Embedding Space, or DES, intervenes in the text encoder's representations, changing how unsafe prompts are communicated to the image generator.

DES moves embeddings from unsafe prompts toward calculated safe regions while reproducing the original embeddings for safe prompts. It also aligns the embedding for nudity with a neutral embedding to strengthen resistance to adversarial attacks. These operations aim to reduce unsafe generation without broadly disrupting the representations that support ordinary image creation.

Experiments report attack success rates of 9.47% on FLUX.1 and 0.52% on Stable Diffusion v1.5. Those are reductions of 76.5% and 63.9% relative to EraseAnything and AdvUnlearn, respectively. Benign-image FID and CLIP scores remain comparable to the original models. The findings show a substantial empirical improvement in defense while retaining measured benign quality, rather than complete prevention of successful attacks.
summary.tldr: DES redirects unsafe text embeddings toward safe regions, reducing adversarial sexual-content generation while maintaining comparable benign-image quality.

title: Mitigating Sexual Content Generation via Embedding Distortion in Text-conditioned Diffusion Models

abstract: Computing eigenvalues of very large matrices is a critical task in many machine learning applications, including the evaluation of log-determinants, the trace of matrix functions, and other important metrics. As datasets continue to grow in scale, the corresponding covariance and kernel matrices become increasingly large, often reaching magnitudes that make their direct formation impractical or impossible. Existing techniques typically rely on matrix-vector products, which can provide efficient approximations, if the matrix spectrum behaves well. However, in settings like distributed learning, or when the matrix is defined only indirectly, access to the full data set can be restricted to only very small sub-matrices of the original matrix. In these cases, the matrix of nominal interest is not even available as an implicit operator, meaning that even matrix-vector products may not be available. In such settings, the matrix is "impalpable", in the sense that we have access to only masked snapshots of it. We draw on principles from free probability theory to introduce a novel method of "free decompression" to estimate the spectrum of such matrices. Our method can be used to extrapolate from the empirical spectral densities of small submatrices to infer the eigenspectrum of extremely large (impalpable) matrices (that we cannot form or even evaluate with full matrix-vector products). We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through a series of examples, comparing its performance against known limiting distributions from random matrix theory in synthetic settings, as well as applying it to submatrices of real-world datasets, matching them with their full empirical eigenspectra.

In such settings, the matrix is "impalpable", in the sense that we have access to only masked snapshots of it. We draw on principles from free probability theory to introduce a novel method of "free decompression" to estimate the spectrum of such matrices. Our method can be used to extrapolate from the empirical spectral densities of small submatrices to infer the eigenspectrum of extremely large (impalpable) matrices (that we cannot form or even evaluate with full matrix-vector products). We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through a series of examples, comparing its performance against known limiting distributions from random matrix theory in synthetic settings, as well as applying it to submatrices of real-world datasets, matching them with their full empirical eigenspectra.

Some estimation methods need only matrix-vector products. This paper studies a more restricted setting where even those operations are unavailable and access consists only of small submatrices.

The authors call these matrices impalpable because the full object cannot be directly accessed or applied as an operator. Their free decompression method draws on free probability theory to extrapolate from the empirical spectral densities of small submatrices. The target is the spectrum of the much larger matrix represented by those limited snapshots.

The paper evaluates the approach using synthetic examples with known limiting distributions from random matrix theory and real-world datasets whose full empirical eigenspectra can be used for comparison. These demonstrations support spectral estimation from restricted matrix access. The contribution addresses a distinct computational obstacle: obtaining useful spectral information when neither forming the matrix nor multiplying by it is feasible.
summary.tldr: Free decompression estimates a large matrix's spectrum from small submatrices when full matrix access and matrix-vector products are unavailable.

title: Spectral Estimation with Free Decompression

abstract: We demonstrate that geometrically distinctive keys during LLM inference tend to have high attention scores. Based on the phenomenon we propose KeyDiff, a training-free KV cache eviction method based solely on key similarity. Unlike other KV cache eviction methods, KeyDiff can process arbitrarily long prompts within strict resource constraints and efficiently generate responses. We provide a theoretical basis for KeyDiff by relating key diversity with attention scores. These results imply KeyDiff can efficiently identify the most important tokens to retain. Notably KeyDiff does not rely on attention scores, allowing the use of optimized attention mechanisms like FlashAttention. Under a strict memory allowance, we demonstrate the effectiveness of KeyDiff for the Llama and Qwen model families by observing a performance gap of less than 0.04\% with 8K cache budget (~23\% KV cache reduction) from the non-evicting baseline on LongBench for Llama 3.1-8B and Llama 3.2-3B. We also observe near baseline performance for Deepseek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B on the Math500 reasoning benchmark and decrease end-to-end inference latency by up to 30\% compared to the other token-eviction methods.

KeyDiff decides what to retain using similarity among keys. The method requires no training and does not directly depend on attention scores. The authors provide a theoretical connection between key diversity and attention, supporting similarity as a basis for eviction. title: KeyDiff: Key Similarity-Based KV Cache Eviction for Long-Context LLM Inference in Resource-Constrained Environments

abstract: Recent advances in text-to-speech synthesis have achieved notable success in generating high-quality short utterances for individual speakers. However, these systems still face challenges when extending their capabilities to long, multi-speaker, and spontaneous dialogues, typical of real-world scenarios such as podcasts. These limitations arise from two primary challenges: 1) long speech: podcasts typically span several minutes, exceeding the upper limit of most existing work; 2) spontaneity: podcasts are marked by their spontaneous, oral nature, which sharply contrasts with formal, written contexts; existing works often fall short in capturing this spontaneity. In this paper, we propose MoonCast, a solution for high-quality zero-shot podcast generation, aiming to synthesize spontaneous podcast-style speech from text-only sources (e.g., stories, technical reports, news in TXT, PDF, or Web URL formats) using the voices of unseen speakers. To enable long audio generation, we employ a language model with parameter, data, and context scaling to process sequences in an innovative format designed for modeling entire multi-speaker, multi-turn speech interactions. To enhance spontaneity, we observe that ASR transcripts capture spontaneous speech details (e.g., filler words indicating hesitations, and specific punctuation and spaces reflecting breathing pauses), suggesting that these transcripts can serve as a partial indicator of speech spontaneity. Building upon this assumption, we utilize a script generation module to generate scripts incorporating these spontaneous elements. Experiments show MoonCast outperforms baselines, with notable improvements in contextual coherence and spontaneity.

summary.tldr: MoonCast combines long-form speech modeling with scripts containing spontaneous speech cues to generate podcasts in unseen speakers' voices.

title: MoonCast: High-Quality Zero-Shot Podcast Generation

abstract: Recent booming time series models have demonstrated remarkable forecasting performance. However, these methods often place greater focus on more effectively modelling the historical series, largely neglecting the forecasting phase, which generates long-term forecasts by separately predicting multiple time points. Given that real-world time series typically consist of various long short-term dynamics, independent predictions over individual time points may fail to express complex underlying patterns and can lead to a lack of global views. To address these issues, this work explores new perspectives from the forecasting phase and proposes a novel Implicit Forecaster (IF) as an additional decoding module. Inspired by decomposition forecasting, IF adopts a more nuanced approach by implicitly predicting constituent waves represented by their frequency, amplitude, and phase, thereby accurately forming the time series. Extensive experimental results from multiple real-world datasets show that IF can consistently boost mainstream time series models, achieving state-of-the-art forecasting performance. Code is available at this repository: [https://github.com/rakuyorain/Implicit-Forecaster](https://github.com/rakuyorain/Implicit-Forecaster).

paragraphs: Time-series forecasting models often devote most of their design effort to understanding historical observations. The paper focuses instead on how they construct future predictions. Predicting multiple future time points separately may fail to capture patterns spanning the forecast, especially when the series combines short-term and long-term dynamics.

Implicit Forecaster is an additional decoding module that represents the forecast through constituent waves. It implicitly predicts their frequencies, amplitudes, and phases, then forms the time series from those components. This connects future values through shared wave descriptions, providing a way to express structure across the forecast rather than handling each predicted time point independently.

Experiments on several real-world datasets show consistent improvements when the module is added to mainstream time-series models, with resulting state-of-the-art forecasting performance. The findings support decoding as an important source of forecasting gains alongside historical-series modeling. The contribution is a reusable forecasting component that translates predicted wave properties into a structured sequence of future values.
summary.tldr: Implicit Forecaster improves time-series models by decoding future sequences through constituent waves defined by frequency, amplitude, and phase.

title: Towards Accurate Time Series Forecasting via Implicit Decoding

abstract: We study the implicit bias of flatness / low (loss) curvature and its effects on generalization in two-layer overparameterized ReLU networks with multivariate inputs---a problem well motivated by the minima stability and edge-of-stability phenomena in gradient-descent training. Existing work either requires interpolation or focuses only on univariate inputs. This paper presents new and somewhat surprising theoretical results for multivariate inputs. On two natural settings (1) generalization gap for flat solutions, and (2) mean-squared error (MSE) in nonparametric function estimation by stable minima, we prove upper and lower bounds, which establish that while flatness does imply generalization, the resulting rates of convergence necessarily deteriorate exponentially as the input dimension grows. This gives an exponential separation between the flat solutions compared to low-norm solutions (i.e., weight decay), which are known not to suffer from the curse of dimensionality. In particular, our minimax lower bound construction, based on a novel packing argument with boundary-localized ReLU neurons, reveals how flat solutions can exploit a kind of "neural shattering" where neurons rarely activate, but with high weight magnitudes. This leads to poor performance in high dimensions. We corroborate these theoretical findings with extensive numerical simulations. To the best of our knowledge, our analysis provides the first systematic explanation for why flat minima may fail to generalize in high dimensions.

Its theory covers both generalization gaps for flat solutions and mean-squared error in function estimation using stable minima. This extends the analysis beyond earlier work requiring interpolation or restricting inputs to one dimension.

Numerical simulations corroborate the theoretical findings. The conclusion is specific to the analyzed network and estimation settings, explaining why flatness alone can offer weak generalization guarantees as dimensionality grows.
summary.tldr: For the studied two-layer ReLU networks, flatness-based generalization rates worsen exponentially with input dimension, unlike known low-norm guarantees.

title: Stable Minima of ReLU Neural Networks Suffer from the Curse of Dimensionality: The Neural Shattering Phenomenon

abstract: Existing acceleration techniques for video diffusion models often rely on uniform heuristics or time-embedding variants to skip timesteps and reuse cached features. These approaches typically require extensive calibration with curated prompts and risk inconsistent outputs due to prompt-specific overfitting. In this paper, we introduce a novel and robust discovery: a unified magnitude law observed across different models and prompts. Specifically, the magnitude ratio of successive residual outputs decreases monotonically, steadily in most timesteps while rapidly in the last several steps. Leveraging this insight, we introduce a Magnitude-aware Cache (MagCache) that adaptively skips unimportant timesteps using an error modeling mechanism and adaptive caching strategy. Unlike existing methods requiring dozens of curated samples for calibration, MagCache only requires a single sample for calibration. Experimental results show that MagCache achieves 2.10×-2.68× speedups on Open-Sora, CogVideoX, Wan 2.1, and HunyuanVideo, while preserving superior visual fidelity. It significantly outperforms existing methods in LPIPS, SSIM, and PSNR, under similar computational budgets.

paragraphs: Video diffusion acceleration often skips computation and reuses stored features, but deciding when to do so can require extensive calibration. Heuristics fitted to curated prompts can also behave inconsistently on other prompts. MagCache bases its decisions on a pattern the authors observe across different video models and prompts.

The pattern concerns ratios between the magnitudes of successive residual outputs. These ratios decrease monotonically, changing steadily through most timesteps and more rapidly near the end. MagCache uses this observation in an error model and an adaptive caching strategy to identify timesteps whose computation can be skipped. Calibration requires only one sample, reducing dependence on a collection of curated examples.

These experiments support magnitude-based adaptation as an effective way to balance feature reuse against output quality.
summary.tldr: MagCache uses observed residual-magnitude patterns to adaptively reuse video diffusion features, delivering reported speedups of 2.10–2.68 times.

title: MagCache: Fast Video Generation with Magnitude-Aware Cache

abstract: Human cognition is punctuated by abrupt, spontaneous shifts between topics—driven by emotional, contextual, or associative cues—a phenomenon known as spontaneous thought in neuroscience. In contrast, self-attention-based models rely on structured patterns over their inputs to predict each next token, lacking spontaneity. Motivated by this distinction, we characterize *spontaneous topic changes* in self-attention architectures and reveal divergences from *spontaneous human thought*. First, we establish theoretical results under a simplified, single-layer self-attention model with suitable conditions by defining a topic as a set of Token Priority Graphs (TPGs). Specifically, we demonstrate that (1) the model maintains the priority order of tokens related to the input topic, (2) a spontaneous topic change can occur only if lower-priority tokens outnumber all higher-priority tokens of the input topic, and (3) unlike human cognition, the longer context length or the more ambiguous input topic does not increase the likelihood of spontaneous change. Second, we empirically validate that the effect of input length or topic ambiguity persists in modern, state-of-the-art LLMs, underscoring a fundamental disparity between human cognition and AI behavior in the context of spontaneous topic changes. To the best of our knowledge, no prior work has explored these questions with a focus so closely aligned to human thought.

The definition makes token ordering central to the analysis.

They also establish a necessary condition for spontaneous topic change: lower-priority tokens must outnumber all higher-priority tokens of that topic. Meeting this count condition is not stated to guarantee a change.

Experiments with modern language models support the reported effects of context length and ambiguity. Together, these findings identify a specific divergence from human spontaneous thought while keeping the formal guarantees tied to the simplified model and its conditions.
summary.tldr: Theory and experiments identify constraints on spontaneous topic changes in self-attention models that differ from patterns of human thought.

title: Dynamics of Spontaneous Topic Changes in Next Token Prediction with Self-Attention

abstract: Process reward models (PRMs) offer fine-grained, step-level evaluations that facilitate deeper reasoning processes in large language models (LLMs), proving effective in complex tasks like mathematical reasoning. However, developing PRMs is challenging due to the high cost and limited scalability of human-annotated data. Synthetic data from Monte Carlo (MC) estimation is a promising alternative but suffers from a high noise ratio, which can cause overfitting and hinder large-scale training. In this work, we conduct a preliminary study on the noise distribution in synthetic data from MC estimation, identifying that annotation models tend to both underestimate and overestimate step correctness due to limitations in their annotation capabilities. Building on these insights, we propose {\bf S}elf-Denoising Monte {\bf C}arlo {\bf An}notation (\textsc{Scan}), an efficient data synthesis and noise-tolerant learning framework. Our key findings indicate that: (1) Even lightweight models (e.g., 1.5B parameters) can produce high-quality annotations through self-denoising strategy, enabling PRMs to achieve superior performance with only 6\% the inference cost required by vanilla MC estimation. (2) With our robust learning strategy, PRMs can effectively learn from this weak supervision, achieving a 39.2 F1 score improvement (from 19.9 to 59.1) in ProcessBench. Despite using only a compact synthetic dataset, our models surpass strong baselines, including those trained on large-scale human-annotated datasets such as PRM800K. Furthermore, performance continues to improve as we scale up the synthetic data, highlighting the potential of \textsc{Scan} for scalable, cost-efficient, and robust PRM training.

Human step annotations are costly, while Monte Carlo estimates offer a scalable alternative with substantial noise. The authors find that annotation models can both underestimate and overestimate whether a step is correct.

The framework combines self-denoising data synthesis with a learning strategy designed to tolerate noisy labels. This addresses annotation quality and the reward model’s ability to learn from imperfect supervision together. The authors report that even a 1.5-billion-parameter annotation model can produce high-quality labels through self-denoising, supporting superior reward-model performance at only 6% of the inference cost of vanilla Monte Carlo estimation.

On ProcessBench, the robust learning strategy raises F1 from 19.9 to 59.1, an increase of 39.2 points. Models trained on a compact synthetic dataset outperform strong baselines, including models trained on large human-annotated datasets such as PRM800K. Performance also improves as synthetic data increases. These findings support denoising and noise-tolerant learning as complementary routes to more scalable step-level reward supervision.
summary.tldr: SCAN combines self-denoising annotations with noise-tolerant learning to improve process reward models at substantially lower annotation cost.

title: SCAN: Self-Denoising Monte Carlo Annotation for Robust Process Reward Learning

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated advanced capabilities in real-world agentic applications. Growing research efforts aim to develop LLM-based agents to address practical demands, introducing a new challenge: agentic scenarios often involve lengthy instructions with complex constraints, such as extended system prompts and detailed tool specifications. While adherence to such instructions is crucial for agentic applications, whether LLMs can reliably follow them remains underexplored. In this paper, we introduce AgentIF, the first benchmark for systematically evaluating LLM instruction following ability in agentic scenarios. AgentIF features three key characteristics: (1) Realistic, constructed from $50$ real-world agentic applications. (2) Long, averaging $1,723$ words with a maximum of $15,630$ words. (3) Complex, averaging $11.9$ constraints per instruction, covering diverse constraint types, such as tool specifications and condition constraints.To construct AgentIF, we collect $707$ human-annotated instructions across $50$ agentic tasks from industrial application agents and open-source agentic systems. For each instruction, we annotate the associated constraints and corresponding evaluation metrics, including code-based evaluation, LLM-based evaluation, and hybrid code-LLM evaluation.We use AgentIF to systematically evaluate existing advanced LLMs. We observe that current models generally perform poorly, especially in handling complex constraint structures and tool specifications. We further conduct error analysis and analytical experiments on instruction length and meta constraints, providing some findings about the failure modes of existing LLMs. We have released the code and data to facilitate future research.

AgentIF tests whether models actually follow these requirements in realistic agent settings. Its focus is instruction adherence when a task involves many interacting constraints, a capability that existing agent demonstrations do not by themselves establish.
