Instructions average 1,723 words and reach 15,630 words, with an average of 11.9 constraints each. The authors annotate individual constraints and assign evaluation procedures using code, language-model judgments, or combinations of both.

The evaluated advanced models generally perform poorly, particularly on complex constraint structures and tool specifications. Additional analyses examine errors, instruction length, and meta constraints to investigate failure patterns. These findings make the benchmark useful for distinguishing an agent’s apparent task competence from its ability to obey detailed operating instructions, while grounding that assessment in requirements collected from actual applications.
summary.tldr: AgentIF exposes weaknesses in advanced language models’ ability to follow long, complex instructions drawn from real agent applications.

title: AGENTIF: Benchmarking Large Language Models Instruction Following Ability in Agentic Scenarios

abstract: Models such as Word2Vec and GloVe construct word embeddings based on the co-occurrence probability $P(i,j)$ of words $i$ and $j$ in text corpora. The resulting vectors $W_i$ not only group semantically similar words but also exhibit a striking linear analogy structure---for example, $W_{\text{king}} - W_{\text{man}} + W_{\text{woman}} \approx W_{\text{queen}}$---whose theoretical origin remains unclear. Previous observations indicate that this analogy structure: (i) already emerges in the top eigenvectors of the matrix $M(i,j) = P(i,j)/P(i)P(j)$, (ii) strengthens and then saturates as more eigenvectors of $M (i, j)$, which controls the dimension of the embeddings, are included, (iii) is enhanced when using $\log M(i,j)$ rather than $M(i,j)$, and (iv) persists even when all word pairs involved in a specific analogy relation (e.g., king--queen, man--woman) are removed from the corpus. To explain these phenomena, we introduce a theoretical generative model in which words are defined by binary semantic attributes, and co-occurrence probabilities are derived from attribute-based interactions. This model analytically reproduces the emergence of linear analogy structure and naturally accounts for properties (i)--(iv). It can be viewed as giving fine-grained resolution into the role of each additional embedding dimension. It is robust to various forms of noise and agrees well with co-occurrence statistics measured on Wikipedia and the analogy benchmark introduced by Mikolov et al.
originalAbstract: Models such as Word2Vec and GloVe construct word embeddings based on the co-occurrence probability $P(i,j)$ of words $i$ and $j$ in text corpora. The resulting vectors $W_i$ not only group semantically similar words but also exhibit a striking linear analogy structure---for example, $W_{\text{king}} - W_{\text{man}} + W_{\text{woman}} \approx W_{\text{queen}}$---whose theoretical origin remains unclear. Previous observations indicate that this analogy structure: (i) already emerges in the top eigenvectors of the matrix $M(i,j) = P(i,j)/P(i)P(j)$, (ii) strengthens and then saturates as more eigenvectors of $M (i, j)$, which controls the dimension of the embeddings, are included, (iii) is enhanced when using $\log M(i,j)$ rather than $M(i,j)$, and (iv) persists even when all word pairs involved in a specific analogy relation (e.g., king--queen, man--woman) are removed from the corpus. To explain these phenomena, we introduce a theoretical generative model in which words are defined by binary semantic attributes, and co-occurrence probabilities are derived from attribute-based interactions. This model analytically reproduces the emergence of linear analogy structure and naturally accounts for properties (i)--(iv). It can be viewed as giving fine-grained resolution into the role of each additional embedding dimension. It is robust to various forms of noise and agrees well with co-occurrence statistics measured on Wikipedia and the analogy benchmark introduced by Mikolov et al.

paragraphs: Word embeddings often represent analogies through vector arithmetic, even though they are learned from word co-occurrence statistics. This paper asks why that structure emerges. It develops a generative model in which words have binary semantic attributes and the interactions between those attributes determine how likely words are to appear together.

The model analytically reproduces several observed patterns. Analogies appear in the leading eigenvectors of a normalized co-occurrence matrix, improve and then saturate as more embedding dimensions are included, and become stronger when the matrix is transformed logarithmically. The model also explains why an analogy can persist after the directly involved word pairs are removed from the corpus.

This account connects individual embedding dimensions to the semantic structure underlying co-occurrence, providing a more detailed explanation than the observation that similar words cluster together. The authors report robustness to several forms of noise and agreement with Wikipedia co-occurrence statistics and an established analogy benchmark. These findings support the proposed attribute-based model as an explanation of the observed patterns.
summary.tldr: A semantic-attribute generative model explains several observed ways that linear analogies emerge from word co-occurrence statistics.

title: On the Emergence of Linear Analogies in Word Embeddings

abstract: Many \textit{Deep Reinforcement Learning} (DRL) algorithms are sensitive to time discretization, which reduces their performance in real-world scenarios. We propose Continuous Soft Actor-Critic, an off-policy actor-critic DRL algorithm in continuous time and space. It is robust to environment time discretization. We also extend the framework to multi-agent scenarios. This \textit{Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning} (MARL) algorithm is suitable for both competitive and cooperative settings. Policy evaluation employs stochastic control theory, with loss functions derived from martingale orthogonality conditions. We establish scaling principles for hyperparameters of the algorithm as the environment time discretization $\delta t$ changes ($\delta t \rightarrow 0$). We provide theoretical proofs for the relevant theorems. To validate the algorithm's effectiveness, we conduct comparative experiments between the proposed algorithm and other mainstream methods across multiple tasks in \textit{Virtual Multi-Agent System} (VMAS). Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed algorithm achieves robust performance across various environments with different time discretization parameter settings, outperforming other methods.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning performance can depend strongly on how an environment divides time into steps. Changing that interval can therefore affect an algorithm even when the underlying task remains similar. Continuous Soft Actor-Critic addresses this sensitivity with an off-policy actor-critic formulation built in continuous time and space, aiming for robustness to the environment's time discretization.

Policy evaluation uses stochastic control theory, with learning losses derived from martingale orthogonality conditions. The paper also establishes how algorithm hyperparameters should scale as the time interval changes and approaches zero, and provides theoretical proofs for the relevant results. This makes the treatment of time resolution an explicit part of the learning framework.

The framework extends to multiple agents in both cooperative and competitive settings. Comparisons with mainstream methods on tasks in the Virtual Multi-Agent System environment show robust performance across different time discretizations and better results than the compared approaches. The contribution joins a continuous-time theoretical formulation with empirical evidence that changing the simulation step need not undermine performance in the evaluated tasks.
summary.tldr: Continuous Soft Actor-Critic uses continuous-time learning and hyperparameter scaling to remain robust across environment time resolutions.

title: Continuous Soft Actor-Critic: An Off-Policy Learning Method Robust to Time Discretization

abstract: We argue that the machine learning value chain is structurally unsustainable due to an economic data processing inequality: each state in the data cycle from inputs to model weights to synthetic outputs refines technical signal but strips economic equity from data generators. We show, by analyzing seventy-three public data deals, that the majority of value accrues to aggregators, with documented creator royalties rounding to zero and widespread opacity of deal terms. This is not just an economic welfare concern: as data and its derivatives become economic assets, the feedback loop that sustains current learning algorithms is at risk. We identify three structural faults - missing provenance, asymmetric bargaining power, and non-dynamic pricing - as the operational machinery of this inequality. In our analysis, we trace these problems along the machine learning value chain and propose an Equitable Data-Value Exchange (EDVEX) Framework to enable a minimal market that benefits all participants. Finally, we outline research directions where our community can make concrete contributions to data deals and contextualize our position with related and orthogonal viewpoints.

paragraphs: This paper argues that the economics of AI training can undermine the people and organizations that originally generate data. Its central claim is that moving from source data to model weights and then synthetic outputs can improve technical usefulness while stripping away the original generators’ economic share. The authors describe this pattern as an economic data processing inequality.

Their analysis covers seventy-three public data deals. They report that aggregators capture most of the value, documented creator royalties round to zero, and deal terms are frequently opaque. They identify three structural contributors: missing records of data origins, unequal bargaining power, and pricing that does not change dynamically. These issues connect the allocation of revenue to how data moves through the machine learning value chain.

The proposed Equitable Data-Value Exchange framework aims to support a minimal market that benefits all participants. The authors also outline research directions for improving data deals. Their broader argument is that compensation affects more than fairness: weakening incentives for data generators could threaten the feedback loop on which learning systems depend.
summary.tldr: An analysis of public data deals motivates a framework intended to give original data generators a more sustainable share of AI’s economic value.

title: A Sustainable AI Economy Needs Data Deals That Work for Generators

abstract: Deepfake detection remains a pressing challenge, particularly in real-world settings where smartphone-captured media from digital screens often introduces Moiré artifacts that can distort detection outcomes. This study systematically evaluates state-of-the-art (SOTA) deepfake detectors on Moiré-affected videos—an issue that has received little attention. We collected a dataset of 12,832 videos, spanning 35.64 hours, from Celeb-DF, DFD, DFDC, UADFV, and FF++ datasets, capturing footage under diverse real-world conditions, including varying screens, smartphones, lighting setups, and camera angles. To further examine the influence of Moiré patterns on deepfake detection, we conducted additional experiments using our DeepMoiréFake, referred to as (DMF) dataset, and two synthetic Moiré generation techniques. Across 15 top-performing detectors, our results show that Moiré artifacts degrade performance by as much as 25.4\%, while synthetically generated Moiré patterns lead to a 21.4\% drop in accuracy. Surprisingly, demoiréing methods, intended as a mitigation approach, instead worsened the problem, reducing accuracy by up to 16\%. These findings underscore the urgent need for detection models that can robustly handle Moiré distortions alongside other real-world challenges, such as compression, sharpening, and blurring. By introducing the DMF dataset, we aim to drive future research toward closing the gap between controlled experiments and practical deepfake detection.

paragraphs: Recording a digital screen with a smartphone can introduce Moiré patterns that interfere with deepfake detection. This paper studies that practical capture condition using DeepMoiréFake, a dataset of 12,832 videos totaling 35.64 hours. The recordings draw from five existing deepfake datasets and vary screens, phones, lighting, and camera angles.

The authors evaluate 15 leading detectors on the captured videos and conduct further experiments with two synthetic Moiré generation methods. Real capture artifacts reduce detector performance by as much as 25.4%, while synthetic patterns produce a reported accuracy decrease of 21.4%. These findings show that the screen-to-camera recording process can materially affect detection outcomes.

Applying demoiréing methods does not solve the problem in the reported tests. Instead, those methods reduce accuracy by up to another reported 16%. The dataset therefore provides a concrete way to evaluate robustness to a distortion that can arise in actual media handling. The results motivate detectors that account for Moiré alongside other practical image changes such as compression, sharpening, and blur.
summary.tldr: DeepMoiréFake shows substantial deepfake-detection failures on screen-recorded videos, with tested Moiré-removal methods also worsening accuracy.

title: Through the Lens: Benchmarking Deepfake Detectors Against Moiré-Induced Distortions

abstract: Recently, Large Language Models (LLMs) have been increasingly used to support various decision-making tasks, assisting humans in making informed decisions. However, when LLMs confidently provide incorrect information, it can lead humans to make suboptimal decisions. To prevent LLMs from generating incorrect information on topics they are unsure of and to improve the accuracy of generated content, prior works have proposed Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG), where external documents are referenced to generate responses. However, previous RAG methods focus only on retrieving documents most relevant to the input query, without specifically aiming to ensure that the human user's decisions are well-calibrated. To address this limitation, we propose a novel retrieval method called Calibrated Retrieval-Augmented Generation (CalibRAG), which ensures that decisions informed by RAG are well-calibrated. Then we empirically validate that CalibRAG improves calibration performance as well as accuracy, compared to other baselines across various datasets.

paragraphs: Language models can influence human decisions even when their answers are confidently wrong. Retrieval-augmented generation brings external documents into response generation to improve the information available to the model. This paper argues that retrieving documents primarily for relevance leaves another important objective insufficiently addressed: how well calibrated the resulting human decisions are.

CalibRAG introduces a retrieval method explicitly oriented toward calibration. In this setting, the concern is whether confidence in decisions informed by the generated response fits their reliability. The approach therefore evaluates the role of retrieved evidence through its contribution to decision-making, extending the aim beyond selecting documents closely related to the original query.

Across multiple datasets, the authors find that CalibRAG improves both calibration and accuracy relative to comparison methods. Those findings support treating calibration as a retrieval objective alongside the usefulness of evidence for answering a question. The central contribution is connecting document retrieval to the reliability of downstream decisions, with empirical results indicating that improved calibration can accompany improved accuracy in the evaluated tasks.
summary.tldr: CalibRAG retrieves evidence with decision calibration in mind, improving both calibration and accuracy across evaluated datasets.

title: Reliable Decision‑Making via Calibration‑Oriented Retrieval‑Augmented Generation

abstract: Despite recent efforts in Large Language Model (LLM) safety and alignment, current adversarial attacks on frontier LLMs can still consistently force harmful generations. Although adversarial training has been widely studied and shown to significantly improve the robustness of traditional machine learning models, its strengths and weaknesses in the context of LLMs are less understood. Specifically, while existing discrete adversarial attacks are effective at producing harmful content, training LLMs with concrete adversarial prompts is often computationally expensive, leading to reliance on continuous relaxations. At the same time, despite their effectiveness and generalization capabilities, training with continuous perturbations does not always capture the full spectrum of vulnerabilities exploited by discrete attacks. In this work, we aim to bridge this gap by introducing MIXAT, a novel method that combines stronger discrete and faster continuous attacks during training. We rigorously evaluate MIXAT across a wide spectrum of state-of-the-art attacks, proposing the *At Least One Attack Success Rate* (ALO-ASR) metric to capture the worst-case vulnerability of models. We show MIXAT achieves substantially better robustness (ALO-ASR $< 20\%$) compared to prior defenses (ALO-ASR $> 50\%$), while maintaining a runtime comparable to methods based on continuous relaxations. We further analyze MIXAT in realistic deployment settings, exploring how chat templates, quantization, low-rank adapters, and temperature affect both adversarial training and evaluation, revealing additional blind spots in current methodologies. Our results demonstrate that MIXAT discrete-continuous defense offers a principled and superior robustness-accuracy tradeoff with minimal computational overhead, highlighting its promise for building safer LLMs. We provide our code and models at https://github.com/insait-institute/MixAT.

Faster continuous perturbations provide an alternative, but they do not always represent the vulnerabilities exposed by discrete prompt attacks. MIXAT combines these two sources of adversarial examples.

The method uses stronger discrete attacks alongside faster continuous attacks during training. Its evaluation introduces At Least One Attack Success Rate, or ALO-ASR, to capture whether any attack in the evaluated collection succeeds. This emphasizes vulnerability across the attack suite instead of allowing strong performance against some attacks to obscure a successful attack elsewhere.

The authors also examine chat templates, quantization, low-rank adapters, and temperature in deployment-oriented training and evaluation. These analyses reveal additional methodological blind spots. The results support combining attack types as a practical robustness improvement with limited added computation, while the reported success rate still reflects remaining vulnerabilities.
summary.tldr: MIXAT combines discrete and continuous adversarial training to reduce measured attack success while retaining runtime comparable to continuous-only approaches.

title: MixAT: Combining Continuous and Discrete Adversarial Training for LLMs

abstract: Compositional Zero-Shot Learning (CZSL) aims to recognize novel attribute-object compositions based on the knowledge learned from seen ones. Existing methods suffer from performance degradation caused by the distribution shift of label space at test time, which stems from the inclusion of unseen compositions recombined from attributes and objects. To overcome the challenge, we propose a novel approach that accumulates comprehensive knowledge in both textual and visual modalities from unsupervised data to update multimodal prototypes at test time. Building on this, we further design an adaptive update weight to control the degree of prototype adjustment, enabling the model to flexibly adapt to distribution shift during testing. Moreover, a dynamic priority queue is introduced that stores high-confidence images to acquire visual knowledge from historical images for inference. Considering the semantic consistency of multimodal knowledge, we align textual and visual prototypes by multimodal collaborative representation learning. Extensive experiments indicate that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on four benchmark datasets under both closed-world and open-world settings. Code will be available at [https://github.com/xud-yan/TOMCAT](https://github.com/xud-yan/TOMCAT).

paragraphs: Compositional zero-shot learning recognizes attribute-object combinations that were absent during training by reusing knowledge of their components. Testing introduces unfamiliar combinations into the label space, creating a distribution shift that can reduce accuracy. TOMCAT responds by adapting the model's multimodal prototypes, its representative descriptions of categories, during testing.

The method gathers textual and visual knowledge from unlabeled data and uses an adaptive weight to control how strongly each prototype changes. A dynamic priority queue retains high-confidence images, allowing later predictions to draw on visual information from earlier inputs. Multimodal collaborative representation learning aligns the textual and visual prototypes so their accumulated knowledge remains semantically consistent.

Experiments report state-of-the-art performance on four benchmark datasets in both closed-world and open-world settings. The approach combines adaptation to current test data with memory of useful past images. Its stated findings support updating category representations at test time as a way to handle the changed composition space, while coordinating the text and image information used in those updates.
summary.tldr: TOMCAT updates aligned text and image prototypes from unlabeled test data to improve recognition of unseen attribute-object combinations.

title: TOMCAT: Test-time Comprehensive Knowledge Accumulation for Compositional Zero-Shot Learning

abstract: Despite the importance of aligning language models with human preferences, crowd-sourced human feedback is often noisy---for example, preferring less desirable responses---posing a fundamental challenge to alignment. A truly robust alignment objective should yield identical model parameters even under severe label noise, a property known as redescending. We prove that no existing alignment methods satisfy this property. To address this, we propose Hölder-DPO, the first principled alignment loss with a provable redescending property, enabling estimation of the clean data distribution from noisy feedback. The aligned model estimates the likelihood of clean data, providing a theoretically grounded metric for dataset valuation that identifies the location and fraction of mislabels. This metric is gradient-free, enabling scalable and automated human feedback valuation without costly manual verification or clean validation dataset. Hölder-DPO achieves state-of-the-art robust alignment performance while accurately detecting mislabels in controlled datasets. Finally, applied to Anthropic HH-RLHF dataset, it reveals substantial noise levels and removing these mislabels significantly improves alignment performance across methods. The code is available at https://github.com/ma921/HolderDPO.

paragraphs: Human preference datasets can contain incorrect judgments, such as labels favoring a less desirable response. This paper studies alignment objectives that remain robust to severe label noise through a property called redescending. In the paper's formulation, this means retaining the same model parameters despite that noise; the authors prove that existing alignment methods do not satisfy the property.

They introduce Hölder-DPO, an alignment loss with a provable redescending property. The resulting aligned model estimates the clean-data likelihood, which also provides a metric for valuing feedback data. The authors report state-of-the-art robust alignment performance and accurate mislabel detection on controlled datasets. Applied to Anthropic HH-RLHF, the method identifies substantial noise, and removing the identified mislabels significantly improves alignment across methods. The contribution connects robust training with dataset assessment: a model trained to withstand corrupted feedback also supplies evidence for finding problematic labels.
summary.tldr: Hölder-DPO combines provably robust preference alignment with a scalable metric for detecting and valuing noisy human feedback.

title: Scalable Valuation of Human Feedback through Provably Robust Model Alignment

abstract: We study the problem of multiclass learning with bandit feedback in both the i.i.d. batch and adversarial online models. In the *uniform* learning framework, it is well known that no hypothesis class $\mathcal{H}$ is learnable in either model when the effective number of labels is unbounded. In contrast, within the *universal* learning framework, recent works by (Hanneke et al., 2025b) and (Hanneke et al., 2025a) have established surprising exact equivalences between learnability under bandit feedback and full supervision in both the i.i.d. batch and adversarial online models, respectively. This raises a natural question: What happens in the *non-uniform* learning framework, which lies between the uniform and universal learning frameworks? Our contributions are twofold: (1) We provide a combinatorial characterization of learnable hypothesis classes in both models, in the realizable and agnostic settings, within the non-uniform learning framework. Notably, this includes elementary and natural hypothesis classes, such as a countably infinite collection of constant functions over some domain that is learnable in both models. (2) We construct a hypothesis class that is non-uniformly learnable under full supervision in the adversarial online model (and thus also in the i.i.d. batch model), but not non-uniformly learnable under bandit feedback in the i.i.d. batch model (and thus also not in the adversarial online model). This serves as our main novel technical contribution that reveals a fundamental distinction between the non-uniform and universal learning frameworks.

paragraphs: This paper studies multiclass learning with limited bandit feedback under the non-uniform learning framework. It considers both independently sampled batch data and adversarial online data. The motivation is a gap between known results: unbounded effective label sets prevent uniform learnability, while universal learning admits exact equivalences between bandit feedback and full supervision.

The authors give combinatorial characterizations of non-uniformly learnable hypothesis classes in both models, covering realizable and agnostic settings. Their results include natural examples such as a countably infinite collection of constant functions that remains learnable in both models. This establishes that the restrictions from uniform learning do not simply carry over unchanged.

The main separation result constructs a class learnable non-uniformly with full supervision even in the adversarial online model, but not learnable non-uniformly with bandit feedback even in the batch model. Thus, the equivalence established for universal learning does not extend to non-uniform learning. The contribution precisely distinguishes these frameworks by showing where the amount of feedback changes which classes can be learned.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes non-uniform multiclass learnability and shows that full supervision can enable learning where bandit feedback cannot.

title: Non-Uniform Multiclass Learning with Bandit Feedback

abstract: Time normalization is the task of converting natural language temporal expressions into machine-readable representations. It underpins many downstream applications in information retrieval, question answering, and clinical decision-making. Traditional systems based on the ISO-TimeML schema limit expressivity and struggle with complex constructs such as compositional, event-relative, and multi-span time expressions. In this work, we introduce a novel formulation of time normalization as a code generation task grounded in the SCATE framework, which defines temporal semantics through symbolic and compositional operators. We implement a fully executable SCATE Python library and demonstrate that large language models (LLMs) can generate executable SCATE code. Leveraging this capability, we develop an automatic data augmentation pipeline using LLMs to synthesize large-scale annotated data with code-level validation. Our experiments show that small, locally deployable models trained on this augmented data can achieve strong performance, outperforming even their LLM parents and enabling practical, accurate, and interpretable time normalization.

paragraphs: Time normalization turns expressions about time into representations that software can use. The difficult cases include expressions composed from several parts, times defined relative to events, and expressions spread across multiple text spans. The paper argues that traditional systems based on ISO-TimeML have limited ability to represent these constructions.

The proposed approach treats normalization as generating executable code. It uses SCATE, a framework whose symbolic operators express how temporal meanings combine, and implements those operators in a Python library. Large language models generate SCATE programs, allowing temporal interpretations to take an explicit, executable form rather than remaining only textual answers.

The authors also use large language models to generate annotated training data, with validation at the code level. Small models trained on this augmented data achieve strong experimental performance and outperform the larger models that generated their training examples. This combination connects expressive temporal representations with locally deployable models, making the resulting interpretations practical to compute and easier to inspect.
summary.tldr: Executable temporal code and validated synthetic training data let small local models outperform their LLM teachers at time normalization.

title: A Semantic Parsing Framework for End-to-End Time Normalization

abstract: The function of biomolecules such as proteins depends on their ability to interconvert between a wide range of structures or conformations. Researchers have endeavored for decades to develop computational methods to predict the distribution of conformations, which is far harder to determine experimentally than a static folded structure. We present ConforMix, an inference-time algorithm that enhances sampling of conformational distributions using a combination of classifier guidance, filtering, and free energy estimation. Our approach upgrades diffusion models---whether trained for static structure prediction or conformational generation---to enable more efficient discovery of conformational variability without requiring prior knowledge of major degrees of freedom. ConforMix is orthogonal to improvements in model pretraining and would benefit even a hypothetical model that perfectly reproduced the Boltzmann distribution. Remarkably, when applied to a diffusion model trained for static structure prediction, ConforMix captures structural changes including domain motion, cryptic pocket flexibility, and transporter cycling, while avoiding unphysical states. Case studies of biologically critical proteins demonstrate the scalability, accuracy, and utility of this method.

paragraphs: Biomolecules function by moving among different structures, so a single folded shape provides only part of the picture. ConforMix improves sampling of these conformational distributions at inference time. It combines classifier guidance, filtering, and free-energy estimation to help diffusion models discover structural variability more efficiently.

The method can be applied to models trained either for static structure prediction or for conformational generation. It does not require prior knowledge of the major degrees of freedom that describe a molecule’s motion. The authors also argue that its sampling benefits are complementary to better pretraining: even a hypothetical model reproducing the Boltzmann distribution perfectly would benefit from the approach.

Applied to a model trained for static structures, ConforMix captures domain motion, flexibility in cryptic pockets, and transporter cycling while avoiding unphysical states in the reported results. Case studies of biologically important proteins demonstrate scalability, accuracy, and utility. The contribution is a way to draw richer structural behavior from diffusion models through the sampling procedure, without requiring that variability to be known beforehand.
summary.tldr: ConforMix improves inference-time sampling of biomolecular conformations, revealing structural variability even from diffusion models trained for static prediction.

title: Unlocking hidden biomolecular conformational landscapes in diffusion models at inference time

abstract: Multimodal learning holds the promise for richer information extraction by capturing dependencies across data sources. Yet, current training methods often underperform due to modality competition, a phenomenon where modalities contend for training resources, leaving some underoptimized. This raises a pivotal question: how can we address training imbalances, ensure adequate optimization across all modalities, and achieve consistent performance improvements as we transition from unimodal to multimodal data? This paper proposes the Multimodal Competition Regularizer (MCR), inspired by a mutual information (MI) decomposition designed to prevent the adverse effects of competition in multimodal training. Our key contributions are: 1) A game-theoretic framework that adaptively balances modality contributions by encouraging each to maximize its informative role in the final prediction. 2) Refining lower and upper bounds for each MI term to enhance the extraction of both task-relevant unique and shared information across modalities. 3) Proposing latent space permutations for conditional MI estimation, significantly improving computational efficiency. MCR outperforms all previously suggested training strategies and simple baselines, demonstrating that training modalities jointly lead to important performance gains on synthetic and large real-world datasets. We release our code and models at https://github.com/kkontras/MCR.

paragraphs: Combining several kinds of data can give a model more useful information, but joint training can leave some inputs underused. The paper calls this modality competition: different data sources compete during optimization, and some never receive adequate training. The Multimodal Competition Regularizer, or MCR, addresses this imbalance by encouraging each modality to contribute useful information to the final prediction.

MCR frames training as a game and uses a decomposition of mutual information to distinguish information that modalities contribute individually from information they share. It refines mathematical bounds used to estimate these contributions. The method also permutes representations in the model’s internal feature space to estimate conditional mutual information more efficiently, making the proposed regularization more computationally practical.

On synthetic and large real-world datasets, the authors report that MCR outperforms the compared training strategies and simple baselines. These findings support the value of actively balancing informative contributions during joint training. They show performance gains from combining modalities in the evaluated settings, rather than assuming that adding data sources automatically improves a model.
summary.tldr: MCR uses game-theoretic regularization to balance information contributions from different modalities and improve joint training.

title: Balancing Multimodal Training Through Game-Theoretic Regularization

abstract: Embodied agents powered by large language models (LLMs), such as Voyager, promise open-ended competence in worlds such as Minecraft. However, when powered by open-weight LLMs they still falter on elementary tasks after domain-specific fine-tuning. We propose MindForge, a generative-agent framework for cultural lifelong learning through explicit perspective taking. We introduce three key innovations: (1) a structured theory of mind representation linking percepts, beliefs, desires, and actions; (2) natural inter-agent communication; and (3) a multi-component memory system. Following the cultural learning framework, we test MindForge in both instructive and collaborative settings within Minecraft. In an instructive setting with GPT-4, MindForge agents powered by open-weight LLMs significantly outperform their Voyager counterparts in basic tasks yielding $3\times$ more tech-tree milestones and collecting $2.3\times$ more unique items than the Voyager baseline. Furthermore, in fully collaborative settings, we find that the performance of two underachieving agents improves with more communication rounds, echoing the Condorcet Jury Theorem. MindForge agents demonstrate sophisticated behaviors, including expert-novice knowledge transfer, collaborative problem solving, and adaptation to out-of-distribution tasks through accumulated cultural experiences.

paragraphs: MindForge studies how embodied language-model agents can improve by learning through interaction with other agents. Its starting problem is that agents using open-weight models can struggle with basic Minecraft tasks even after domain-specific fine-tuning. The framework makes perspective taking and accumulated social experience explicit parts of the agent’s operation.

Three components support this approach: a structured representation connecting perceptions, beliefs, desires, and actions; natural communication between agents; and a memory system with multiple components. Together, these provide mechanisms for representing perspectives, exchanging knowledge, and retaining experience. The authors evaluate both instruction-based learning and fully collaborative activity in Minecraft.

In the instructive setting involving GPT-4, open-weight MindForge agents reach three times as many technology-tree milestones and collect 2.3 times as many unique items as Voyager counterparts. In collaborative settings, two initially underperforming agents improve with additional communication rounds. The authors also observe knowledge transfer between experts and novices, joint problem solving, and adaptation to unfamiliar tasks through accumulated cultural experience. These findings support social learning as a useful component of the evaluated embodied agents.
summary.tldr: MindForge combines perspective taking, communication, and memory to help Minecraft agents learn from instruction and collaboration.

title: MindForge: Empowering Embodied Agents with Theory of Mind for Lifelong Cultural Learning

abstract: The success of DeepSeek-R1 demonstrates the immense potential of using reinforcement learning (RL) to enhance LLMs' reasoning capabilities. This paper introduces Retrv-R1, the first R1-style MLLM specifically designed for multimodal universal retrieval, achieving higher performance by employing step-by-step reasoning to produce more accurate retrieval results. We find that directly applying the methods of DeepSeek-R1 to retrieval tasks is not feasible, mainly due to (1) the high computational cost caused by the large token consumption required for multiple candidates with reasoning processes, and (2) the instability and suboptimal results when directly applying RL to train for retrieval tasks. To address these issues, Retrv-R1 introduces an information compression module with a details inspection mechanism, which enhances computational efficiency by reducing the number of tokens while ensuring that critical information for challenging candidates is preserved. Additionally, a new training paradigm is proposed, including an activation stage using a retrieval-tailored synthetic CoT dataset for more effective optimization, followed by RL with a novel curriculum reward to improve both performance and efficiency. Incorporating these novel designs, Retrv-R1 achieves SOTA performance, high efficiency, and strong generalization ability, as demonstrated by extensive experiments across multiple benchmarks and tasks.

paragraphs: Retrv-R1 uses step-by-step reasoning to improve multimodal retrieval. The authors identify two obstacles to transferring R1-style reinforcement learning directly to this task. Reasoning over multiple candidates consumes many tokens, making retrieval expensive. Direct reinforcement-learning training also produces instability and suboptimal results, motivating changes to both information processing and training.

The framework compresses candidate information to reduce token use and adds a mechanism for inspecting details. This is intended to retain critical information when a candidate is difficult to judge. Its training begins with an activation stage using synthetic reasoning examples tailored to retrieval. Reinforcement learning follows, with a curriculum reward designed to improve both retrieval performance and efficiency.

Across multiple benchmarks and tasks, the authors report state-of-the-art performance, high efficiency, and strong generalization. The contribution is the coordinated design: compression addresses the cost of considering candidates, detail inspection protects difficult judgments, and staged training addresses optimization problems. Together, these changes make reasoning-based retrieval more effective in the reported evaluations.
summary.tldr: Retrv-R1 combines compressed candidate information, selective detail inspection, and staged reinforcement learning to improve multimodal retrieval.

title: Retrv-R1: A Reasoning-Driven MLLM Framework for Universal and Efficient Multimodal Retrieval

abstract: The rapid advancement of generative models, such as GANs and Diffusion models, has enabled the creation of highly realistic synthetic images, raising serious concerns about misinformation, deepfakes, and copyright infringement. Although numerous Artificial Intelligence Generated Image (AIGI) detectors have been proposed, often reporting high accuracy, their effectiveness in real-world scenarios remains questionable. To bridge this gap, we introduce AIGIBench, a comprehensive benchmark designed to rigorously evaluate the robustness and generalization capabilities of state-of-the-art AIGI detectors. AIGIBench simulates real-world challenges through four core tasks: multi-source generalization, robustness to image degradation, sensitivity to data augmentation, and impact of test-time pre-processing. It includes 23 diverse fake image subsets that span both advanced and widely adopted image generation techniques, along with real-world samples collected from social media and AI art platforms. Extensive experiments on 11 advanced detectors demonstrate that, despite their high reported accuracy in controlled settings, these detectors suffer significant performance drops on real-world data, limited benefits from common augmentations, and nuanced effects of pre-processing, highlighting the need for more robust detection strategies. By providing a unified and realistic evaluation framework, AIGIBench offers valuable insights to guide future research toward dependable and generalizable AIGI detection.

paragraphs: High accuracy on a controlled image dataset does not necessarily show that an AI-image detector will work reliably on images encountered elsewhere. This paper introduces AIGIBench to examine that gap. Its purpose is to test robustness and generalization under conditions that better reflect the variety of generated images and their real-world presentation.

The benchmark covers four questions: whether detectors generalize across image sources, withstand image degradation, benefit from data augmentation, and respond well to preprocessing at test time. It includes 23 fake-image subsets spanning different generation techniques, together with samples collected from social media and AI art platforms. This makes the evaluation broader than testing one familiar source of synthetic images.

Experiments with 11 advanced detectors reveal substantial performance drops on real-world data despite strong reported results in controlled settings. Common augmentations offer limited benefits, and preprocessing has nuanced effects. These findings show why detection cannot be judged from a single accuracy figure and provide a shared framework for developing more dependable methods.
summary.tldr: AIGIBench finds that strong controlled-test accuracy does not translate into reliable real-world AI-image detection for the 11 detectors evaluated.

title: Is Artificial Intelligence Generated Image Detection a Solved Problem?

abstract: Matrix factorization is among the most successful techniques for collaborative filtering. One challenge of collaborative filtering is how to utilize available auxiliary information to improve prediction accuracy. In this paper, we study the problem of utilizing auxiliary information as features of factorization and propose formalizing the problem as general functional matrix factorization, whose model includes conventional matrix factorization models as its special cases. Moreover, we propose a gradient boosting based algorithm to efficiently solve the optimization problem. Finally, we give two specific algorithms for efficient feature function construction for two specific tasks. Our method can construct more suitable feature functions by searching in an infinite functional space based on training data and thus can yield better prediction accuracy. The experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms the baseline methods on three real-world datasets.

paragraphs: Matrix factorization is a widely used approach to collaborative filtering, but useful auxiliary information can be difficult to incorporate into its predictions. This paper treats that information as features of the factorization and introduces general functional matrix factorization. Conventional matrix factorization models are included as special cases of the proposed formulation.

The authors develop a gradient-boosting algorithm to solve the associated optimization problem efficiently. They also give two specialized algorithms for constructing feature functions for two particular tasks. The central flexibility is that feature functions are learned from training data through a search over an infinite function space, allowing the representation to adapt to the prediction problem.

That flexibility can produce more suitable features and thereby improve prediction accuracy. On three real-world datasets, the proposed method outperforms the baseline methods used in the experiments. The contribution combines a more general modeling formulation with a practical optimization procedure, showing how auxiliary information can become part of the factorization itself.
summary.tldr: General functional matrix factorization uses gradient boosting to learn auxiliary-information features, improving predictions over the reported baselines.

title: General Functional Matrix Factorization Using Gradient Boosting

abstract: Canonical correlation analysis (CCA) is a well established technique for identifying linear relationships among two variable sets. Kernel CCA (KCCA) is the most notable nonlinear extension but it lacks interpretability and robustness against irrelevant features. The aim of this article is to introduce two nonlinear CCA extensions that rely on the recently proposed Hilbert-Schmidt independence criterion and the centered kernel target alignment. These extensions determine linear projections that provide maximally dependent projected data pairs. The paper demonstrates that the use of linear projections allows removing irrelevant features, whilst extracting combinations of strongly associated features. This is exemplified through a simulation and the analysis of recorded data that are available in the literature.

paragraphs: Canonical correlation analysis identifies relationships between two sets of variables by finding suitable linear combinations of each. Kernel CCA extends the search to nonlinear relationships, but the paper identifies difficulties with interpreting its results and handling irrelevant features. The aim is to capture richer dependence while retaining projections that remain connected to the original variables.

The authors introduce two extensions based on the Hilbert-Schmidt independence criterion and centered kernel target alignment. Both methods seek linear projections whose resulting data pairs are maximally dependent according to their chosen criterion. The nonlinear aspect lies in how dependence is measured, while the projections themselves remain linear.

This design allows the methods to remove irrelevant features and extract combinations of features with strong associations. A simulation and an analysis of previously available recorded data illustrate these capabilities. The contribution is a way to combine nonlinear dependence assessment with a more interpretable representation, making the selected combinations of original features part of the explanation of the relationship.
summary.tldr: Two CCA extensions use nonlinear dependence criteria with linear projections to identify associated feature combinations and remove irrelevant features.

title: Canonical Correlation Analysis based on Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion and Centered Kernel Target Alignment

abstract: Online learning with delayed feedback has received increasing attention recently due to its several applications in distributed, web-based learning problems. In this paper we provide a systematic study of the topic, and analyze the effect of delay on the regret of online learning algorithms. Somewhat surprisingly, it turns out that delay increases the regret in a multiplicative way in adversarial problems, and in an additive way in stochastic problems. We give meta-algorithms that transform, in a black-box fashion, algorithms developed for the non-delayed case into ones that can handle the presence of delays in the feedback loop. Modifications of the well-known UCB algorithm are also developed for the bandit problem with delayed feedback, with the advantage over the meta-algorithms that they can be implemented with lower complexity.

paragraphs: Online learners may need to make new decisions before receiving feedback on earlier ones. This is relevant to distributed and web-based learning systems. The paper studies how such delays affect regret, the performance gap used to assess an online learner relative to a comparison strategy.

The analysis distinguishes adversarial from stochastic problems. In the studied adversarial setting, delay affects regret multiplicatively; in the stochastic setting, it contributes additively. This distinction matters because the same practical obstacle has a different mathematical effect depending on how the learning environment is modeled.

The authors provide general meta-algorithms that adapt existing methods for immediate feedback to delayed feedback through a black-box transformation. They also develop versions of UCB specifically for bandit problems with delays. These specialized versions can be implemented with lower complexity than the general transformations. The paper therefore offers both an account of the cost of delay and practical ways to modify learning algorithms to handle it.
summary.tldr: The paper analyzes delay's differing effects on adversarial and stochastic regret and adapts online learners to delayed feedback.

title: Online Learning under Delayed Feedback

abstract: We introduce a novel algorithm to compute nonnegative sparse principal components of positive semidefinite (PSD) matrices. Our algorithm comes with approximation guarantees contingent on the spectral profile of the input matrix A: the sharper the eigenvalue decay, the better the approximation quality. If the eigenvalues decay like any asymptotically vanishing function, we can approximate nonnegative sparse PCA within any accuracy εin time polynomial in the matrix size n and desired sparsity k, but not in 1/ε. Further, we obtain a data-dependent bound that is computed by executing an algorithm on a given data set. This bound is significantly tighter than a-priori bounds and can be used to show that for all tested datasets our algorithm is provably within 40%-90% from the unknown optimum. Our algorithm is combinatorial and explores a subspace defined by the leading eigenvectors of A. We test our scheme on several data sets, showing that it matches or outperforms the previous state of the art.

paragraphs: The paper studies principal components that must be both sparse and nonnegative for a positive semidefinite input matrix. These requirements constrain which components are allowed, making approximation quality an important concern. The proposed combinatorial algorithm searches a subspace determined by the matrix’s leading eigenvectors.

Its guarantees depend on the input spectrum: faster eigenvalue decay yields better approximation quality. When eigenvalues decay according to an asymptotically vanishing function, the algorithm can reach any requested accuracy with running time polynomial in matrix size and desired sparsity. The running time is not polynomial in inverse accuracy, so requesting greater precision has a distinct computational cost.

The authors also compute a dataset-specific bound by running an algorithm on the observed data. This bound is substantially tighter than the advance guarantees and certifies the reported proximity to the unknown optimum on every tested dataset. Empirically, the method matches or exceeds the compared state of the art. The contribution combines competitive solutions with evidence about their approximation quality.
summary.tldr: A combinatorial algorithm for nonnegative sparse PCA provides spectrum-dependent guarantees and tighter dataset-specific certificates of approximation quality.

title: Nonnegative Sparse PCA with Provable Guarantees

abstract: We investigate a new Follow the Perturbed Leader (FTPL) algorithm for online structured prediction problems. We show a regret bound which is comparable to the state of the art of FTPL algorithms and is comparable with the best possible regret in some cases. To better understand FTPL algorithms for online structured learning, we present a lower bound on the regret for a large and natural class of FTPL algorithms that use logconcave perturbations. We complete our investigation with an online shortest path experiment and empirically show that our algorithm is both statistically and computationally efficient.

To better understand FTPL algorithms for online structured learning, we present a lower bound on the regret for a large and natural class of FTPL algorithms that use logconcave perturbations. We complete our investigation with an online shortest path experiment and empirically show that our algorithm is both statistically and computationally efficient.

paragraphs: Online structured prediction involves making a sequence of decisions whose outputs have internal structure. This paper investigates a new Follow the Perturbed Leader algorithm for such problems. Its analysis centers on regret, which measures the accumulated cost of the learner's decisions relative to a comparison choice over the same sequence.

The authors prove a regret bound comparable to existing leading FTPL bounds and, in some cases, comparable to the best achievable regret. They also establish a lower bound for a broad, natural class of FTPL algorithms using logconcave perturbations. This second result helps characterize the limits of that algorithmic class alongside the performance guarantee for the new method.

An online shortest-path experiment provides an empirical test involving structured decisions. The results show both statistical and computational efficiency in that setting. The paper thus combines an algorithm, an upper bound on its regret, and a lower bound for a related class, while reserving the strongest comparison to optimal regret for the cases where it applies.
summary.tldr: A new FTPL algorithm offers competitive regret for online structured prediction, alongside a lower bound for algorithms with logconcave perturbations.

title: Following the Perturbed Leader for Online Structured Learning

abstract: We introduce a new anomaly detection methodology for data with latent dependency structure. As a particular instantiation, we derive a hidden Markov anomaly detector that extends the regular one-class support vector machine. We optimize the approach, which is non-convex, via a DC (difference of convex functions) algorithm, and show that the parameter v can be conveniently used to control the number of outliers in the model. The empirical evaluation on artificial and real data from the domains of computational biology and computational sustainability shows that the approach can achieve significantly higher anomaly detection performance than the regular one-class SVM.

paragraphs: Anomaly detection seeks observations that do not fit the pattern a model treats as normal. This paper focuses on data whose dependencies involve hidden structure. Its central idea is to account for those latent relationships when deciding what counts as an anomaly, extending the modeling framework beyond the regular one-class support vector machine.

As a specific instance of the broader methodology, the authors derive a hidden Markov anomaly detector. The resulting optimization problem is nonconvex, and they address it with a difference-of-convex-functions algorithm. They also show that the parameter v provides a convenient way to control the number of outliers in the model.

Experiments use artificial data and real data from computational biology and computational sustainability. The results show that the approach can achieve significantly better anomaly detection than a regular one-class SVM. This is an empirical finding about the potential benefit of representing latent dependencies, supporting their inclusion when building an anomaly detector for structured data.
summary.tldr: A hidden Markov extension of the one-class SVM models latent dependencies and can substantially improve anomaly detection.

title: Hidden Markov Anomaly Detection

abstract: The rank aggregation problem has been studied with varying desiderata in varied communities such as Theoretical Computer Science, Statistics, Information Retrieval and Social Welfare Theory. We introduce a variant of this problem we call distributional rank aggregation, where the ranking data is only available via the induced distribution over the set of all permutations. We provide a novel translation of the usual social welfare theory axioms to this setting. As we show this allows for a more quantitative characterization of these axioms: which then are not only less prone to misinterpretation, but also allow simpler proofs for some key impossibility theorems. Most importantly, these quantitative characterizations lead to natural and novel relaxations of these axioms, which as we show, allow us to get around celebrated impossibility results in social choice theory. We are able to completely characterize the class of positional scoring rules with respect to our axioms and show that Borda Count is optimal in a certain sense.

paragraphs: Rank aggregation combines ranking information into an overall ordering. This paper studies a version in which the available information is a probability distribution over all possible rankings. That shift changes how desirable properties of an aggregation rule should be expressed, since the input is distributional rather than presented directly as a collection of individual rankings.

The authors translate familiar social welfare axioms into this setting and give them quantitative characterizations. Making the axioms quantitative helps clarify their meaning and simplifies proofs of some impossibility theorems. More significantly, it creates natural ways to relax the requirements. Under those relaxed requirements, the authors show how to avoid certain celebrated impossibility results in social choice theory.

The paper also completely characterizes positional scoring rules with respect to its axioms and establishes an optimality result for Borda Count in a particular sense. That qualification is essential: it is an optimality statement within the proposed analysis, not universal superiority over every ranking method. The work connects distributional information with precisely adjustable aggregation requirements.
summary.tldr: Distributional rank aggregation makes social choice axioms quantitative, enabling relaxations and a qualified optimality result for Borda Count.

title: Distributional Rank Aggregation, and an Axiomatic Analysis

abstract: Recently, there has been considerable progress on designing algorithms with provable guarantees —typically using linear algebraic methods—for parameter learning in latent variable models. Designing provable algorithms for inference has proved more difficult. Here we take a first step towards provable inference in topic models. We leverage a property of topic models that enables us to construct simple linear estimators for the unknown topic proportions that have small variance, and consequently can work with short documents. Our estimators also correspond to finding an estimate around which the posterior is well-concentrated. We show lower bounds that for shorter documents it can be information theoretically impossible to find the hidden topics. Finally, we give empirical results that demonstrate that our algorithm works on realistic topic models. It yields good solutions on synthetic data and runs in time comparable to a single iteration of Gibbs sampling.

paragraphs: Learning a topic model's parameters and inferring the topic proportions of a document are distinct tasks. The paper addresses the latter, where provable algorithms have been harder to develop. It aims to recover the unknown mixture of topics in a document, including when the document contains relatively little text.

The authors exploit a property of topic models to construct simple linear estimators with small variance. Their estimates also identify a point around which the posterior distribution is concentrated. This connects the computationally simple estimate to the model's distribution of plausible topic proportions, providing more justification than a point prediction alone.

The paper also proves lower bounds showing that sufficiently short documents can make hidden-topic recovery information-theoretically impossible. This establishes a real data limitation alongside the positive inference results. Empirically, the algorithm works with realistic topic models, gives good solutions on synthetic data, and takes time comparable to a single Gibbs-sampling iteration. The combined message is efficient, justified inference within the information available in the document.
summary.tldr: Low-variance linear estimators enable provable topic-proportion inference, alongside lower bounds on what short documents can reveal.

title: Provable Algorithms for Inference in Topic Models

abstract: We introduce Mix and match (M&M) – a training framework designed to facilitate rapid and effective learning in RL agents that would be too slow or too challenging to train otherwise.The key innovation is a procedure that allows us to automatically form a curriculum over agents. Through such a curriculum we can progressively train more complex agents by, effectively, bootstrapping from solutions found by simpler agents.In contradistinction to typical curriculum learning approaches, we do not gradually modify the tasks or environments presented, but instead use a process to gradually alter how the policy is represented internally.We show the broad applicability of our method by demonstrating significant performance gains in three different experimental setups: (1) We train an agent able to control more than 700 actions in a challenging 3D first-person task; using our method to progress through an action-space curriculum we achieve both faster training and better final performance than one obtains using traditional methods.(2) We further show that M&M can be used successfully to progress through a curriculum of architectural variants defining an agents internal state. (3) Finally, we illustrate how a variant of our method can be used to improve agent performance in a multitask setting.

paragraphs: Some reinforcement learning agents are difficult to train because their policy representations are complex from the outset. Mix and Match addresses this by constructing a curriculum over agents themselves. It progressively trains more complex agents using solutions discovered by simpler ones, allowing earlier learning to support later stages of training.

The curriculum changes how the policy is represented internally, rather than gradually changing the tasks or environments. The framework can progress through action spaces or through architectural variants that define an agent’s internal state. This makes agent design part of the training progression instead of fixing its full complexity at the beginning.

The authors report significant performance gains in three experimental setups. In a challenging 3D first-person task with more than 700 actions, an action-space curriculum produces faster training and better final performance than traditional methods. They also demonstrate successful architectural curricula and a variant that improves multitask performance. These examples support the framework’s applicability across several forms of agent complexity.
summary.tldr: Mix and Match trains increasingly complex reinforcement learning agents by building on simpler agents through curricula over policy representations.

title: Mix & Match Agent Curricula for Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Probabilistic programming languages are a flexible tool for specifying statistical models, but this flexibility comes at the cost of efficient analysis. It is currently difficult to compactly represent the subtle independence properties of a probabilistic program, and exploit independence properties to decompose inference. Classical graphical model abstractions do capture some properties of the underlying distribution, enabling inference algorithms to operate at the level of the graph topology. However, we observe that graph-based abstractions are often too coarse to capture interesting properties of programs. We propose a form of sound abstraction for probabilistic programs wherein the abstractions are themselves simplified programs. We provide a theoretical foundation for these abstractions, as well as an algorithm to generate them. Experimentally, we also illustrate the practical benefits of our framework as a tool to decompose probabilistic program inference.

paragraphs: Probabilistic programs offer a flexible way to express statistical models, but their structure can be difficult to exploit for efficient inference. In particular, useful independence relationships may be subtle. Graphical abstractions expose some distributional structure, yet the authors argue that graphs can be too coarse to capture properties that matter within programs.

Their alternative is to represent an abstraction as a simplified program. Keeping a program-shaped representation gives the framework another way to express structure relevant to decomposing inference. The authors provide a theoretical foundation for sound abstractions and an algorithm that generates them, connecting the representation choice to a principled construction procedure.

Experiments illustrate practical benefits when the framework is used to split probabilistic inference into components. The contribution therefore spans both formal reasoning and computational organization: simplified programs serve as abstractions that help expose opportunities for decomposition. The reported evidence illustrates the utility of this approach without asserting that every probabilistic program admits the same degree of simplification.
summary.tldr: Sound abstractions expressed as simplified programs expose structure that can help decompose probabilistic inference.

title: Sound Abstraction and Decomposition of Probabilistic Programs

abstract: Image generation has been successfully cast as an autoregressive sequence generation or transformation problem. Recent work has shown that self-attention is an effective way of modeling textual sequences. In this work, we generalize a recently proposed model architecture based on self-attention, the Transformer, to a sequence modeling formulation of image generation with a tractable likelihood. By restricting the self-attention mechanism to attend to local neighborhoods we significantly increase the size of images the model can process in practice, despite maintaining significantly larger receptive fields per layer than typical convolutional neural networks. While conceptually simple, our generative models significantly outperform the current state of the art in image generation on ImageNet, improving the best published negative log-likelihood on ImageNet from 3.83 to 3.77. We also present results on image super-resolution with a large magnification ratio, applying an encoder-decoder configuration of our architecture. In a human evaluation study, we find that images generated by our super-resolution model fool human observers three times more often than the previous state of the art.

paragraphs: The Image Transformer adapts a self-attention architecture to image generation formulated as a sequence modeling problem. Its autoregressive formulation provides a tractable likelihood, allowing the model to assign an evaluable probability to an image. The work extends an architecture used for textual sequences to the dependencies involved in generating images.

The main practical adjustment restricts attention to local neighborhoods. This lets the model process substantially larger images while still giving each layer a larger receptive field than typical convolutional networks. The approach therefore uses local attention to balance the amount of image context available to a layer with the computational demands of processing that context.

On ImageNet, the authors improve the best published negative log-likelihood from 3.83 to 3.77. They also apply an encoder-decoder version to image super-resolution with a large magnification ratio. In a human evaluation, its outputs fool observers three times as often as the previous leading method. These findings cover both probabilistic image generation and the perceived realism of enlarged images.
summary.tldr: Local self-attention makes Transformer image generation practical and improves reported image likelihood and super-resolution realism.

title: Image Transformer

abstract: Bandit is a framework for designing sequential experiments, where a learner selects an arm $A \in \mathcal{A}$ and obtains an observation corresponding to $A$ in each experiment. Theoretically, the tight regret lower-bound for the general bandit is polynomial with respect to the number of arms $|\mathcal{A}|$, and thus, to overcome this bound, the bandit problem with side-information is often considered. Recently, a bandit framework over a causal graph was introduced, where the structure of the causal graph is available as side-information and the arms are identified with interventions on the causal graph. Existing algorithms for causal bandit overcame the $\Omega(\sqrt{|\mathcal{A}|/T})$ simple-regret lower-bound; however, their algorithms work only when the interventions $\mathcal{A}$ are localized around a single node (i.e., an intervention propagates only to its neighbors). We then propose a novel causal bandit algorithm for an arbitrary set of interventions, which can propagate throughout the causal graph. We also show that it achieves $O(\sqrt{ \gamma^*\log(|\mathcal{A}|T) / T})$ regret bound, where $\gamma^*$ is determined by using a causal graph structure. In particular, if the maximum in-degree of the causal graph is a constant, then $\gamma^* = O(N^2)$, where $N$ is the number of nodes.

paragraphs: A bandit learner chooses an experiment, observes its outcome, and uses that information to guide later choices. In a causal bandit problem, experiments are interventions on a causal graph whose structure is available to the learner. This structure supplies information beyond the list of possible actions and can improve on general bandit guarantees that depend strongly on the number of actions.

Earlier causal bandit algorithms considered interventions restricted to effects around a single node. The proposed algorithm handles an arbitrary intervention set, allowing effects to propagate throughout the causal graph. This extends the framework to experiments whose consequences travel beyond the immediate neighborhood of an intervention.

The authors bound regret by a quantity of order sqrt(gamma* log(|A|T)/T), where T is the experiment count and gamma* depends on graph structure. If the maximum number of incoming edges per node is constant, gamma* is O(N²) for N nodes. The guarantee therefore connects learning difficulty to causal structure, with the stated incoming-edge condition giving a concrete bound.
summary.tldr: A causal bandit algorithm handles interventions whose effects propagate through the graph, with regret controlled by a graph-dependent quantity.

title: Causal Bandits with Propagating Inference

abstract: We study the problem of off-policy evaluation (OPE) in Reinforcement Learning (RL), where the aim is to estimate the performance of a new policy given historical data that may have been generated by a different policy, or policies. In particular, we introduce a novel doubly-robust estimator for the OPE problem in RL, based on the Targeted Maximum Likelihood Estimation principle from the statistical causal inference literature. We also introduce several variance reduction techniques that lead to impressive performance gains in off-policy evaluation. We show empirically that our estimator uniformly wins over existing off-policy evaluation methods across multiple RL environments and various levels of model misspecification. Finally, we further the existing theoretical analysis of estimators for the RL off-policy estimation problem by showing their $O_P(1/\sqrt{n})$ rate of convergence and characterizing their asymptotic distribution.

paragraphs: Off-policy evaluation estimates how a new decision policy would perform using historical data collected by other policies. This is challenging because the available observations reflect earlier decision-making behavior. The paper introduces a doubly robust estimator for reinforcement-learning evaluation, drawing on Targeted Maximum Likelihood Estimation, a principle developed in statistical causal inference.

The authors also develop several variance-reduction techniques to improve the estimator’s performance. Reducing variance addresses how much an evaluation estimate fluctuates with the available data. Their empirical comparisons span multiple reinforcement-learning environments and different degrees of model misspecification, allowing the evaluation to include settings where modeling choices do not accurately capture the underlying problem.

Across the tested conditions, the proposed estimator beats the existing methods considered. The paper also advances the theoretical analysis of off-policy estimators by establishing a convergence rate proportional to one over the square root of sample size, in probability, and characterizing their asymptotic distribution. These results combine favorable experimental comparisons with a description of estimation behavior as data increases.
summary.tldr: A targeted-learning estimator with variance reduction improves off-policy evaluation across tested environments and comes with asymptotic statistical analysis.

title: More Efficient Off-Policy Evaluation through Regularized Targeted Learning

abstract: Causal inference requires assumptions about the data generating process, many of which are unverifiable from the data. Given that some causal assumptions might be uncertain or disputed, formal methods are needed to quantify how sensitive research conclusions are to violations of those assumptions. Although an extensive literature exists on the topic, most results are limited to specific model structures, while a general-purpose algorithmic framework for sensitivity analysis is still lacking. In this paper, we develop a formal, systematic approach to sensitivity analysis for arbitrary linear Structural Causal Models (SCMs). We start by formalizing sensitivity analysis as a constrained identification problem. We then develop an efficient, graph-based identification algorithm that exploits non-zero constraints on both directed and bidirected edges. This allows researchers to systematically derive sensitivity curves for a target causal quantity with an arbitrary set of path coefficients and error covariances as sensitivity parameters. These results can be used to display the degree to which violations of causal assumptions affect the target quantity of interest, and to judge, on scientific grounds, whether problematic degrees of violations are plausible.
