paragraphs: Causal conclusions depend on assumptions about how data were generated, and some of those assumptions cannot be verified from observations alone. This paper develops a systematic way to ask how a conclusion changes when uncertain assumptions are violated. Its scope is arbitrary linear structural causal models.

The authors formulate sensitivity analysis as a constrained identification problem and introduce an efficient graph-based algorithm. The algorithm uses nonzero constraints on directed and bidirected edges. Researchers can select path coefficients and error covariances as sensitivity parameters, allowing the analysis to represent uncertainty about different aspects of the causal model.

The resulting sensitivity curves show how a target causal quantity changes as those parameters vary. This makes the consequences of assumption violations explicit and helps identify violations large enough to alter a substantive conclusion. Researchers can then use scientific knowledge to judge whether those violations are plausible. The contribution broadens algorithmic sensitivity analysis beyond methods tailored to particular model structures, while retaining the linear-model setting.
summary.tldr: A graph-based framework derives sensitivity curves showing how causal quantities in linear structural models respond to assumption violations.

title: Sensitivity Analysis of Linear Structural Causal Models

abstract: Graph sparsification has been used to improve the computational cost of learning over graphs, e.g., Laplacian-regularized estimation and graph semi-supervised learning (SSL). However, when graphs vary over time, repeated sparsification requires polynomial order computational cost per update. We propose a new type of graph sparsification namely fault-tolerant (FT) sparsification to significantly reduce the cost to only a constant. Then the computational cost of subsequent graph learning tasks can be significantly improved with limited loss in their accuracy. In particular, we give theoretical analyze to upper bound the loss in the accuracy of the subsequent Laplacian-regularized estimation and graph SSL, due to the FT sparsification. In addition, FT spectral sparsification can be generalized to FT cut sparsification, for cut-based graph learning. Extensive experiments have confirmed the computational efficiencies and accuracies of the proposed methods for learning on dynamic graphs.

paragraphs: Graph sparsification reduces the computational burden of learning on graphs by providing a smaller graph representation. When the graph changes over time, repeatedly rebuilding that representation can itself become expensive. The paper focuses on this maintenance problem, where previous repeated sparsification requires computational work of polynomial order for each update.

The authors introduce fault-tolerant sparsification to reduce that update cost to a constant. The resulting sparse graphs can also make subsequent learning computations substantially cheaper while limiting accuracy loss. The paper gives theoretical upper bounds on the accuracy degradation caused by sparsification for Laplacian-regularized estimation and graph semi-supervised learning.

The framework extends from spectral sparsification to cut sparsification, making it relevant to learning methods based on graph cuts as well. Extensive experiments support the claimed computational efficiency and accuracy on changing graphs. The contribution therefore addresses both sides of using a compact graph representation: keeping it inexpensive to maintain as the graph evolves, and controlling how much its simplification affects the learning task performed afterward.
summary.tldr: Fault-tolerant sparsification reduces graph-update costs to a constant while bounding accuracy loss for subsequent graph learning.

title: Improved Dynamic Graph Learning through Fault-Tolerant Sparsification

abstract: Unordered, variable-sized inputs arise in many settings across multiple fields. The ability for set- and multiset-oriented neural networks to handle this type of input has been the focus of much work in recent years. We propose to represent multisets using complex-weighted multiset automata and show how the multiset representations of certain existing neural architectures can be viewed as special cases of ours. Namely, (1) we provide a new theoretical and intuitive justification for the Transformer model’s representation of positions using sinusoidal functions, and (2) we extend the DeepSets model to use complex numbers, enabling it to outperform the existing model on an extension of one of their tasks.

paragraphs: Many learning problems involve inputs whose size varies and whose ordering is irrelevant. Multisets provide a way to describe such collections while allowing repeated elements. This paper proposes representing them with complex-weighted multiset automata, creating a framework for examining how neural architectures encode unordered data.

The authors show that representations used by certain existing architectures fit within this framework as special cases. One consequence is a new theoretical and intuitive explanation for the sinusoidal functions used to represent positions in Transformers. This connects a familiar neural-network design choice to a broader account of representation using complex weights.

The framework also suggests a concrete modification to DeepSets: extending the model to use complex numbers. The resulting model outperforms the existing version on an extension of one of its tasks. The contribution therefore spans explanation and design, both clarifying existing representations and motivating a tested modification. The reported performance advantage is specific to that task extension, rather than a claim about every unordered-data problem.
summary.tldr: Complex-weighted multiset automata connect existing neural representations and motivate a complex-valued DeepSets extension with a demonstrated task-specific improvement.

title: Representing Unordered Data Using Complex-Weighted Multiset Automata

abstract: A complementary label (CL) simply indicates an incorrect class of an example, but learning with CLs results in multi-class classifiers that can predict the correct class. Unfortunately, the problem setting only allows a single CL for each example, which notably limits its potential since our labelers may easily identify multiple CLs (MCLs) to one example. In this paper, we propose a novel problem setting to allow MCLs for each example and two ways for learning with MCLs. In the first way, we design two wrappers that decompose MCLs into many single CLs, so that we could use any method for learning with CLs. However, the supervision information that MCLs hold is conceptually diluted after decomposition. Thus, in the second way, we derive an unbiased risk estimator; minimizing it processes each set of MCLs as a whole and possesses an estimation error bound. We further improve the second way into minimizing properly chosen upper bounds. Experiments show that the former way works well for learning with MCLs but the latter is even better.

Unfortunately, the problem setting only allows a single CL for each example, which notably limits its potential since our labelers may easily identify multiple CLs (MCLs) to one example. In this paper, we propose a novel problem setting to allow MCLs for each example and two ways for learning with MCLs. In the first way, we design two wrappers that decompose MCLs into many single CLs, so that we could use any method for learning with CLs. However, the supervision information that MCLs hold is conceptually diluted after decomposition. Thus, in the second way, we derive an unbiased risk estimator; minimizing it processes each set of MCLs as a whole and possesses an estimation error bound. paragraphs: A complementary label tells a classifier which class an example does not belong to. Such labels can still support learning to predict the correct class, but allowing only one excluded class per example wastes information when annotators can identify several. This paper introduces a learning setting that accepts multiple complementary labels for each example.

The authors develop two routes for using that information. The first provides two wrappers that split a set of excluded classes into individual complementary labels, allowing existing single-label methods to be reused. The paper argues that this decomposition conceptually dilutes the supervision carried by the original set.

The second route keeps each set intact and derives an unbiased estimator of the classification risk, together with an estimation error bound. The authors further develop this approach by minimizing appropriately chosen upper bounds. Experiments show that decomposition works well, but the set-based approach performs better. The findings favor using the joint information in several excluded classes rather than relying solely on their separate contributions.
summary.tldr: Learning from sets of incorrect labels preserves supervision that splitting them into individual labels can dilute, and performs better in the reported experiments.

title: Learning with Multiple Complementary Labels

abstract: Randomized smoothing, using just a simple isotropic Gaussian distribution, has been shown to produce good robustness guarantees against $\ell_2$-norm bounded adversaries. In this work, we show that extending the smoothing technique to defend against other attack models can be challenging, especially in the high-dimensional regime. In particular, for a vast class of i.i.d. smoothing distributions, we prove that the largest $\ell_p$-radius that can be certified decreases as $O(1/d^{\frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{p}})$ with dimension $d$ for $p > 2$. Notably, for $p \geq 2$, this dependence on $d$ is no better than that of the $\ell_p$-radius that can be certified using isotropic Gaussian smoothing, essentially putting a matching lower bound on the robustness radius. When restricted to \emph{generalized} Gaussian smoothing, these two bounds can be shown to be within a constant factor of each other in an asymptotic sense, establishing that Gaussian smoothing provides the best possible results, up to a constant factor, when $p \geq 2$. We present experimental results on CIFAR to validate our theory. For other smoothing distributions, such as, a uniform distribution within an $\ell_1$ or an $\ell_\infty$-norm ball, we show upper bounds of the form $O(1 / d)$ and $O(1 / d^{1 - \frac{1}{p}})$ respectively, which have an even worse dependence on $d$.

paragraphs: Randomized smoothing can provide certificates that a model withstands bounded adversarial perturbations. Gaussian smoothing already offers useful guarantees for perturbations measured with the l2 norm. This paper asks how well smoothing can extend to other norms, particularly when the input has many dimensions.

For a broad class of independent, identically distributed smoothing distributions, the authors prove that the largest certifiable lp radius scales no better than O(1/d^(1/2 − 1/p)) for p greater than 2. Here, d is input dimension. The certificate therefore shrinks as dimension increases. For p at least 2, the dimension dependence does not improve on isotropic Gaussian smoothing.

Within generalized Gaussian smoothing, the relevant bounds asymptotically agree up to a constant factor, making Gaussian smoothing optimal to that precision. The paper also gives worse dimension-dependent upper bounds for uniform smoothing within l1 and l-infinity balls. Experiments on CIFAR support the theory. The result identifies limits on the certificates obtainable through these smoothing families, rather than claiming that every robustness approach faces the same restriction.
summary.tldr: For broad smoothing families, certifiable robustness under lp perturbations with p greater than 2 deteriorates with dimension and cannot improve on Gaussian dimension scaling.

title: Curse of Dimensionality on Randomized Smoothing for Certifiable Robustness

abstract: Tensor network (TN) decomposition is a promising framework to represent extremely high-dimensional problems with few parameters. However, it is challenging to search the (near-)optimal topological structures for TN decomposition, since the number of candidate solutions exponentially grows with increasing the order of a tensor. In this paper, we claim that the issue can be practically tackled by evolutionary algorithms in an affordable manner. We encode the complex topological structures into binary strings, and develop a simple genetic meta-algorithm to search the optimal topology on Hamming space. The experimental results by both synthetic and real-world data demonstrate that our method can effectively discover the ground-truth topology or even better structures with a small number of generations, and significantly boost the representational power of TN decomposition compared with well-known tensor-train (TT) or tensor-ring (TR) models.

In this paper, we claim that the issue can be practically tackled by evolutionary algorithms in an affordable manner. We encode the complex topological structures into binary strings, and develop a simple genetic meta-algorithm to search the optimal topology on Hamming space. The experimental results by both synthetic and real-world data demonstrate that our method can effectively discover the ground-truth topology or even better structures with a small number of generations, and significantly boost the representational power of TN decomposition compared with well-known tensor-train (TT) or tensor-ring (TR) models.

paragraphs: Tensor networks represent very high-dimensional problems using relatively few parameters. Their effectiveness depends on topology: the pattern of connections among the components of the decomposition. Choosing that pattern becomes difficult as tensor order increases because the number of candidate structures grows exponentially. The paper investigates whether evolutionary search can make this choice practically manageable.

The authors encode network topologies as binary strings and develop a genetic meta-algorithm to search over them. This converts complicated structural choices into a search in Hamming space, where candidate encodings differ in their binary entries. The proposal is a practical way to explore topology choices without fixing a standard structure in advance.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world data show that the method can discover the ground-truth topology, or structures reported to be better, within a small number of generations. The resulting decompositions have substantially stronger representational power than tensor-train and tensor-ring models in those evaluations. The findings support evolutionary search as an affordable empirical approach to this large structural search problem.
summary.tldr: Encoding tensor-network topologies as binary strings enables evolutionary search that finds effective structures in relatively few generations in experiments.

title: Evolutionary Topology Search for Tensor Network Decomposition

abstract: The attribution problem, that is the problem of attributing a model’s prediction to its base features, is well-studied. We extend the notion of attribution to also apply to feature interactions. The Shapley value is a commonly used method to attribute a model’s prediction to its base features. We propose a generalization of the Shapley value called Shapley-Taylor index that attributes the model’s prediction to interactions of subsets of features up to some size $k$. The method is analogous to how the truncated Taylor Series decomposes the function value at a certain point using its derivatives at a different point. In fact, we show that the Shapley Taylor index is equal to the Taylor Series of the multilinear extension of the set-theoretic behavior of the model. We axiomatize this method using the standard Shapley axioms—linearity, dummy, symmetry and efficiency—and an additional axiom that we call the interaction distribution axiom. This new axiom explicitly characterizes how interactions are distributed for a class of functions that model pure interaction. We contrast the Shapley-Taylor index against the previously proposed Shapley Interaction index from the cooperative game theory literature. We also apply the Shapley Taylor index to three models and identify interesting qualitative insights.

title: The Shapley Taylor Interaction Index

abstract: When machine predictors can achieve higher performance than the human decision-makers they support, improving the performance of human decision-makers is often conflated with improving machine accuracy. Here we propose a framework to directly support human decision-making, in which the role of machines is to reframe problems rather than to prescribe actions through prediction. Inspired by the success of representation learning in improving performance of machine predictors, our framework learns human-facing representations optimized for human performance. This “Mind Composed with Machine” framework incorporates a human decision-making model directly into the representation learning paradigm and is trained with a novel human-in-the-loop training procedure. We empirically demonstrate the successful application of the framework to various tasks and representational forms.

We empirically demonstrate the successful application of the framework to various tasks and representational forms.

paragraphs: A more accurate machine predictor does not automatically establish that the human using it will make better decisions. This paper makes human performance the direct target of learning. The machine’s role is to change how a problem is represented to a person, with the person still responsible for making the decision.

The proposed Mind Composed with Machine framework adapts representation learning to this human-facing purpose. It incorporates a model of human decision-making into the representation-learning process and uses a new human-in-the-loop training procedure. The representation is therefore optimized in connection with how people make decisions, rather than assessed solely by the accuracy of a machine predictor.

The authors empirically demonstrate successful applications across multiple tasks and forms of representation. These results support learning how to present a problem as a route to better human decision support. The broader contribution is to frame the machine and human as a combined decision-making process, so that the learning objective addresses the performance of the person the system is meant to help.
summary.tldr: Mind Composed with Machine learns problem representations optimized for human decision-making through a human-in-the-loop procedure.

title: Learning Representations by Humans, for Humans

abstract: We consider an online revenue maximization problem over a finite time horizon subject to lower and upper bounds on cost. At each period, an agent receives a context vector sampled i.i.d. from an unknown distribution and needs to make a decision adaptively. The revenue and cost functions depend on the context vector as well as some fixed but possibly unknown parameter vector to be learned. We propose a novel offline benchmark and a new algorithm that mixes an online dual mirror descent scheme with a generic parameter learning process. When the parameter vector is known, we demonstrate an $O(\sqrt{T})$ regret result as well an $O(\sqrt{T})$ bound on the possible constraint violations. When the parameter is not known and must be learned, we demonstrate that the regret and constraint violations are the sums of the previous $O(\sqrt{T})$ terms plus terms that directly depend on the convergence of the learning process.

paragraphs: The paper considers an agent making revenue-seeking decisions over a finite sequence of periods while respecting lower and upper cost bounds. Each period brings a context sampled independently from an unknown distribution. Revenue and cost also depend on a fixed parameter vector, which may itself need to be learned as decisions are made.

The proposed algorithm combines online dual mirror descent with a generic parameter-learning procedure. This creates a framework in which learning the unknown parameters and managing constrained decisions occur together. The authors also introduce an offline benchmark against which the online procedure’s revenue performance can be assessed.

When the parameter vector is known, both regret and possible constraint violations are bounded by terms of order √T, where T is the time horizon. When parameters must be learned, each bound adds a term directly related to the learning procedure’s convergence. This makes the effect of imperfect knowledge explicit: the decision algorithm retains a baseline guarantee, while additional performance and feasibility costs depend on how well the learning component progresses.
summary.tldr: Dual mirror descent combines constrained online decisions with parameter learning, yielding bounds that explicitly reflect learning progress.

title: Joint Online Learning and Decision-making via Dual Mirror Descent

abstract: Offline reinforcement learning is a promising approach for practical applications since it does not require interactions with real-world environments. However, existing offline RL methods only work well in environments with continuous or small discrete action spaces. In environments with large and discrete action spaces, such as recommender systems and dialogue systems, the performance of existing methods decreases drastically because they suffer from inaccurate value estimation for a large proportion of out-of-distribution (o.o.d.) actions. While recent works have demonstrated that online RL benefits from incorporating semantic information in action representations, unfortunately, they fail to learn reasonable relative distances between action representations, which is key to offline RL to reduce the influence of o.o.d. actions. This paper proposes an action representation learning framework for offline RL based on a pseudometric, which measures both the behavioral relation and the data-distributional relation between actions. We provide theoretical analysis on the continuity of the expected Q-values and the offline policy improvement using the learned action representations. Experimental results show that our methods significantly improve the performance of two typical offline RL methods in environments with large and discrete action spaces.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning learns from existing data without further environment interaction. Large discrete action spaces create a particular difficulty: many possible actions fall outside the data distribution, making their values difficult to estimate accurately. The paper targets this problem in settings such as recommendation and dialogue, where the number of available actions can be large.

The proposed framework learns action representations through a pseudometric that measures both behavioral relationships and relationships arising from the data distribution. Relative distances between actions are central to the design. The aim is to organize actions in a way that helps reduce the influence of out-of-distribution actions on offline learning.

The authors analyze continuity of expected Q-values and offline policy improvement with the learned representations. Experiments show significant improvements when the framework is applied to two typical offline reinforcement learning methods in large discrete action spaces. The results support using behavior and data coverage together when constructing representations for actions in this setting.
summary.tldr: Action representations based on behavioral and data-distribution relationships improve offline reinforcement learning with large discrete action spaces.

title: Learning Pseudometric-based Action Representations for Offline Reinforcement Learning

abstract: As a seminal tool in self-supervised representation learning, contrastive learning has gained unprecedented attention in recent years. In essence, contrastive learning aims to leverage pairs of positive and negative samples for representation learning, which relates to exploiting neighborhood information in a feature space. By investigating the connection between contrastive learning and neighborhood component analysis (NCA), we provide a novel stochastic nearest neighbor viewpoint of contrastive learning and subsequently propose a series of contrastive losses that outperform the existing ones. Under our proposed framework, we show a new methodology to design integrated contrastive losses that could simultaneously achieve good accuracy and robustness on downstream tasks. With the integrated framework, we achieve up to 6% improvement on the standard accuracy and 17% improvement on the robust accuracy.

paragraphs: Contrastive learning builds representations using positive and negative sample pairs. Those comparisons also determine which examples become neighbors in the learned feature space. This paper examines that connection through neighborhood component analysis, offering a stochastic nearest-neighbor interpretation of contrastive learning.

The interpretation becomes a basis for designing new training losses. Rather than treating pairwise comparisons only as isolated attractions and separations, the framework relates them to neighborhood information in the representation. The authors propose a series of losses that outperform existing ones and develop an integrated loss-design methodology intended to support both accuracy and robustness on downstream tasks.

With the integrated framework, the authors report improvements of up to 6% in standard accuracy and 17% in robust accuracy. These are the reported upper ends of the improvements, rather than gains promised for every task. The contribution is both conceptual and practical: a neighborhood-based account of contrastive learning leads to concrete objective functions with experimentally improved downstream performance.
summary.tldr: A stochastic nearest-neighbor view of contrastive learning guides new losses that improve standard and robust downstream accuracy.

title: Revisiting Contrastive Learning through the Lens of Neighborhood Component Analysis: an Integrated Framework

abstract: The Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK), defined as the outer product of the neural network (NN) Jacobians, has emerged as a central object of study in deep learning. In the infinite width limit, the NTK can sometimes be computed analytically and is useful for understanding training and generalization of NN architectures. At finite widths, the NTK is also used to better initialize NNs, compare the conditioning across models, perform architecture search, and do meta-learning. Unfortunately, the finite width NTK is notoriously expensive to compute, which severely limits its practical utility. We perform the first in-depth analysis of the compute and memory requirements for NTK computation in finite width networks. Leveraging the structure of neural networks, we further propose two novel algorithms that change the exponent of the compute and memory requirements of the finite width NTK, dramatically improving efficiency. Our algorithms can be applied in a black box fashion to any differentiable function, including those implementing neural networks. We open-source our implementations within the Neural Tangents package at https://github.com/google/neural-tangents.

paragraphs: The neural tangent kernel is built from derivatives describing how a neural network’s outputs change with its parameters. It is useful for studying training and generalization. Although some infinitely wide networks permit analytical kernel calculations, practical finite networks require computations that can be prohibitively expensive in both time and memory.

This paper analyzes those computational and memory requirements in depth. Using the internal structure of neural networks, the authors develop two algorithms that change the exponents governing these costs. The improvement therefore concerns how resource requirements scale with problem size, making finite-width kernel calculations substantially more efficient.

The methods apply as black-box procedures to differentiable functions, including neural networks, and are released in the Neural Tangents package. More efficient computation supports uses already associated with finite-width kernels, including initialization, comparisons of model conditioning, architecture search, and meta-learning. The paper’s central contribution is computational infrastructure that makes this analytical tool more practical to use on finite models.
summary.tldr: Two algorithms improve the scaling of time and memory costs for computing finite-width neural tangent kernels.

title: Fast Finite Width Neural Tangent Kernel

abstract: Discrete black-box optimization problems are challenging for model-based optimization (MBO) algorithms, such as Bayesian optimization, due to the size of the search space and the need to satisfy combinatorial constraints. In particular, these methods require repeatedly solving a complex discrete global optimization problem in the inner loop, where popular heuristic inner-loop solvers introduce approximations and are difficult to adapt to combinatorial constraints. In response, we propose NN+MILP, a general discrete MBO framework using piecewise-linear neural networks as surrogate models and mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) to optimize the acquisition function. MILP provides optimality guarantees and a versatile declarative language for domain-specific constraints. We test our approach on a range of unconstrained and constrained problems, including DNA binding, constrained binary quadratic problems from the MINLPLib benchmark, and the NAS-Bench-101 neural architecture search benchmark. NN+MILP surpasses or matches the performance of black-box algorithms tailored to the constraints at hand, with global optimization of the acquisition problem running in a few minutes using only standard software packages and hardware.

paragraphs: Searching over discrete choices is difficult when evaluating each candidate requires access to a black-box function and valid choices must satisfy combinatorial constraints. Model-based optimization adds another challenge: each search step requires optimizing an acquisition function that selects what to evaluate next. Heuristic solvers approximate this inner problem and can be awkward to adapt to constraints.

MILP supplies a flexible way to state domain-specific constraints and provides optimality guarantees for the acquisition problem. Those guarantees concern candidate selection within the model-based procedure.

The authors test constrained and unconstrained tasks involving DNA binding, binary quadratic optimization, and neural architecture search. Their framework matches or exceeds specialized black-box algorithms in these experiments. Acquisition optimization takes a few minutes with standard software and hardware, showing that a general constrained solver can be practically useful in the reported settings.
summary.tldr: NN+MILP combines neural surrogates with mixed-integer programming to select discrete candidates while handling combinatorial constraints.

title: Constrained Discrete Black-Box Optimization using Mixed-Integer Programming

abstract: Learning effective policies for real-world problems is still an open challenge for the field of reinforcement learning (RL). The main limitation being the amount of data needed and the pace at which that data can be obtained. In this paper, we study how to build lightweight simulators of complicated systems that can run sufficiently fast for deep RL to be applicable. We focus on domains where agents interact with a reduced portion of a larger environment while still being affected by the global dynamics. Our method combines the use of local simulators with learned models that mimic the influence of the global system. The experiments reveal that incorporating this idea into the deep RL workflow can considerably accelerate the training process and presents several opportunities for the future.

paragraphs: Deep reinforcement learning needs substantial experience, so the speed at which training data can be generated can limit its practicality. This paper studies how to construct lightweight simulators for complicated systems. It focuses on environments where an agent directly interacts with only a small part of a larger system but still feels the effects of global dynamics.

The method pairs a local simulator with a learned model of the wider system’s influence. The local component handles the portion with which the agent interacts, while the learned component mimics effects arriving from outside that portion. This combination addresses the central difficulty of local simulation: the agent’s immediate surroundings do not evolve independently of the larger environment.

Experiments show that incorporating these influence-augmented local simulators into a deep reinforcement learning workflow can considerably accelerate training. The finding supports simulator design as a way to address the pace of experience generation. Its relevance is tied to the stated setting, where local interactions and wider influences can be treated through complementary simulation components.
summary.tldr: Local simulators augmented with learned global influences can considerably accelerate reinforcement learning in the studied networked systems.

title: Influence-Augmented Local Simulators: a Scalable Solution for Fast Deep RL in Large Networked Systems

abstract: Out-of-distribution (OOD) detection is the problem of identifying inputs which are unrelated to the in-distribution task. The OOD detection performance when the in-distribution (ID) is ImageNet-1K is commonly being tested on a small range of test OOD datasets. We find that most of the currently used test OOD datasets, including datasets from the open set recognition (OSR) literature, have severe issues: In some cases more than 50$%$ of the dataset contains objects belonging to one of the ID classes. These erroneous samples heavily distort the evaluation of OOD detectors. As a solution, we introduce with NINCO a novel test OOD dataset, each sample checked to be ID free, which with its fine-grained range of OOD classes allows for a detailed analysis of an OOD detector’s strengths and failure modes, particularly when paired with a number of synthetic “OOD unit-tests”. We provide detailed evaluations across a large set of architectures and OOD detection methods on NINCO and the unit-tests, revealing new insights about model weaknesses and the effects of pretraining on OOD detection performance. We provide code and data at https://github.com/j-cb/NINCO.

paragraphs: Out-of-distribution detection asks whether an input falls outside the task a model is intended to handle. This paper examines evaluations where ImageNet-1K defines the in-distribution classes. The authors find serious problems in commonly used outside-distribution test datasets: in some cases, more than half of the samples contain objects belonging to an ImageNet-1K class.

Those samples distort the evaluation because the test treats them as outside the task even though they contain in-distribution objects. To address this, the authors introduce NINCO, a test dataset whose samples have each been checked to exclude in-distribution content. Its fine-grained selection of outside-distribution classes supports a more detailed examination of where detectors succeed or fail.

The paper also introduces synthetic OOD unit tests and evaluates many architectures and detection methods using both these tests and NINCO. The evaluations reveal insights into model weaknesses and the effects of pretraining on detection performance. The contribution centers on improving the evidence used to judge detectors: cleaner test membership and more targeted analyses make performance differences more interpretable.
summary.tldr: NINCO addresses contamination in ImageNet OOD benchmarks with individually checked samples and targeted tests of detector behavior.

title: In or Out? Fixing ImageNet Out-of-Distribution Detection Evaluation

abstract: We study fine-grained error bounds for differentially private algorithms for counting under continual observation. Our main insight is that the matrix mechanism when using lower-triangular matrices can be used in the continual observation model. More specifically, we give an explicit factorization for the counting matrix $M_\mathsf{count}$ and upper bound the error explicitly. We also give a fine-grained analysis, specifying the exact constant in the upper bound. Our analysis is based on upper and lower bounds of the completely bounded norm (cb-norm) of $M_\mathsf{count}$. Along the way, we improve the best-known bound of 28 years by Mathias (SIAM Journal on Matrix Analysis and Applications, 1993) on the cb-norm of $M_\mathsf{count}$ for a large range of the dimension of $M_\mathsf{count}$. Furthermore, we are the first to give concrete error bounds for various problems under continual observation such as binary counting, maintaining a histogram, releasing an approximately cut-preserving synthetic graph, many graph-based statistics, and substring and episode counting. Finally, we note that our result can be used to get a fine-grained error bound for non-interactive local learning and the first lower bounds on the additive error for $(\epsilon,\delta)$-differentially-private counting under continual observation. Subsequent to this work, Henzinger et al. (SODA, 2023) showed that our factorization also achieves fine-grained mean-squared error.

paragraphs: Differentially private counting under continual observation requires releasing useful counts as data arrives while protecting privacy. This paper studies the resulting error in fine detail, including constants that coarse growth-rate descriptions can hide. The goal is to make the accuracy guarantees more explicit across counting and related tasks.

The key observation is that the matrix mechanism can operate in this continual setting when it uses lower-triangular matrices. The authors provide an explicit factorization of the counting matrix and derive an error upper bound with a specified constant. These contributions clarify both achievable accuracy and restrictions on accuracy within the stated privacy setting.
summary.tldr: An explicit matrix factorization yields fine-grained privacy error bounds, including constants, for continually released counts and related statistics.

title: Constant Matters: Fine-grained Error Bound on Differentially Private Continual Observation

abstract: In reinforcement learning from human feedback, it is common to optimize against a reward model trained to predict human preferences. Because the reward model is an imperfect proxy, optimizing its value too much can hinder ground truth performance, in accordance with Goodhart’s law. This effect has been frequently observed, but not carefully measured due to the expense of collecting human preference data. In this work, we use a synthetic setup in which a fixed “gold-standard” reward model plays the role of humans, providing labels used to train a proxy reward model. We study how the gold reward model score changes as we optimize against the proxy reward model using either reinforcement learning or best-of-$n$ sampling. We find that this relationship follows a different functional form depending on the method of optimization, and that in both cases its coefficients scale smoothly with the number of reward model parameters. We also study the effect on this relationship of the size of the reward model dataset, the number of reward model and policy parameters, and the coefficient of the KL penalty added to the reward in the reinforcement learning setup. We explore the implications of these empirical results for theoretical considerations in AI alignment.

The authors optimize the proxy using either reinforcement learning or best-of-n sampling and track the resulting gold-model score. They find that the relationship follows different functional forms for the two optimization methods. In both cases, the fitted coefficients vary smoothly with the number of parameters in the reward model.

The study also examines reward-model dataset size, reward-model and policy size, and the strength of the KL penalty used during reinforcement learning. These empirical relationships help characterize how optimization pressure and model scale interact in this setup. Because the reference judge is itself a fixed model, the measured target is its score. The paper explores what these findings may imply for theoretical questions in AI alignment.
summary.tldr: A synthetic reward-model study finds method-dependent scaling relationships describing how proxy optimization affects a gold-standard model's score.

title: Scaling Laws for Reward Model Overoptimization

abstract: Normalizing flows (NF) are a class of powerful generative models that have gained popularity in recent years due to their ability to model complex distributions with high flexibility and expressiveness. In this work, we introduce a new type of normalizing flow that is tailored for modeling positions and orientations of multiple objects in three-dimensional space, such as molecules in a crystal. Our approach is based on two key ideas: first, we define smooth and expressive flows on the group of unit quaternions, which allows us to capture the continuous rotational motion of rigid bodies; second, we use the double cover property of unit quaternions to define a proper density on the rotation group. This ensures that our model can be trained using standard likelihood-based methods or variational inference with respect to a thermodynamic target density. We evaluate the method by training Boltzmann generators for two molecular examples, namely the multi-modal density of a tetrahedral system in an external field and the ice XI phase in the TIP4P water model. Our flows can be combined with flows operating on the internal degrees of freedom of molecules and constitute an important step towards the modeling of distributions of many interacting molecules.

paragraphs: This paper develops a normalizing flow for distributions over the positions and orientations of multiple rigid objects in three dimensions. Molecules arranged in a crystal provide the motivating example. The challenge is to represent rotations smoothly while assigning valid probabilities to physical orientations, which have a different geometry from ordinary position coordinates.

The authors construct expressive flows on unit quaternions, a representation of three-dimensional rotations. Two opposite unit quaternions describe the same rotation, so the method explicitly accounts for this double representation when defining a density over orientations. That step enables standard likelihood-based training or variational inference against a thermodynamic target distribution.

The method is evaluated through Boltzmann generators for a tetrahedral system with multiple density modes in an external field and for ice XI using the TIP4P water model. The flows can also be combined with models of molecules’ internal degrees of freedom. The contribution is thus a probability-consistent component for molecular sampling, with demonstrations on two systems and a route toward combining rigid motion with internal molecular variation.
summary.tldr: Quaternion-based normalizing flows model rigid molecular positions and orientations while preserving valid probabilities over three-dimensional rotations.

title: Rigid Body Flows for Sampling Molecular Crystal Structures

abstract: Although disentangled representations are often said to be beneficial for downstream tasks, current empirical and theoretical understanding is limited. In this work, we provide evidence that disentangled representations coupled with sparse task-specific predictors improve generalization. In the context of multi-task learning, we prove a new identifiability result that provides conditions under which maximally sparse predictors yield disentangled representations. Motivated by this theoretical result, we propose a practical approach to learn disentangled representations based on a sparsity-promoting bi-level optimization problem. Finally, we explore a meta-learning version of this algorithm based on group Lasso multiclass SVM predictors, for which we derive a tractable dual formulation. It obtains competitive results on standard few-shot classification benchmarks, while each task is using only a fraction of the learned representations.

paragraphs: Disentangled representations are often expected to help downstream learning, but the paper notes that supporting understanding remains limited. It studies their interaction with sparse task-specific predictors: predictors that use only a subset of the available representation. The authors provide evidence that this combination improves generalization.

In multi-task learning, the paper proves an identifiability result giving conditions under which maximally sparse predictors yield disentangled representations. The conditions are central: the result does not say that sparsity always produces disentanglement. Motivated by this connection, the authors formulate a practical learning approach as a bilevel optimization problem that promotes sparsity.

They also develop a meta-learning version using group Lasso multiclass support vector machine predictors and derive a tractable dual formulation. It achieves competitive results on standard few-shot classification benchmarks while each task uses only a fraction of the learned representation. The findings connect a theoretical route to disentanglement with a practical method for learning shared features that individual tasks can use selectively.
summary.tldr: Sparse task-specific predictors can support disentangled representations under stated conditions and yield competitive few-shot learning performance.

title: Synergies between Disentanglement and Sparsity: Generalization and Identifiability in Multi-Task Learning

abstract: Embedding text sequences is a widespread requirement in modern language understanding. Existing approaches focus largely on constant-size representations. This is problematic, as the amount of information contained in text often varies with the length of the input. We propose a solution called Nugget, which encodes language into a representation based on a dynamically selected subset of input tokens. These nuggets are learned through tasks like autoencoding and machine translation, and intuitively segment language into meaningful units. We demonstrate Nugget outperforms related approaches in tasks involving semantic comparison. Finally, we illustrate these compact units allow for expanding the contextual window of a language model (LM), suggesting new future LMs that can condition on significantly larger amounts of content.

paragraphs: Text embeddings often compress every input into a representation of the same size. Nugget starts from the observation that inputs do not all contain the same amount of information, and longer text may need more representational capacity. The paper proposes a representation built from a dynamically selected subset of input tokens instead of relying only on a constant-size summary.

These selected units, called nuggets, are learned through tasks such as autoencoding and machine translation. They intuitively divide language into meaningful pieces, providing several compact units through which a text can be represented. Dynamic selection makes the representation responsive to the input rather than imposing the same representation size on every sequence.

The authors show that Nugget outperforms related approaches on tasks involving semantic comparison. They also illustrate how compact nugget representations can expand a language model’s contextual window. This suggests a route toward future models that condition on substantially more content, while the stated demonstration is the use of these compact units to extend context.
summary.tldr: Nugget represents text through dynamically selected token units, improving semantic comparison and illustrating a way to expand language-model context.

title: Nugget: Neural Agglomerative Embeddings of Text

abstract: The top-$k$ operator returns a $k$-sparse vector, where the non-zero values correspond to the $k$ largest values of the input. Unfortunately, because it is a discontinuous function, it is difficult to incorporate in neural networks trained end-to-end with backpropagation. Recent works have considered differentiable relaxations, based either on regularization or perturbation techniques. However, to date, no approach is fully differentiable and sparse. In this paper, we propose new differentiable and sparse top-$k$ operators. We view the top-$k$ operator as a linear program over the permutahedron, the convex hull of permutations. We then introduce a $p$-norm regularization term to smooth out the operator, and show that its computation can be reduced to isotonic optimization. Our framework is significantly more general than the existing one and allows for example to express top-$k$ operators that select values in magnitude. On the algorithmic side, in addition to pool adjacent violator (PAV) algorithms, we propose a new GPU/TPU-friendly Dykstra algorithm to solve isotonic optimization problems. We successfully use our operators to prune weights in neural networks, to fine-tune vision transformers, and as a router in sparse mixture of experts.

paragraphs: The top-k operator keeps the largest input values and sets the others to zero. This produces sparse selections, but abrupt changes in which values are selected make the operator difficult to train through with backpropagation. The paper seeks operators that combine differentiability with sparsity, properties that earlier relaxations had not fully provided together.

The authors express top-k selection as a linear optimization problem over the permutahedron, a shape formed from permutations. Adding a p-norm regularization term smooths the operation. They show that computing the resulting operators reduces to isotonic optimization, which imposes ordering constraints, and their framework also accommodates selection according to magnitude.

For computation, the paper provides pool adjacent violator algorithms and introduces a Dykstra algorithm designed to suit GPUs and TPUs. The operators are successfully used for neural-network weight pruning, vision-transformer fine-tuning, and routing in sparse mixtures of experts. These applications illustrate how a trainable selection mechanism can retain sparsity while becoming usable inside larger end-to-end learning systems.
summary.tldr: A convex-optimization framework produces differentiable sparse top-k operators with algorithms suited to modern accelerators.

title: Fast, Differentiable and Sparse Top-k: a Convex Analysis Perspective

abstract: Recent score-based diffusion models (SBDMs) show promising results in unpaired image-to-image translation (I2I). However, existing methods, either energy-based or statistically-based, provide no explicit form of the interfered intermediate generative distributions. This work presents a new score-decomposed diffusion model (SDDM) on manifolds to explicitly optimize the tangled distributions during image generation. SDDM derives manifolds to make the distributions of adjacent time steps separable and decompose the score function or energy guidance into an image "denoising" part and a content "refinement" part. To refine the image in the same noise level, we equalize the refinement parts of the score function and energy guidance, which permits multi-objective optimization on the manifold. We also leverage the block adaptive instance normalization module to construct manifolds with lower dimensions but still concentrated with the perturbed reference image. SDDM outperforms existing SBDM-based methods with much fewer diffusion steps on several I2I benchmarks.

paragraphs: Unpaired image-to-image translation changes images between domains without paired training examples. Score-based diffusion methods have shown promise, but the paper identifies a difficulty in explicitly describing the intermediate distributions affected during generation. SDDM addresses this by organizing the generation process on manifolds so that the intertwined distributions can be optimized explicitly.

The method derives manifolds that separate distributions at adjacent time steps. It then splits the score function or energy guidance into denoising and content-refinement parts. Equalizing the refinement components allows multiple objectives to be optimized on a manifold while keeping refinement at the same noise level, giving these two roles a more explicit mathematical treatment.

SDDM also uses block adaptive instance normalization to construct lower-dimensional manifolds concentrated around the perturbed reference image. On several image-translation benchmarks, it outperforms existing score-based diffusion methods while using substantially fewer diffusion steps. The findings support separating denoising from content refinement as a way to improve both translation results and the number of generation steps required.
summary.tldr: SDDM separates denoising and content refinement on manifolds, improving unpaired image translation with fewer diffusion steps.

title: SDDM: Score-Decomposed Diffusion Models on Manifolds for Unpaired Image-to-Image Translation

abstract: In machine learning applications, it is well known that carefully designed learning rate (step size) schedules can significantly improve the convergence of commonly used first-order optimization algorithms. Therefore how to set step size adaptively becomes an important research question. A popular and effective method is the Polyak step size, which sets step size adaptively for gradient descent or stochastic gradient descent without the need to estimate the smoothness parameter of the objective function. However, there has not been a principled way to generalize the Polyak step size for algorithms with momentum accelerations. This paper presents a general framework to set the learning rate adaptively for first-order optimization methods with momentum, motivated by the derivation of Polyak step size. It is shown that the resulting techniques are much less sensitive to the choice of momentum parameter and may avoid the oscillation of the heavy-ball method on ill-conditioned problems. These adaptive step sizes are further extended to the stochastic settings, which are attractive choices for stochastic gradient descent with momentum. Our methods are demonstrated to be more effective for stochastic gradient methods than prior adaptive step size algorithms in large-scale machine learning tasks.

paragraphs: Choosing a learning rate strongly affects how an optimization algorithm converges. The Polyak step size offers an adaptive choice for gradient descent and stochastic gradient descent without estimating the objective’s smoothness parameter. This paper addresses how to extend that principle systematically to methods that also use momentum.

The authors develop a general framework motivated by the derivation of the Polyak rule. It adjusts step sizes for first-order methods with momentum rather than treating the learning rate and momentum behavior as unrelated choices. The resulting techniques are reported to be much less sensitive to the momentum parameter and may avoid heavy-ball oscillations on ill-conditioned problems.

The framework is also extended to stochastic optimization, providing adaptive choices for stochastic gradient descent with momentum. On large-scale machine learning tasks, the proposed methods are demonstrated to be more effective than earlier adaptive step-size algorithms for stochastic gradient methods. The contribution is thus a principled route from an established adaptive rule to momentum-based training, with reported benefits for parameter sensitivity and practical effectiveness.
summary.tldr: A generalized Polyak framework adapts learning rates for momentum methods, reducing momentum sensitivity and improving reported stochastic optimization performance.

title: Generalized Polyak Step Size for First Order Optimization with Momentum

abstract: Recent works have demonstrated the benefits of capturing long-distance dependency in graphs by deeper graph neural networks (GNNs). But deeper GNNs suffer from the long-lasting scalability challenge due to the neighborhood explosion problem in large-scale graphs. In this work, we propose to capture long-distance dependency in graphs by shallower models instead of deeper models, which leads to a much more efficient model, LazyGNN, for graph representation learning. Moreover, we demonstrate that LazyGNN is compatible with existing scalable approaches (such as sampling methods) for further accelerations through the development of mini-batch LazyGNN. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate its superior prediction performance and scalability on large-scale benchmarks. The implementation of LazyGNN is available at https: //github.com/RXPHD/Lazy_GNN.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks can benefit from information located far away in a graph. Increasing depth is one way to capture these dependencies, but it creates a scalability problem: the neighborhoods involved in computation can expand rapidly. On large graphs, this neighborhood explosion makes deeper models expensive to train and use.

LazyGNN pursues long-distance dependencies with a shallower model. The contribution is to separate the goal of capturing distant graph information from the need to make the model deeper. The authors also develop a mini-batch version and show compatibility with existing scaling techniques, including sampling methods, so those techniques can provide further acceleration.

Comprehensive experiments report superior prediction performance and scalability on large-scale benchmarks. These results suggest that the shallower approach can preserve useful distant dependencies while improving efficiency in the tested settings. The compatibility result also matters practically: LazyGNN can work alongside established methods for managing large graphs, expanding the available options for reducing the cost of graph representation learning.
summary.tldr: LazyGNN captures long-distance graph dependencies with shallower models and supports sampling-based acceleration.

title: LazyGNN: Large-Scale Graph Neural Networks via Lazy Propagation

abstract: The renowned difference-in-differences (DiD) estimator relies on the assumption of ’parallel trends,’ which may not hold in many practical applications. To address this issue, economists are increasingly considering the triple difference estimator as a more credible alternative. Both DiD and triple difference are limited to assessing average effects exclusively. An alternative avenue is offered by the changes-in-changes (CiC) estimator, which provides an estimate of the entire counterfactual distribution by relying on assumptions imposed on the distribution of potential outcomes. In this work, we extend the triple difference estimator to accommodate the CiC framework, presenting the ‘triple changes estimator’ and its identification assumptions, thereby expanding the scope of the CiC paradigm. Subsequently, we empirically evaluate the proposed framework and apply it to a study examining the impact of Medicaid expansion on children’s preventive care.

paragraphs: Difference-in-differences estimates policy effects using a parallel-trends assumption that may fail in practice. Triple difference is increasingly considered as an alternative, but both approaches focus on average effects. This paper asks how to expand that perspective to the distribution of outcomes that would have occurred under a counterfactual policy setting.

The starting point is changes-in-changes, which estimates an entire counterfactual distribution using assumptions about potential-outcome distributions. The authors extend triple difference into this framework and call the resulting method the triple changes estimator. They also state its identification assumptions, specifying the conditions under which the desired counterfactual distribution can be recovered.

The paper empirically evaluates the framework and applies it to Medicaid expansion and children’s preventive care. Its methodological contribution is to connect the additional comparisons of triple difference with the distributional scope of changes-in-changes. This broadens the questions that can be studied beyond an average effect, while keeping identification dependent on the proposed assumptions. The supplied findings describe the framework and application without asserting a particular direction of the policy’s effect.
summary.tldr: The triple changes estimator combines triple-difference reasoning with changes-in-changes to identify counterfactual outcome distributions under stated assumptions.

title: Triple Changes Estimator for Targeted Policies

abstract: Machine learning techniques often lack formal correctness guarantees, evidenced by the widespread adversarial examples that plague most deep-learning applications. This lack of formal guarantees resulted in several research efforts that aim at verifying Deep Neural Networks (DNNs), with a particular focus on safety-critical applications. However, formal verification techniques still face major scalability and precision challenges. The over-approximation introduced during the formal verification process to tackle the scalability challenge often results in inconclusive analysis. To address this challenge, we propose a novel framework to generate Verification-Friendly Neural Networks (VNNs). We present a post-training optimization framework to achieve a balance between preserving prediction performance and verification-friendliness. Our proposed framework results in VNNs that are comparable to the original DNNs in terms of prediction performance, while amenable to formal verification techniques. This essentially enables us to establish robustness for more VNNs than their DNN counterparts, in a time-efficient manner.

paragraphs: Formal verification aims to establish guarantees about neural-network behavior, including robustness against adversarial changes. Its practical difficulty is partly a tradeoff between scale and precision. To handle large computations, verifiers use approximations that can be too loose to establish whether the desired property holds, leaving the analysis inconclusive.

This paper proposes modifying a trained network to make it more amenable to verification. Its post-training optimization framework balances preservation of prediction performance against verification-friendliness. The resulting Verification-Friendly Neural Networks, or VNNs, are intended to retain useful predictive behavior while making formal analysis more effective.

The authors report prediction performance comparable to the original networks and time-efficient verification that establishes robustness for more VNNs than their original counterparts. The contribution therefore concerns both the network and the proof process: changing the trained model can improve the ability to certify its behavior. The claim is that more robustness properties can be established for the resulting networks, rather than that every transformed network is automatically robust.
summary.tldr: Post-training optimization makes neural networks easier to verify while preserving comparable prediction performance and enabling more time-efficient robustness certificates.

title: VNN: Verification-Friendly Neural Networks with Hard Robustness Guarantees

abstract: Modern ML systems increasingly augment input instances with additional relevant information to enhance final prediction. Despite growing interest in such retrieval-augmented models, their fundamental properties and training are not well understood. We propose a statistical framework to study such models with two components: 1) a retriever to identify the relevant information out of a large corpus via a data-dependent metric; and 2) a predictor that consumes the input instances along with the retrieved information to make the final predictions. We present a principled method for end-to-end training of both components and draw connections with various training approaches in the literature. Furthermore, we establish excess risk bounds for retrieval-augmented models while delineating the contributions of both retriever and predictor towards the model performance.We validate the utility of our proposed training methods along with the key takeaways from our statistical analysis on open domain question answering task where retrieval augmentation is important.

paragraphs: Retrieval-augmented models make predictions using both an input and relevant information selected from a larger collection. This paper develops a statistical framework for understanding that combined system. It treats retrieval and prediction as distinct components: the retriever selects information using a data-dependent measure of relevance, while the predictor uses the selected information alongside the original input.

The authors propose a principled way to train both components together, connecting their method to existing training approaches. Joint training matters because the usefulness of retrieved information depends on how the predictor consumes it. Studying the components together provides a way to reason about that interaction rather than evaluating retrieval as an isolated preliminary step.

The theoretical contribution is a set of excess-risk bounds that distinguish the contributions of the retriever and predictor to overall performance. The authors also test their training methods and conclusions from the analysis on open-domain question answering. These experiments support the framework’s usefulness in a setting where finding relevant information is central to answering correctly.
summary.tldr: A statistical framework explains how retrievers and predictors jointly affect performance and provides a principled way to train them together.

title: A Statistical Framework for Data-dependent Retrieval-Augmented Models

abstract: We study the classic problem of correlation clustering in dynamic vertex streams. In this setting, vertices are either added or randomly deleted over time, and each vertex pair is connected by a positive or negative edge. The objective is to continuously find a partition which minimizes the sum of positive edges crossing clusters and negative edges within clusters. We present an algorithm that maintains an $O(1)$-approximation with $O(\text{polylog} n)$ amortized update time. Prior to our work Behnezhad et al. in SODA 2023 achieved a $5$-approximation with $O(1)$ expected update time in edge streams which translates in vertex streams to an $O(D)$-update time where $D$ is the maximum possible degree. Finally we complement our theoretical analysis with experiments on real world data.

The objective is to continuously find a partition which minimizes the sum of positive edges crossing clusters and negative edges within clusters. We present an algorithm that maintains an $O(1)$-approximation with $O(\text{polylog} n)$ amortized update time. Prior to our work Behnezhad et al. in SODA 2023 achieved a $5$-approximation with $O(1)$ expected update time in edge streams which translates in vertex streams to an $O(D)$-update time where $D$ is the maximum possible degree. paragraphs: Correlation clustering groups vertices using positive and negative relationships. Positive edges favor putting their endpoints together, while negative edges favor separating them. The objective counts disagreements: positive edges split across clusters and negative edges kept inside a cluster. This paper studies maintaining such a grouping while vertices arrive or are randomly deleted.

The authors give an algorithm that maintains a constant-factor approximation with amortized update time polynomial in log n. Amortized time describes the cost averaged across a sequence of updates. The guarantee therefore combines an approximately good clustering with a small average maintenance cost as the vertex stream changes.

This improves on the stated vertex-stream cost obtained from an earlier edge-stream algorithm, whose update time becomes proportional to the maximum possible degree. The distinction matters because adding or removing one vertex can involve many relationships. Experiments on real-world data complement the theoretical analysis. The result specifically covers the stated insertion and random-deletion setting, making that deletion model part of the guarantee.
summary.tldr: The algorithm maintains a constant-factor correlation clustering approximation with polylogarithmic amortized updates under vertex arrivals and random deletions.

title: Dynamic Correlation Clustering in Sublinear Update Time

abstract: The core of clustering lies in incorporating prior knowledge to construct supervision signals. From classic k-means based on data compactness to recent contrastive clustering guided by self-supervision, the evolution of clustering methods intrinsically corresponds to the progression of supervision signals. At present, substantial efforts have been devoted to mining internal supervision signals from data. Nevertheless, the abundant external knowledge such as semantic descriptions, which naturally conduces to clustering, is regrettably overlooked. In this work, we propose leveraging external knowledge as a new supervision signal to guide clustering. To implement and validate our idea, we design an externally guided clustering method (Text-Aided Clustering, TAC), which leverages the textual semantics of WordNet to facilitate image clustering. Specifically, TAC first selects and retrieves WordNet nouns that best distinguish images to enhance the feature discriminability. Then, TAC collaborates text and image modalities by mutually distilling cross-modal neighborhood information. Experiments demonstrate that TAC achieves state-of-the-art performance on five widely used and three more challenging image clustering benchmarks, including the full ImageNet-1K dataset. The code can be accessed at https://github.com/XLearning-SCU/2024-ICML-TAC.

Nevertheless, the abundant external knowledge such as semantic descriptions, which naturally conduces to clustering, is regrettably overlooked. In this work, we propose leveraging external knowledge as a new supervision signal to guide clustering. To implement and validate our idea, we design an externally guided clustering method (Text-Aided Clustering, TAC), which leverages the textual semantics of WordNet to facilitate image clustering. Specifically, TAC first selects and retrieves WordNet nouns that best distinguish images to enhance the feature discriminability. Then, TAC collaborates text and image modalities by mutually distilling cross-modal neighborhood information. Experiments demonstrate that TAC achieves state-of-the-art performance on five widely used and three more challenging image clustering benchmarks, including the full ImageNet-1K dataset. The code can be accessed at https://github.com/XLearning-SCU/2024-ICML-TAC.

paragraphs: Image clustering depends on signals that indicate which images belong together. Many methods derive these signals from the images themselves, such as compactness or self-supervised relationships. This paper investigates external semantic knowledge as an additional source of guidance, using language to help distinguish visual groups.

The proposed Text-Aided Clustering method draws on nouns from WordNet. It first selects and retrieves nouns that best distinguish the images, using their textual meaning to improve feature discriminability. It then lets the text and image representations exchange neighborhood information through mutual distillation. This step links the relationships found in each modality so that both can contribute to the grouping process.

The authors report state-of-the-art results on five widely used benchmarks and three more challenging ones, including the full ImageNet-1K dataset. These experiments support external textual semantics as a useful clustering signal. The contribution combines a concrete source of outside knowledge with a mechanism for integrating that knowledge into image relationships, extending the supervision available beyond the visual dataset alone.
summary.tldr: Text-Aided Clustering uses WordNet semantics and mutual text-image distillation to improve image grouping.

title: Image Clustering with External Guidance

abstract: For the first time, this position paper introduces a fundamental link between tensor networks (TNs) and Green AI, highlighting their synergistic potential to enhance both the inclusivity and sustainability of AI research. We argue that TNs are valuable for Green AI due to their strong mathematical backbone and inherent logarithmic compression potential. We undertake a comprehensive review of the ongoing discussions on Green AI, emphasizing the importance of sustainability and inclusivity in AI research to demonstrate the significance of establishing the link between Green AI and TNs. To support our position, we first provide a comprehensive overview of efficiency metrics proposed in Green AI literature and then evaluate examples of TNs in the fields of kernel machines and deep learning using the proposed efficiency metrics. This position paper aims to incentivize meaningful, constructive discussions by bridging fundamental principles of Green AI and TNs. We advocate for researchers to seriously evaluate the integration of TNs into their research projects, and in alignment with the link established in this paper, we support prior calls encouraging researchers to treat Green AI principles as a research priority.

paragraphs: Green AI emphasizes the sustainability and inclusivity of AI research, making efficiency part of how research value is assessed. This position paper argues that tensor networks deserve serious consideration within that agenda. Its case rests on their mathematical foundations and their potential for logarithmic compression.

The authors review discussions of Green AI and assemble an overview of efficiency metrics proposed in that literature. They then use those metrics to evaluate tensor-network examples in kernel machines and deep learning. This links the broader argument to concrete ways of assessing efficiency, rather than presenting compression potential alone as sufficient evidence of practical value.

The paper's conclusion is a research recommendation: investigate tensor networks as a possible tool for making AI more sustainable and accessible, and give Green AI principles greater priority. The stated contribution is the connection between these research areas, supported by a review and evaluated examples. It presents tensor networks as a valuable option to examine within particular projects, with efficiency metrics providing a basis for that examination.
summary.tldr: This position paper argues that tensor networks' mathematical structure and compression potential make them valuable candidates for sustainable, inclusive AI research.

title: Position: Tensor Networks are a Valuable Asset for Green AI

abstract: The emergence of In-Context Learning (ICL) in LLMs remains a remarkable phenomenon that is partially understood. To explain ICL, recent studies have created theoretical connections to Gradient Descent (GD). We ask, do such connections hold up in actual pre-trained language models? We highlight the limiting assumptions in prior works that make their setup considerably different from the practical setup in which language models are trained. For example, their experimental verification uses *ICL objective* (training models explicitly for ICL), which differs from the emergent ICL in the wild. Furthermore, the theoretical hand-constructed weights used in these studies have properties that don't match those of real LLMs. We also look for evidence in real models. We observe that ICL and GD have different sensitivity to the order in which they observe demonstrations. Finally, we probe and compare the ICL vs. GD hypothesis in a natural setting. We conduct comprehensive empirical analyses on language models pre-trained on natural data (LLaMa-7B). Our comparisons of three performance metrics highlight the inconsistent behavior of ICL and GD as a function of various factors such as datasets, models, and the number of demonstrations. We observe that ICL and GD modify the output distribution of language models differently. These results indicate that *the equivalence between ICL and GD remains an open hypothesis* and calls for further studies.

paragraphs: In-context learning lets a language model respond to examples placed in its prompt. Some theoretical work connects this behavior to gradient descent. This position paper examines whether those connections explain the behavior of actual pretrained language models, focusing on the gap between theoretical constructions and practical training.

The authors identify assumptions that make earlier evidence difficult to transfer directly. Some experiments train models explicitly for in-context learning, whereas the ability emerges under a different training setup in ordinary language models. Some theoretical constructions also rely on hand-designed weights with properties unlike those of real models.

The paper then compares in-context learning and gradient descent empirically, including analyses of LLaMa-7B pretrained on natural data. The two processes respond differently to demonstration order and change output distributions differently. Comparisons across three performance metrics also reveal inconsistent relationships as datasets, models, and demonstration counts vary. These findings leave equivalence as an open hypothesis requiring further study, rather than establishing that all gradient-descent explanations are impossible.
summary.tldr: Theoretical assumptions and empirical behavioral differences leave the equivalence between in-context learning and gradient descent unresolved.

title: Position: Do pretrained Transformers Learn In-Context by Gradient Descent?

abstract: Compositional reasoning capabilities are usually considered as fundamental skills to characterize human perception. Recent studies show that current Vision Language Models (VLMs) surprisingly lack sufficient knowledge with respect to such capabilities. To this end, we propose to thoroughly diagnose the composition representations encoded by VLMs, systematically revealing the potential cause for this weakness. Specifically, we propose evaluation methods from a novel game-theoretic view to assess the vulnerability of VLMs on different aspects of compositional understanding, e.g., relations and attributes. Extensive experimental results demonstrate and validate several insights to understand the incapabilities of VLMs on compositional reasoning, which provide useful and reliable guidance for future studies. The deliverables will be updated here.
