paragraphs: Compositional understanding concerns how parts of a description or scene fit together, including attributes and relationships. This paper investigates why vision-language models can struggle with that ability. Its focus is the composition information represented inside the models and how weaknesses in those representations may help explain their reasoning failures.

The authors introduce evaluation methods grounded in a game-theoretic perspective. These methods assess vulnerability across different aspects of composition, including relations and attributes. Separating these aspects gives the investigation a more specific target than a single overall assessment of compositional ability: it asks which kinds of composition knowledge appear weak in the evaluated models.

Extensive experiments are reported to establish and validate insights into those weaknesses. The contribution is primarily diagnostic, offering evidence intended to guide later research on compositional reasoning. The abstract presents the evaluation approach as a way to investigate potential causes of limited understanding. Its practical significance is that a structured account of failure can help future work focus on the particular representations that need improvement.
summary.tldr: Game-theoretic evaluations diagnose weaknesses in vision-language models' representations of compositional information, including attributes and relations.

title: Diagnosing the Compositional Knowledge of Vision Language Models from a Game-Theoretic View

abstract: This paper introduces diffusion protein language model (DPLM), a versatile protein language model that demonstrates strong generative and predictive capabilities for protein sequences. We first pre-train scalable DPLMs from evolutionary-scale protein sequences within a generative self-supervised discrete diffusion probabilistic framework, which generalizes language modeling for proteins in a principled way. After pre-training, DPLM exhibits the ability to generate structurally plausible, novel and diverse protein sequences for unconditional generation. We further demonstrate the proposed diffusion generative pre-training make DPLM possess a better understanding of proteins, making it a superior representation learner, which can be fine-tuned for various predictive tasks, comparing favorably to ESM2. Moreover, DPLM can be tailored for various needs, which showcases its prowess of conditional generation in several ways: (1) conditioning on partial peptide sequences, e.g., generating scaffolds for functional motifs with high success rate; (2) incorporating other modalities as conditioners, e.g., structure-conditioned generation for inverse folding; and (3) steering sequence generation towards desired properties, e.g., satisfying specified secondary structures, through a plug-and-play classifier guidance.

paragraphs: The diffusion protein language model, DPLM, is designed to both generate protein sequences and learn representations useful for prediction. It is pretrained on evolutionary-scale sequence data using a self-supervised discrete diffusion framework. The same generative training foundation supports several downstream uses, rather than restricting the model to a single protein task.

After pretraining, DPLM generates novel, diverse sequences with plausible structures without requiring a conditioning input. Its learned representations can also be fine-tuned for predictive tasks, where the paper reports favorable comparisons with ESM2. These findings connect generative pretraining with both sequence creation and useful representations of protein information.

The authors additionally demonstrate several forms of controlled generation. DPLM can build scaffolds around partial peptide sequences, including functional motifs, with a reported high success rate. It can use structural information for inverse folding or classifier guidance to steer sequences toward desired properties such as specified secondary structures. Together, these applications demonstrate flexibility in what information can guide sequence generation.
summary.tldr: DPLM uses diffusion pretraining to support protein generation, predictive representation learning, and several forms of controlled sequence design.

title: Diffusion Language Models Are Versatile Protein Learners

abstract: We propose a two-stage optimization formulation for the memory retrieval dynamics of modern Hopfield models, termed $\mathtt{U\text{-}Hop}$. Our key contribution is a learnable feature map $\Phi$ which transforms the Hopfield energy function into a kernel space. This transformation ensures convergence between the local minima of energy and the fixed points of retrieval dynamics within the kernel space. Consequently, the kernel norm induced by $\Phi$ serves as a novel similarity measure. It utilizes the stored memory patterns as learning data to enhance memory capacity across all modern Hopfield models. Specifically, we accomplish this by constructing a separation loss $\mathcal{L}_\Phi$ that separates the local minima of kernelized energy by separating stored memory patterns in kernel space. Methodologically, $\mathtt{U\text{-}Hop}$ memory retrieval process consists of: (Stage I:) minimizing separation loss for a more uniformed memory (local minimum) distribution, followed by (Stage II:) standard Hopfield energy minimization for memory retrieval. This results in significant reduction of possible meta-stable states in the Hopfield energy function, thus preventing memory confusion. Empirically, with real-world datasets, we demonstrate that $\mathtt{U\text{-}Hop}$ outperforms all existing modern Hopfield models and SOTA similarity measures, achieving a substantial margin in both associative memory retrieval and deep learning tasks. Code is available at GitHub; future updates are on arXiv.

paragraphs: Modern Hopfield models retrieve stored patterns through energy minimization. This paper introduces U-Hop, a two-stage method that changes the representation of memories before performing retrieval. Its goal is to increase memory capacity and reduce confusion caused by competing or metastable states in the energy landscape.

A learnable feature map transforms the energy function into a kernel space, where its induced norm supplies a new similarity measure. The stored memories themselves provide the learning data. In the first stage, a separation loss pushes stored patterns apart in that space, spreading the associated energy minima more uniformly. The second stage performs standard Hopfield energy minimization to retrieve a memory.

The formulation aligns local energy minima with retrieval fixed points in the kernel space and substantially reduces possible metastable states. On real-world datasets, the authors report substantial gains over existing modern Hopfield models and state-of-the-art similarity measures in associative retrieval and deep-learning tasks. The results support learning a memory-specific similarity representation before running the retrieval dynamics.
summary.tldr: U-Hop learns to separate stored memories in kernel space before retrieval, increasing capacity and reducing memory confusion.

title: Uniform Memory Retrieval with Larger Capacity for Modern Hopfield Models

abstract: We study partially observable assistance games (POAGs), a model of the human-AI value alignment problem which allows the human and the AI assistant to have partial observations. Motivated by concerns of AI deception, we study a qualitatively new phenomenon made possible by partial observability: would an AI assistant ever have an incentive to interfere with the human’s observations? First, we prove that sometimes an optimal assistant must take observation-interfering actions, even when the human is playing optimally, and even when there are otherwise-equivalent actions available that do not interfere with observations. Though this result seems to contradict the classic theorem from single-agent decision making that the value of perfect information is nonnegative, we resolve this seeming contradiction by developing a notion of interference defined on entire policies. This can be viewed as an extension of the classic result that the value of perfect information is nonnegative into the cooperative multiagent setting. Second, we prove that if the human is simply making decisions based on their immediate outcomes, the assistant might need to interfere with observations as a way to query the human’s preferences. We show that this incentive for interference goes away if the human is playing optimally, or if we introduce a communication channel for the human to communicate their preferences to the assistant. Third, we show that if the human acts according to the Boltzmann model of irrationality, this can create an incentive for the assistant to interfere with observations. Finally, we use an experimental model to analyze tradeoffs faced by the AI assistant in practice when considering whether or not to take observation-interfering actions.

paragraphs: This paper studies assistance games in which a human and an AI have incomplete observations. It asks whether an assistant can have an incentive to alter what the human observes. The authors prove that some optimal assistants must take observation-interfering actions, even with an optimal human and otherwise-equivalent noninterfering actions available.

That result appears to conflict with the principle that perfect information has nonnegative value in single-agent decisions. The authors resolve the tension by defining interference over whole policies rather than isolated actions, extending the information-value perspective to cooperation. This distinction matters because judging an individual action and judging an entire decision strategy need not yield the same conclusion.

Other incentives depend on human behavior. With a human focused on immediate outcomes, interference may help query preferences; this particular incentive disappears with optimal human play or a preference-communication channel. A Boltzmann model of irrationality can also create interference incentives. An experimental model explores practical tradeoffs, showing why the source of an incentive matters when interpreting or addressing it.
summary.tldr: Partially observable assistance games reveal several distinct incentives for AI assistants to interfere with human observations, including some involving optimal humans.

title: Observation Interference in Partially Observable Assistance Games

abstract: Effectively scaling up deep reinforcement learning models has proven notoriously difficult due to network pathologies during training, motivating various targeted interventions such as periodic reset and architectural advances such as layer normalization. Instead of pursuing more complex modifications, we show that introducing static network sparsity alone can unlock further scaling potential beyond their dense counterparts with state-of-the-art architectures. This is achieved through simple one-shot random pruning, where a predetermined percentage of network weights are randomly removed once before training. Our analysis reveals that, in contrast to naively scaling up dense DRL networks, such sparse networks achieve both higher parameter efficiency for network expressivity and stronger resistance to optimization challenges like plasticity loss and gradient interference. We further extend our evaluation to visual and streaming RL scenarios, demonstrating the consistent benefits of network sparsity.

paragraphs: Increasing the size of a deep reinforcement learning network does not automatically make it easier to train or more effective. The paper connects this difficulty to training pathologies that have motivated interventions such as periodic resets and layer normalization. It investigates whether a simpler structural change can improve scaling.

The proposed change is static random sparsity. Before training begins, a predetermined fraction of weights is randomly removed in a single pruning step. The authors show that this alone can provide additional scaling potential beyond dense counterparts using state-of-the-art architectures. Their analysis finds greater parameter efficiency for expressivity and stronger resistance to optimization problems, including loss of plasticity and interference between gradients.

These findings connect network connectivity to both what a model can represent and how well it continues learning. Evaluations extend to visual and streaming reinforcement learning, where sparsity shows consistent benefits. The stated result supports one-time random pruning as a useful scaling intervention in the tested settings, without requiring an increasingly elaborate training modification.
summary.tldr: Removing random weights once before training improves the scaling and optimization behavior of evaluated deep reinforcement learning networks.

title: Network Sparsity Unlocks the Scaling Potential of Deep Reinforcement Learning

abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are becoming more capable and widespread, the study of their failure cases is becoming increasingly important. Recent advances in standardizing, measuring, and scaling test-time compute suggest new methodologies for optimizing models to achieve high performance on hard tasks. In this paper, we apply these advances to the task of model jailbreaking: eliciting harmful responses from aligned LLMs. We develop an adversarial reasoning approach to automatic jailbreaking that leverages a loss signal to guide the test-time compute, achieving SOTA attack success rates against many aligned LLMs, even those that aim to trade inference-time compute for adversarial robustness. Our approach introduces a new paradigm in understanding LLM vulnerabilities, laying the foundation for the development of more robust and trustworthy AI systems.

paragraphs: This paper studies whether additional computation at inference time can strengthen automated attempts to bypass a language model’s safety behavior. The target task is jailbreaking: eliciting harmful responses from models trained to avoid them. The authors bring ideas developed for spending computation on difficult reasoning tasks into the study of these failures.

Their approach uses adversarial reasoning guided by a loss signal. That signal directs the computation spent during the attack, connecting the search process to an indication of how well the attack is working. The central contribution is therefore an approach to allocating and guiding attack-time reasoning, rather than simply treating an attack as a single fixed request.

The authors report state-of-the-art attack success rates against many aligned language models. These include models designed to use additional inference-time computation for adversarial robustness. The findings show that such defenses can still be vulnerable to this approach in the reported evaluations. The work offers a way to investigate vulnerabilities that could inform the development of more robust systems.
summary.tldr: Loss-guided adversarial reasoning achieves leading jailbreak success rates against many aligned language models, including some that spend extra computation on robustness.

title: Adversarial Reasoning at Jailbreaking Time

abstract: Large-scale text encoders in text-to-image (T2I) diffusion models have demonstrated exceptional performance in generating high-quality images from textual prompts. Unlike denoising modules that rely on multiple iterative steps, text encoders require only a single forward pass to produce text embeddings. However, despite their minimal contribution to total inference time and floating-point operations (FLOPs), text encoders demand significantly higher memory usage, up to eight times more than denoising modules. To address this inefficiency, we propose Skip and Re-use layers (Skrr), a simple yet effective pruning strategy specifically designed for text encoders in T2I diffusion models. Skrr exploits the inherent redundancy in transformer blocks by selectively skipping or reusing certain layers in a manner tailored for T2I tasks, thereby reducing memory consumption without compromising performance. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Skrr maintains image quality comparable to the original model even under high sparsity levels, outperforming existing blockwise pruning methods. Furthermore, Skrr achieves state-of-the-art memory efficiency while preserving performance across multiple evaluation metrics, including the FID, CLIP, DreamSim, and GenEval scores.

paragraphs: Text encoders in diffusion-based image generators run only once to convert a prompt into embeddings. Despite contributing little to overall inference time and arithmetic cost, they can consume up to eight times as much memory as the denoising modules. This paper targets that imbalance by reducing the encoder's memory requirements.

Skrr is a pruning strategy that selectively skips or reuses transformer layers. It exploits redundancy between blocks in a way tailored to text-to-image generation. The aim is to retain the prompt representation's usefulness for image generation while reducing the amount of encoder machinery that must be stored.

Experiments show image quality comparable to the original model even at high sparsity levels, with better results than existing blockwise pruning methods. The authors report state-of-the-art memory efficiency while preserving performance across FID, CLIP, DreamSim, and GenEval evaluations. The findings highlight why memory optimization deserves attention independently of inference-time optimization: a component can be computationally inexpensive during generation yet still dominate the memory needed to run the system.
summary.tldr: Skrr reduces text-to-image encoder memory by skipping and reusing layers while preserving comparable image quality in the reported evaluations.

title: Skrr: Skip and Re-use Text Encoder Layers for Memory Efficient Text-to-Image Generation

abstract: Recent advances in conditional diffusion models have shown promise for generating realistic TalkingFace videos, yet challenges persist in achieving consistent head movement, synchronized facial expressions, and accurate lip synchronization over extended generations. To address these, we introduce the Motion-priors Conditional Diffusion Model (MCDM), which utilizes both archived and current clip motion priors to enhance motion prediction and ensure temporal consistency. The model consists of three key elements: (1) an archived-clip motion-prior that incorporates historical frames and a reference frame to preserve identity and context; (2) a present-clip motion-prior diffusion model that captures multimodal causality for accurate predictions of head movements, lip sync, and expressions; and (3) a memory-efficient temporal attention mechanism that mitigates error accumulation by dynamically storing and updating motion features. We also introduce the TalkingFace-Wild dataset, a multilingual collection of over 200 hours of footage across 10 languages. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of MCDM in maintaining identity and motion continuity for long-term TalkingFace generation.

paragraphs: Generating a convincing talking face over a long video requires more than plausible individual frames. Head movement, facial expression, lip synchronization, and identity must remain coherent across time. This paper introduces the Motion-priors Conditional Diffusion Model, or MCDM, to use information from both earlier footage and the current clip when predicting motion.

An archived-clip component combines historical frames with a reference frame to preserve identity and context. A present-clip diffusion component models multimodal causal relationships for predicting head movement, expressions, and lip synchronization. A memory-efficient temporal attention mechanism stores and updates motion features dynamically, helping reduce errors that accumulate over an extended generation.

The authors also introduce TalkingFace-Wild, a multilingual dataset containing more than 200 hours of footage across 10 languages. Experiments demonstrate that MCDM maintains identity and motion continuity in long-term talking-face generation. The approach matters because it makes continuity an explicit part of motion prediction, combining the immediate clip’s requirements with a maintained representation of preceding motion.
summary.tldr: MCDM combines historical and current motion information to preserve identity and movement continuity in long talking-face videos.

title: Long-Term TalkingFace Generation via Motion-Prior Conditional Diffusion Model

abstract: Training reinforcement learning (RL) agents requires extensive trials and errors, which becomes prohibitively time-consuming in systems with costly reward evaluations. To address this challenge, we propose adaptive reward modeling (AdaReMo) which accelerates RL training by decomposing the complicated reward function into multiple localized fast reward models approximating direct reward evaluation with neural networks. These models dynamically adapt to the agent’s evolving policy by fitting the currently explored subspace with the latest trajectories, ensuring accurate reward estimation throughout the entire training process while significantly reducing computational overhead. We empirically show that AdaReMo not only achieves over 1,000 times speedup but also improves the performance by 14.6% over state-of-the-art approaches across three expensive-to-evaluate systems—molecular generation, epidemic control, and spatial planning. Code and data for the project are provided at https://github.com/tsinghua-fib-lab/AdaReMo.
originalAbstract: Training reinforcement learning (RL) agents requires extensive trials and errors, which becomes prohibitively time-consuming in systems with costly reward evaluations. To address this challenge, we propose adaptive reward modeling (AdaReMo) which accelerates RL training by decomposing the complicated reward function into multiple localized fast reward models approximating direct reward evaluation with neural networks. These models dynamically adapt to the agent’s evolving policy by fitting the currently explored subspace with the latest trajectories, ensuring accurate reward estimation throughout the entire training process while significantly reducing computational overhead. We empirically show that AdaReMo not only achieves over 1,000 times speedup but also improves the performance by 14.6% over state-of-the-art approaches across three expensive-to-evaluate systems—molecular generation, epidemic control, and spatial planning. Code and data for the project are provided at https://github.com/tsinghua-fib-lab/AdaReMo.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning needs repeated feedback about how well actions perform. When evaluating that reward is expensive, the feedback calculation can make training prohibitively slow. AdaReMo addresses this bottleneck by approximating a complicated reward function with multiple localized neural models that can provide reward estimates quickly.

These approximations adapt as the agent's policy changes. Each model fits the currently explored part of the system using recent trajectories, keeping its focus aligned with the decisions the agent is actually making. This adaptation is central to the approach: the reward approximation follows the evolving training process rather than remaining fixed while the policy moves into different regions.

Across molecular generation, epidemic control, and spatial planning, the authors report more than a thousandfold speedup and a 14.6% performance improvement over state-of-the-art approaches. The empirical findings indicate that faster reward evaluation can accompany improved outcomes in these expensive-to-evaluate systems. The contribution is a way to concentrate reward-modeling effort where the current policy needs it while reducing computational overhead.
summary.tldr: AdaReMo adapts localized reward models to an evolving policy, reporting over 1,000-fold speedup across three expensive-to-evaluate systems.

title: Reinforcement Learning with Adaptive Reward Modeling for Expensive-to-Evaluate Systems

abstract: We propose CAL (Complete Anything in Lidar) for Lidar-based shape-completion in-the-wild. This is closely related to Lidar-based semantic/panoptic scene completion. However, contemporary methods can only complete and recognize objects from a closed vocabulary labeled in existing Lidar datasets. Different to that, our zero-shot approach leverages the temporal context from multi-modal sensor sequences to mine object shapes and semantic features of observed objects. These are then distilled into a Lidar-only instance-level completion and recognition model. Although we only mine partial shape completions, we find that our distilled model learns to infer full object shapes from multiple such partial observations across the dataset. We show that our model can be prompted on standard benchmarks for Semantic and Panoptic Scene Completion, localize objects as (amodal) 3D bounding boxes, and recognize objects beyond fixed class vocabularies.

Existing scene-completion methods are often restricted to the object categories labeled in their training datasets. Complete Anything in Lidar, or CAL, introduces a zero-shot approach intended to extend completion and recognition beyond those fixed vocabularies.

CAL uses temporal information from multimodal sensor sequences to extract object shapes and semantic features. It then distills that information into a model that performs instance-level completion and recognition from Lidar alone. Although the extracted shape targets are only partial, the authors find that learning from multiple partial observations across the dataset enables the distilled model to infer complete object shapes.

The model can be prompted for standard semantic and panoptic scene-completion benchmarks. It can also localize objects with amodal 3D bounding boxes, which describe their full extent, and recognize objects outside fixed class vocabularies. The contribution connects richer training-time sensor sequences with a Lidar-only model capable of broader object-level understanding.
summary.tldr: CAL learns from partial shapes in multimodal sequences to support Lidar-only completion and recognition beyond fixed object vocabularies.

title: Towards Learning to Complete Anything in Lidar

abstract: Pre-trained Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are becoming increasingly popular across various visual tasks, and several open-sourced VLM variants have been released. However, selecting the best-performing pre-trained VLM for a specific downstream task is challenging since no single VLM can achieve promising performance on all downstream tasks, and evaluating all available VLMs is impossible due to time and data limitations. To address this problem, this paper proposes a novel paradigm to select and reuse VLM for downstream tasks, called Model Label Learning (MLL). The proposal contains three key modules: model labeling, which assigns labels to each VLM to describe their specialty and utility; model selection, which matches the requirements of the target task with model labels; and model reuse, which applies selected VLMs to the target task in an ensemble manner. The proposal is highly computationally efficient and growable since the model labeling process is completed target task independent and the ability could grow with the number of candidate VLMs. We also introduce a new benchmark for evaluating VLM selection methods, including 49 VLMs and 17 target task datasets. Experimental results clearly demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method for selecting and reusing VLMs.

paragraphs: Different pretrained vision-language models have different strengths, making the choice of model consequential for a downstream task. Evaluating every available candidate can exceed the available time or data. Model Label Learning addresses this selection problem by giving models reusable descriptions of their specialties and utility, then matching those descriptions to a task's requirements.

The framework has three stages. Model labeling characterizes candidate models; model selection uses those labels to identify suitable candidates; model reuse combines selected models in an ensemble for the target task. Labeling is performed independently of the target task, so the characterization work can be reused. The framework can also grow as additional candidate models become available.

The authors introduce a benchmark containing 49 vision-language models and 17 target-task datasets, and report experiments supporting effective selection and reuse. The approach connects efficient model discovery with ensemble-based adaptation. Its practical significance is that choosing among pretrained models becomes a structured matching process, supported by reusable model information rather than requiring a fresh evaluation of every candidate for every task.
summary.tldr: Model Label Learning characterizes vision-language models once, matches them to downstream tasks, and reuses selected models through ensembles.

title: Vision-Language Model Selection and Reuse for Downstream Adaptation

abstract: K-Means clustering is a classical and effective unsupervised learning method attributed to its simplicity and efficiency. However, it faces notable challenges, including sensitivity to random initial centroid selection, a limited ability to discover the intrinsic manifold structures within nonlinear datasets, and difficulty in achieving balanced clustering in practical scenarios. To overcome these weaknesses, we introduce a novel framework for K-Means that leverages manifold learning. This approach eliminates the need for centroid calculation and utilizes a cluster indicator matrix to align the manifold structures, thereby enhancing clustering accuracy. Beyond the traditional Euclidean distance, our model incorporates Gaussian kernel distance, K-nearest neighbor distance, and low-pass filtering distance to effectively manage data that is not linearly separable. Furthermore, we introduce a balanced regularizer to achieve balanced clustering results. The detailed experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed methodology.

paragraphs: K-means is simple and efficient, but its results can depend on initial centroid choices, and ordinary Euclidean geometry can miss nonlinear structure in data. It can also struggle to produce balanced clusters. This paper develops a unified clustering framework that incorporates manifold learning to address these weaknesses.

The approach removes centroid calculation and uses a cluster indicator matrix to align manifold structures. That matrix represents cluster assignments within the learning process. The framework also extends beyond Euclidean distance by incorporating Gaussian-kernel, nearest-neighbor, and low-pass-filtering distances. These alternatives provide ways to account for relationships that ordinary straight-line distance may not capture in data that are not linearly separable.

A balancing regularizer further encourages balanced clustering results. The reported experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the overall methodology. Its contribution is to bring assignment information, nonlinear data structure, and cluster balance into one formulation. This changes both how relationships among data points are represented and how cluster assignments are encouraged, while retaining k-means as the starting point.
summary.tldr: The framework combines centroid-free k-means, manifold-aware distances, and a balancing regularizer to improve clustering.

title: Unified K-Means Clustering with Label-Guided Manifold Learning

abstract: This paper studies the problem of differentially private empirical risk minimization (DP-ERM) for binary linear classification. We obtain an efficient $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-DP algorithm with an empirical zero-one risk bound of $\tilde{O}\left(\frac{1}{\gamma^2\varepsilon n} + \frac{|S_{\mathrm{out}}|}{\gamma n}\right)$ where $n$ is the number of data points, $S_{\mathrm{out}}$ is an arbitrary subset of data one can remove and $\gamma$ is the margin of linear separation of the remaining data points (after $S_{\mathrm{out}}$ is removed). Here, $\tilde{O}(\cdot)$ hides only logarithmic terms. In the agnostic case, we improve the existing results when the number of outliers is small. Our algorithm is highly adaptive because it does not require knowing the margin parameter $\gamma$ or outlier subset $S_{\mathrm{out}}$. We also derive a utility bound for the advanced private hyperparameter tuning algorithm.

paragraphs: This paper studies private learning for binary linear classification when most examples may be easy to separate, even if some are not. Its central question is whether a learner can benefit from a large separation margin on a subset of the data while maintaining differential privacy and tolerating the remaining examples.

The authors give an efficient algorithm with an empirical classification-error bound governed by two terms. Ignoring logarithmic factors, one scales as 1/(γ²εn), and the other as |S_out|/(γn). Here, n is the dataset size, ε controls privacy, and γ is the separation margin after removing an arbitrary subset S_out. Larger margins and fewer removed examples make this guarantee more favorable.

Crucially, the algorithm does not need to know either the margin or which examples belong to the removable subset. In the agnostic setting, the bound improves existing results when there are few outliers. The paper also derives a utility bound for advanced private hyperparameter tuning, extending its analysis to choosing learning settings under privacy constraints.
summary.tldr: A private linear-classification algorithm adapts to large-margin subsets without knowing their margins or outliers in advance.

title: Adapting to Linear Separable Subsets with Large-Margin in Differentially Private Learning

abstract: Solving partial differential equations (PDEs) using neural methods has been a long-standing scientific and engineering research pursuit. Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) have emerged as a promising alternative to traditional numerical methods for solving PDEs. However, the gap between domain-specific knowledge and deep learning expertise often limits the practical application of PINNs. Previous works typically involve manually conducting extensive PINNs experiments and summarizing heuristic rules for hyperparameter tuning. In this work, we introduce PINNsAgent, a novel surrogation framework that leverages large language models (LLMs) to bridge the gap between domain-specific knowledge and deep learning. PINNsAgent integrates Physics-Guided Knowledge Replay (PGKR) for efficient knowledge transfer from solved PDEs to similar problems, and Memory Tree Reasoning for exploring the search space of optimal PINNs architectures. We evaluate PINNsAgent on 14 benchmark PDEs, demonstrating its effectiveness in automating the surrogation process and significantly improving the accuracy of PINNs-based solutions.

paragraphs: Physics-informed neural networks offer a neural approach to solving partial differential equations, but building an effective model requires both domain knowledge and deep learning expertise. Existing practice often involves extensive manual experiments followed by heuristic tuning rules. PINNsAgent aims to automate this surrogation process using large language models.

The framework combines two mechanisms. Physics-Guided Knowledge Replay transfers knowledge from already solved equations to similar problems. Memory Tree Reasoning explores the space of possible PINN architectures. Together, these components connect reusable problem-solving experience with architecture search, addressing both how earlier solutions can inform a new problem and how candidate network designs can be explored.

The authors evaluate PINNsAgent on 14 benchmark partial differential equations and report effective automation with significantly improved solution accuracy. The result supports using an LLM-centered framework to coordinate the design of physics-informed neural surrogates. Its practical contribution is to reduce the reliance on manually accumulated tuning experience while using similarities among equations to make previous work useful for subsequent problems.
summary.tldr: PINNsAgent combines knowledge replay and architecture search to automate neural PDE surrogation and improve solution accuracy.

title: PINNsAgent: Automated PDE Surrogation with Large Language Models

abstract: Recent theoretical studies (Kou et al., 2023; Cao et al., 2022) revealed a sharp phase transition from benign to harmful overfitting when the noise-to-feature ratio exceeds a threshold—a situation common in long-tailed data distributions where atypical data is prevalent. However, such harmful overfitting rarely happens in overparameterized neural networks. Further experimental results suggested that memorization is necessary for achieving near-optimal generalization error in long-tailed data distributions (Feldman & Zhang, 2020). We argue that this discrepancy between theoretical predictions and empirical observations arises because previous feature-noise data models overlook the heterogeneous nature of noise across different data classes. In this paper, we refine the feature-noise data model by incorporating class-dependent heterogeneous noise and re-examine the overfitting phenomenon in neural networks. Through a comprehensive analysis of the training dynamics, we establish test loss bounds for the refined model. Our findings reveal that neural networks can leverage "data noise" to learn implicit features that improve the classification accuracy for long-tailed data. Our analysis also provides a training-free metric for evaluating data influence on test performance. Experimental validation on both synthetic and real-world datasets supports our theoretical results.

paragraphs: This paper revisits why memorizing unusual training examples can coexist with good generalization in neural networks. Earlier feature-noise theories predicted harmful overfitting beyond a noise threshold, yet the abstract describes a mismatch with empirical behavior on long-tailed data. The authors argue that those models miss an important detail: noise can differ across classes.

They refine the data model to include class-dependent heterogeneous noise and analyze the resulting training dynamics in two-layer networks. The analysis establishes bounds on test loss. Its central finding is that what the model calls noise can contain implicit features that neural networks use to improve classification accuracy on long-tailed data.

The analysis also yields a metric for estimating how data influences test performance without training. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets support the theoretical results. The contribution changes how noise is represented in the explanation of overfitting, showing that class-dependent structure can make some apparent noise useful for prediction under the studied model.
summary.tldr: A refined theory shows how class-dependent noise can contain useful features, helping explain benign overfitting on long-tailed data.

title: Rethinking Benign Overfitting in Two-Layer Neural Networks

abstract: Deep graph clustering (DGC), which aims to unsupervisedly separate the nodes in an attribute graph into different clusters, has seen substantial potential in various industrial scenarios like community detection and recommendation. However, the real-world attribute graphs, e.g., social networks interactions, are usually large-scale and attribute-missing. To solve these two problems, we propose a novel DGC method termed Complementary Multi-View Neighborhood Differentiation ($\textit{CMV-ND}$), which preprocesses graph structural information into multiple views in a complete but non-redundant manner. First, to ensure completeness of the structural information, we propose a recursive neighborhood search that recursively explores the local structure of the graph by completely expanding node neighborhoods across different hop distances. Second, to eliminate the redundancy between neighborhoods at different hops, we introduce a neighborhood differential strategy that ensures no overlapping nodes between the differential hop representations. Then, we construct $K+1$ complementary views from the $K$ differential hop representations and the features of the target node. Last, we apply existing multi-view clustering or DGC methods to the views. Experimental results on six widely used graph datasets demonstrate that CMV-ND significantly improves the performance of various methods.

paragraphs: Graph clustering groups nodes without requiring cluster labels, using their connections and available attributes. Real-world graphs can be both large and incomplete, with some node attributes missing. CMV-ND addresses these challenges by preparing complementary views of graph structure that existing clustering methods can use.

The method first recursively expands a node’s neighborhood across different hop distances to capture local structural information completely. It then differentiates those neighborhoods so their representations contain no overlapping nodes across hops. This removes redundancy between views of nearby and more distant connections. Combining K differential neighborhood representations with the target node’s features produces K plus one complementary views.

Existing multi-view clustering or deep graph clustering methods operate on the resulting representations. Experiments on six commonly used graph datasets show significant performance improvements across various methods. The contribution therefore lies in how graph information is organized before clustering: preserving the explored neighborhood information while avoiding repeated inclusion of the same nodes at different distances. This makes the preprocessing useful across multiple downstream clustering approaches.
summary.tldr: CMV-ND builds nonoverlapping neighborhood views that improve existing clustering methods on graphs with missing attributes.

title: Scalable Attribute-Missing Graph Clustering via Neighborhood Differentiation

abstract: Deep neural networks often degrade under distribution shifts. Although domain adaptation offers a solution, privacy constraints often prevent access to source data, making Test-Time Adaptation (TTA)—which adapts using only unlabeled test data—increasingly attractive. However, current TTA methods still face practical challenges: (1) a primary focus on instance-wise alignment, overlooking CORrelation ALignment (CORAL) due to missing source correlations; (2) complex backpropagation operations for model updating, resulting in overhead computation and (3) domain forgetting. To address these challenges, we provide a theoretical analysis to investigate the feasibility of Test-time Correlation Alignment (TCA), demonstrating that correlation alignment between high-certainty instances and test instances can enhance test performances with a theoretical guarantee. Based on this, we propose two simple yet effective algorithms: LinearTCA and LinearTCA+. LinearTCA applies a simple linear transformation to achieve both instance and correlation alignment without additional model updates, while LinearTCA+ serves as a plug-and-play module that can easily boost existing TTA methods. Extensive experiments validate our theoretical insights and show that TCA methods significantly outperforms baselines across various tasks, benchmarks and backbones. Notably, LinearTCA achieves higher accuracy with only 4% GPU memory and 0.6% computation time compared to the best TTA baseline. It also outperforms existing methods on CLIP over 1.86%. Code: https://github.com/youlj109/TCA

paragraphs: Test-time adaptation adjusts predictions using unlabeled test data when the deployment distribution differs from training. Access to source data may be restricted, making source correlations unavailable. This paper investigates whether correlations among high-certainty test instances can instead provide a useful alignment reference for the broader test population.

The authors give a theoretical analysis supporting performance improvement through this form of correlation alignment. LinearTCA implements the idea with a linear transformation that aligns both instances and correlations without further model updates. LinearTCA+ provides a plug-in version for existing adaptation methods, allowing the same principle to supplement their adaptation procedures.

Across evaluated tasks, benchmarks, and backbones, the methods outperform the compared baselines. LinearTCA achieves higher accuracy while using 4% of the GPU memory and 0.6% of the computation time of the best TTA baseline in the reported comparison. The authors also report an improvement exceeding 1.86% over existing methods on CLIP. These findings combine predictive gains with a particularly low computational burden for the update-free variant.
summary.tldr: Test-time correlation alignment uses high-certainty instances as a reference, improving reported adaptation accuracy with very low computational cost.

title: Test-time Correlation Alignment

abstract: Preference alignment in Large Language Models (LLMs) has significantly improved their ability to adhere to human instructions and intentions. However, existing direct alignment algorithms primarily focus on relative preferences and often overlook the qualitative aspects of responses, despite having access to preference data that includes reward scores from judge models during AI feedback. Striving to maximize the implicit reward gap between the chosen and the slightly inferior rejected responses can cause overfitting and unnecessary unlearning of the high-quality rejected responses. The unawareness of the reward scores also drives the LLM to indiscriminately favor the low-quality chosen responses and fail to generalize to optimal responses that are sparse in data. To overcome these shortcomings, our study introduces reward-conditioned LLM policies that discern and learn from the entire spectrum of response quality within the dataset, helping extrapolate to more optimal regions. We propose an effective yet simple data relabeling method that conditions the preference pairs on quality scores to construct a reward-augmented dataset. The experiments across various benchmarks and diverse models demonstrate that our approach consistently boosts DPO by a considerable margin. Through comprehensive ablation studies, we demonstrate that our method not only maximizes the utility of preference data but also mitigates the issue of unlearning, demonstrating its broad effectiveness beyond mere data expansion. Our code is available at https://github.com/shenao-zhang/reward-augmented-preference.

paragraphs: Preference training often records which response is better while overlooking how good either response actually is. The paper argues that this can penalize a strong response merely because another is slightly better, or encourage a weak response because its alternative is worse. Both problems arise from treating relative preference as the whole training signal.

The proposed approach uses reward scores already available from judge models. It relabels preference pairs to condition them on quality scores, producing a reward-augmented dataset and reward-conditioned language-model policies. This allows training to distinguish different levels of response quality and aims to help the model generalize toward better responses that are sparse in the original data.

Experiments across multiple models and benchmarks consistently improve DPO by a considerable margin. Ablation studies also support reduced unlearning of useful responses and show benefits beyond simply expanding the dataset. The central finding is that preserving quality information within preference training can make better use of the same underlying judgments and reduce harmful pressure against relatively rejected but valuable answers.
summary.tldr: Conditioning preference data on reward scores improves DPO and helps reduce unlearning of high-quality rejected responses.

title: Reward-Augmented Data Enhances Direct Preference Alignment of LLMs

abstract: Data sets used in recent work on graph similarity scoring and matching tasks suffer from significant limitations.  Using Graph Edit Distance (GED) as a showcase, we highlight pervasive issues such as train-test leakage and poor generalization, which have misguided the community's understanding and assessment of the capabilities of a method or model.These limitations arise, in part, because preparing labeled data is computationally expensive for combinatorial graph problems.We establish some key properties of GED that enable scalable data augmentation for training, and adversarial test set generation.Together, our analysis, experiments and insights establish new, sound guidelines for designing and evaluating future neural networks, and suggest open challenges for future research.

Using Graph Edit Distance (GED) as a showcase, we highlight pervasive issues such as train-test leakage and poor generalization, which have misguided the community's understanding and assessment of the capabilities of a method or model.These limitations arise, in part, because preparing labeled data is computationally expensive for combinatorial graph problems.We establish some key properties of GED that enable scalable data augmentation for training, and adversarial test set generation.Together, our analysis, experiments and insights establish new, sound guidelines for designing and evaluating future neural networks, and suggest open challenges for future research.

paragraphs: Graph matching and similarity systems depend on datasets that let researchers judge whether their methods work beyond the examples used in training. This paper argues that datasets used in recent research have serious weaknesses. Using Graph Edit Distance as its main example, it highlights training and test leakage and poor generalization that have distorted assessments of model capabilities.

The authors connect part of the problem to the computational expense of preparing labeled examples for combinatorial graph tasks. They establish properties of Graph Edit Distance that support scalable augmentation of training data and the generation of adversarial test sets. This connects an analysis of the task itself to practical ways of constructing better evaluation data.

The resulting contribution combines analysis, experiments, and guidelines for designing and evaluating future neural systems. Its significance is that a benchmark can give a misleading impression of progress when its construction does not adequately challenge generalization. The paper offers ways to improve that construction and identifies remaining research challenges, making dataset quality a central part of assessing graph matching methods.
summary.tldr: The paper exposes weaknesses in graph matching benchmarks and uses Graph Edit Distance properties to support better training and adversarial evaluation data.

title: Position: Graph Matching Systems Deserve Better Benchmarks

abstract: Quantile estimation and inference play essential roles in diverse scientific and industrial applications, and their accuracy can often be enhanced by integrating auxiliary data from multiple sites. However, developing efficient aggregation methods for quantile inference under potential privacy constraints, particularly with heterogeneous datasets, remains challenging. To address these issues, we propose a systematic framework for quantile estimation and inference under potential local differential privacy (LDP). The key idea is to construct weighted estimators by adaptively aggregating quantile estimates from target and source sites. The adaptive weights are determined by minimizing the asymptotic variance, incorporating an additional $\ell_2$ penalty to account for parameter shift. A parallel stochastic gradient descent algorithm under LDP constraints is developed for weight estimation and valid inference. Additionally, we introduce a conservative weighted estimator to ensure robust inference across diverse heterogeneous scenarios. Rigorous theoretical analysis establishes the consistency, normality, and effectiveness of the proposed methods. Extensive numerical studies and real data application corroborate our theoretical findings.

abstract: Classifying protein topology is essential for deciphering biological function, but progress is held back by the lack of large-scale benchmarks that avoid duplicates and by models that do not scale well. We introduce TEDBench, a large-scale, non-redundant benchmark for protein fold classification constructed from the Encyclopedia of Domains (TED) and Foldseek-clustered AlphaFold structures. We show that on TEDBench, current protein representation learning methods either require very large models or fail to deliver strong performance. To address this challenge, we propose Masked Invariant Autoencoders (MiAE), a self-supervised framework for protein structure representation learning. MiAE uses an extremely high masking ratio of up to $90%$ with an $\mathrm{SE(3)}$-invariant encoder and a lightweight decoder that reconstructs backbone coordinates from the latent representation and mask tokens. MiAE scales well and outperforms supervised counterparts and state-of-the-art baselines on TEDBench, establishing a strong recipe for protein fold classification. To test transfer beyond AlphaFold structures, we further benchmark on a curated dataset from experimental structures of CATH v4.4. TEDBench is available at https://github.com/BorgwardtLab/TEDBench.

title: Protein Fold Classification at Scale: Benchmarking and Pretraining

abstract: Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models enable conditional computation but face deployment challenges due to the memory wall: while few experts are activated per token, the entire model must reside in memory. Existing expert pruning methods primarily rely on independent ranking, failing to account for the complex inter-dependencies and redundancies between experts. In this paper, we formulate post-training MoE pruning as a reconstruction-driven subset selection problem, aiming to minimize layer-output distortion under a cardinality constraint. We introduce SCHUR-A, an algorithm that leverages A search to achieve globally optimal expert selection within each layer. To maintain computational tractability, we derive a novel, admissible heuristic upper bound using a Schur-complement-based relaxation of the reconstruction objective. This tight bound allows for aggressive pruning of the search space while mathematically guaranteeing optimality. Furthermore, we propose an automated strategy to balance fidelity and memory reduction across heterogeneous layers via knee-point detection. Extensive experiments on Qwen3-30B-A3B demonstrate that SCHUR-A* significantly outperforms greedy and ranking-based baselines, maintaining comparable performance even under aggressive pruning ratios.

This paper formulates pruning as choosing a subset that minimizes distortion of a layer’s output under a limit on the number retained.

SCHUR-A* uses A* search to find the globally optimal subset within each layer for this reconstruction objective. The work demonstrates the value of evaluating experts jointly: a subset’s ability to reconstruct a layer’s behavior depends on how its members work together, which independent importance scores can fail to capture.
summary.tldr: SCHUR-A* uses mathematically guided search to select optimal expert subsets within each layer while balancing reconstruction fidelity and memory savings.

title: SCHUR-A*: Layer-wise Optimal Expert Pruning for MoEs via Schur-Complement Guided A* Search

abstract: Model merging in the pretrain-finetune paradigm has proven effective by combining multiple finetuned models into one with multi-task capabilities. However, existing methods rely on fix or manually tuned merging coefficients, making the unified model sensitive to the initial merging strategy and suboptimal for downstream adaptation. Thus, this paper proposed an innovative model merging framework called MetaMerging, a novel meta-learning algorithm to adaptively optimize the merging coefficients to construct a unified model tailored for task-specific adapter training. By simulating adapter updates in an inner loop and meta-optimizing merging coefficients in an outer loop, MetaMerging produces more balanced and generalizable unified models. Extensive experiments on CV and NLP fields show strong performance of MetaMerging on various downstream tasks and demonstrate the effectiveness of meta-learning in our method compared to other parameter merging methods. Our code is available at https://github.com/cjcj46262/MetaMerging.

paragraphs: Model merging combines separately fine-tuned models into one model with multiple capabilities. The weights assigned to those source models influence the result, yet existing approaches often fix these coefficients or tune them manually. MetaMerging instead learns coefficients with a specific downstream goal: creating a shared model that is well suited to task-specific adapter training.

The method uses two nested learning loops. The inner loop simulates adapter updates for downstream tasks. The outer loop adjusts merging coefficients based on that adaptation process. This makes the merge sensitive to how the resulting model will be used, connecting the initial combination of parameters to subsequent task-specific learning.

Experiments in computer vision and natural language processing report strong downstream performance and demonstrate the value of meta-learning compared with other parameter-merging methods. The resulting models are described as more balanced and generalizable. The contribution is an adaptive way to construct a multi-task starting point, with the merging decision evaluated through its usefulness for later adapter training.

title: Learn to Merge: Meta-Learning for Adaptive Multi-Task Model Merging

abstract: Inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) is typically formulated as maximizing entropy subject to matching the distribution of expert trajectories. Classical (dual-ascent) IRL guarantees monotonic performance improvement but requires fully solving an RL problem each iteration to compute dual gradients. More recent adversarial methods avoid this cost at the expense of stability and monotonic dual improvement, by directly optimizing the primal problem and using a discriminator to provide rewards. In this work, we bridge the gap between these approaches by enabling monotonic improvement of the reward function and policy without having to fully solve an RL problem at every iteration. Our key theoretical insight is that a trust-region-optimal policy for a reward function update can be globally optimal for a smaller update in the same direction. This smaller update allows us to explicitly optimize the dual objective while only relying on a local search around the current policy. In doing so, our approach avoids the training instabilities of adversarial methods, offers monotonic performance improvement, and learns a reward function in the traditional sense of IRL—one that can be globally optimized to match expert demonstrations. Our proposed algorithm, Trust Region Inverse Reinforcement Learning (TRIRL), outperforms state-of-the-art imitation learning methods across multiple challenging tasks by a factor of 2.4x in terms of aggregate inter-quartile mean, while recovering reward functions that generalize to system dynamics shifts.

title: Trust Region Inverse Reinforcement Learning: Explicit Dual Ascent using Local Policy Updates

abstract: As real-world knowledge continues to evolve, the parametric knowledge acquired by multimodal models during pretraining becomes increasingly difficult to remain consistent with real-world knowledge. Existing research on multimodal knowledge updating focuses only on learning previously unknown knowledge, while overlooking the need to update knowledge that the model has already mastered but that later changes; moreover, evaluation is limited to the same modality, lacking a systematic analysis of cross-modal consistency. To address these issues, this paper proposes MMKU-Bench, a comprehensive evaluation benchmark for multimodal knowledge updating, which contains over 25k knowledge instances and more than 49k images, covering two scenarios, updated knowledge and unknown knowledge, thereby enabling comparative analysis of learning across different knowledge types. On this benchmark, we evaluate a variety of representative approaches, including supervised fine-tuning (SFT), reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), and knowledge editing (KE). Experimental results show that SFT and RLHF are prone to catastrophic forgetting, while KE better preserve general capabilities but exhibit clear limitations in continual updating. Overall, MMKU-Bench provides a reliable and comprehensive evaluation benchmark for multimodal knowledge updating, advancing progress in this field. The code and dataset are available at https://github.com/baochenfu/MMKU-Bench.

paragraphs: Updating a multimodal model involves two distinct situations: teaching it something previously unknown and replacing something it learned correctly before the world changed. MMKU-Bench evaluates both. It also addresses cross-modal consistency, extending evaluation beyond whether updated knowledge works within the same modality in which it was assessed.

The benchmark contains more than 25,000 knowledge instances and over 49,000 images. Its two knowledge scenarios enable comparisons between learning new information and revising established knowledge. The authors use it to evaluate supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning from human feedback, and knowledge editing, bringing these approaches into a common evaluation framework.

The experiments reveal different weaknesses. Supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning from human feedback are prone to catastrophic forgetting, meaning updates can undermine previously learned capabilities. Knowledge editing better preserves general capabilities but has clear limitations when updates continue over time. These findings make the benchmark useful for examining both successful knowledge change and the ability to sustain broader model competence through repeated updating.
summary.tldr: MMKU-Bench evaluates learning new and changed multimodal knowledge, revealing forgetting and continual-update weaknesses in representative methods.

title: MMKU-Bench: A Multimodal Update Benchmark for Diverse Visual Knowledge

abstract: Machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) have proven to be wildly useful for molecular dynamics simulations, powering countless drug and materials discovery applications. However, MLIPs face two primary bottlenecks preventing them from reaching realistic simulation scales: inference time and memory consumption. In this work, we address both issues by challenging the long-held belief that the cutoff radius for the MLIP must be held to a fixed, constant value. For the first time, we introduce a dynamic cutoff formulation that still leads to stable, long timescale molecular dynamics simulation. In introducing the dynamic cutoff, we are able to induce sparsity onto the underlying atom graph by targeting a specific number of neighbors per atom, significantly reducing both memory consumption and inference time. We show the effectiveness of a dynamic cutoff by implementing it onto 4 state of the art MLIPs: MACE, Nequip, Orbv3, and TensorNet, leading to 2.26x less memory consumption and 2.04x faster inference time, depending on the model and atomic system. We also perform an extensive error analysis and find that the dynamic cutoff models exhibit minimal accuracy dropoff compared to their fixed cutoff counterparts on both materials and molecular datasets. All model implementations and training code will be fully open sourced.

title: Smooth Dynamic Cutoffs for Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials

abstract: Large language models can be steered at inference time through prompting or activation interventions, but activation steering methods often underperform compared to prompt-based approaches. We investigate whether activation steering can be improved by learning to mimic the interventions that prompt steering triggers within the model. To this end, we introduce Prompt Steering Replacement (PSR) models, a new family of activation steering methods that distill prompt steering behavior into interpretable interventions on model activations. A PSR is an activation steering method that estimates position-specific steering coefficients and is trained to imitate prompt-based interventions. Experiments on persona steering and instruction following across multiple language models demonstrate that PSR models consistently outperform constant-coefficient interventions that are frequently used in the literature and achieve performance close to or exceeding prompt steering while maintaining interpretability.

paragraphs: Language models can be directed through written prompts or through changes to their internal activations. Activation steering often performs worse than prompting. This paper investigates whether it can improve by learning to reproduce the internal interventions that a steering prompt itself induces, using prompting as the behavior to imitate.

The proposed Prompt Steering Replacement models estimate position-specific steering coefficients. That lets the intervention vary across positions instead of applying the constant coefficients common in existing approaches. Training distills prompt-induced behavior into interpretable activation interventions, connecting a successful external instruction to a structured internal control mechanism.

Experiments cover persona steering and instruction following across multiple language models. PSR consistently outperforms the constant-coefficient interventions tested and reaches performance close to, or above, prompt steering while maintaining interpretability. These results support the usefulness of adapting steering strength by position and learning from the model’s own response to prompts. The demonstrated advantage concerns the evaluated tasks and models, while the broader contribution is a family of interventions trained to mimic prompt-based control.
summary.tldr: Prompt Steering Replacement learns position-specific activation interventions that match or approach prompting performance in the reported evaluations.

title: Steer Like the LLM: Activation Steering that Mimics Prompting

abstract: Quantized neural network training optimizes a discrete, non-differentiable objective. The straight-through estimator (STE) enables backpropagation through surrogate gradients and is widely used. While previous studies have primarily focused on the properties of surrogate gradients and their convergence, the influence of quantization hyperparameters, such as bit width and quantization range, on learning dynamics remains largely unexplored. We theoretically show that in the high-dimensional limit, STE dynamics converge to a deterministic ordinary differential equation. This reveals that STE training exhibits a plateau followed by a sharp drop in generalization error, with plateau length depending on the quantization range. A fixed-point analysis quantifies the asymptotic deviation from the unquantized linear model. We also extend analytical techniques for stochastic gradient descent to nonlinear transformations of weights and inputs.

paragraphs: Quantized models use discrete representations, making their training objective non-differentiable. The straight-through estimator enables training by substituting surrogate gradients for derivatives that cannot be used directly. This paper examines how quantization choices shape the resulting learning trajectory, extending attention beyond whether those surrogate gradients converge.

The authors show theoretically that, in a high-dimensional limit, the training dynamics converge to a deterministic ordinary differential equation. This provides a tractable description of how learning evolves. The analysis reveals a plateau in generalization error followed by a sharp decline, with the plateau’s duration depending on the quantization range.

A fixed-point analysis then measures the eventual deviation from an unquantized linear model. The paper also extends analytical tools for stochastic gradient descent to nonlinear transformations of weights and inputs. Its contribution is therefore both an explanation of delayed progress during quantized training and a framework for studying its long-term behavior. The conclusions about the trajectory arise in the stated high-dimensional theoretical setting.
summary.tldr: A high-dimensional theory links straight-through training of quantized models to deterministic dynamics, explaining plateaus and quantization-dependent long-term behavior.

title: High-Dimensional Learning Dynamics of Quantized Models with Straight-Through Estimator

abstract: Data plays an invaluable role in large-scale ML training pipelines. Multiple factors, including the need to incentivize the creation of high-quality data and efforts to compensate creative data work, have led to increased interest in data pricing. Data pricing mechanisms seek to establish a market where data providers are compensated based (in part) on the value of their data to the data buyer, e.g., frontier AI labs. However, assessing the exact value that each provider’s data adds to the data buyer’s objective requires repeated re-training, which is infeasible in practice. Our work studies data pricing under compute constraints. In our setting, data buyers cannot make data acquisition decisions optimally due to limited compute. Inspired by existing practice in the field of data selection, we propose a model for this problem called “pricing with an attribution oracle,” and provide a theoretical analysis of compute-efficient acquisition and pricing.

paragraphs: Pricing training data requires some way to connect a provider’s payment to the value their data creates for a buyer. This matters both for encouraging useful data production and for compensating the people who produce it. The paper examines this market-design problem when the buyer has a limited amount of computation.

The obstacle is that exact valuation can require repeatedly retraining a model to determine how different data contributions affect the buyer’s objective. At large training scales, that process is infeasible. Consequently, the buyer cannot simply calculate every contribution precisely and make optimal acquisition decisions on that basis.

The authors introduce a framework called pricing with an attribution oracle, inspired by existing data-selection practices. They use it to theoretically analyze acquisition and pricing under computational constraints. The contribution is a model for reasoning about what a data market can do when valuation itself consumes scarce resources. It brings the feasibility of assessing data value into the pricing problem, rather than assuming that value is already available at no computational cost.
summary.tldr: The paper develops a theoretical framework for acquiring and pricing training data when limited computation prevents exact valuation.

title: A Theory of Data Acquisition and Pricing at Scale

abstract: Partial differential equations (PDEs) are fundamental for modeling complex natural and physical phenomena. In many real-world applications, however, observational data are extremely sparse, which severely limits the applicability of both classical numerical solvers and existing neural approaches. While neural methods have shown promising results under moderately sparse observations, their inference efficiency at high resolutions is limited, and their accuracy degrades substantially in the extremely sparse regime. In this work, we propose the Di-BiLPS, a unified neural framework that effectively handle both forward and inverse PDE problems under extremely sparse observations. Di-BiLPS combines a variational autoencoder to compress high-dimensional inputs into a compact latent space, a latent diffusion module to model uncertainty, and contrastive learning to align representations. Operating entirely in this latent space, the framework achieves efficient inference while retaining flexible input–output mapping. In addition, we introduce a PDE-informed denoising algorithm based on a variance-preserving diffusion process, which further improves inference efficiency. Extensive experiments on multiple PDE benchmarks demonstrate that Di-BiLPS consistently achieves SOTA performance under extremely sparse inputs (as low as 3%), while substantially reducing computational cost. Moreover, Di-BiLPS enables zero-shot super-resolution, as it allows predictions over continuous spatial–temporal domains.

It also addresses the computational cost of producing high-resolution predictions, which can limit existing neural approaches even when their inputs are less sparse.

The framework compresses high-dimensional inputs through a variational autoencoder, represents uncertainty with latent diffusion, and uses contrastive learning to align representations. Performing its core operations in the compact latent space supports efficient inference and flexible input-output mappings. A PDE-informed denoising algorithm based on variance-preserving diffusion further improves inference efficiency.

Across multiple PDE benchmarks, the authors report state-of-the-art performance with observed inputs as sparse as 3%, together with substantially lower computational cost. The framework can also predict over continuous spatial and temporal domains, enabling zero-shot super-resolution. These results connect sparse-data reconstruction and efficient high-resolution prediction within the same latent-space approach, covering both directions of the PDE modeling problem.
summary.tldr: Di-BiLPS uses compact latent representations and PDE-informed diffusion to solve forward and inverse problems from extremely sparse observations.

title: Di-BiLPS: Denoising induced Bidirectional Latent-PDE-Solver under Sparse Observations

abstract: Fine-grained traffic prediction is critically important for mitigating traffic congestion in key urban areas and for providing lane-change guidance in autonomous vehicles and navigation systems. However, task-specific models are not efficient enough, city-scale pre-trained models often overlook fine-grained requirements, and the demand for extensive computational resources hinders practical deployment. To address this issue, we developed a lightweight pre-training framework, MiniTraffic. This framework leverages abundant road-level data to address lane-level data scarcity through a frequency domain stability augmentation module and captures road-lane correlations via contrastive clustering to construct small-scale graph structures, significantly reducing model parameters. Fine-tuning with minimal target data provides a unified and efficient solution for fine-grained traffic prediction. In multi-granularity traffic prediction tasks across six fine-grained datasets, MiniTraffic demonstrated superior performance compared to existing baselines.

Such predictions can support congestion management and lane-change guidance, but lane-level data are scarce and computationally demanding models can be difficult to deploy. MiniTraffic addresses both the data shortage and the need for smaller models.

The framework uses abundant road-level observations to support learning for lane-level tasks. A frequency-domain stability augmentation module helps address the scarcity of detailed data, while contrastive clustering captures relationships between roads and lanes. These relationships are organized into small graph structures, substantially reducing the number of model parameters. The pretrained model is then fine-tuned using a small amount of target-task data.

Across six fine-grained datasets covering traffic prediction at multiple granularities, MiniTraffic outperforms the evaluated baselines. The approach matters because it connects information available at a broad scale with predictions needed at a finer scale. Its reported results support compact pretraining as a practical route to detailed traffic prediction without requiring extensive target data.
summary.tldr: MiniTraffic transfers road-level information into compact models for fine-grained traffic prediction using little target data.

title: Being More Lightweight and Practical: Mini-sized Contrastive Learning Pre-trained Models for Fine-grained Traffic Task

abstract: Model merging offers an appealing route to multi-task learning by composing independently fine-tuned checkpoints without centralized data or retraining. However, this convenience can come with a hidden cost. Model merging may amplify performance disparities across subgroups, raising fairness concerns even when average accuracy remains competitive. To explain this phenomenon, we develop a sensitivity-based theoretical analysis that upper bounds the fairness gap induced by model merging. Theoretical analysis with empirical verifications reveals that the resulting fairness gap is governed by two coupled factors, a merging magnitude term that measures how far the merged parameters move from the target model and global sensitivity terms that determine how unevenly the perturbation affects subgroup losses. Guided by these insights, we propose FairMerging, a two-stage merging framework that first reduces the sensitivity of the target model and then performs fairness-aware coefficient optimization with orthogonally normalized task vectors. Experiments across multiple datasets, backbones, and merging baselines demonstrate that FairMerging substantially mitigates unfairness while retaining competitive multi-task performance.
