This paper examines how merging itself can amplify those disparities. Its analysis asks how moving model parameters changes subgroup losses, bringing fairness directly into the study of model composition.

The authors derive an upper bound on the fairness gap induced by merging. Two coupled quantities matter: how far the merged parameters move from a target model, and how unevenly subgroup losses respond to that movement. This connects fairness to both the size of the parameter change and the target model’s sensitivity to it.

FairMerging turns that analysis into a two-stage procedure. It first reduces target-model sensitivity, then optimizes merging coefficients with fairness in mind using orthogonally normalized task vectors. Experiments across datasets, backbones, and merging baselines report substantially reduced unfairness while maintaining competitive multi-task performance. The findings show why controlling parameter movement alone may leave an important source of disparity unaddressed.
summary.tldr: FairMerging reduces subgroup disparities by addressing model sensitivity and fairness when choosing how to combine task-specific models.

title: FairMerging: Rethinking Model Merging through the Lens of Fairness

abstract: Conveying complex objectives to reinforcement learning (RL) agents often requires meticulous reward engineering. Preference-based RL (PbRL) offers a promising alternative by learning reward functions from human feedback, but its scalability is hindered by high labeling costs. Inspired by advances in Video Foundation Models (ViFMs), we present Video-based Optimal Transport Preference (VOTP), a semi-supervised framework that learns effective reward functions from only a handful of labels. By leveraging optimal transport to align visual trajectories within the rich representation space of ViFMs, VOTP effectively generates high-fidelity pseudo-labels for large amounts of unlabeled data, substantially reducing human supervision. Extensive experiments across locomotion and manipulation benchmarks demonstrate the superiority of VOTP, which outperforms state-of-the-art offline PbRL methods under limited feedback budgets. We also showcase the robustness of VOTP in the presence of visual distractors and validate its utility on real robotic tasks, where it learns meaningful rewards with minimal human input.

Its practical difficulty is the amount of human labeling required. VOTP addresses this cost in offline learning by combining a small set of preference labels with a much larger collection of unlabeled visual trajectories.

The framework represents those trajectories using a video foundation model and aligns them with optimal transport. This alignment generates high-fidelity pseudo-labels for unlabeled data, extending the supervision available for learning a reward function. The approach is semi-supervised: the human labels provide an initial source of guidance, while visual representations and trajectory matching help carry that guidance across additional data.

Experiments on locomotion and manipulation benchmarks show that VOTP outperforms state-of-the-art offline preference-based methods under limited feedback budgets. The authors also report robustness to visual distractors and demonstrate meaningful reward learning on real robotic tasks with minimal human input. These results support trajectory alignment as a way to reduce labeling demands while retaining useful reward information in the tested settings.
summary.tldr: VOTP uses video representations and optimal transport to generate preference pseudo-labels, improving offline reward learning with limited human feedback.

title: Video-Based Optimal Transport for Feedback-Efficient Offline Preference-Based Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Distinguishing Large Language Model (LLM) generated text from human writing is a critical and difficult challenge. While LLMs are trained to write like humans, we hypothesize that this training leaves an indelible mark. LLMs develop a particularly strong aversion to token repetition very early in training. This bias persists as a “Vestigial Heuristic” (a developmental artifact) that is activated in LLM-generated text, separating LLM from human writing. To probe this phenomenon, we introduce Telescope Perplexity, a metric that evaluates the token repetition of the model, $P(s_i | s_{1:i})$. Our empirical investigation reveals that the Telescope Perplexity signature emerges early in pre-training, and Telescope Perplexity empirically enables highly effective zero-shot LLM detection. We show state-of-the-art or competitive performance across diverse datasets (including modern evaluation sets we introduce), reference models, and perturbation schemes with greater efficiency than other methods.

paragraphs: Detecting machine-generated writing is difficult because language models are trained to resemble human text. This paper investigates a possible trace of that training: a strong tendency to avoid repeating tokens. The authors hypothesize that the tendency develops early and persists as a developmental artifact that behaves differently on model-generated and human-written text.

They introduce Telescope Perplexity to probe this behavior. Its probability measure asks about a token after the context already includes that token, directly examining repetition probability. This gives the detector a signal tied to the model's treatment of repetition. The empirical study finds that the signature appears early in pretraining, supporting the proposed account of its origin.

Telescope Perplexity enables effective zero-shot detection in the reported evaluations. It achieves state-of-the-art or competitive performance across multiple datasets, reference models, and text perturbations, with greater efficiency than comparison methods. The authors also introduce modern evaluation sets. The results establish repetition probability as a useful empirical detection signal, while the developmental explanation remains framed as the paper's hypothesis.
summary.tldr: Telescope Perplexity uses token-repetition probabilities as an efficient signal for zero-shot detection of model-generated writing.

title: Telescope: Improving Zero Shot Detection of LLM Generated Content By Measuring Token Repetition Probability

abstract: Supervised convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are widely used to solve imaging inverse problems, achieving state-of-the-art performance in numerous applications. However, despite their empirical success, these methods are poorly understood from a theoretical perspective and often treated as black boxes. To bridge this gap, we analyze trained neural networks through the lens of the Minimum Mean Square Error (MMSE) estimator, incorporating functional constraints that capture two fundamental inductive biases of CNNs: translation equivariance and locality via finite receptive fields. Under the empirical training distribution, we derive an analytic, interpretable, and tractable formula for this constrained variant, termed Local-Equivariant MMSE (LE-MMSE). Through extensive numerical experiments across various inverse problems (denoising, inpainting, deconvolution), datasets (FFHQ, CIFAR-10, FashionMNIST), and architectures (U-Net, ResNet, PatchMLP), we demonstrate that our theory matches the neural networks outputs (PSNR $\gtrsim25$ dB). Furthermore, we provide insights into the differences between physics-aware and physics-agnostic estimators, the impact of high-density regions in the training (patch) distribution, and the influence of other factors (dataset size, patch size, etc).

paragraphs: Convolutional networks can reconstruct images from corrupted or incomplete measurements, but their successful predictions are difficult to explain analytically. This paper studies those predictions through minimum mean square error estimation, an approach that selects an estimate to minimize expected squared reconstruction error.

The authors constrain that estimator to reflect two architectural properties: translation equivariance and a finite receptive field. These capture how a network responds to shifted inputs and how much nearby information it can use. Under the empirical training distribution, they derive Local-Equivariant MMSE, an explicit formula that is interpretable and computationally tractable. This gives a concrete mathematical account of behavior associated with these architectural biases.

Experiments cover denoising, inpainting, and deconvolution across several datasets and architectures. The analytic predictions match network outputs at approximately 25 dB PSNR or higher. The analysis also examines the role of dense regions in the training patch distribution, dataset size, patch size, and whether an estimator incorporates imaging physics. These results help connect reconstruction behavior to training data and structural constraints.
summary.tldr: A constrained minimum-error estimator provides an analytic explanation of image reconstruction networks through locality and translation equivariance.

title: An analytic theory of convolutional neural network inverse problems solvers

abstract: Real-world datasets often follow a long-tailed distribution, making generalization to tail classes difficult. We revisit this problem through the lens of shortcut learning, where models prefer the easiest predictive cues (e.g., background or textures) over object-centric semantics, especially under scarce and biased supervision. We find that this tendency is amplified for tail classes: limited examples often share similar contexts, making non-semantic signals highly correlated and thus tempting shortcuts, whereas head classes with diverse appearances and environments encourage more stable object-focused representations. Motivated by this observation, we propose Shortcut-Resistant CAM Distillation (SRCD), a plug-and-play framework that transfers object-focused explanations from head to tail classes. SRCD operates in the Class Activation Map (CAM) space, where a CAM provides a class-specific spatial evidence map for a prediction. SRCD aggregates CAMs from a small set of head-class candidates into a shortcut-resistant teacher using an energy-model weighting based on coherence and concentration, and distills it to the tail-class CAM. We provide a theoretical analysis that quantifies shortcut reliance as shortcut-region evidence mass in CAM space and shows that SRCD suppresses tail shortcuts. Extensive experiments on long-tailed benchmarks consistently improve strong baselines. The code is available at https://github.com/Haifeng3/SRCD.

paragraphs: In long-tailed recognition, some classes have many examples while others have very few. The paper finds that rare classes are especially vulnerable to shortcuts: their limited examples often share backgrounds or textures that correlate with the label. Common classes have more varied appearances and environments, encouraging representations that focus more consistently on the object.

Shortcut-Resistant CAM Distillation transfers object-focused evidence from common classes to rare ones. It works with Class Activation Maps, which locate spatial evidence for a class prediction. The method combines maps from a small set of common-class candidates into a teacher, weighting them through an energy model based on coherence and concentration, then distills that teacher into the rare-class map.

The theoretical analysis measures shortcut reliance as the amount of activation-map evidence assigned to shortcut regions and shows that SRCD suppresses rare-class shortcuts. Experiments consistently improve strong baselines on long-tailed benchmarks. The approach uses explanation maps as a training mechanism, directing rare-class learning toward object-related evidence when scarce examples otherwise make contextual cues unusually tempting.
summary.tldr: SRCD transfers object-focused activation maps from common classes to rare classes, reducing shortcut reliance and improving long-tailed recognition.

title: Shortcut-Resistant CAM Distillation for Long-Tailed Recognition

abstract: Coupled spatiotemporal forecasting is important for predicting the future evolution of multiple interacting dynamical systems, such as in climate models. However, existing methods are severely constrained by the persistent bottleneck of compounding errors. In coupled systems, errors from each subsystem simulator propagate and amplify one another, a phenomenon we term Reciprocal Error Amplification leading to a rapid collapse of long-range predictions. To address this challenge, we propose a universal framework called PnP-Corrector (Plug-and-Play Corrector). The core idea of our framework is to decouple the physical simulation from the error correction process: it freezes pre-trained physics simulation engines and exclusively trains a correction agent to proactively counteract the systematic biases emerging from the coupled system. Furthermore, we design an efficient predictive model architecture, DSLCast, to serve as the backbone of this framework. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method significantly enhances the long-term stability and accuracy of coupled forecasting systems. For instance, in the challenging task of a 300-day global ocean-atmosphere coupled forecast, our PnP-Corrector framework reduces the prediction error of the baseline model by 28% and surpasses state-of-the-art models on several key metrics. Codes link: https://github.com/Alexander-wu/PnP-Corrector.

abstract: Federated learning increasingly faces deletion requests that require client-level unlearning without sacrificing model quality, yet a client’s influence is often deeply entangled after many rounds of aggregation. We aim to make unlearning fast, stable, and predictable by reducing the gap to leave-one-out retraining under realistic heterogeneity. We propose Influence-Disentangled Federated Training (IDFT), which instruments standard FedAvg with training-time influence logging: each round’s updates are decomposed into shared covarying directions and a client-separable residual trace, and an entanglement-aware shrinkage suppresses non-removable components. Deletion then becomes a single subtraction followed by a short anchored repair, yielding a stability-style characterization of retrain fidelity driven by the unremoved residual. Across representative benchmarks, IDFT consistently attains the lowest retrain gap (Avg. Gap) on multiple dataset–architecture pairs and improves the fidelity–cost frontier, matching retrain-level forgetting with substantially lower communication/compute than history-heavy baselines. These results suggest a practical pathway to unlearning-friendly federated systems by designing for removability during training rather than relying solely on post-hoc corrections.

paragraphs: IDFT prepares a federated model for later requests to remove a client’s contribution. Repeated aggregation can entangle that contribution with other clients’ updates, making deletion difficult. The paper aims to make removal faster and more predictable while keeping the resulting model close to one retrained without the deleted client, including when clients have heterogeneous data.

During ordinary FedAvg training, IDFT records influence by splitting updates into shared directions that vary together and a residual trace separable by client. A shrinkage mechanism suppresses components that are difficult to remove. A deletion request then triggers one subtraction and a short anchored repair. The accompanying analysis relates fidelity to retraining to the residual influence that remains unremoved.

Across representative benchmarks and multiple dataset–architecture combinations, IDFT reports the lowest average gap to retraining. It also matches retraining-level forgetting with substantially less communication and computation than history-heavy baselines. These results support designing removability into training itself, so later deletion can use a prepared influence record instead of relying entirely on corrections after training.
summary.tldr: IDFT records and separates client influence during federated training, enabling efficient deletion that closely matches retraining without the client.

title: Influence-Disentangled Federated Training: Learning Models That Are Easy to Unlearn

abstract: Split Federated Learning (SFL) enables privacy-preserving collaborative training by partitioning models between clients and a server. However, under non-IID data distributions, SFL often suffers from biased optimization and unstable convergence, while existing solutions largely adapt techniques from conventional federated learning. In this work, we observe that the split architecture of SFL inherently alters how client information is represented and coordinated, opening opportunities for bias compensation beyond parameter-level aggregation. Based on this insight, we propose BESplit, an architecture-aware framework that exploits the intrinsic structure of SFL to mitigate non-IID effects. First, to prevent biased local data from dominating global updates, we introduce Evidential Aggregation (EA) to perform fine-grained reweighting of client contributions based on evidential uncertainty. Second, to further reduce distributional skew, we develop Bias-Compensated Collaboration (BCC) to align split-layer representations by pairing complementary clients. Finally, Dual-Teacher Distillation (DTD) is incorporated to synchronize knowledge between decoupled client and server models, enabling independent local inference. Extensive experiments on five benchmark datasets demonstrate that BESplit consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods in accuracy, convergence stability, and computational efficiency under diverse non-IID settings.

paragraphs: Split federated learning divides a model between participating clients and a server. When clients hold differently distributed data, their contributions can bias the shared training process and make convergence unstable. BESplit starts from the observation that this split also creates opportunities to coordinate information through intermediate representations, beyond simply combining model parameters.

The framework uses three complementary mechanisms. Evidential Aggregation reweights client contributions using uncertainty derived from evidence, aiming to prevent biased local data from dominating updates. Bias-Compensated Collaboration pairs complementary clients and aligns their representations at the split layer. Dual-Teacher Distillation then synchronizes knowledge between the separated client and server models, supporting inference locally without requiring the server.

Together, these mechanisms address contribution weighting, representation mismatch, and knowledge synchronization. Experiments on five benchmark datasets report consistently better accuracy, convergence stability, and computational efficiency than state-of-the-art methods across diverse non-IID settings. The findings support treating the split architecture itself as a resource for handling client differences, rather than relying only on adaptations of conventional federated-learning aggregation.
summary.tldr: BESplit uses uncertainty weighting, complementary client pairing, and distillation to improve split federated learning with uneven client data.

title: BESplit: Bias-Compensated Split Federated Learning with Evidential Aggregation

abstract: The integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) with automated theorem proving has shown immense promise, yet is constrained by challenges in scaling up both training-time reinforcement learning (RL) and inference-time compute. This paper introduces BFS-Prover-V2, a step-level theorem proving system designed to address this dual scaling problem. We present two primary innovations. The first is a novel multi-turn off-policy RL framework for continually improving the performance of the LLM step-prover at training time. This framework, inspired by the principles of AlphaZero, utilizes a multi-stage expert iteration pipeline featuring adaptive tactic-level data filtering and periodic retraining to surmount the performance plateaus that typically curtail long-term RL in LLM-based agents. The second innovation is a planner-enhanced multi-agent system that scales reasoning capabilities at inference time. This architecture employs a general reasoning model as a high-level planner to iteratively decompose complex theorems into a sequence of simpler subgoals. This hierarchical approach substantially reduces the search space, enabling a team of parallel prover agents to collaborate efficiently by leveraging a shared proof cache. We demonstrate that this dual approach to scaling yields state-of-the-art results on established formal mathematics benchmarks. BFS-Prover-V2 achieves 95.08% and 41.4% on the miniF2F and ProofNet test sets respectively. While demonstrated in the domain of formal mathematics, the RL and inference techniques presented in this work are of broader interest and may be applied to other domains requiring long-horizon multi-turn reasoning and complex search.

paragraphs: BFS-Prover-V2 tackles two ways to improve automated theorem proving: train a stronger model for individual proof steps, and organize more effective search when solving a theorem. The paper treats these as complementary scaling problems, since better training and more inference-time computation each need mechanisms that make continued investment useful.

For training, it introduces multi-turn off-policy reinforcement learning with repeated expert iteration. Adaptive filtering selects tactic-level training data, and periodic retraining aims to overcome performance plateaus. For inference, a general reasoning model plans by repeatedly decomposing a difficult theorem into simpler subgoals. Parallel prover agents work on the resulting search while sharing a proof cache, helping coordinate their efforts.

The authors report state-of-the-art benchmark results, including 95.08% on miniF2F and 41.4% on ProofNet test sets. These results support combining stronger step-level learning with hierarchical, collaborative search. The paper also suggests that the techniques may transfer to other long-horizon reasoning and search problems, but the reported demonstration is in formal mathematics.
summary.tldr: BFS-Prover-V2 combines iterative reinforcement learning with planner-guided parallel proof search to improve formal theorem proving.

title: BFS-Prover-V2: Scaling up Multi-Turn Off-Policy RL and Multi-Agent Tree Search for LLM Step-Provers

abstract: Automating User Interface (UI) generation substantially improves productivity and accelerates development by reducing engineering time and manual effort. Despite recent progress of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) in UI2Code, most existing approaches focus on a single HTML/CSS form and fail to systematically incorporate front-end frameworks such as React, Vue, and Angular. Moreover, their outputs are often verbose and hard to reuse at the component level. To address those issues, we propose Deterministic Component Mining (DCM), a multi-stage pipeline that couples MLLMs with a compact intermediate representation to enable multi-framework and component-oriented code generation. Firstly, a lightweight structure model predicts the representation of the DOM tree in JSON format, capturing the coarse layout from a webpage screenshot. Subsequently, we formulate deterministic rules to normalize the predicted DOM tree and mine reusable components with repetitive patterns via structural hashing and clustering, thereby yielding a portable intermediate representation. Finally, we employ a framework-conditioned prompting strategy governed by a binding specification and a file-block protocol to emit HTML/React/Vue/Angular code with explicit component props and repeat constructs. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DCM significantly outperforms baselines on automatic evaluation metrics and component-level reuse, while delivering consistent gains in multi-framework portability and overall code structural quality.

Deterministic Component Mining addresses these goals through a staged pipeline that combines multimodal language models with explicit structural processing.

The contribution is a way to make screenshot-derived structure reusable across frameworks, with component discovery handled explicitly before final code generation.
summary.tldr: DCM extracts reusable page components into a portable representation, improving screenshot-to-code generation across HTML, React, Vue, and Angular.

title: Deterministic Component Mining for Multi-Framework UI2Code Generation

abstract: Conformal prediction offers finite-sample coverage guarantees under minimal assumptions. However, existing methods treat the entire modeling process as a black box, overlooking opportunities to exploit and understand modular structure. We introduce a conformal prediction framework for two-stage sequential models, where an upstream predictor generates intermediate representations for a downstream model. By decomposing the overall prediction residual into stage-specific components, our method enables practitioners to attribute uncertainty to specific pipeline stages. We develop a risk-controlled parameter selection procedure using family-wise error rate (FWER) control to calibrate stage-wise scaling parameters, and introduce an adaptive extension for non-stationary settings. Experiments on synthetic distribution shifts, as well as real-world supply chain and stock market data, demonstrate that our approach improves coverage under structural, stage-wise shifts compared to standard conformal methods, while identifying stage-wise error contribution. This framework offers diagnostic advantages and robust coverage that standard conformal methods lack.

paragraphs: In a two-stage prediction pipeline, one model produces an intermediate representation that another model uses for its final prediction. Treating this entire process as one black box can hide where uncertainty originates. This paper develops a conformal prediction framework that uses the pipeline’s modular structure to make uncertainty more informative.

The method decomposes the final prediction residual into components associated with individual stages. It then calibrates scaling parameters for those components through a risk-controlled selection procedure using family-wise error rate control. This gives practitioners a way to connect uncertainty with particular parts of the pipeline. An adaptive extension addresses settings whose distributions change over time.

Experiments cover synthetic distribution shifts and real supply chain and stock market data. Under structural shifts affecting individual stages, the framework improves coverage relative to standard conformal methods while identifying stage-specific error contributions. The stated benefit combines stronger empirical coverage in these settings with diagnostic information about which pipeline stage contributes to the observed errors.
summary.tldr: This conformal prediction framework separates uncertainty by pipeline stage and improves coverage under evaluated stage-specific distribution shifts.

title: Decomposition-Based Modular Conformal Prediction for Two-Stage Modeling

abstract: While recent advancements in Vector Quantization (VQ) models have successfully achieved complete codebook utilization, a critical bottleneck remains largely unexplored: the effective dimensionality of the codebook embedding space. We observe that discrete codebook representations tend to degenerate into low-dimensional subspaces, characterized by significantly lower effective rank than continuous representations during quantization. Through comprehensive spectral analysis, we identify that this dimensional collapse stems from the suppression of low-variance components inherent to the vector quantization process, thereby severely limiting the expressive capacity of VQ models. To mitigate this fundamental issue, we propose a simple yet effective codebook regularization strategy designed to restore low-variance components, effectively bridging the spectral gap between discrete codebook spaces and continuous representations. Extensive experiments demonstrate that this regularization objective is compatible with diverse VQ training paradigms, yielding significant improvements in reconstruction fidelity and downstream performance in autoregressive image generative models.

paragraphs: Using every entry in a vector-quantization codebook does not necessarily mean its representations are expressive. This paper finds that codebook embeddings can concentrate in a low-dimensional subspace even when utilization is complete. Their effective rank is substantially lower than that of the continuous representations being quantized, revealing a bottleneck that entry-usage statistics alone can miss.

Through spectral analysis, the authors attribute this dimensional collapse to suppression of low-variance components during vector quantization. They propose a codebook regularization objective that restores those components and narrows the spectral gap between discrete and continuous representations. The intervention therefore targets the geometry of the representation space, complementing efforts focused on ensuring codebook entries are used.

Experiments show compatibility with different vector-quantization training paradigms and significant improvements in reconstruction fidelity. They also report better downstream performance in autoregressive image generation. These results support the paper’s central distinction: the number of active codebook entries and the effective dimensionality of their embeddings capture different aspects of representation quality.
summary.tldr: A codebook regularizer restores suppressed low-variance components, reducing dimensional collapse and improving reconstruction and autoregressive image generation.

title: Unveiling And Addressing Dimensional Collapse In Vector Quantization Models Via Codebook Regularization

abstract: Collaborative agentic AI is projected to transform entire industries by enabling AI-powered agents to autonomously perceive, plan, and act within digital environments. Yet, current solutions in this field are all built in isolation, and we are rapidly heading toward a landscape of fragmented, incompatible ecosystems. In this position paper, we argue that interoperability, achieved by the adoption of minimal standards, is essential to ensure open, secure, web-scale, and widely-adopted agentic ecosystems. To this end, we devise a minimal architectural foundation for collaborative agentic AI, named Web of Agents, which is composed of four components: agent-to-agent messaging, interaction interoperability, state management, and agent discovery. Web of Agents adopts existing standards and reuses existing infrastructure where possible. With Web of Agents, we take a first but critical step toward interoperable agentic systems and offer a pragmatic path forward before ecosystem fragmentation becomes the norm.

paragraphs: Collaborative agents are intended to perceive digital environments, make plans, and act autonomously. This paper argues that developing such systems in isolated ecosystems risks making collaboration depend on incompatible infrastructure. Its central proposal is to establish minimal shared standards before fragmentation becomes entrenched, so agents can cooperate across ecosystem boundaries.

The authors introduce an architectural foundation called Web of Agents. It has four components: messaging between agents, interoperability of interactions, management of state, and discovery of agents. Together, these identify the basic areas in which independently developed systems need common arrangements. The architecture uses existing standards and infrastructure where possible, making reuse part of the proposed route toward broader compatibility.

The paper positions this foundation as an initial step toward open, secure agent ecosystems that can operate at web scale and gain widespread adoption. It argues that interoperability is essential to that ambition. The contribution is a minimal architecture and a practical direction for coordination, with the emphasis on enabling collaboration across systems as the field develops.
summary.tldr: The proposed Web of Agents defines minimal shared foundations for agents to collaborate across otherwise incompatible ecosystems.

abstract: Variational inference methods, including mean field methods and loopy beliefpropagation, have been widely used for approximate probabilistic inference ingraphical models. While often less accurate than MCMC, variational methodsprovide a fast deterministic approximation to marginal and conditionalprobabilities. Such approximations can be particularly useful in highdimensional problems where sampling methods are too slow to be effective. Alimitation of current methods, however, is that they are restricted toparametric probabilistic models. MCMC does not have such a limitation;indeed, MCMC samplers have been developed for the Dirichlet process (DP), anonparametric distribution on distributions (Ferguson, 1973) that is thecornerstone of Bayesian nonparametric statistics~\citep (Escobar and West,1995; Neal, 2000}. In this paper, we develop a mean-field variationalapproach to approximate inference for the Dirichlet process, where theapproximate posterior is based on the truncated stick-breaking construction(Ishwaran and James, 2001). We compare our approach to DP samplers forGaussian DP mixture models.

paragraphs: Approximate probabilistic inference often involves a tradeoff between computational speed and accuracy. Variational methods offer fast, deterministic approximations, although they are often less accurate than sampling-based MCMC methods. This paper addresses a restriction of existing variational approaches: their focus on parametric models, while MCMC methods already support the nonparametric Dirichlet process.

The authors develop a mean-field variational method for Dirichlet process inference. The approximate posterior uses a truncated stick-breaking construction, giving the approximation a finite representation of the process. This makes it possible to bring the variational approach into a setting central to Bayesian nonparametric statistics.

The method is compared with Dirichlet process samplers for Gaussian mixture models. Its motivation is particularly relevant to high-dimensional problems where sampling can be too slow to be effective. The contribution is an approximate inference route for the Dirichlet process that extends the reach of deterministic variational methods, while retaining the explicit approximation introduced by the truncated posterior construction.
summary.tldr: A truncated stick-breaking posterior enables mean-field variational inference for the nonparametric Dirichlet process.

title: Variational methods for the Dirichlet process

abstract: The effort necessary to construct labeled sets of examples in a supervisedlearning scenario is often disregarded, though in many applications, it is atime-consuming and expensive procedure. While this already constitutes a majorissue in classification learning, it becomes an even more serious problem whendealing with the more complex target domain of total orders over a set ofalternatives. Considering both the pairwise decomposition and the constraintclassification technique to represent label ranking functions, we introduce anovel generalization of pool-based active learning to address this problem.
originalAbstract: The effort necessary to construct labeled sets of examples in a supervisedlearning scenario is often disregarded, though in many applications, it is atime-consuming and expensive procedure. While this already constitutes a majorissue in classification learning, it becomes an even more serious problem whendealing with the more complex target domain of total orders over a set ofalternatives. Considering both the pairwise decomposition and the constraintclassification technique to represent label ranking functions, we introduce anovel generalization of pool-based active learning to address this problem.

paragraphs: Supervised learning depends on labeled examples, but obtaining those labels can require substantial human effort. That burden becomes especially important when the requested answer is a complete ordering of alternatives rather than a single class. A ranking asks the annotator to supply relationships among multiple choices, making the labeling problem richer and potentially more expensive.

This paper generalizes pool-based active learning to label ranking. The central idea is to treat the selection of examples for labeling as part of the learning problem. Instead of taking the available training examples as fixed, the learner can choose from a pool when seeking additional ranking information.

The authors consider both pairwise decomposition and constraint classification as ways to represent ranking functions. Pairwise decomposition organizes the task around comparisons between alternatives, while constraint classification supplies another representation for the ordering problem. The contribution is a generalization of active learning that addresses these ranking representations and makes annotation effort an explicit concern in learning preferences.
summary.tldr: The paper extends pool-based active learning to learning complete rankings, addressing the cost of obtaining ranking labels.

abstract: We show how nonlinear embedding algorithms popular for use with shallow semi-supervised learning techniques such as kernel methods can be applied to deep multi-layer architectures, either as a regularizer at the output layer, or on each layer of the architecture. This provides a simple alternative to existing approaches to deep learning whilst yielding competitive error rates compared to those methods, and existing shallow semi-supervised techniques.
originalAbstract: We show how nonlinear embedding algorithms popular for use with shallow semi-supervised learning techniques such as kernel methods can be applied to deep multi-layer architectures, either as a regularizer at the output layer, or on each layer of the architecture. This provides a simple alternative to existing approaches to deep learning whilst yielding competitive error rates compared to those methods, and existing shallow semi-supervised techniques.

paragraphs: The paper connects nonlinear embedding methods used in shallow semi-supervised learning with deep, multi-layer architectures. Its starting point is that embedding algorithms already used with approaches such as kernel methods can also help shape a deep model. The contribution is a way to apply those existing ideas within a different kind of architecture.

The embedding can act as a regularizer at the output layer, or regularization can be applied at every layer. These choices determine where the embedding influences learning: at the final output or throughout the sequence of intermediate representations. The paper therefore offers more than one place to incorporate semi-supervised embedding into a deep architecture.

The authors describe this as a simple alternative to existing deep learning approaches and report competitive error rates. The comparisons cover both other deep methods and shallow semi-supervised techniques. Competitive performance supports the usefulness of this connection between embedding and deep learning, while stopping short of claiming that the approach consistently outperforms either class of alternatives.
summary.tldr: Nonlinear semi-supervised embeddings can regularize deep networks at the output or throughout their layers, yielding competitive error rates.

title: Deep learning via semi-supervised embedding

abstract: Trajectory planning and optimization is a fundamental problem in articulated robotics. Algorithms used typically for this problem compute optimal trajectories from scratch in a new situation. In effect, extensive data is accumulated containing situations together with the respective optimized trajectories - but this data is in practice hardly exploited. The aim of this paper is to learn from this data. Given a new situation we want to predict a suitable trajectory which only needs minor refinement by a conventional optimizer. Our approach has two essential ingredients. First, to generalize from previous situations to new ones we need an appropriate situation descriptor - we propose a sparse feature selection approach to find such well-generalizing features of situations. Second, the transfer of previously optimized trajectories to a new situation should not be made in joint angle space - we propose a more efficient task space transfer of old trajectories to new situations. Experiments on trajectory optimization for a simulated humanoid reaching problem show that we can predict reasonable motion prototypes in new situations for which the refinement is much faster than an optimization from scratch.

paragraphs: Robot trajectory optimization generates useful experience: each solved problem provides a situation paired with an optimized motion. This paper proposes learning from those accumulated examples. For a new situation, the goal is to predict a suitable trajectory that a conventional optimizer can refine, reducing the need to solve the entire planning problem from scratch.

The approach has two main components. First, sparse feature selection identifies situation descriptors that generalize to new cases. Second, previously optimized trajectories are transferred through task space rather than joint-angle space. Together, these components address how to recognize relevant past situations and how to adapt their motions to a new task.

Experiments use a simulated humanoid reaching problem. The method predicts reasonable motion prototypes in new situations, and refining those prototypes is much faster than optimizing from scratch in the reported experiments. The learned prediction therefore acts as a useful starting point for optimization, with conventional refinement remaining part of the process that produces the resulting motion.
summary.tldr: Learning situation features and transferring past motions through task space produces robot trajectories that can be refined much faster in simulated reaching experiments.

title: Trajectory prediction: learning to map situations to robot trajectories

abstract: Relational learning is becoming increasingly important in many areas of application. Here, we present a novel approach to relational learning based on the factorization of a three-way tensor. We show that unlike other tensor approaches, our method is able to perform collective learning via the latent components of the model and provide an efficient algorithm to compute the factorization. We substantiate our theoretical considerations regarding the collective learning capabilities of our model by the means of experiments on both a new dataset and a dataset commonly used in entity resolution. Furthermore, we show on common benchmark datasets that our approach achieves better or on-par results, if compared to current state-of-the-art relational learning solutions, while it is significantly faster to compute.

Here, we present a novel approach to relational learning based on the factorization of a three-way tensor. We show that unlike other tensor approaches, our method is able to perform collective learning via the latent components of the model and provide an efficient algorithm to compute the factorization. We substantiate our theoretical considerations regarding the collective learning capabilities of our model by the means of experiments on both a new dataset and a dataset commonly used in entity resolution. Furthermore, we show on common benchmark datasets that our approach achieves better or on-par results, if compared to current state-of-the-art relational learning solutions, while it is significantly faster to compute.

paragraphs: Relational learning concerns data described through connections, potentially involving several kinds of relationships. This paper proposes representing such data with a three-way tensor and learning a factorization of that tensor. The factorization provides latent components through which the model can organize the information contained in the different relationships.

The key contribution is collective learning through those latent components. Rather than treating every relationship as an isolated learning problem, the model can use its shared internal representation to connect their learning. The authors explain this capability theoretically and supply an efficient algorithm for computing the factorization, linking the modeling idea to a practical procedure.

Experiments on a new dataset and an established entity-resolution dataset support the discussion of collective learning. On common benchmarks, the method also obtains results that match or improve on the compared state-of-the-art relational learning approaches while requiring significantly less computation. These findings support both the usefulness of the latent sharing and the computational efficiency of the proposed factorization.
summary.tldr: A three-way tensor factorization shares latent components across relationships, achieving competitive relational learning results with faster computation.

title: A Three-Way Model for Collective Learning on Multi-Relational Data
